This procedure provides the guidance necessary to release suspended benefits and to reinstate terminated benefits when a client's initial or ongoing eligibility is confirmed.

CPP benefits When a suspended or terminated CPP benefit is released or reinstated, the recurring payment schedule is reactivated. Any former deduction amounts on a suspended account are reactivated. On a terminated account, any former deduction amounts are not reactivated (e.g. a voluntary tax withhold). When a client requests to cancel or withdraw a CPP benefit, a new application for benefits must be submitted to put the benefit back in pay. When a suspended CPP pension or benefit is resumed or a terminated CPP pension or benefit is reinstated, the recurring payment schedule is reactivated. Any amounts formerly deducted (e.g. a voluntary tax withhold) from a suspended account are reactivated, if applicable.

When a Date of Death (DOD) is entered on a client's account in error, it must be corrected as soon as it is discovered. You must remove the DOD from the client's account and notify the Social Insurance Registry (SIR) and other program areas (e.g. CPP, OAS and International Operations) immediately. For instructions on completing and sending an urgent email to the SIR and reinstating any suspended or cancelled benefits, Reporting an Incorrect Date of Death to the Social Insurance Registry (Action) To notify another program, follow your regional procedures.

When it has been determined that a Date of Death (DOD) is entered on a client's account in error, it must be corrected as soon as it is discovered. You must immediately remove the DOD from the client's account and notify the Social Insurance Registry (SIR) and other program areas. For instructions on completing and sending an urgent email to notify the SIR and reinstating any suspended or cancelled benefits, Reporting an Incorrect Date of Death to the Social Insurance Registry (Action) To notify another program, follow your regional procedures.

This procedure provides you with the steps to notify the Social Insurance Registry (SIR) when there is a discrepancy in the Date of Death (DOD) entered on a deceased client's SIN record or when a client has been marked deceased in error. In cases where a DOD was entered on a client's account in error, this procedure provides instruction on how to reinstate any suspended or cancelled benefits.

Although procedures have always instructed processing staff to notify the SIR when addressing a DOD discrepancy or removing an erroneous DOD from a client's account, Reporting an Incorrect Date of Death to the Social Insurance Registry (Action) and this announcement have been developed to emphasize the importance of timely notifications to the SIR to ensure the DOD is corrected, or the death flag is removed from the client's account. When the Department is advised that a client has disappeared and remains absent without apparent reason, you must consider a presumption of death. A Presumption of Death Certificate (ISP-3511) form is required to approve or stop the payment of certain CPP and OAS benefits. The Department's manager has authority to issue an ISP-3511 form and declare the date on which the client's death is presumed to have occurred. For more information, refer to Documentary Evidence—Death (Policy) and Documentary Evidence—Death (Policy) Presumption of Death (Action)

You must consider a presumption of death when a client disappears and remains absent from their customary location or home for an extended period, with or without apparent reason. When the Department confirms a client is dead, you must confirm the date of death and issue a Presumption of Death Certificate (ISP-3511) form to approve or stop certain CPP and OAS benefits. A Service Canada manager has the authority to issue an ISP-3511 form and declare the date on which a client's death is presumed to have occurred. Presumption of Death (Action)

Gather and review information to validate the death of a contributor, then send a request for a Presumption of Death Certificate (ISP3511) form to a manager. A presumption of death is considered when an applicant or a client disappears and continues to be absent from their customary location or home for an extended period of time, without any apparent reason.

The circumstances surrounding the disappearance of an applicant or client and the length of time of the absence are important factors to consider when determining if an applicant or a client is dead. You must provide the manager with information to confirm the date of death and to approve or end specific CPP and OAS benefits. A Service Canada manager has the authority to issue an ISP3511 form and to declare the date on which an applicant’s or client’s death is presumed to have occurred. However, the following conditions apply: OAS authority is restricted to the presumption of death of applicants and beneficiaries only. CPP authority declares the date of presumed death of the: contributor or beneficiary; spouse or common-law partner; former spouse or former common-law partner.

Entering a Date of Death (DOD) in ITRDS affects any interrelated accounts by putting an end date on all interrelationships. If an interrelationship is added after death, you must manually enter the DOD as the End Date of the interrelationship.

Entering the date of death terminates all CPP benefits in pay in ITRDS and prevents payments from being issued when there is no entitlement. Adding or changing a client's Date of Death can affect eligibility and entitlement to benefits for all interrelated accounts. When a Date of Death is entered on a client's account, the system ends all existing interrelationships. If you delete or modify the Date of Death , you must manually delete or modify the End Date from those interrelationships. For more information, Interrelationships in ITRDS (Scenario)

For the deceased disabled contributor's -18 child to continue receiving benefit payments, the surviving spouse or common-law partner or other individual or agency with decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the surviving child must submit an application or request in writing. The Surviving Child's benefit and the Disabled Contributor's Child Benefit ( DCCB ) cease the month after the month in which any of the following occur: the child reaches age 18 and does not attend school on a full-time or part-time basis; the child who is 18 years of age or older stops attending school on a full-time or part-time basis; the child who is 18 years of age or older who attends school on a full-time or part-time basis reaches the age of 25; or the child dies. In addition, DCCB payments cease the month after the month in which any of the following events occur: the DSB or PRDB ceases because the contributor ceases to be disabled; the contributor dies; the child is legally or "in fact" adopted by someone other than the disabled contributor or their spouse or common-law partner; the "in fact" adoption relationship changes to the extent that the parent DSB or PRDB beneficiary-child-contributor relationship has permanently ended, not merely that some of the circumstances have changed. The DCCB can be reinstated if it can be demonstrated that the child-contributor DSB or PRDB beneficiary relationship is re-established; the disabled contributor ceases to have decision-making responsibility or parenting time with respect to the child; the child ceases to be under the legal or "in fact" decision-making responsibility or parenting time of the DSB or PRDB beneficiary, where the child was originally a child of the beneficiary by reason of legal or "in fact" . The DCCB can be reinstated if it can be demonstrated that the child- DSB or PRDB beneficiary relationship is re-established; or the conversion of a DCCB for a child over the age 18 to a Surviving Child's benefit. A DCCB in pay or payable to a child between the ages of 18 and 25 at the time of the DSB or PRDB beneficiary's death is converted automatically to a Surviving Child's benefit without the need to complete an application providing that all conditions of eligibility for a Surviving Child's benefit are met.

Once the date of death is added or updated on the Birth and Death Details evidence and activated, Cúram will run a reassessment to ensure that the account is in balance. When a death notification is received, the DOD must be added to the Birth and Death Details evidence as soon as possible because it will impact any OAS pension and benefits that the client is currently receiving. Once the DOD is added or updated on the Birth and Death Details evidence and activated, Cúram will run a reassessment to ensure that the account is in balance. A task will be generated for manual review if, at any time during the reassessment process: the account is not in balance; or the system cannot perform actions automatically. As part of the reassessment process, Cúram will automatically: Update the spouse's Marital Relationship evidence to Surviving Spouse/Common Law Partner , if applicable. All CPP pensions or benefits and the OAS pension are taxable. However, income-tested benefits (i.e. GIS, ALW , ALWS ) are non-taxable. Tax slips inform clients, the CRA and Revenu Québec of the total amount of benefits paid and any amounts withheld during a calendar year. This includes: Regular benefit payments; Arrears payments; Underpayments; Tax withholds; and Overpayment recovery. For CPP accounts, tax slip information and credit slips originate from CPMS . For OAS accounts, tax slip information originates from Cúram. The reissuing and amending of tax slips are recorded through CPMS or Cúram. A CPP client will receive: a Statement of Canada Pension Plan Benefits T4A(P) (ISP-0136) form for periods when they are in receipt of a CPP pension or benefit and are a resident of Canada; a Statement of Amounts Paid or Credited to Non-residents of Canada NR4 (CPP) (ISP-0139) form for periods when they are in receipt of a CPP pension or benefit and are a non-resident of Canada; or a Reimbursement Of Benefit Paid During A Previous Year (ISP-1611) (credit slip) form when the recovery of an overpayment exceeds the total pension or benefit payments issued during the same calendar year. An OAS client will receive: a Statement of Old Age Security T4A(OAS) (ISP-0137) form for periods when they are in receipt of an OAS pension or an income-tested benefit and are a resident of Canada; a Statement of Old Age Security Pension Paid or Credited to Non-residents of Canada NR4(OAS) (ISP-0138) form for periods when they are in receipt of an OAS pension and/or an income-tested benefit and are a non-resident of Canada. CPP and OAS tax slips are generated at the beginning of January of a given calendar year. Tax slip mailing occurs the year following the tax year (e.g. in 2026 for the 2025 tax year). Clients will receive their tax slips by the end of February. Each year, some accounts are excluded from the automatic annual tax slip bulk mail-out because they do not meet the pre-set criteria. For CPP, these accounts are identified through scans and exception reports, which are used as the basis for specific instruction to staff. This annual instruction outlines the corrective action required to ensure clients who were excluded from the bulk mail-out will receive their correct tax slip by the end of February. Refer to T4 and NR4 Tax Slips Mail-out for 2025—Cyclical (Knowledge) . T4 and NR4 Tax Slips Mail-out for 2025—Cyclical (Knowledge) For OAS, National Headquarters handles all tax slips with various issues to ensure correct formatting before distribution. Tax Information Slips Online Tax slip information is loaded into Tax Information Slips Online (TISO). Clients can view and print official copies of their tax slips for the current year and the past 6 years through My Service Canada Account (MSCA) for CPP and the Client Portal via their MSCA for OAS. Clients can also choose to modify the mailing options of their tax slips online in TISO through MSCA. Third party representatives cannot use the online tax slip services via MSCA. CPP OAS

Tax slips reflect benefit and payment information for an entire calendar year. They are issued on an annual basis for monthly CPP and OAS benefits and for the one-time death benefit payment received within a calendar year. T4As are issued to a CPP or OAS client for periods during which they were a resident of Canada. NR4s are issued to a CPP or OAS client for periods during which they were not a resident of Canada. Credit slips are issued when a client refunds a sum of money that was deposited during the previous tax year to offset an overpayment. For CPP, you must create a manual tax slip ( T4A (P) Statement of Canada Pension Plan Benefits (ISP-0136), NR4 (CPP) Statement of amounts paid or credited to non-residents of Canada (ISP-0139) or Reimbursement Of Benefit Paid During A Previous Year (ISP-1611) (credit slip)) in CPMS or E-Forms when the system has not produced one for various reasons. These reasons are identified during the year-end T4A and NR4 scans. For OAS, you must create a tax slip ( T4A (OAS) Statement of Old Age Security (ISP-0137) or NR4 (OAS) Statement of Old Age Security Pension paid or credited to non-residents of Canada (ISP-0138)) in Cúram. There should never be a systematic reason where an original tax slip for 2023 or later could not be generated in Cúram. If you encounter a situation where a tax slip cannot be created, you must create a National Service Desk ticket to report the issue.

If a client's eligibility for CPPD benefits is being reassessed, you must send them the Benefit Status - Suspend (ISS-6190) letter. This letter does not imply an immediate suspension of benefits. However, it does notify the client that a suspension is possible while their eligibility is being reassessed. A Medical Adjudicator (MA) must consider the nature of the disability and the medical prognosis when deciding to suspend benefits. Suspension of the CPPD benefit depends on the MA's consideration of the client's medical condition and circumstances. When suspending the CPPD benefit in ITRDS , the system will also automatically suspend all related Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefits.

If the suspension of a parent's CPPD benefit occurs as a result of a reassessment, you must also suspend any Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ). The Medical Adjudicator (MA) will send a Disability Suspensions Request (MD16B) form to the SCBO . The MA will also provide the date to suspend the benefit and the reason for the suspension. The SCBO must suspend the CPPD benefit according to the MA's request. They must also suspend any related DCCB . Go to the Suspend the pension or benefit section below.

Effective January 1, 2025, when a credit split application is received and approved for separated legal spouses, there is no eligibility to a CPP SVR pension when one of the separated legal spouses dies. If a separated legal spouse is receiving an SVR pension and the Department receives a credit split application on or after January 1, 2025 for the same deceased separated legal spouse, the SVR pension ceases as of the effective date of the credit split approval. This applies regardless of whether it is the estate of the deceased contributor, or the living separated legal spouse who makes the application or request for the credit split. An SVR pension that remains in pay awaiting processing of the credit split could result in an SVR pension overpayment. This overpayment is valid and collectable. To avoid an overpayment situation for the SVR recipient you must: ensure you screen the credit split application at the time of receipt; and suspend or terminate the SVR pension. In some situations, you must suspend the SVR pension before continuing to review the credit split application or request. Suspension of the SVR pension should only occur when more information is required to determine eligibility to the credit split. Some examples of when you must suspend are (this is not an exhaustive list): when the credit split application meets the criteria to be processed by the Dual Processing Unit in Timmins, ON; when there is a CPPD application in PWS or on hold in ITRDS ; when a letter of representation must be sent to the deceased separated legal spouse's estate; when the period of separation is less than 12 months; when the applicant has indicated they have a spousal agreement with their legal separated spouse but did not provide it, and it was signed: before June 4, 1986; in British Columbia on or after July 1, 1995; in Quebec on or after July 1, 1989; in Saskatchewan on or after January 1, 1987; or in Alberta on or after October 1, 2005. For information on contacting the client to notify them of the suspension of the SVR pension, as well as instructions on how to suspend the SVR pension, Suspend Benefits (Scenario) When no additional information is required to determine eligibility to the credit split, or you have requested and received the required information, you must terminate the SVR pension before continuing to process the credit split application or request. If the SVR pension applicant is the separated legal spouse of the deceased contributor and was approved for a credit split submitted on or after January 1, 2025 during their separation from the same contributor, they are not eligible to a CPP SVR pension. The separated legal spouse who applied for the credit split (or their executor, if it was the estate who applied on behalf of a deceased legal spouse) has up to 60 days after they receive their credit split Notice of Canada Pension Plan Credit Split Approval (ISP-1900C) form to request to withdraw the credit split. If a request to withdraw the credit split is received and approved, the SVR pension applicant may be eligible to the SVR pension, if they meet all of the other eligibility requirements. You must determine when the ISP-1900C form was sent. If you are within or at 60 days of the date, verify PWS for a request to withdraw the credit split received from the credit split applicant. If there is one, a decision must be made on the request to withdraw the credit split before data capturing the SVR pension application. If there is no request to withdraw the credit split, proceed with processing the SVR pension application. Additionally, the SVR pension applicant may be eligible to the SVR pension if, after the credit split was submitted and approved, they reconciled and resumed their spousal relationship with their separated legal spouse for a period of one year or more immediately before the contributor died. If this is a possibility, given the date the credit split was submitted, you must determine the status of the relationship between the applicant and the deceased contributor at the time of death and the length of time during which they were reconciled, if applicable. If this information already provided to the Department is on file or has been provided on the SVR pension application itself and there are no discrepancies, you do not need to request additional information from the applicant. If you require information from the applicant to determine if they resumed their spousal relationship with the deceased contributor for a period of one year or more immediately before the contributor's death, send the Development - Marital Status (ISS-6182) letter to the applicant. Follow the bring forward procedures to allow the applicant to reply. Bring Forward (BF) (Action) For more information about the impact of a credit split on a separated legal spouse's eligibility to an SVR pension, Survivor's Pension—Eligibility Requirements and Disqualifying Conditions (Policy)

Before January 2019, survivors under the age of 35 could only qualify for the SVR pension if they had a dependant or were disabled (also known as a qualifier or qualifying condition). Survivors aged between 35 and 45 without any dependants or not disabled received a reduced SVR rate. The SVR DSB Periods screen in ITRDS was used to enter disability periods to qualify a survivor for a full SVR pension. Effective January 1, 2019, these qualifying conditions are no longer required. Between January 1, 2019 and May 21, 2022 when a previous Survivor's pension application existed in ITRDS for the same deceased spouse prior to January 1, 2019, with a status of Eligible but no Entitlement , the SVR DSB Periods screen was used to override the age restrictions and the receipt date of the original application. For these cases, the Start Date on the SVR DSB Periods screen in ITRDS was entered as the latest of: the month following the month of death of the contributor; or 11 months before the receipt date of the second application; and no earlier than January 2019. Effective May 21, 2022 this procedure is no longer applicable due to the changes to the functionality in ITRDS. For more information, Survivor's Pension Application

Effective January 1, 2019, the prescribed qualifying conditions that a survivor aged 35 to 45 either must have a dependent child or be considered disabled as per CPP to receive an unreduced SVR pension were removed. Before January 2019, the amount of an SVR pension was established by some or all of the following factors: the earnings and contributions of the deceased contributor; the age of the survivor at the time of the contributor's death; whether or not the survivor had any dependent children at the time of the contributor's death; whether or not the survivor was considered disabled as per the CPP.

Effective January 1, 2019, the prescribed qualifying conditions that a survivor under age 35 either must have a dependent child or be considered disabled as per CPP to be eligible for the SVR pension were removed. In order to determine if they meet eligibility requirements, survivors need to apply, or re-apply if they were previously denied.

Before January 2019, a surviving spouse under the age of 35 could only qualify for the CPP SVR pension if: they had a dependent child or children at the time of the contributor's death; they were disabled; or both. Surviving spouses between the ages of 35 and 45 without any dependents and who were not disabled received a reduced SVR pension entitlement. Effective January 2019, applicants under the age of 45 are no longer required to have dependent children or be considered disabled under the Canada Pension Plan legislation to qualify for the full under-65 SVR pension. The SCBO must advise the Medical Adjudicator (MA) if the applicant: was under the age of 45 at the time of the deceased contributor's date of death; and has received a reduced SVR pension, if applicable. The MA will determine if and when the applicant met the severe and prolonged criteria to assess entitlement to a full SVR pension prior to 2019. Applicants who were under the age of 35 at the time of the contributor's death and who have an account status of Eligible but No Entitlement in ITRDS , must re-apply for the CPP SVR pension to be considered under the post-January 2019 rules. For more information, SVR Pension Application (Scenario)

New Effective January 1, 2025 Disentitlement to CPP SVR pension in cases of Credit Splitting effective January 1, 2025: An individual who receives a credit split on or after January 1 st , 2025 would not be eligible for an SVR pension due to the death of their separated spouse. For more information, Credit Splitting (Policy) Effective January 1, 2019 An SVR pension is payable up to and including the month: that the survivor dies; a written request to cancel the SVR pension is submitted by the survivor within the prescribed timeframes; or the survivor becomes eligible for another SVR pension of greater value. In such cases, the first SVR pension is cancelled effective the month after the death of the second spouse or common-law partner. Before January 1, 2019 An SVR pension was payable up to and including the month the survivor: dies; or who was under the age of 35, ceased to have dependent children and was not disabled. Before January 1, 1987 If a survivor remarried before January 1, 1987, their SVR pension ceased with the final payment occurring the month of remarriage. This only applied in cases of legal marriage. A common-law union did not terminate an SVR pension. Had the new marriage been terminated by divorce (recognized by Canadian law) before January 1987 or had been annulled at any time, the SVR pension was payable again upon notification by the former beneficiary. In such cases, the SVR pension was reinstated effective the month after the divorce. In the case of annulment, however, the pension was reinstated retroactively back to the month it was cancelled due to the remarriage.

Survivors under age 35 Effective January 1, 2019, the prescribed qualifying conditions that a survivor under age 35 must either have a dependent child or be considered disabled according to the CPP to be eligible for the Survivor’s (SVR) pension, were removed. In such cases, survivors must apply or re-apply. For new eligibility determinations, the maximum retroactive period will continue to be 11 months before the date of application. However, in no case is an SVR pension payable without the prescribed qualifying conditions for any month before January 2019. Survivors aged 35 to 45 Effective January 1, 2019, the prescribed qualifying conditions that a survivor aged 35 to 45 must either have a dependent child or be considered disabled according to the CPP to receive an unreduced SVR pension, were removed. For new eligibility determinations, the maximum retroactive period will continue to be 11 months before the date of application.

An individual may request to cancel any CPP benefit, including CPPD benefits, provided the following conditions are met: the request is made in writing; and the cancellation request is received within 12 months of the date the first payment commenced. The pension or benefit may then be cancelled provided the following conditions are met: the beneficiary repays all amounts received no later than 12 months after the day in which their request for a cancellation is granted; and the request is not an "in-favour" request to cancel a CPP RTR pension "in-favour" of a CPP DSB benefit. When the written cancellation request is received, as long as the request is granted and all amounts are repaid within the prescribed timeframes, the pension or benefit is cancelled retroactive to the initial effective date. The application is considered never to have been made and the pension or benefit is considered never to have been paid. Therefore, if an individual wishes to receive a pension or benefit at a future date, they must submit a new application. If the beneficiary does not repay the amounts within the 12-month period, the pension and any related benefits are reinstated and any amounts already recovered are returned to the beneficiary.

The Minister has the authority to refuse or cancel a credit split for a couple that is divorced, legally annulled or separated on or after January 1, 1987, when it is apparent upon data capturing or within 60 days after data capturing the credit split that negatively affects both spouses. When a request to split credits between former spouses upon divorce or annulment is approved, the credit split cannot be withdrawn by either of the individuals. With the exception of the Minister's power to refuse or cancel a credit split if detrimental to both individuals, the division of credits between former spouses upon divorce or annulment is permanent. When a request to split credits between separated legal spouses or common-law partners is approved, the applicant may ask to withdraw their Application for Canada Pension Plan Credit Split (upon separation or divorce) (ISP-1901) form within 60 days of being notified of the credit split. For more information on withdrawing a credit split, Withdraw an Application (Scenario)

Separated legal spouses or former common-law partners can request to withdraw their Application for Canada Pension Plan Credit Split (upon separation or divorce) (ISP-1901) form. The request to withdraw the credit split application must be made by the applicant and received by the Department within 60 days after the date the applicant receives their Notice of Canada Pension Plan Credit Split Approval (ISP-1900C) form. After approving the request to withdraw the credit split application, you must send a written notice of the withdrawal to the applicant's separated legal spouse or former common-law partner. If the applicant's separated legal spouse or former common-law partner is deceased, you must send the written notice of the withdrawal letter to the executor if there is an estate. When there is no estate, you are not required to send a letter. There is no authority to withdraw a credit split if the legal spouses divorced after January 1, 1987. However, the Minister has the authority to refuse a credit split if it is detrimental to both spouses. In such situations, you can reverse the division if both contributors are receiving a CPP benefit. For more information on the withdrawal of a CPP credit split, Credit Splitting (Policy)

Credit splitting for former common-law partners may only be considered if the following eligibility requirements are met: Cancellation Where credit splitting is detrimental to both common-law partners. It must be evident, immediately before credit splitting or within 60 days after, that credit splitting would adversely affect both common-law partners. This is only applicable when both common-law partners are beneficiaries at the time of credit splitting or both common-law partners become beneficiaries within 60 days of credit splitting. Having 2 benefits in pay is the only way it can be determined with any accuracy that credit splitting is detrimental to both common-law partners. Withdrawal The legislation allows the withdrawal of an application in those cases where: Separation occurred after January 1, 1987; and A written notice of withdrawal is submitted to the Department no later than 60 days after receiving notification of the division. The 60 days refers to the initial decision and not decisions which may be communicated as the result of a reconsideration or appeal. After the 60 days have passed, there is no discretion to withdraw the application even if both parties make a request; If the request for withdrawal is approved, the former common-law partner must be notified in writing of the withdrawal; When an application is withdrawn, the application cannot be used at a later date. A new application must be submitted.

When legal spouses are separated, credit splitting may only be considered if the following eligibility requirements are met: Cancellation A credit split is not permitted where credit splitting is detrimental to both spouses. It must be evident, immediately before credit splitting or within 60 days after, that credit splitting would adversely affect both spouses. This is only applicable when both spouses are beneficiaries at the time of credit splitting or both spouses become beneficiaries within 60 days of credit splitting. Having 2 benefits in pay is the only way it can be determined with any accuracy that credit splitting is detrimental to both spouses. Withdrawal The legislation allows the withdrawal of an application in cases where: separation occurred after January 1, 1987, but the couple have not obtained a divorce; and a written notice of withdrawal is submitted to the Department no later than 60 days after receiving notification of the division of credits. The 60 days refers to the initial decision and not decisions which may be communicated as the result of a reconsideration or appeal. After the 60 days have passed, there is no discretion to withdraw the application even if both parties make a request. if the request for withdrawal is approved, the former spouse must be notified in writing of the withdrawal; when an application is withdrawn, the application cannot be used at a later date. A new application must be submitted.

Pension Sharing (PNSH) stops with the earliest of the: cancellation of either spouse or common-law partner's RTR pension in favour of the DSB ; month in which either spouse or common-law partner dies; month following the month the Department approves a written cancellation request signed by both spouses or common-law partners; month in which a divorce or annulment is granted; month the Department is notified that the non-contributor spouse or common-law partner becomes a contributor; or 12th month following the month in which the spouses or common-law partners start living separate and apart. In cases where the couple is requesting a cancellation of their PNSH and there is no breakdown in their relationship, both parties must sign the request. Clients are encouraged to use the Cancellation of Pension Sharing for Canada Pension Plan Retirement Pension(s) (ISP-1014) form. For dual benefits, refer to Dual Workflow Charts for CPP and CPPD Processors (PDF, 301 KB) Download link . Dual Workflow Charts for CPP and CPPD Processors

PNSH stops with the earliest of the: cancellation of either the spouse or common-law partner's RTR pension in favour of DSB ; month in which either the spouse or common-law partner dies; month following the month the Department approves a written request signed by both spouses or common-law partners to stop PNSH; month in which a divorce or annulment is granted; month the Department is notified that the non-contributor spouse or common-law partner becomes a contributor; or 12th month following the month in which the spouses or common-law partners start living separate and apart for voluntary reasons. In cases where the couple is requesting a cancellation of their PNSH and there is no breakdown in their relationship, both parties must sign a written request. Pension Sharing (PNSH) ends at the time of the earliest of the following events: When either spouse or common-law partner dies, the PNSH ceases the month of death. Example: the spouse or common-law partner dies in July the last shared pension payment is July. The PNSH ceases as of August. For a single PNSH, sharing ends the month in which the non-contributor spouse or common-law partner becomes a contributor. When the PNSH involves only CPP RTR pensions, sharing ends the 12th month following the month in which the spouses or common-law partners start voluntarily living separate and apart. When the PNSH involves both CPP and QPP RTR pensions, sharing ends the earliest of the 12th month after the spouses or common-law partners separated or the month in which the spouses legally separated. Example: if the date of separation was July 15, 2003, the last month their RTR pensions would be shared would be July 2004 and the pension sharing would end effective August 2004. The month in which a divorce is granted or a judgment of nullity of a marriage is issued. The last month the pensions would be shared is the month in which the divorce is granted or a judgment of nullity of a marriage is issued. The month after the month in which the Minister approves a written request(s) from both spouses or common-law partners to cancel the PNSH. If only one spouse or common-law partner requests a cancellation, the PNSH continues. When spouses or common-law partners voluntarily choose to end the PNSH, a written request, signed by both spouses or common-law partners must be made. If one or both spouses are incapable of signing, the spouses' representative(s) must sign the request to end PNSH on their behalf. Contributors or their authorized representative(s) may choose to submit a completed and signed form specifically for this purpose: Cancellation of Pension Sharing for Canada Pension Plan Retirement Pension(s) (ISP-1014). Alternatively, they may submit a written request. Ceasing the PNSH retroactively There are cases where the Department does not become aware of an event that results in the termination of a PNSH until after the event. As a result, a spouse or common-law partner will have received a portion of the pension to which they were not entitled. In cases of divorce, separation, or where one spouse or common-law partner becomes a contributor, the result will be an overpayment on one account and underpayment on the other account. When this happens, the Department will release the resulting underpayment to the contributor and will collect the overpayment. The contributor must receive their full entitlement for the months after the PNSH cease date. When there is both an underpayment and an overpayment on the same account, the underpayment can be applied to the overpayment. Any balance remaining on the overpayment will be recovered. When either spouse or common-law partner dies, the PNSH ceases the month of death. Any shared pension payment after death is a debt to the Crown and must be recovered. In cases where both spouses or common-law partners request to have the PNSH cancelled, this would not result in any overpayment or underpayment. The PNSH in this situation is cancelled the month after the month the Minister approves the written request, therefore the cancellation does not have monetary implications.

If the benefits for the spouse or common-law partner are affected, they must be notified in writing. The client can request in writing to have their OAS pension reinstated at any time without having to reapply. However, no retroactivity will be paid earlier than the received date of the reinstatement request. Entitlement resumes the later of: the month following the month the written request is received; or the date indicated on the request. For more information, refer to: Cessation—OAS Pension and Benefits (Policy) ; and Cessation—OAS Pension and Benefits (Policy) Reinstatement (Policy) . If the request is granted, the pension and any related benefits (GIS and ALW benefit) must be repaid no later than 6 months after the day on which the cancellation request was granted. If the client does not repay the amounts within the 6 months, the pension and any related benefits are reinstated and any recovered amounts are returned to the client and their spouse or common law partner, if applicable. Once an OAS pension is cancelled, the application is deemed to have never been made and the individual will have to reapply if they wish to receive the OAS pension. They will continue to accumulate residence or to increase their OAS pension through an actuarial adjustment. An application for a CPP benefit or an OAS pension can be withdrawn if: the applicant requests in writing to withdraw their application; and the request is received before the benefit or pension payment is issued. It is not necessary to withdraw an application for a CPP benefit or an OAS pension if the applicant requests a change to the effective date and the new date they request is within one year (before or after) of the date the application was received, the requested change can be made if the Department has not yet: finalized a decision on the application; communicated a decision to the applicant ; and issued any payments. After an application is withdrawn, applicants must be advised in writing that a new application is required if and when they decide to re-apply in the future. Eligibility to a pension or a benefit will be based on the new application and not on the application that was withdrawn. CPP Credit Split (Division of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings) For the policy and parameters on the withdrawal of a CPP Credit Split, CPP Credit Splitting (Policy) Guaranteed Income Supplement, Allowance and Allowance for the Survivor benefits There is no authority in the OAS Act to withdraw an application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), the Allowance ( ALW ) and the Allowance for the Survivor ( ALWS ). A beneficiary may, however, request in writing that the GIS, ALW or ALWS cease .

An individual may request to cancel the OAS pension and/or the GIS provided the following conditions are met: the request is made in writing; and the cancellation request is received within 6 months of the date the first payment commenced. The pension or benefit may then be cancelled provided the beneficiary repays all amounts received no later than 6 months after the day on which their request for a cancellation is granted. When the written cancellation request is received, as long as the request is granted and all amounts are repaid within the prescribed timeframes, the OAS pension or GIS is cancelled retroactively to the initial effective date. When an OAS pension or GIS are cancelled, the application(s) is considered never to have been made (or the individual never automatically enrolled), and the pension and/or benefit are considered never to have been paid. In addition, the GIS beneficiary no longer has a lifetime renewable designation. If the individual wishes to receive a pension or GIS at a future date, they must submit a new application. After the pension is cancelled, individuals can continue to: accumulate Canadian residence; or increase their OAS pension amount through an actuarial adjustment (voluntary deferral). Cancellation of the OAS pension and/or GIS and its effects on the ALW benefit When the OAS pensioner has requested to cancel their OAS pension and/or the GIS, the ALW benefit must also be repaid no later than 6 months after the day on which the request for the cancellation is granted. As a result of the cancellation of the OAS pension or GIS, the ALW benefit application is considered never to have been made and the benefit never to have been paid. In addition, the ALW beneficiary no longer has a lifetime renewable designation and an application for the ALW is required in the future. If the ALW beneficiary fails to repay the amounts owed within the 6-month period, the OAS pension or GIS, and any related benefits (i.e. ALW benefit) are reinstated, and any recovered amounts are returned to the beneficiary. Automatic enrolment for the OAS pension and GIS The Minister retains the right to: cancel the OAS automatic enrolment process; and request an application before the individual's 65th birthday. ALW and ALWS There is no authority in the OAS Act to cancel an ALW or an ALWS benefit. However, a beneficiary may make a request, in writing, that the ALW or ALWS benefit be ceased.

Beneficiaries request the cancellation of their pensions and benefits for a variety of reasons. For instance, the individual's financial needs may have changed or the individual has simply decided to cancel the benefit for personal reasons. A pension or benefit may be cancelled when an individual's request is made within the prescribed period of time: The CPP Regulations provide for the cancellation of a CPP pension or benefit if a request is made within 12 months of receipt of the first payment; The OAS Act provides for cancellation of the OAS pension and/or the GIS if a request is made within 6 months of the first payment. If it is determined that a beneficiary is no longer eligible to receive a CPP or an OAS pension or benefit, it is cancelled. In such cases, the term "cancellation" means the termination of payment of a benefit as the individual is no longer eligible to receive the benefit.

A cessation of an OAS pension is an action initiated by a pensioner to voluntarily stop receiving their pension for a period of time or indefinitely. It is different from a suspension of benefits. Cessation of the OAS pension A pensioner can make a request in writing that their OAS pension be ceased. Cessation of the OAS pension also results in the cessation of other supplementary benefits such as the GIS and the ALW benefit. If the benefits for the spouse or common-law partner are impacted, the spouse or common-law partner must be notified in writing. The pension ceases to be payable effective: the month in which the pensioner's request is actioned; or the month indicated by the pensioner (if it is in the future). Should a pensioner choose to receive their pension at a later date, it can be reinstated. Cessation of the GIS, ALW or ALWS A beneficiary is not obligated to accept a GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit for any particular period that they do not wish. After completing an application, the individual can decide not to receive the benefit right away or, if they are already receiving the benefit, may discontinue that payment for a period of time. The GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits cease to be payable effective: the month in which the request is actioned by the Department; or the month indicated by the pensioner (if it is in the future). When a beneficiary chooses to cease the payment of the GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit, the lifetime renewal designation ends. Should a beneficiary choose to receive their benefit at a later date, it can be reinstated: however, a new application is required. When the request to cease is approved for the GIS or the ALW and if the benefits for the spouse or common-law partner are impacted, the spouse or common-law partner must be notified in writing.

At any time after the ALWS benefit payments begin, a client can request to cease their payment of the ALWS benefit provided the request is made in writing. When a client chooses to cease the payment of the ALWS benefit, the lifetime renewal designation ends. If the client wishes to receive the ALWS benefit in the future, they must submit a new application. A client can request the cancellation of: the OAS pension; the OAS pension and the GIS; or the GIS alone. If the request is granted, any related benefits may be affected, including the spouse or common-law partner's income-tested benefits. A cancellation request can be granted if the request is: made in writing; and received by the Department within 6 months of the date the first payment was issued. Although a signature is not required on the written request, you must call the client if an unsigned request for cancellation is received to confirm that they submitted it. When a cancellation request is received, it must be processed as a priority so that the applicable actions are performed in Cúram to stop the payment of benefits, minimizing the repayment amount. If the request is granted, the affected pension and any related benefits must be repaid no later than 6 months after the day on which the request for cancellation is granted. A client may request to change the effective date of a CPP RTR pension or an OAS pension because they want to receive the pension at an earlier or later date. You can change the effective date of a CPP RTR pension or an OAS pension when requested by the client in writing if the new effective date is 12 months or less from the date of receipt of application and the client has not received any payments. You can also change the effective date of a CPP, CPPD or OAS pension or benefit in the following situations: a protected date has been provided by using an International Social Security Agreement; a claim of incapacity is approved; a claim of erroneous advice or administrative error is approved; or it is recommended following an investigation by the Integrity Services Branch. For all other situations, the date of receipt of the application or the date of death determines the effective date. An RTR effective date cannot be earlier than the month after the receipt date of the application for applicants aged 60 to 64. RTR and OAS applicants 65 and over can receive retroactive benefits for up to 12 months if they qualify, but not for any months before they reached age 65. Requests for change to an effective date must be made in writing. For more information, refer to Receipt Date and Date Protection (Action) and Receipt Date and Date Protection (Action) Applications Date of Receipt (Policy)

If the client has been informed of the approval decision but they have not received a payment, they must submit a written request to change the effective date. To withdraw the application, refer to Withdraw an Application . The receipt date of the application, the date of death or the effective date of other benefits determines the effective date.

For OAS and CPP pension and benefit payments, an account can have: the same payment destination for both; and different payment destinations for OAS and CPP payments. A payment destination can be: the client or their legal representative's mailing address if they receive payments by paper cheques; or the client or their legal representative's financial institution if they receive payments by direct deposit. The Government of Canada seeks to issue all federal government payments, including CPP and OAS benefits, by direct deposit. OAS and CPP payments can only be deposited into: the client's bank account; a bank account held jointly by the client and another person; or the bank account of a legal representative appointed to administer an incapable individual's financial affairs (e.g. a trustee, bulk payee, committee, or guardian). For more information, refer to Legal Representation (Policy) . Legal Representation (Policy) Some CPP and OAS clients contact the Department and indicate that they are unable to receive direct deposit payments. The most common reasons are: the client lives in a remote location or country where the direct deposit service is not offered; the agency or provincial department (e.g. the public trustee) does not maintain a bank account for direct deposit; the client has a low income and cannot afford a bank account due to banking fees; and the financial institution refuses to open a bank account for a client.

Direct deposit information should only be data captured for CPP and OAS clients currently receiving payments or applying for a new benefit. If you receive a request from an individual not in receipt of a CPP or OAS benefit, you must securely destroy the request in compliance with Information Management practices. Payments can only be deposited into: the client's bank account; the bank account held jointly by the client and another person; or the bank account of a legal representative appointed to administer an incapable individual's financial affairs. For more information, refer to Legal Representation (Policy) . Legal Representation (Policy)

Some private and public nursing homes ask their clients to sign a form giving the home authorization to deposit benefits directly into the home's bank account. If these clients are capable of handling their own affairs and do not require a trustee, the Department cannot comply because such action is considered an assignment of benefits and is against program legislation. The course of action for the nursing home is to arrange with the client to have pre-authorized withdrawals from their chequing account.

Some nursing homes ask their clients to sign a form giving the home authorization to deposit benefits directly into the nursing home's bank account even if the client is capable of managing their own affairs. This type of authorization must not be accepted as it is considered an assignment of benefits and is not permitted by legislation.

Some private and public nursing homes ask their residents to sign a form, giving the home authorization to direct deposit pension benefits directly into the home's bank account. This type of authorization must not be accepted as it is considered an assignment of benefits and is not permitted by legislation.

ITRDS automatically readjudicates a benefit when a change to a client's information (e.g. updating the client's date of birth) affects their benefit eligibility or entitlement. The result of the readjudication is displayed immediately when you refresh the Benefits screen. You must understand which parts of a client's account activity are automated and when processing staff intervention is required. When there are system issues or problems with the client data which prevents the system from readjudicating, you may need to manually readjudicate a benefit. Each benefit has a status and a reason for the status. The reason assists you in understanding why the benefit is in the specific status (i.e. which eligibility rule was not met for a denied benefit). When an automatic or manual readjudication occurs, ITRDS determines if the benefit rate and status have changed. In certain circumstances, ITRDS does not automatically change the benefit entitlement, but instead amends the benefit's status to indicate that further steps must be taken. Manual intervention is then required.

ITRDS automatically readjudicates a benefit when a change to a client's information (e.g. updating the client's date of birth) affects their benefit eligibility or entitlement. The result of the readjudication is displayed immediately when you refresh the Benefits screen. Occasionally, you will need to manually readjudicate a benefit when system issues or problems with the client data prevents the system from readjudicating. For example, the system does not automatically readjudicate when a child-contributor relationship is modified. For accounts requiring readjudication using the Program Exception Process (PEP) or Super PEP functionality, you must manually determine benefit eligibility and recalculate the benefit amounts, if applicable. Any changes must be made by an authorized user by modifying the applicable fields in the PEP and Super PEP data capture after you manually determine benefit eligibility and recalculate the benefit amount on all interrelated accounts. Provincial or territorial courts can send the Department documents—such as court orders and certificates—appointing one or more individuals to act on behalf of an incapable client. The court appoints a guardian or committee only after considering factors that include whether the incapable individual had a personal directive in place before becoming incapable (e.g. an enduring power of attorney). Therefore, the guardian or committee takes precedence over all others who applied to become trustees on behalf of a CPP and OAS client. As a result, the Department will accept a court-appointed guardian or committee to act on behalf of a CPP and OAS client. Some court orders may pertain only to the personal care of the incapable individual and not their property. You must examine the authorizing document to ensure that it is for property purposes before accepting it. For more information, refer to Court Orders, Committees and Guardianship (Work Tool) or Court Orders, Committees and Guardianship (Work Tool) Legal Representation (Policy)

Certain provincial legislative laws require the appointment of a committee. A committee can consist of one or more persons. If a client is found to be incapable of managing their own affairs, the public trustee may be automatically appointed as the committee. This only happens if there is no existing valid legal representative (e.g. enduring POA). If the public trustee becomes the committee of an incapable client, that client's POA (other than an enduring POA) is void. A third party can be appointed as the committee in place of the public trustee when the third party applies to the provincial court. Since a committee may be given authority over the client's financial affairs, their personal affairs, or both, it is very important to read the authorizing document carefully. The Department only pays benefits to committees managing the financial affairs of incapable clients. The committee is responsible for managing the client's affairs, such as: the administration of the client's income. This includes: conducting banking; paying expenses; budgeting for the client and their family; preparing income tax returns. the client's real estate and personal assets. This includes: selling if it is in the client's best interest; entering into contracts; operating all existing businesses; bringing or defending any lawsuits on the client's behalf. the preparation of a complete inventory of the client's assets and liabilities. This includes: expenses; assets; debts; a detailed accounting when required. A committee remains in effect until one of the following occurs: the court makes an order appointing another committee to replace the existing committee; the client's capability to make decisions is restored; the client or committee applies to the court for an order terminating the committee; or the client or committee dies. Before amending the client's account, you must verify the committee has been terminated by requesting the court order declaring the termination of the committee.

The Department often receives applications and court orders, certificates, or letters from provincial or territorial public trustees, (or public guardian and trustees) stating that they or another third party (individual or agency) have been appointed to administer an individual's financial affairs. A legal representative, public trustee, guardian or committee is appointed under provincial or territorial legislation to act on behalf of an incapable individual only after many factors have been considered by the province or territory, including whether the individual had granted an enduring POA before they became incapable of managing their affairs. However, a court ruling may remove a POA and replace it with a public trustee if the attorney is not acting in the best interests of the grantor. As each province or territory has its own process for appointing the public trustee, not every public trustee will submit the same document to prove that they have been appointed to act on behalf of an incapable individual. When a public trustee does not send in a court order or a certificate of guardianship, but sends a letter that identifies the following criteria, the letter can be accepted as proof of appointment in order to pay CPP or OAS benefits to the public trustee: the name of the individual they are assisting; their role on behalf of the individual (the letter must state that the representative must be appointed to administer the property of the incapable individual and not their personal care); that the individual is incapable; and the legislation under which they are acting. OAS and CPP benefits are paid directly to federally, provincially or territorially appointed administrators on behalf of an incapable individual when the Department is notified of the arrangement by the Province or Territory and the administrator sends in proof of their appointment as described above. Legal representatives appointed by a court or by the public trustee are accountable to the Court for monies received on behalf of incapable individuals. Court orders Where a province or territory requires the Court to decide whether a guardian, committee, or trustee needs to be appointed to manage the finances of an incapable adult, the process is as follows: The Court makes a decision on capacity taking into consideration evaluations made by a qualified capacity assessor, and then issues a court order which may have a seal and a docket number. The court order designates the public trustee, a private citizen or an agency as the committee or guardian to handle either the personal care or property, or both for an individual who is deemed not competent. The public trustee, agency or individual(s) identified above may be given permanent or temporary custody of the individual. The Department has no authority to cancel or revoke a court order unless the Department receives: another court order revoking the first one; or a certificate from the public trustee naming a private citizen responsible for administering the individual's benefits. Committees Certain provincial or territorial legislative statutes specify the appointment of a committee. A committee may consist of one or more individuals. If an individual is found to be incapable of managing their own affairs, the public trustee may be appointed automatically (without a court hearing) as committee when there is no existing valid legal representative (i.e. an existing committee, or an enduring POA). Upon application to the applicable provincial or territorial court, a third party may be appointed as committee in place of the public trustee to manage the financial affairs of the incapable individual. Since committees may be given authority over the individual's financial affairs, their personal affairs, or both it is very important that staff read the authorizing document carefully. Guardianships Some provinces and territories allow the appointment of guardians for incapable individuals. Guardianship law falls under provincial or territorial legislation and guardianship orders, or certificates are unique to each province or territory. A guardian may be appointed by the provincial or territorial court or by the public trustee. A private guardianship order or certificate is issued by a court after it approves an application made by a private citizen to look after the affairs of an incapable individual. A statutory guardianship means that a statute or law allows a guardian to be appointed without court involvement. When someone is appointed by the public trustee without a court order, this type of appointment is called statutory guardianship. The guardian is usually a relative, spouse or partner of the incapable individual. In some provinces or territories, where an incapable adult is in need of assistance and there is no legal representative, and no family or friends willing or able to act as a committee or private guardian, the public trustee may be appointed as statutory guardian without a court hearing. After a medical and a functional assessment is submitted to a designated health authority (a government-appointed medical officer), this official has the authority to issue a certificate of incapability which allows the public trustee to automatically become the incapable adult's statutory guardian and take over their financial and legal affairs. Some guardianships are for personal matters (guardianships of the individual), while others are for financial matters (guardianships of property). If a party is appointed a guardian of the individual, they have the legal authority to make or assist the beneficiary in making decisions about their personal care but not their financial matters. A guardian of property cares for and manages all property belonging to the incapable individual or minor that is not otherwise held in trust.

A Power of Attorney (POA) document is a legal contract between the client (grantor) and any authorized individual (attorney) named in the document. In Quebec, a Power of Attorney can also be called a mandate, in which the legal contract binds the client (mandator) and their legal representative (mandatary). When it is determined that the document is valid for CPP and OAS purposes, the legal representative has all the rights and responsibilities of the person they represent. The client can only grant POA or mandate to a third party when they are mentally capable and in control of their own affairs. If the client is not mentally capable, a trustee or tutor (in Quebec) may be appointed to administer their affairs. For more information, Trusteeship (Scenario) The Department will not accept different POA or mandate documents for the same grantor or mandator. There can only be one POA or mandate per client for both OAS and CPP. If two POA or mandate documents are received naming different parties, the documents will not be accepted. Confirmation as to which POA or mandate document to use for both programs is required. When an attorney or mandatary is on file, the client may continue to act on the account. The existence of a POA or mandate does not necessarily mean the client is no longer able or no longer wishes to administer their own affairs. You must review the document carefully to: identify who is being appointed attorney or mandatary. If there is more than one individual appointed, confirm whether they must act together (jointly) or can act alone (severally); identify if there is an alternate attorney or mandatary named, if the primary attorney or mandatary is unwilling or unable to act or dies. The Department will require written notification of the primary's resignation or proof of their death before the Department will recognize the alternate's authority to act on behalf of the grantor or mandator; ensure the type of POA or mandate document is recognized for the administration of CPP and OAS pension and benefits; ensure the type of POA or mandate document is recognized for the administration of CPP and OAS pension and benefits. The POA or mandate must be intended for property, not personal care; determine if the attorney or mandatary's authority will continue or end if the grantor or mandator becomes incapable. A POA or mandate in Quebec is not enduring. A protection mandate is required to name one or more individuals to manage the mandator's property if they become incapable and must be homologated (approved by a court) to become effective.
