A POA is executed (written and signed) according to the laws of the province, territory, or country where they are drafted; and, therefore, may be executed differently. A POA is said to exist when an individual authorizes another individual or agency to act on their behalf. The individual giving the power is called the “grantor”; the individual receiving it is called the “attorney”. The grantor must be mentally capable of making their own decisions at the time the POA is executed. The relationship between the grantor and the attorney is governed, except in the province of Quebec, by the common law of agency and by provincial statutes and legislation. In Quebec, it is governed by the Civil Code. The POAs and Protection Mandates in Quebec section below provides more information on this topic. A general POA gives the attorney the authority to do anything the grantor could do themselves, within the terms listed in the POA document. A limited POA gives the attorney authority to act for a specific purpose (e.g. to buy or sell a particular piece of property). As a general rule, the POA will be recognized for CPP and OAS purposes if it complies with the laws of the place where it was executed. However, ultimately, it is up to the discretion of the Department whether it will accept a POA. A POA document may authorize the appointment of one or more attorneys to act jointly (together), severally (independently) or successively (independently but successive by order of attorney named). If a POA specifies that co-attorneys must act jointly and there is not an option for them to act severally, the signatures of both attorneys are required to make a decision on behalf of the grantor. If the POA names more than one attorney and does not state whether they can act alone, then it is to be assumed that they must act jointly. If a POA allows the attorneys to act jointly and severally, and a signature is required on a document, the signature of one attorney is sufficient. If a POA requires attorneys to act jointly, signatures of all attorneys are required on a document. The Department can however for communication purposes communicate with each attorney separately. The authority given in a POA may come into effect on a date specified in the document, or it may only “spring” into effect once an event that is specified in the document occurs (i.e. disability, incapability or an overseas posting). This is known as a "springing" POA. If there is no specified date or event, a POA starts immediately upon execution. POAs usually cover 2 areas of decision-making: decisions about property; and decisions about personal care. The Department will only recognize a POA that is intended for property, as CPP and OAS benefits are considered property. A POA that has been given for banking purposes only will not be recognized. A POA for personal care is not acceptable for the administration of CPP and OAS pensions and benefits. A POA may be described as "ordinary" or as "enduring" (also known as "general" or as "continuing"). If the POA document does not contain wording that it will continue or endure despite the incapability of the grantor, then it is an ordinary POA. An ordinary POA ends automatically when the grantor becomes incapable. While both types of POA are acceptable for CPP and OAS purposes, it is important to note on file if it is an ordinary or enduring POA to indicate when the authority of the attorney will end. If the Department accepts a POA, it will be applied to both programs, OAS and CPP. If the Department already has a POA on file for an individual, and then receives a POA that was executed more recently, the Department must confirm with the grantor they have revoked the previously issued POA. Springing POA A springing POA takes effect when the event that is specified in the POA document takes place. The event may be: the physical or mental incapability of the grantor; or a non-medical event. For example, the grantor requires someone to manage their affairs while they are residing outside of Canada temporarily. The POA springs into effect when the grantor leaves Canada. When the grantor returns to Canada, the POA ends. If the springing event is incapability of the beneficiary (grantor), confirmation of the grantor's incapability is required before recognizing the authority of the attorney. Confirmation can be an assessment from a medical professional or a court document. A Certificate of Incapability (ISP-3505) form is also acceptable; however, it is not required as the form's intended purpose is for appointing a trustee and not for recognizing a springing POA. A springing POA that comes into effect when the grantor becomes incapable is an enduring POA. If the springing POA is not conditional on a physical or mental incapability (as in the example of a temporary absence from Canada), confirmation that the springing event has occurred could be a phone call or letter from the grantor informing the Department of the springing event, or the Department confirming the event with the grantor. The type of notification required would depend on the wording in the POA. On the other hand, the POA itself could provide specific terms that make it clear that the event has occurred, and confirmation is not required. For example, the POA document may state that the lawyer can only provide a copy of the POA document to the attorney to inform them they have been given POA when the springing event has taken place. When the attorney presents a copy of the POA to the Department, this proves that the springing condition has been met. POAs and Protection Mandates in Quebec In Quebec, an individual can choose to grant a POA and a protection mandate. A POA in Quebec is similar to a general POA, but it is not enduring. The POA allows the grantor to name one or more individuals to manage their property, but not their personal care, and to perform administrative duties such as paying bills, withdrawing money from a bank account or other financial transactions as described in the POA document. The POA only provides authority for the attorneys to act on behalf of the grantor while the grantor has the mental capability to act on their own and to oversee the actions of the attorney. In Quebec, a grantor can also name one or more individuals to look after their personal care and to manage their property in the event that they become incapacitated. This is called a protection mandate; the grantor is the mandator and the attorney is the mandatary. The protection mandate only comes into effect once 2 conditions are met: an attorney or notary, at the request of the mandatary, applies for homologation of the mandate; and a medical assessment confirms that the mandator is incapacitated. Once a protection mandate is in force, it replaces the POA for CPP and OAS purposes. Since the beneficiary/mandator has been deemed incapable of managing their affairs, benefits will be made payable to the mandatary. Since the mandatary has the authority to act on the mandator's behalf they will have access to the mandator's account and finances in order to manage their benefits. As of November 1, 2022, there are also 3 types of representatives that may be relevant for CPP and OAS purposes: tutor; assistant; and temporary representative. Tutor A tutor is a court-appointed individual who represents an individual who is incapable of caring for themselves or of administering their property. The role of tutor may also be assigned to the public curator by the court. The court must issue a judgment specifying: the acts that the incapable individuals can perform themselves, either alone or with the assistance of their tutor; and the acts that they cannot perform alone and that must be done by their tutor. As of November 1, 2022, a previous form of protective supervision—the curator— will no longer exist. Any outstanding curators will become tutors. Assistant An assistant is an individual chosen by someone living with a difficulty to help with the administration of their property or the exercise of their rights. Although assistants are not court-appointed, they are recognized by the public curator and are publicly registered to act as an intermediary between the individual living with a difficulty and third parties, including government departments. Temporary Representative A temporary representative of an incapable individual is a court-authorized individual who performs a specific act on their behalf. The court sets the terms and conditions of the exercise of the temporary representative's powers. Given that this is a temporary measure, there is an end to the period of the temporary representation, after which the incapable individual regains their rights. When is a POA valid? In Canada, since legal representation is legislated provincially or territorially and is unique to each province and territory, a POA is valid when it meets the legislated standards of the province or territory in which it is issued. An authorizing instrument issued in one province or territory is acceptable in another province or territory, provided it meets the requirements of the province or territory receiving the POA. Therefore, should the grantor move to another province or territory after executing the POA, the POA executed in the one province or territory will be honoured in whatever province or territory the grantor resides as long as the initial authorizing instrument meets the requirements of the province or territory. Provincial or territorial legislation allow for a POA to be executed without the involvement of a lawyer, but it must be executed according to the laws of the province or territory where it is being executed. The provinces or territories provide direction on how POAs should be written and signed if they are executed without legal assistance (a lawyer or notary public). They often provide a template that the grantor can use. An individual can grant a POA to whomever, with whatever duties, and under whatever conditions they choose, which could include allowing the appointed attorney to delegate their duties to others. Although it is the individual's right to grant their authority to someone that they trust to act on their behalf, accepting a POA for CPP and OAS purposes is up to the discretion of the Department. A POA document executed with or without legal assistance may be a valid POA for CPP or OAS purposes if it meets the legal requirements under the provincial or territorial Act in which it is executed. The following list provides some general information needed to determine if a POA is valid (including a foreign-issued POA) for CPP or OAS purposes: a title that describes the contents; the name or names of individuals who have the power to act on behalf of the grantor (jointly and severally) (independently); a description of what the appointed third party or parties can do on behalf of the grantor; the date the POA takes effect (on the date it is executed or upon a specific event for a springing POA); the duration of the appointment; information about whether the power continues to act after the grantor becomes incapable (enduring or continuing); the conditions under which the POA continues; the name and signature of the grantor; the date on which the document was drafted; the name and signature of the individual (s) named to act on behalf of the grantor (the signature of an individual who has been granted POA is only required on the POA document where the requirement is prescribed by legislation. Not all Acts require the attorney named in the POA to sign the POA document); the names and signatures of the witness(es). The POA will only be acceptable for program purposes if it is witnessed in accordance with the appropriate Act. If there is only one witness, they cannot be the same individual that is being given the POA, an individual related to the grantor by blood, adoption, adoption-in-fact or through marriage, or someone of minor age; and in the case of a foreign POA, it must be witnessed either by a lawyer and accompanied by legal advice and witness certificate in the prescribed form; or by two adults who are not named as the POA or who are not family members of either the POA or grantor. The POA must contain the grantor's signature. It must indicate where it was executed and that its purpose is for property and not for personal care. Although a POA does not have to be enduring or continuing, it is important to take note whether the POA is enduring or continuing should the grantor become incapable. When a POA is signed with a mark instead of a signature A POA signed by a mark is acceptable. The mark might be anything from an “x” to a thumbprint. A statement from the witness(es) or a lawyer must accompany the POA document that has been signed with a mark confirming they saw the grantor sign the document with their mark and that they appeared to understand what they were signing. POAs and payment of benefits Unlike trusteeship, when the Department has been advised that a third party has been granted a POA, whether springing or enduring, it does not result in changing the payee to that third party. Even if the grantor becomes incapable, payments continue to be made payable to the grantor in care of the POA. When is a POA not valid? A POA document that does not meet the legal requirements under provincial or territorial law cannot be accepted, nor will a written statement be accepted as a substitute. A third party indicating that they are the holder of a POA who cannot produce a copy of the document cannot be recognized by the Department as the individual's legal representative. When does a POA end? A POA remains in effect until: it is voluntarily revoked. The grantor can only revoke a POA while they are mentally capable. This revocation must be done in writing and witnessed by a lawyer, notary public or 1 to 2 witnesses (depending on the province or territory where it is being signed); the grantor completes a new POA. The Department will need to confirm with the grantor that they have revoked the previous POA; or it is involuntarily revoked through: bankruptcy of the grantor; mental incapability of the grantor (if the POA is not an enduring or continuing POA); or death of the grantor. it is revoked by a Court order, either through a direct order or by the appointment of another representative, which automatically rescinds the POA (the appointment of the public trustee, or a guardian, etc.). The authority of an attorney under an enduring POA ends if a court is satisfied, on the application of any interested individual, that an attorney has abused their authority and a guardian is subsequently appointed under provincial or territorial law; the individual having the POA: advises the Department in writing that they no longer have POA (e.g. the POA has been revoked); has renounced their role as POA and there is no joint or substitute attorney named in the POA document; is no longer physically or mentally capable of performing duties; or dies. A POA document may name an alternate attorney in case the primary attorney is unwilling or unable to act or dies. If the primary attorney is unwilling or unable to act on behalf of the grantor, the Department will require written notification of the primary's resignation or proof of their death before the Department will recognize the alternate's authority to act on behalf of the grantor for OAS and CPP purposes. Protection of employees of the Department Generally, some protection is given under the various provincial Acts when the actual notice of revocation of the POA is not received by the attorney or by the Department. If the attorney and the Department act in good faith and without knowledge that the grantor has terminated or revoked the POA, the Department's actions resulting from the attorney's requests are valid and binding.

Dire need situations exist when a client can suffer severe financial hardship if the payment of benefits is delayed. Severe financial hardship puts the client at risk of being unable to satisfy basic needs (e.g. food, housing, medical services). Dire Need You must issue a priority payment immediately if the client's situation meets the dire need criteria. Split Payable—Add or Adjust in CPMS (Action)

A client is in a dire need situation if a delay in benefit payments will cause them to suffer severe financial hardship. Severe financial hardship is defined as a risk of being unable to satisfy basic needs, such as food, medical services or housing. Examples of factors demonstrating dire need situations include: an inability to pay medical bills or expenses (including medications) or to pay for the transportation required to access medications or medical services; an inability to buy food; a risk of eviction from housing due to an inability to pay the rent or mortgage; a risk of disconnection of utilities. Every individual’s circumstances are unique. A situation that seems dire need to one individual may not seem dire to another. You must make every effort to ensure that the client’s situation meets the following dire need criteria. An inability to satisfy basic needs such as food, medical services or housing. The benefit application's status has been verified in ITRDS, OAS Online or in the International Agreements (IA) system. All required supporting documents have been submitted . There is no pattern of past claims of dire need. Review the claimant's file to see if there is a history of such claims. Dire need situations must be escalated on an urgent basis. If a client who is in receipt of ongoing benefits has not received their payments due to an error by Service Canada: You must apologize to the client for any inconvenience caused. You must issue a priority payment immediately; an. You do not need to assess dire need criteria. Dire need notifications received by email or telephone When an email is received from either an in-person centre or a call centre with “Dire Need” in the subject line: Review the file immediately . Contact the client within 24 hours to tell them: the outcome of the review; and when they will likely receive their CPP or OAS payment. If you can issue a payment to the client, follow existing procedures to issue a priority payment within 72 hours of receiving the notification. If the situation requires faster delivery of the payment, discuss arrangements with your manager. Dire need notifications received by mail There are instances when correspondence is received in the mail processing centre indicating that the client is in dire need. In such cases, you must: Review the file immediately ; Contact the client within 24 hours of file review; If you can issue a payment to the client, follow existing procedures to issue a priority payment within 72 hours of receiving the notification.

Review the client's account to determine if the conversion of benefits will occur automatically in the system (i.e. without an application and using the information already on file) or if confirmation of information (e.g. address and payment destination) or an application is required. This will depend on the following conditions: the current ALW or ALWS benefit status (e.g. eligible and entitled, eligible but not entitled); the number of years of residence in Canada at the time of approval of the ALW or ALWS benefit; and the lifetime renewal designation. When the conversion of benefits does not occur automatically in the system, the client may be required to complete one of the following, depending on their situation: the Conversion Application (OAS/GIS) (ISP-3045) form; the Application for the Old Age Security Pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement (ISP-3550) form; or the OAS, Conversion of benefits, Confirm Existence (ISS-0629) letter, if you are unable to reach the client by phone to confirm their address and direct deposit information. This requirement can be waived if certain conditions are met. Conversion— ALW or ALWS to the OAS pension and GIS (Policy) Cúram will automatically convert a client's ALW or ALWS benefit to an OAS pension and the GIS when they reach age 65 if the following conditions are met: The client has 40 years of residence in Canada as of their most recent ALW or ALWS benefit application, determined by overrides or residence period evidence, in this order. The ALW or ALWS benefit is not suspended; and The client is eligible and entitled to an amount greater than $0 for the ALW or ALWS benefit in the current calendar month; or The client's account was not migrated from a legacy system and: they are eligible but not entitled (including excess income); and they meet the conditions outlined in the policy to waive the requirement to confirm the client's existence and information. If Cúram cannot automatically convert the client's benefits at age 65, a manual review of the account will be required to determine if they are eligible for conversion or if additional information or an application is required. The following table describes when you must confirm information or send an application or letter to the client: Effect of the conversion of benefits on the spouse or common-law partner's GIS When a client's ALW benefit is converted to an OAS pension and the GIS, their spouse or common-law partner's entitlement to the GIS is affected. Since the ALW benefit client is now receiving the OAS pension and the GIS, the rate table on which their spouse or common-law partner's GIS entitlement is based will change. If the change is retroactive, Cúram will recalculate the spouse or common-law partner's GIS entitlement for the retroactive period where the ALW benefit client has converted to the OAS pension and the GIS. Couples living apart for reasons beyond their control refers to specific situations where a married couple or common-law partners are unable to reside together, and it does not reflect a breakdown in the marriage or common-law relationship. The following describes how CPP and OAS benefits are affected when a client's marital status changes to "living apart for reasons beyond their control": Program Benefits CPP The SVR pension or Pension Sharing is not affected if the couple begins living apart for reasons beyond their control. The couple is still considered married or common-law. Program Benefits OAS The GIS is calculated based on single income the month following the month the couple began living apart, if it is to their advantage. The ALW benefit is calculated based on single income the month following the month the couple began living apart but not before January 1, 2017, if it is to their advantage. For more information, Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control (Scenario)

This provision applies to couples where: one member of the couple is eligible for the GIS; both members of the couple are eligible for the GIS; or one member of the couple is eligible for the GIS and the other member is eligible for the ALW benefit. Before the Department can consider applying the provision, the client or their spouse or common-law partner must provide the required information about the separation in writing and be living apart for a reason that is considered beyond their control. For more information about the eligibility requirements and the required documentation to support them, refer to: Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control—OAS (Policy) ; and Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control—OAS (Policy) Examples—Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control (Work Tool) . Examples—Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control (Work Tool)

The couple will continue to have their entitlement calculated based on living apart for reasons beyond their control until the circumstances have changed and the provision no longer applies. Refer to Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control—OAS (Policy) for detailed requirements. Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control—OAS (Policy)

Once it has been established that a couple is living apart for reasons beyond their control, manual calculations are required to determine if applying the provision results in an advantage or disadvantage to either member of the couple. The provision should only be applied if it is advantageous to the couple. This means that they would receive a higher amount as a couple based on their individual incomes than they would receive as a couple based on their combined income. There may be situations where the entitlement based on individual income is advantageous for the couple but results in a higher monthly benefit amount for one member of the couple and a lower monthly benefit amount for the other member. When this occurs, you must obtain authorization from the disadvantaged client or their legal representative to receive a lower entitlement before the provision can be applied. For examples on how to determine if the provision is advantageous to the couple or not, Examples—Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control (Work Tool)

Couples living apart for reasons beyond their control refers to specific situations where a married couple or common-law partners are unable to reside together in a dwelling maintained by either of them because of circumstances not attributable to either party. It does not reflect a breakdown in the marriage or common-law relationship. The Old Age Security Act has a provision that allows couples to be paid income-tested benefits based on their individual incomes rather than combined income if it is more advantageous. For more information, Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control—OAS (Policy)

A couple will continue to be paid at the single rate because of living apart for reasons beyond their control until such time that the circumstances change and the provision no longer applies. For instance, the provision no longer applies when: the couple begins to share a dwelling that is maintained by them (e.g. when they both start living in the matrimonial home again); the couple separates; one of them dies.

In recognition of the difficulties that couples face when they are forced to live apart as a result of circumstances beyond their control, the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act) has a provision that allows the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) and the Allowance ( ALW ) benefits to be calculated at a more favourable rate. To use their income for the purposes of calculating a more favourable benefit rate, the couple must: be living apart as a result of circumstances not attributable to either party; and not be living together in a dwelling maintained by either of them. For the GIS and the ALW benefits, where it has been determined that a couple is living apart for reasons beyond their control and there is no change in their marital status, their benefit(s) may be calculated at a more favourable rate. This provision is applicable to couples where: One person is eligible for the GIS benefit Both persons are eligible for the GIS benefit or One person is eligible for the GIS benefit and the other person is eligible for the ALW benefit. It allows each member of the couple to have their entitlement calculated at the single rate based on their individual income and it is not intended to place the couple in a worse financial situation. If the single rate is calculated on individual income and it is not advantageous to the couple, the benefit(s) will continue to be calculated based on the couple's combined income. If, as a result of applying this provision, the benefit of one person in the couple is reduced or no longer entitled, but it is to the overall advantage of the couple, written authorization by that person or their Power of Attorney, trustee or legal representative must be obtained before benefits can be recalculated.

The Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Control evidence exists on the Application Case and Integrated Case and impacts entitlement for income-tested benefits. It captures the reason why a client and their spouse or common-law partner are living apart when this living arrangement is beyond their control. A client can have multiple periods of living apart for reasons beyond their control resulting in multiple evidence records. If the client indicates on their paper application that they are living apart for reasons beyond their control, the Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Control evidence is automatically created when the application is captured in Cúram. The Reason for Living Apart field will indicate Unknown since this question is not included on paper benefit applications. However, as the Reason for Living Apart field is mandatory, Cúram will automatically generate an Evidence Issue(s) task which must be manually resolved before authorizing the application. Further documentation may be required. When a couple is living apart for reasons beyond their control, if it is to the overall advantage of the couple but to the disadvantage of one member to be paid on individual income, the client who is disadvantaged must give consent to receive a lower entitlement amount. Cúram will generate an Evidence Verification Request task and a request for consent to be disadvantaged must be manually sent to the client. Cúram will continue to pay the couple on combined income until consent is received. If it is received, the consent is manually captured in the Consent to be Disadvantaged evidence and Cúram will then apply the provision. If a client has multiple separate time periods of living apart for reasons beyond their control in the same marital relationship, they must give consent for each period. Each Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Control evidence can only have a single related Consent to be Disadvantaged evidence. A client can change their consent at any point during a period when they are living apart for a reason beyond their control. Consent for each new payment period is not required if the time period that the couple lives apart for reasons beyond their control is uninterrupted. As long as the period of living apart for reasons beyond their control is ongoing, the consent remains valid unless revoked by the disadvantaged client. For more information, Couples Living Apart for Reasons Beyond Their Control (Scenario)

The following are situations in which the requirement for an application cannot be waived by the Department: The pensioner or beneficiary is absent from Canada for more than 6 months (not including the month of departure), and it is established that the absence is due to a permanent change in residence. The Department chooses not to waive the annual requirement for an application for a reason related to eligibility and entitlement. The pensioner or beneficiary no longer ha s a lifetime renewal designation . The pensioner is no longer in receipt of the OAS pension. The pensioner or beneficiary requests in writing that their benefit be ceased. An ALW beneficiary is no longer eligible for the ALW if a pensioner has their OAS pension cancelled upon request or is no longer eligible for the OAS pension (e.g. if the pensioner requested to cancel their OAS pension and the cancellation is granted, the beneficiary is no longer eligible for the ALW and they lose their lifetime renewal designation . If the Department chooses not to waive the requirement for an application, legislation requires that the pensioner or beneficiary be notified at least 15 days in advance to submit a subsequent application. Communicating to the pensioner/beneficiary that the Department is not waiving their renewal application means that the pensioner/beneficiary no longer has a lifetime renewal designation until a new application is received and approved (e.g. a new application (GIS, ALW or ALWS)). It is required to confirm eligibility and entitlement if a pensioner or beneficiary loses their lifetime renewal designation .

Lifetime renewal designation Before May 3, 2007, pensioners or beneficiaries were only eligible to automatically renew their GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit without an application if they were in receipt of a benefit in the month before the start of the next payment period (i.e. June). Effective May 3, 2007, pensioners or beneficiaries are eligible to be automatically renewed for benefits without an application beginning with the 2008-2009 payment period, provided they meet the following requirements: A GIS, ALW or ALWS beneficiary was in receipt of benefits on May 3, 2007. An applicant's initial GIS, ALW or ALWS application was received before May 3, 2007, but processed and approved on or after this date. In this situation, even if the applicant is not entitled due to excess income, they are still considered a lifetime renewal applicant. An applicant's initial GIS, ALW or ALWS application is received and approved on or after May 3, 2007. In this situation, even if the applicant is not entitled due to excess income, they are still considered a lifetime renewal applicant. Requirement for an application is waived The requirement for a GIS, ALW or ALWS benefit application can be waived for any subsequent year for which the pensioner or beneficiary's income information is provided to the Department via the CRA one-way transmission, or by a statement of income received directly from the pensioner or beneficiary where they must have a lifetime renewal designation. Lifetime renewal designation lost Communicating to the pensioner or beneficiary that the Department is not waiving their renewal application means the pensioner or beneficiary no longer has a lifetime renewal designation until a new application is received and approved (e.g. a new application (GIS, ALW or ALWS )). It is required to confirm eligibility and entitlement if a pensioner or beneficiary loses their lifetime renewal designation. Situations in which the lifetime renewal designation is no longer applicable: The ALW or ALWS beneficiary: ALW beneficiary becomes divorced or separated for more than 3 months from their pensioner spouse or common-law partner; or ALWS beneficiary no longer meets the definition of survivor. If the pensioner is no longer eligible for the OAS pension, the pensioner or beneficiary is no longer eligible to receive the GIS or ALW benefits and their lifetime renewal designation ends. When the pensioner or beneficiary leaves Canada for more than 6 months, their entitlement stops 6 months after the month of departure. If their absence is considered: permanent (i.e. involving a change in residence) and they no longer reside in Canada, they are no longer eligible to receive GIS, ALW or ALWS benefits, and their lifetime renewal designation ends. temporary (i.e. not involving a change in residence), they will continue to be eligible to receive GIS, ALW or ALWS benefits and will retain their lifetime renewal designation. Sponsored immigrants Sponsored individuals who have applied for a GIS, an ALW or an ALWS benefit and who meet all other eligibility and entitlement criteria can be approved for the benefit but may not be entitled for payment because they are under a sponsorship agreement. The approval of their benefits allows the Department to consider them a lifetime renewal applicant. This allows them to have subsequent applications for their respective benefits waived as part of the lifetime renewal designation process. The decision to waive a future application is at the discretion of the Department.

As of May 3, 2007, when an income-tested benefit application is approved, the client qualifies for a lifetime renewal designation. Once the client has a lifetime renewal designation, the ITB for Life status in Cúram will be set to Yes . Any subsequent income received from the CRA will automatically be used to calculate the client's benefit entitlement for the renewal of their income-tested benefits. As a result, a client who files their annual income tax return will never have to submit a statement of income. This designation remains on the account until the client is no longer eligible for the benefit. If the designation is lost, the client will have to submit a new application to have it reinstated. Following the eligibility assessment in Cúram, the ITB for Life status will be updated to reflect the client’s eligibility to the yearly renewal of income-tested benefits. The ITB for Life status cannot be manually modified. The designation and effective date are set automatically based on actions performed in the system. There are situations where the client can be eligible for the benefit, but not in pay. In these cases, the lifetime renewal designation remains on the account. Here are some examples where the client is not entitled to income-tested benefits, but they retain their lifetime renewal designation: the income is in excess; no income was received for a payment year; the client or their spouse or common-law partner is temporarily outside of Canada longer than 6 months and entitlement is affected; or the client or their spouse or common-law partner is under a sponsorship agreement and entitlement is limited. Once the client becomes entitled again (e.g. income is received, client returns to Canada, sponsorship ends), the benefit can be reinstated without having to reapply, as long as the required income has been received from the client or the CRA. An authorized contact can : provide and receive information relating to the client's benefits; change the client's telephone number, home address and correspondence mailing address (the mailing address cannot be changed if the client's payments are being issued by cheque); request application forms, T4 slips, Statements of Contributions or letters to be mailed; and submit a written request for documentation from the client's file. An authorized contact cannot : add, change or remove a payment destination (e.g. direct deposit information or a mailing address where cheques are sent); add, change or remove a voluntary tax withhold; sign an application or form for the client; make a decision for the client (e.g. appeal a decision); and apply for or cancel benefits on the client's behalf.

With the exception of an individual with a Power of Attorney (POA) or mandate, individuals in the role of an authorized contact cannot act as a legal representative on behalf of the client. Authorized contacts are for sharing information only and are not authorized to sign, make decisions or receive benefit payments on behalf of a client. Payment request from a lawyer At times, a lawyer will advise a client to designate them as the recipient of their first benefit payment. Legislation does not allow for any benefit to be assigned, attached, anticipated or given as security. Upon receipt of such a request: verify that the letter of advice is dated and signed by the lawyer and the client; and inform the lawyer that they will be sent the first retroactive cheque but that it will be payable to the client.

Authority to communicate is different than authority to legally act on behalf of an individual and the two must not be confused. Lawyers Lawyers are "authorized contacts" and cannot make decisions on behalf of applicants or beneficiaries unless they have also been given POA. As a contact, their scope is limited to communication and the parameters described in the authorizing document. The exception is signing a request for a reconsideration or appeal as this is prescribed in legislation. Legislation allows anyone to request a reconsideration on behalf of an applicant. The authorizing letter should be read carefully to see what lawyer is the individual's authorized contact. A written notice from the individual is not required. A letter written on a lawyer's letterhead that advises the Department that they are representing an individual is sufficient proof that the lawyer or the paralegal working for the lawyer is the individual's authorized contact. A written notice from the individual is not required. Other authorized contacts An individual or organization who has been given authority to communicate on behalf of a beneficiary through a consent to communicate form or letter is also known as an "authorized contact". Although the consent is a legal document, it only provides the individual with the authority to receive and provide information. The individual or organization is not authorized to make decisions on behalf of the beneficiary, such as initiate voluntary tax withholds, or change payment details.

The Department must obtain written consent in cases where the individual is seeking to allow the Department to disclose their information to another individual, agency or organization (who is not a legal representative) over a continuous period of time. A departmental form that is available for this purpose: Consent to Communicate Information to an Authorized Person (ISP-1603) form. The intended use of the ISP-1603 form is not to communicate with an agency or organization. An agency or organization's form is acceptable consent as long as it provides all the required information. The individual can also provide all the required information to the Department with their own written statement authorizing us to communicate with that agency or organization. As it is an individual's right to share their personal information with whomever and however they choose, the Department cannot insist on the individual using a departmental consent form for communication purposes with an authorized person or agency. However, to protect the privacy of the individual and the integrity of the programs, the consent needs to be in writing, signed and dated. If the individual uses a letter of authorization or another agency or organization's form for consent to communicate their personal information, it should provide: the name, address and telephone number of the authorized person, agency or organization; what information can be shared; and any restrictions. For example, a consent may be received restricting the purpose for communication with the authorized person to the reconsideration process. Once a decision is made on the reconsideration, the consent expires. By signing the consent form or letter, the individual is declaring they understand that they are allowing the Department to communicate their personal information to a third party. The Department will only release information that is permitted by the form or letter and under the specified circumstances and conditions stated on the consent form or letter. If an individual has provided written consent, they may withdraw their consent at any time. For records and audit purposes, it would be preferable the withdrawal bein writing. However, if the individual cannot send a written request and the employee had validated their identity over the phone, the Department can accept their verbal request to withdraw their consent. The staff must document the withdrawal request.

An authorized contact can be anyone who is authorized by the individual to communicate on their behalf. They can be an individual, an agency or an organization. In order to release any personal information to an authorized contact, the Department must first have on file the written consent of the individual to whom the personal information relates to. Consent can be a letter of authorization, or a departmental or other organization's consent form. Upon receiving written consent from the individual, the Department can communicate information about the individual's file with the authorized contact based on the specified information in the letter or form. Only information not restricted by the individual, by the legislation and by the Department can be discussed with the contact. Copies of documents from the individual's file cannot be released to a contact unless the letter of authorization instructs the Department to do so. If it does, the release of information must follow the rules set out by Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP). When in doubt regarding what information to release from a file to an authorized contact, the ATIP coordinator can provide assistance.

Undue hardship occurs when the repayment of an overpayment (in whole or in part) causes financial stress for the debtor because of limited household income. Hardship exists when the debtor is unable to repay a portion of the overpayment without being deprived of the necessities of life such as food, shelter, medical services, clothing and utilities (water, electricity and heating). When an overpayment is established on a debtor's account, they are notified of the amount and recovery rate. The proposed recovery rate is based on the Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) When the debtor or their legal representative claims financial difficulty and cannot repay the debt at the proposed recovery rate, you can accept or negotiate an amended recovery rate without requesting a Statement of Income and Expenses (ISP-0100) form. However, you must ensure that the overpayment can be recovered within the applicable 5- or 10-year period. For more information, Overpayments—Recovery and Collection (Policy) If the overpayment cannot be recovered within the 5- or 10-year period, the debtor must indicate their inability to afford repayment on the ISP-0100 form or in a written statement, including their income and expenses. The income stated on the ISP-0100 form or written statement should be current amounts, and if the debtor is married or living common-law, the spouse or common-law partner's income must also be included. Other household members' income should not be included (e.g. children, parents, etc.). Use your judgment to determine if the expenses listed are reasonable. If an expense appears too high, you must contact the debtor to request clarification or supporting documentation. For example, if a client has 2 people in their household and claims $5,000.00 per month in grocery expense, you must request clarification. When a new recovery rate is set or the recovery is deferred, you must send a letter to notify the debtor. You must assess each undue hardship case on an individual basis.

When an individual claims the recovery of their overpayment (as a whole or in parts) would cause suffering or privation due to their limited household income, undue hardship may be considered. Household income is the total combined income of the individual and their spouse or common-law partner. Children's income is not considered when determining household income. In addition, assets and liabilities are excluded when determining a claim of undue hardship. Undue hardship exists when the individual cannot repay any portion of the overpayment, however small, without being deprived of the necessities of life. These necessities include food, shelter, medical attention, clothing and utilities (i.e. water, electricity and heating). A claim of undue hardship must come from the individual or from someone acting on their behalf. Reduced recovery rates for active accounts When an individual claims undue hardship, they indicate that they cannot repay at the established or proposed recovery rate. In response, the Department has the authority to reduce, suspend or defer recovery action for a period of time, while keeping with the key principles. In most cases, an individual must provide information about their household income and expenses on a Statement of Income and Expenses (ISP-0100) form. They must also provide documentation to the Department to support their claim. The Department has the discretion to accept or negotiate a reduced recovery rate without the need to request an ISP-0100 form. This reduced recovery is allowed as long as the overpayment will still be recovered within the suggested 5-year or 10-year time frames. In cases where the overpayment will not be recovered in the suggested time frames above based on the proposed reduced recovery rate, information about the individual's income and expenses is required. Once the ISP-0100 form is received, it is reviewed and the individual's ability or inability to repay their overpayment is determined. Additional information or clarification of details can be requested, if required. If the amount of an expense does not seem reasonable, the individual can be asked to provide an explanation. If the individual indicates they are currently making payments on loans and/or credit cards, they can be asked when these payments are expected to end. If the individual's yearly reasonable expenses are more than, equal to or approximate the yearly income, it may be concluded that undue hardship does exist. Discretion and judgement must be applied in each case. If it is determined that the individual is experiencing undue hardship and is not capable of repaying their overpayment at the proposed or established recovery rate, the recovery rate can be reduced. As a guideline for undue hardship claims, the reduced rate should be sufficient to recover the bulk of the overpayment within 10 years, but this is not always possible. Therefore, recovery rates are discretionary and can be reduced depending on the individual's financial situation. If the assessment of the individual's financial situation does not allow a reduced recovery rate, the original recovery rate should be maintained. If a reduced recovery rate is established and there is a possibility that the individual's financial situation may change in the future (i.e. loan payment is expected to end in the near future), the account can be reviewed every 6 to 12 months. Increased recovery rates for active accounts When it is determined that the individual can pay more than the established recovery rate, the recovery rate can be increased. However, the individual needs to agree on an increased recovery rate before it is implemented. Deferred recovery rate When it is determined that the individual is in a temporary (6 to 12 months) or long-term (5 years or less) situation of undue hardship, the recovery rate can be suspended (if recovery has started) or deferred (if recovery has not started). The account must be reviewed in 6 to 12 months or in 5 years or less, as applicable. Recovery after a period of deferral or suspension Before recovery begins or is restarted, individuals must be advised in writing of the intended recovery action after a period of deferral or suspension. They must also be provided with the opportunity to respond within a reasonable time frame. Individuals will be given a minimum of 30 days to reply. If the individual objects, negotiations must take place before restarting recovery.

ITRDS uses the data in the client's profile with the information that you enter when you perform a data capture simulation. A simulated data capture performed in ITRDS does not affect any of the client's current benefits. Data capture simulations in ITRDS allow you to: calculate a single or combined benefit estimate dollar amount; determine the potential eligibility for a benefit; or determine the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) for benefit eligibility purposes. A compromise settlement is an agreement to settle a debt by accepting a partial payment in lieu of the full debt repayment. This procedure will guide you on how to process the request from the debtor or their representative.

A compromise settlement offer is an agreement between a debtor and Service Canada to finalize a debt by accepting a partial payment of the debt as full repayment. A debtor or their representative must request a compromise settlement offer in writing. They must give the reason for the request and details of the proposal. All requests for a compromise settlement are forwarded to the Collections Litigations and Advisory Services section of Canada Revenue Agency. The Collections Litigations and Advisory Services is the delegated authority to negotiate and accept such requests. After a compromise settlement offer is accepted, the balance owing on the debt is permanently written off from the accounts receivable records, and the debtor is released from any obligation to pay the remaining balance. For more information, refer to the policy Overpayments—Recovery and Collection

A compromise settlement is an agreement to finalize an overpayment by accepting a partial payment as full repayment of the overpayment. The individual is released from any obligation to pay the balance owed. A compromise settlement will only be considered when it is in the best interest of the Department. The individual or their representative must initiate the compromise settlement in writing. They must clearly indicate the reason for the request and the details of the proposal. All requests for a compromise settlement are forwarded to the Collections Litigations and Advisory Services section of the Canada Revenue Agency. They are the delegated authorities of the Department to negotiate and accept these requests. After a compromise settlement is finalized, the remaining balance of an overpayment is written-off.

Residence periods are the amount of time a client has resided in and outside of Canada. You will data capture all residence periods a client has declared from age 18 to present. The data capture in ITRDS must be complete and accurate in order to determine the client's: eligibility (to approve or deny the application); and entitlement (to avoid an incorrect payment). Once all residence periods are captured, ITRDS calculates the total years of residence based on: total periods of valid Canadian residence to date; total periods of creditable foreign residence to date; or a combination of both. When entering periods on the Residence screen, ITRDS will determine the client’s eligibility to the OAS pension and benefits based on the following: For any residence period outside of Canada, you must select a Reason for Absence associated with the Type of period.

When establishing residence for an OAS pension or benefit, any absences interrupting residence in Canada are excluded from the Canadian residence calculation. An applicant is considered absent from Canada when they are not physically present in Canada. However, not all absences interrupt residence and they must be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. When evaluating an absence, consider the following: Length of the absence Temporary absences lasting less than one year do not necessarily interrupt residence and may not need to be investigated unless they are part of a larger pattern of absences. An absence lasting more than one year, depending on its nature, can interrupt residence. Reason for the absence The applicant may need to clarify whether the absence was temporary in nature for it to be considered as residence in Canada. Frequency of absences Absences that are a part of a larger pattern of absences may indicate residential ties to another country. When reviewing the length, nature or frequency of an absence, consider the applicant's residential ties to Canada when they are outside of the country. The applicant may need to demonstrate that they maintained significant ties to Canada during the period(s) that they were absent. If residential ties cannot be verified, the period of absence is excluded from the Canadian residence calculation. For factors to consider when reviewing an applicant’s residential ties, refer to the Residential Ties work tool. For a residence statement to be considered complete, it must include all periods of residence in Canada and absence from Canada relevant to eligibility and entitlement. Documentary Evidence—Residence (Policy) This includes all periods of Canadian residence and all absences from Canada greater than 6 months: from the latest of: the applicant’s 18th birthday; or the date of initial arrival into Canada; and up to and including the date the applicant submits their application. If an applicant selects Yes in response to the question about having lived continuously in Canada since birth or age 18 on an OAS pension or benefit application, this is considered a complete residence statement. While the residence history is considered complete if it includes only the years of residence, clarification is required if months are missing. If an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) is needed for the applicant to be eligible for an OAS pension or benefit, all residence periods, including those outside of Canada, from age 18 to the date the applicant submits their application are required in writing. When an application is submitted early, confirmation of the applicant's continued residence up to their pension or benefit effective date is required if the additional time affects the residence calculation.

For the residence history to be considered complete, it must state all periods of residence in Canada and absences from Canada relevant to eligibility and entitlement. For example, if an applicant born outside of Canada qualifies under domestic legislation, only the residence history from the date of initial entry into Canada is required. If an applicant qualifies under an International Social Security Agreement, a complete residence history from age 18 to present is required. In general, absences of less than one year do not necessarily interrupt residence and may not need to be investigated. The application should be processed based on the stated residence history, unless there is a pattern of frequent absences over a period of several years, as it could be indicative of presence rather than residence. Absences from Canada over one year can interrupt residence unless the absence is: of a temporary nature; for the purpose of attending school or university; or deemed as residence in Canada under a specified circumstance. When an individual claims a large number of separate periods as Canadian residence, the decision regarding the periods of residence must be based on a judgment of the particular circumstances of the case. In certain situations, there will be no alternative but to accept the statement of the applicant for at least part of the claimed residence. In dealing with these cases, it is reasonable to require something more than a signed statement from a reference supporting an applicant’s claim. An agent should contact the applicant and the references by telephone and interviewed whenever possible, as interviews can turn up pertinent information. If, after an interview, the applicant's claim still lacks credibility, or that there is concern about potential impropriety, the file should be referred to the Integrity Services Branch. In difficult residence cases, if, after a thorough review, judgment dictates that there is insufficient proof of residence or that there is a lack of credibility in the applicant’s statement, then any decision to deny the application should be made on that basis. Contact the individual when: there is information on the residence history or the application that indicates their residence in Canada can be deemed residence for OAS purposes; there are contradictions on the residence history itself; or the residence history is not complete. After contacting the individual, if the number of 40ths changes, obtain additional information and/or amendments to the residence history in writing.

Each absence is evaluated based on its duration. If there are numerous absences throughout the individual's residence history, these absences must be reviewed collectively. Updated Absences of less than one year In most cases, an absence of less than one year does not interrupt residence. However, if there is a pattern of frequent short-term absences from Canada, an individual's residence history must be reviewed to determine if the pensioner was and still can be considered a resident of Canada. In cases where it is clearly indicated that the individual has severed all residential ties with Canada, a review of an applicant's residence during a short-term absence is required. Updated Absences greater than one year An absence from Canada greater than one year may be determined to have interrupted residence. As a rule of thumb, the longer the absence from Canada, the greater the chance that residence may have been interrupted. Any absence may be considered temporary if the individual can prove residential ties to Canada and that they: were a resident of Canada at the time of departure; did not establish residence in the other country; maintained strong ties with Canada during their absence; and showed intent of returning to Canada within a reasonable time period. This determination can only be made upon return to Canada. The individual may be required to submit supporting evidence of the reason for the prolonged absence. Frequent absences of 6 months or more within a period of several years may constitute a break in Canadian residence or they may be determined to be temporary absences.

An absence is defined as a period of absence from Canada of a Canadian resident that is of a temporary nature and: does not exceed one year; is for the purpose of attending school or university; or is a specified circumstance. Exceptions to residence rules can be deemed not to have interrupted an individual's residence in Canada. Residence in Canada may include temporary absences (i.e. periods of time during which an individual was outside of Canada). Temporary absences are of a nature and duration which do not interrupt residence in Canada. To maintain residence in Canada during periods of temporary absences, an individual must be able to demonstrate 2 distinct ties with Canada: that a centralized mode of living in Canada was established before the period of absence; and that a principle and centralized mode of living was maintained during the period of absence. To prove continuing residence in Canada, evidence is required to show that the absences were temporary in nature (i.e. there was a clear intent to return to Canada and the individual maintained factual ties with Canada). A determination of residence must be made on a case by case basis. There is no single rule to determine whether an individual is a resident of Canada. Many factors must be considered and analyzed. If there is greater evidence showing a continuing residential relationship with Canada, the individual's residence in Canada may be assumed. If it is determined that an individual maintained residence in Canada during periods of temporary absences, the individual is considered to have been in Canada throughout the period of absence. For qualification and benefit calculation purposes, the period of absence will contribute to the residence requirements.

Translation services are available in all regions and at National Headquarters to: translate business documents; translate documents from clients; or communicate out to clients in the official language (i.e. English or French) of their choice. Translation requests are sent to internal translation units first, then to the Translation Bureau—Public Services and Procurement Canada, if necessary. You can accept documents translated by Canadian federal, provincial or territorial governments, foreign missions (e.g. embassies, consulates, High Commissions) and certified translators for the purpose of administering CPP and OAS benefits. You do not have to translate documents provided by clients in a foreign language if the material is not relevant to the consideration of the application or the ongoing receipt of benefits. For example: A client who came to Canada in 1988 attaches a copy of his foreign passport from 1980 to 1985 while he did not reside in Canada. A client indicates in a letter the nature of attached documents and you know they are not relevant. You must not assume the nature of the documen ts, the client must specify it in writing . Departmental employees can review and edit translated work. For technical translations of one or two words, employees can use a program lexicon to identify the word in the other official language. Best practices You must send translation requests as early as possible before the deadline in order to reduce costs. A minimum 24-hour turnaround time is required for all requests sent to the Translation Bureau. Translating l ong documents can take several weeks. Ensure that you follow the Government of Canada’s security directions Internal link on how to classify and transmit documents. For example, client documents can require Protected B classification and transmittal. Government of Canada’s security directions You should provide: translated reference material with related vocabulary in both languages. Providing existing translations improves accuracy and reduces timelines; a clean copy with few questions or clearly marked revisions (e.g. tracked changes, yellow highlighting). For revision, include the original translation; and content that is clear and professional with proper punctuation, grammar, names, titles, etc.

For the purpose of administering CPP and OAS benefits, you may need to have foreign documents translated. However, translation is not required when the documents received are translated by: a Canadian, provincial or territorial, government; or foreign missions (e.g. embassies, consulates, High Commissions), Government departments and certified translators. You do not have to translate documents provided in a foreign language if: the material is not relevant to the consideration of the application or the ongoing receipt of benefits; or the relevant details are provided by the foreign agency. For more information, Translation (Action)

When an OAS pensioner residing outside Canada has not accumulated enough Canadian residence (i.e. 20 years) to allow portability of the pension, the totalization provisions of Canada's International Social Security Agreements (ISSAs) can be used to satisfy these requirements. While the way Canadian residence is measured under the various agreements may vary, the basic premise is that years of residence or contributions in an ISSA country can be added to an applicant's Canadian residence (totalization). If the combination of Canadian residence and qualifying international residence or contributions is greater than 20 years, the OAS pension becomes fully portable. If a pensioner leaves Canada permanently and their pension is not portable, entitlement may be reinstated if they accrue creditable periods in a country with whom Canada has an ISSA without having to return to Canada.

Portability is the term used to refer to a pensioner's ability to receive their pension abroad. After an OAS pensioner leaves Canada, the portability rules determine the length of time that the Department can continue to pay the pension. The basic intent of the OAS pension is to provide seniors with modest economic support. The amount of support and an individual's eligibility for the support is based on their contribution to Canadian society. The primary targets of the OAS pension are seniors living in Canada. For OAS purposes, the contribution that an individual makes to Canadian society is measured by the amount of time an applicant has been a resident of Canada. After having made a significant contribution to our society, many seniors may choose to leave Canada to live elsewhere.

As a rule, OAS income-tested benefits (i.e. GIS, ALW and ALWS ) are not portable. These benefits are intended to provide immediate economic support to lower income Canadians while they are residents of Canada. The payment of OAS income tested benefits is extended for 6 months beyond the month of departure from Canada but are not continued beyond that point.

To satisfy the portability requirements, an applicant must have accumulated a minimum of 20 years of Canadian residence, at which time an OAS pensioner is considered to have made a significant enough contribution to warrant the continued payment (portability) of the OAS pension after leaving Canada. However, this requirement is not applied at the time of application unless the applicant applies from outside of Canada. Instead, the portability requirement is applied 6 months after the month that a pensioner left Canada. This means that pensioners who were originally entitled to an OAS pension based on less than 20 years of Canadian residence could have accumulated sufficient residence to allow portability of the pension. A pensioner may be paid a full pension under the 10 Year Rule or the 3 for 1 Rule but may not have accumulated the required 20 years of residence in Canada after the age of 18 for the pension to be portable. The same applies to a pensioner in receipt of a partial pension in which they have not accumulated the required 20 years of Canadian residence. A partial pension based on 18/40ths will, after 2 additional years of Canadian residence (from the effective date of the OAS pension), become fully portable. It was not portable at the time of application but later becomes so; however, there will be no adjustment to the rate. If an applicant chooses to voluntarily defer a partial pension for a higher pension amount, the adjustment to the pension may be based on the actuarial adjustment, not on the further accumulation of residence. However, residence will continue to be accumulated for portability purposes.

For the purpose of OAS benefits (i.e. partial OAS pension, GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits), absences of sufficient duration (temporary or otherwise) will stop the continuing payment of benefits. Payment of these benefits will continue for only 6 months after the month of departure. An individual's absence may be considered temporary for the purpose of initial eligibility, but this determination will not supersede the restrictions on the payment of benefits outside of Canada. The rules regarding the portability of benefits must be applied, regardless of whether the Department considers the absence to be temporary in nature.

IO processes benefit applications using provisions set out in the International Social Security Agreements (ISSA) to assist individuals to qualify for Canadian benefits to which they would not otherwise be entitled. These agreements coordinate the administration and operation of the CPP and OAS programs with the comparable social security program of another country. When determining eligibility for an OAS pension or benefit, an ISSA allows periods of residence and/or contributions in a country with which Canada has an agreement in force to be added to an applicant's years of residence in Canada after reaching age 18 to meet the minimum residence requirements to qualify. While an ISSA can assist in qualifying a client for an OAS pension, the client's entitlement (40th) will be based only on their actual number of years of residence in Canada. An ISSA can also allow periods of residence and/or contributions in a country with which Canada has an agreement in force to be added to an applicant's CPP contributions to meet the minimum contributory requirement for a CPP pension or benefit. In all cases, the terms and provisions of an ISSA can only be applied on or after the entry into force date. An agreement enters into force when the terms and conditions of the ISSA take effect. The terms of most ISSAs allow for foreign creditable periods to be added to residence in Canada to meet the minimum residence requirements. This is known as "totalization" and it is completed by staff in International Operations (IO). While totalization can assist an applicant to meet the minimum residence requirements, entitlement is still based on actual years of residence in Canada. International Social Security Agreements Canada has reciprocal agreements related to social benefits in force with many countries. These International Social Security Agreements (ISSA) allow social program credits from other countries to be considered when determining eligibility for benefits in Canada. Some applicants may have lived and worked in Canada and in other countries. Their work activity in another country may occur before or after their work in Canada. The social security systems of certain countries allow voluntary contributions to be made without work activity. Such voluntary contributions can also be used in determining an individual's eligibility for benefits in Canada. The DTH benefit payment can be made to the individual or institution who paid for or is responsible for paying the deceased contributor's funeral expenses if: there is no estate; or the estate has not applied within 60 days from the date of death of the contributor. The individual or institution may be required to submit the receipt (i.e evidence of payment) and the invoice or contract (i.e. evidence of responsibility to pay). Proof of funeral expenses (e.g. funeral receipt or contract) are not required from the individual or institution who has paid or was responsible for the payment of the funeral expenses. The Minister reserves the right to request proof of funeral expenses at any time. The information regarding the amount of the funeral expenses or service provider may be obtained by a phone call if it is not submitted on the application. The DTH benefit payment can be made to another eligible applicant if: there is no estate; the estate has not applied within 60 days from the date of death of the contributor; or the DTH benefit is less than $2,387 (the amount prescribed in the CPP regulations). Before paying the DTH benefit to someone other than an estate representative (e.g. executor, court-appointed administrator, public trustee), the Minister must make reasonable enquiries to ensure that the estate representative has sufficient time to apply (i.e. 60 days). If there is no estate or the benefit amount is below the amount prescribed in the legislation, the payment of the benefit can be made immediately to the appropriate applicant as per the hierarchy prescribed in the legislation.

Once the CPP Death (DTH) benefit eligibility criteria are met, the payee must be determined. When the payment of a DTH benefit has been approved, the benefit is payable to the estate of a deceased contributor except when indicated in the legislation. For the CPP DTH benefit, estate means that an estate representative has been appointed and has accepted the responsibility to administer the deceased contributor's assets and debts, including the distribution of any benefits, and is considered the first payee. The estate representative can be: an individual or agency (e.g. law firm) appointed by the deceased contributor in their last will and testament as their executor; an individual appointed by the court of the relevant provincial jurisdiction; or a provincial public trustee. The legislation allows for the payment of the DTH benefit (in whole or in part) to be made to an individual or agency other than the estate when: there is no estate; or the estate has not applied for the DTH benefit within the prescribed time of 60 days following the contributor's death. In the absence of a DTH benefit application by the deceased contributor's estate, the hierarchy for paying the DTH benefit is as follows: to an individual, agency or institution who has paid or is responsible for the payment of a deceased contributor's funeral expenses; in the absence of an individual or institution described in paragraph (a), to the survivor of the deceased contributor; or in the absence of an individual or institution referred to in paragraph (a) and a survivor referred to in paragraph (b), to the next of kin of the deceased contributor. For the DTH benefit, an institution is an organization who has taken responsibility for the funeral expenses of the deceased contributor (e.g. Last Post Fund, Community and Social Services).

Each program will determine the delegated authority for remitting overpayments as there are 2 distinct provisions under the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act . If the remission request is for multiple overpayments, complete a separate form for each program and each benefit payment. Refer to the following examples to determine if you must submit multiple forms: If a client is in pay for an OAS pension and GIS but payments are made after their date of death, the total amount of the OAS pension and GIS is one benefit payment. If a client has a GIS and an ALW benefit overpayment due to change in marital status, the amount of each debt is treated separately as they are separate benefit payments. If a client has a DSB and RTR pension overpayment due to a change to their Record of Earnings (ROE), the amount of each debt is treated separately as they are separate benefit payments. If a client is in pay for a combined RTR and SVR pension but payments are made after their date of death, the total amount of the RTR / SVR pension is one benefit payment. If a client has a RTR pension and a PRB overpayment due to a change to their ROE, the total amount of the RTR pension and PRB is one benefit payment. If a client has a RTR pension and a PRDB overpayment due to a change to their ROE, the total amount of the RTR pension and the PRDB is one benefit payment. If a client, due to a change to their ROE, has a combined RTR / SVR pension and a PRDB overpayment, the total amount of the combined RTR / SVR pension and the PRDB is one benefit payment.
