Reversals of remissions are only done in exceptional circumstances. For more information, Overpayments—Remissions (Policy) To request a reversal of remissions, proceed as follows: For CPP, a request for review and reversal, if required, must be sent to CPP Operations via the National Business Expertise Tool (NEXO) Internal link (access is required). National Business Expertise Tool For OAS, reversals of remissions are completed automatically in Cúram. In exceptional cases when the Public Sector Collections and Disbursements system interface is unable to transmit or receive data and the interface fails, a task will be generated for staff to reverse the remission in Cúram. When you reverse a remission in CPMS or Cúram, the debt becomes collectable again. In CPMS , the remission amount will be automatically adjusted on the Remissions/Write Offs screen. In Cúram, the liability is increased by the amount of the reversal in the Person record. Proceed to recover the debt. Departmental Receivables (Overpayments) (Scenario)

Manual reversals of remissions or write-offs under the Financial Administration Act are only done in Cúram in exceptional cases when the Public Sector Collections and Disbursements system interface is unable to transmit or receive data. When you reverse a write-off or remission, the initial liability amount or outstanding debt balance is increased by the amount of the reversal in the Person record. As a result, the debt becomes collectible again. The write-off may or may not be able to be reversed in the future depending on the write-off reason. For example, a compromise settlement or a discharged bankruptcy cannot be reversed. However, write-offs coded as Benefit Cancellation Deductions , Reconciliation – RD and Other can be reversed.

A write-off is an accounting action that removes, in whole or in part, a legally enforceable debt from the accounts receivable records. A write-off does not mean that the debt is forgiven. The debt continues to exist but the recovery is deferred so that the debt can be collected in the future. After you review the file, you may determine that the debt should be recommended for a write-off. The following situations are examples where a write-off should be recommended: The debtor is deceased and there is no known estate or person responsible for the deceased debtor's affairs (e.g. there is no response to the Department's request for repayment when sent to the deceased's last known address); The debtor is a non-resident and there is no apparent means of collecting the debt at this time; The debtor cannot be located; The debtor is experiencing long term hardship with the possibility of future recovery; A balance of a debt remains after a compromised settlement is accepted; A balance of a debt remains after a discharged bankruptcy; A balance of a debt remains after an undischarged bankruptcy; A balance of a debt remains after the closure of a consumer proposal; The Department determined the debt was the result of misrepresentation and it cannot be recovered despite all collection attempts. The debtor has a debt arising from a conviction of fraud and it cannot be recovered despite all collection attempts. For more information, refer to Overpayments—Write-Offs (Policy) and Overpayments—Write-Offs (Policy) Write-Off an Overpayment (Scenario)

A write-off under the Financial Administration Act is an accounting action that removes, in whole or in part, a legally enforceable debt from the accounts receivable records. A write-off does not mean that the debt is forgiven. Since the debt will continue to exist, a write-off simply defers the recovery so that the debt can be collected in the future, except if you are recommending a write-off in any one of these 3 situations: a balance remains after a compromise settlement is accepted; a balance remains after the closure of a consumer proposal; or a balance remains after a bankruptcy discharge is granted. Once the debt or any remaining balance is written off, it cannot be collected at a future date as the debtor is released from the obligation to repay the debt and the debt no longer exists. For more information, refer to Compromise Settlement (Scenario) and Compromise Settlement (Scenario) Bankruptcy (Scenario) An overpayment should only be written-off when every possible effort to recover or collect the debt is exhausted. For more information, refer to Overpayments—Write-Offs (Policy) and Overpayments—Write-Offs (Policy) Overpayments—Key Principles (Policy) To write off a debt, you must make a recommendation to the Chief Financial Officer Branch (CFOB) via the CFOB F&A Portal External link . Only the CFOB has the authority to approve the write-off of a debt. CFOB F&A Portal Once approved, the recommendation is sent directly to the Public Sector Collections and Disbursements system. The following are common examples of when to recommend a write-off as there is potential to recover the debt in the future: the debtor is deceased and there is no known estate or person responsible for the deceased debtor's affairs (e.g. no response to the Department's request for repayment when sent to the deceased's last known address); the debtor is a non-resident (e.g. debtor resides outside of Canada and currently does not have residential ties with Canada) and there are no apparent means of collecting the debt at this time; the debtor cannot be located; the debtor is experiencing long-term hardship with the possibility of future recovery; the Department determined the debt was the result of misrepresentation and it cannot be recovered despite all collection attempts; or the debtor has a debt arising from a conviction of fraud and it cannot be recovered despite all collection attempts.

There are 2 different types of write-offs: write-offs under the Financial Administration Act ; and write-offs in Cúram. A write-off under the Financial Administration Act is the removal of an overpayment, in whole or in part, from the accounts receivable records. Depending on the write-off reason, it may be a permanent or temporary forgiveness of the debt. For more information, refer to Write-Off an Overpayment (Scenario) . You will not manually add this type of write-off to Cúram unless you are directed to do so by the Chief Financial Officer Branch (CFOB). Once the recommendation has been approved by the CFOB, it will be added to Cúram automatically. Write-Off an Overpayment (Scenario) A write-off in Cúram is an adjustment that reduces the initial liability amount of a debt. It is not an actual forgiveness of the debt, and it could be recovered at some point in the future.

A remission is the decision to forgive an otherwise legally enforceable debt. Remissions should only be used when the Department cannot recover or collect a debt in the future. For OAS, remissions are managed through the write-off functionality in Cúram. CPP and OAS staff have delegated authority to remit debts on active and inactive accounts, depending on the amount of the debt. To ensure that the remission is approved by the applicable delegated authority, refer to the Delegation of Authorities (PDF, 313 KB) Download link . Delegation of Authorities For situations in which overpayments may be remitted, and situations requiring recovery of debt efforts prior to remission, Overpayments—Remissions (Policy) If a decision has been made to remit an overpayment due to erroneous advice/administrative error, any portion of the overpayment already recovered should not be refunded. Any payment received after the debt has been remitted must be refunded to the client. If the debtor, their legal representative or another third party insists on repaying the debt after it has been remitted, the Minister can accept the payment as a donation. For the process on how to accept a donation, send an enquiry via the National Business Expertise Tool (NEXO) Internal link (access is required). National Business Expertise Tool

The remission of a debt is a decision to forgive the debt. The Department cannot resume recovery or collect the debt once the remission is approved. After you review the file, you may determine that the debt should be remitted instead of written-off in the following situations: the debt cannot be collected in the reasonably foreseeable future (e.g. debtor is deceased and a written statement is received from an executor or individual taking care of the deceased's affairs confirming that there are no funds available to pay the debt); the cost of recovery exceeds the debt (e.g. initial debt is $100.00 or less per benefit payment on an inactive account); the debt is the result of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error; or the debtor is experiencing undue hardship (e.g. permanent and ongoing). For more information, refer to the Overpayments—Remissions (Policy) and Overpayments—Remissions (Policy) Remit an Overpayment (Scenario)

According to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act) and the Financial Administration Act , a remission is the decision to forgive an otherwise legally enforceable debt. This means that the debt is forgiven and the Crown gives up the right to resume collection at a future date. The debtor is released from the obligation to repay their overpayment. After a remission is approved on the overpayment or a specified portion of the overpayment, the Department gives up the right to resume recovery or collection of the overpayment at a future date. The individual is released from the obligation to repay because the overpayment is forgiven and no longer exists. As a rule, decisions to remit or not to remit an overpayment are upheld by the delegated official and will not be re-visited except in cases where there is: a gross error or misapplication of the legislation; new information that is discovered; or a jurisdictional error. Any payment received from an individual after their overpayment has been remitted must be returned to them since the overpayment no longer exists. However, if the individual insists on repaying the overpayment after it has been remitted, the Minister may accept the payment as a donation. In situations where a portion of an overpayment has already been recovered or repaid and a subsequent decision is made to remit the overpayment, the balance of the overpayment is remitted. There is no authority to reissue the already recovered funds to the individual when the Department has determined there was originally no entitlement to those funds. This includes situations where the cause of the overpayment was due to Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE).

The remission of a debt (i.e. a receivable) is a decision to forgive the debt. After a debt is remitted, the Department cannot resume recovery or collect the debt. For more information on remitting a receivable, refer to Remit an Overpayment . A write-off is an accounting action that removes a debt from the accounts receivable record. However, the debt is not forgiven and it can generally still be collected . Some write-off codes cannot be collected in the future as per the Financial Administration Act . After you receive the approval, you must review CPMS to ensure that all actions have been taken. Remit an Overpayment

There is no time limit on the certification of a document as long as there is no reason to doubt the document's authenticity. An individual certifying a copied document is attesting to the fact that they have compared it to the original document and found it to be a true copy of the original and unaltered in any way. For a complete list of officials who can certify a photocopy of a document, Documentary Evidence—Treatment and Use (Policy)

A certified true copy means that a copy bears a stamp or written statement attesting to the fact that it is exactly the same as the original document. There is no set formal or standardized legal wording to use when certifying documents. When certifying documents, you must do so in writing using phrases or stamps such as the following: Certified copy of the original; This copy conforms to the original; or I certify this to be a true copy of the original. The Department uses the following standard statement: “This photocopy conforms to the original document which has not been altered in any way.” There are a number of other conditions that must be met before you can accept a certified copy. For more information, Documentary Evidence—Treatment and Use (Policy)

A certified photocopy is a copy of an original document that is made and certified by an official from the list below. An individual certifying a photocopied document is attesting to the fact that they have compared it to the original document and found it to be a true copy of the original and unaltered in any way. There is no time limit on the certification if there is no reason to doubt the document's authenticity. There is no formal or legal wording that needs to be used with certifying documents. However, the individual performing the certification must do so in writing and use phrases or stamps that say such things as: "Certified copy of the original"; "This copy conforms to the original"; or "I certify this to be a true copy of the original", etc. The following officials can certify a photocopy of a document: Accountant; Chief of First Nations Band; Commissioner for Oaths; Employee of a Service Canada Centre acting in an official capacity; Funeral Director; Justice of the Peace; Lawyer, Magistrate, Notary; Manager of a financial institution; Medical and Health Practitioner: Chiropractor; Dentist; Doctor; Ophthalmologist; Optometrist; Pharmacist; Psychologist; Naturopathic Doctor; Nurse Practitioner; or Registered Nurse; Member of Parliament or their staff; Member of Provincial Legislature or their staff; Minister of Religion; Municipal Clerk; Official of a country with which Canada has a reciprocal social security agreement; Official of a federal or provincial government department or one of its agencies; Official of an Embassy, Consulate or High Commission; Police Officer; Professional Engineer; Social Worker; Teacher; or University Professor. Acceptable certified photocopies To be considered an acceptable certified true copy of an original document, a certified photocopy must: be clear and readable; contain the signature, name and official position or title of the individual who certified the document; contain the date when it was certified; and include a statement attesting to the fact that the document is a true copy of the original and has been compared to the original to ensure it was not amended or altered in any way. (This may be evident in a stamp that has been pre-formatted for this purpose.) The certified photocopy can be certified by a notary public or by a lawyer or solicitor and does not need to be returned to the individual. A government or court-issued document contains an official stamp and/or seal and is signed by the government or court official (domestic or foreign). A certified true copy of a government or court-issued document is accepted as an original document as the original document is retained by the government or court. A notarized copy is a document that is certified as a true copy by a: notary public; or lawyer/solicitor. Notarized copies bear an embossed seal or stamp along with complete certification and a signature. Multiple page documents often have a stapled blue paper corner or the certified documents are enclosed in a special envelope or folder. Unacceptable certified photocopies A photocopied document that does not contain the standard statement attesting to the fact that the document is a true copy that has been compared to the original which was not amended or altered in any way, is not acceptable. A certified photocopy is not acceptable if the document's appearance gives rise to doubts about its authenticity. This includes such items as family bibles and privately held records, where the date when the record was made is not normally given. Regardless of the certification, a certified true copy is not acceptable if it appears that the original has been altered in any way. Sometimes a document or form is received as a stamped certified copy of a certified true copy. Copies of certified true copies are unacceptable as documentary evidence, when a certified or original copy is requested. An individual cannot certify an already certified copy of a document. It is impossible for the individual performing the certification to make a proper attestation when they do not have access to the original document.

OAS Time Bar Provision When an overpayment for an OAS pension, the Guaranteed Income Sup plement (GIS), the Allowance (ALW) or th e Allowance f or the Survivor (ALWS) ben efits covers a period before April 1, 1994, the full amount of the overpayment—including the time bar portion—must be set up as an overpayment. The time bar portion must be remitted before the debtor is advised of the outstanding debt due. For more information on actioning a remission, Remit an Overpayment If there is an outstanding OAS overpayment balance after the time bar portion has been remitted, follow standard recovery proced ures to collect the overpayment. Refer t o Departmental Receivable (Overpayments) The following are examples of common recovery situations involving the time bar provision: Common-law adjustments on income-tested benefits Updated Bill C-23 came into force in July 2000 and its purpose was to: recognize same-sex relationships; extend CPP and OAS benefits and obligations to all individuals in common-law relationships; and establish a common definition of spouse and common-law partner in the CPP and OAS programs. If you are informed or become aware of an existing common-law relationship that impacts entitlement to an income-tested benefit (e.g., GIS, ALW or ALWS), the affected accounts must be recalculated back to the effective date of the common-law relationship, but no earlier than July 2000. If the recalculation results in an overpayment, follow standard recovery procedures to collect the overpayment. Refe r to Departmental Receivable (Overpayments)

Before Bill C-54, overpayments for OAS benefits (OAS pension, GIS, Allowance (ALW), Allowance for the Survivor (ALWS) were recorded in their entirety, but recovery could only be enforced for amounts accrued in both the current year and the preceding fiscal year. The intent was that all overpayments over 2 years would be statute barred from recovery. This was based on the time bar provision of the OAS Act. After July 13, 1995, when Bill C-54 was given Royal Assent, the time bar provision was removed. At passage of the legislation, recovery of overpayments was limited to 2 years, but each passing year would increase the number of years that could be recovered. The Department will not recover any OAS pension, GIS, ALW or ALWS overpayment amount accrued before April 1, 1994 unless the overpayment was set-up before that date. Time bar provisions do not apply in cases where fraud or misrepresentation is proven. The full amount of the overpayment, including the time bar portion, must be set up as an overpayment. The time bar portion is remitted before the individual is advised of the outstanding overpayment. Overpayments due to recalculation of accounts with common-law adjustments are not recoverable earlier than July 2000 (the effective date of Bill C-23 where the definition of common-law was harmonized for CPP and OAS) unless they were established before that date. This means that adjustments to accounts can only be made back to July 2000. The individual is advised of the outstanding overpayment calculated on or after July 2000. T he Department will continue to collect overpayments on those accounts where overpayments were established before July 2000 and the individual has alrea dy been informed.

The debtor was overpaid from June 1990 to September 1995 for a total amount of $25,000. The overpayment was not discovered and set up until September 1995; The overpayment for the period from June 1990 to March 1994 of $15,000 is not recoverable, because it was not established and set up before the removal of the time bar provisions of April 1, 1994. The total overpayment amount that is owing is from April 1, 1994, to September 1995 and is $10,000. The full $25,000 amount must be set up in the system. The $15,000 for the period of June 1990 to March 1994 must be remitted. The $10,000 for the period of April 1994 to September 1995 must be recovered in full.

A debtor was overpaid from March 1985 to September 1993, for a total amount of $12,000. The overpayment was discovered and set up in December 1993. The overpayment for the period from March 1985 to September 1993 is $12,000. The full amount is recoverable, because it was established and set up before the removal of the time bar provisions of April 1, 1994.

Example A The client was overpaid from March 1985 to September 1993 in the amount of $12,000.00. The overpayment was discovered and set up in December 1993. This is a debt to the Crown and is recoverable because it was established and set up before the removal of the time bar provisions of April 1, 1994. Example B The client was overpaid from June 1990 to September 1995 in the amount of $25,000.00. The overpayment was not discovered and set up until September 1995. The overpayment for the period from June 1990 to March 1994 of $15,000.00 is not considered a debt due to the Crown. Neither is it recoverable because it was not established and set up before the removal of the time bar provisions of April 1, 1994. The total overpayment amount that is considered a debt due to the Crown is from April 1994 to September 1995 in the amount of $10,000.00. The entire amount of the overpayment ($25,000.00) must be set up in the system. The $15,000.00 for the period of June 1990 to March 1994 must be remitted, but the $10,000.00 for April 1994 to September 1995 must be recovered in full.

If a debtor is not satisfied with an OAS or CPP decision, they have the right to request a reconsideration or administrative review of the decision. The debtor can request a reconsideration or an appeal of the circumstances that caused the overpayment if the circumstances meet the criteria for an appeal or reconsideration. If the debtor has requested a reconsideration or an appeal, refer to Reconsideration or to Reconsideration Actioning Appeal If you receive a reconsideration or an appeal, you must stop recovery of the overpayment until you know the outcome of the reconsideration or appeal. If the recovery action has already been initiated, suspend the recovery action until you know the outcome of the reconsideration or appeal. Modify a Departmental Receivable Recovery Rate

An individual can request a reconsideration or an appeal on: the decision to impose a penalty; the penalty amount; or both. If you receive a request for reconsideration within 90 days of the OAS – CPP, Penalty, Overpayment, Interest (ISS-0867) letter, verify if the collection of the penalty and recovery of the debt has already started. If yes, you must suspend both the collection of the penalty amount and recovery of the overpayment pending the outcome of the reconsideration. For more information, Reconsideration (Scenario)

If a debtor requests a reconsideration or appeals the circumstances which caused the overpayment, you must defer or suspend all recovery actions until a decision is rendered. If an underpayment becomes available, do not hold it to wait for the outcome of the reconsideration or appeal. Release the underpayment to the client or their legal representative, as applicable. Reconsideration (Scenario)

Under the CPP and the OAS Act, all individuals who have had a penalty imposed have the right to ask for a reconsideration or an appeal on: the decision to impose a penalty; and the amount of the penalty. If the Minister receives a request for a reconsideration within 90 days of the date of the letter of imposition of a penalty, and collection of the penalty and recovery of the overpayment has already begun, both the collection of the penalty and the recovery of the overpayment are suspended until the outcome of the reconsideration or subsequent appeal has been communicated to the individual.

An individual (or any individual acting on their behalf) who was subject to an administrative monetary penalty and is dissatisfied with the decision or the penalty amount can request that the Minister reconsider that decision.

If an individual is not satisfied with the decision to impose an administrative penalty or the penalty amount, they have the right to request a reconsideration. These requests must be considered urgent . You can only action the reconsideration request if you did not make the initial decision. If you made the original decision, you must contact your designated Business Expertise Consultant to have the request reassigned to another designated SCBO determine who will action the reconsideration. Overpayments are normally recovered from monthly OAS or CPP payments, or from other eligible payments received from the same program from which the benefit was initially paid. However, if the overpayment cannot be recovered from the same program, it can be recovered from the other program. This process is known as the cross-program recovery . Cross Program Recovery (Scenario)

Before releasing any underpayment, you must verify if there is an overpayment under your own program and under the other program (e.g. CPP or OAS, including under an International Social Security Agreement). If the other program's overpayment can be recovered from the underpayment, contact the other program area to ask them to submit a cross program recovery request. For more information, Cross Program Recovery (Scenario)
An overpayment recovery is normally through a set-off of the same program’s benefits. If there is an OAS overpayment but no OAS benefit in pay, the overpayment can be recovered from the CPP benefits.

When an individual has an overpayment, it may be recovered from any pension or benefit payable under any act or program administered by the Minister. Recovery of an overpayment can be deducted and retained from the whole or a portion of a pension or benefit payment. This will ensure recovery of the overpayment (i.e. single payment or instalments) will not cause undue hardship in accordance with recovery rates of undue hardship and with the agreement of the paying program. Once a standard recovery rate is established based on the amount of all CPP and OAS pensions and benefits in pay, recovery of the overpayment is normally through a set-off or deduction from the same program's pension or benefit payments. If the Department is not able to recover the overpayment from the same program, a set-off from other programs within the Department (i.e. CPP and OAS) is considered.

When a program identifies available funds that can be used to recover an overpayment made by another program, they must notify the program with the potential debt. This enables the program with the potential debt to assess the situation and initiate a cross program recovery request, if appropriate. To support this process, the following workflow outlines the necessary communication steps for a cross program recovery request. When you establish an overpayment on a client's account, including cases of Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE), you must promptly send an initial overpayment letter to the debtor or their legal representative. This letter is to inform the debtor about the amount of the overpayment and any changes to their entitlement amount. You must also request full repayment of the overpayment, except in cases of EA/AE. However, if the overpayment is $100 or less on an active account, you must notify the debtor of the amount and advise them that it will be automatically recovered from their next monthly payment. When sending an overpayment letter for an EA/AE case that you are investigating, you must ensure you: inform the debtor or legal representative that their file is under review and that information regarding recovery will be provided later; and do not request repayment or inform them that the overpayment may be remitted. When the investigation of the EA/AE is complete and if it is determined that the overpayment was due to EA/AE, you must obtain necessary approval to remit the overpayment either fully or partially before requesting any repayment, if applicable. If the overpayment: is fully remitted, send another letter to the debtor or legal representative to inform them that the overpayment was remitted; is partially remitted, send another letter to the debtor or legal representative to inform them about the remitted amount and request repayment of the remaining balance; is determined not to be due to EA/AE, send another letter to the debtor or legal representative to inform them that the review of the file is complete and to request repayment. Refer to the applicable tab within this procedure for instructions on recovery. For more information, Overpayments—Remissions (Policy) In cases of a sensitive nature (e.g. a large overpayment, recovery may cause undue hardship), it is recommended that you call the debtor or their legal representative before initiating recovery to inform them that they will receive a letter about their overpayment. For information regarding calling the debtor or legal representative, Authenticate a Client or an Authorized Representative During a Phone Call (Action) You must give a debtor or legal representative a minimum of 30 days to reply to the letter, except when recovering from arrears or overpayments of $100 or less on active accounts. The deadline to reply varies based on each situation (e.g. the debtor lives outside Canada or is ill). If the debtor or legal representative does not respond within 30 days: for an active account with overpayments over $100, you can initiate recovery from the debtor's monthly benefit payments. for an inactive account: with a CPP or CPPD receivable in CPMS , the CRA Collections Unit will be responsible for collecting the overpayment. A monthly Statement of Account will be sent to the debtor until the overpayment is fully recovered. with an overpayment in Cúram, the CRA Collections Unit will be responsible for collecting the overpayment. A monthly Statement of Account will be sent to the debtor until the overpayment it is fully recovered. Reconsiderations and appeals The letter informing the client about the overpayment and the reason for the overpayment must include the debtor's reconsideration or appeal rights. If the debtor or their legal representative is not satisfied with the CPP or OAS decision: they have the right to request a reconsideration or appeal regarding the reason for the overpayment; and they cannot request a reconsideration or appeal regarding the amount of the overpayment or the recovery rate. Reconsideration or appeal rights are not provided for CPP or CPPD overpayments, for an account dependent on another beneficiary's eligibility and the beneficiary is no longer eligible. Reconsideration or appeal rights for OAS overpayments are provided for all benefits. This includes when an ALW beneficiary loses eligibility due to the OAS pensioner no longer being eligible for OAS and GIS. For more information, Reconsideration (Scenario)

When the overpayment is $100.00 or less and there is a monthly benefit in pay in ITRDS , CPMS recovers the full overpayment from the debtor's next monthly benefit payment. If the monthly entitlement amount is insufficient to recover the full amount of the overpayment, the outstanding balance will be recovered from the subsequent payments. When the overpayment is more than $100.00 and there is a monthly benefit in pay in ITRDS , CPMS automatically sets the recovery rate at 25% against the debtor's monthly CPP entitlement. You must adjust the recovery rate if the debtor is also in receipt of an OAS pension or benefit (i.e. GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit), including in the International Agreements system. If the CPP debtor is also in receipt of: an OAS pension only (i.e. no GIS), you must calculate the recovery rate at 25% of the total CPP and OAS monthly entitlement amounts; or an OAS pension and a GIS, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit, you must calculate the recovery rate at 10% of the total CPP and OAS monthly entitlement amounts. If the OAS program is currently recovering their own overpayment, you must: set the applicable recovery rate (e.g. 25% or 10%) in CPMS based only on the CPP monthly entitlement amount; and notify the OAS program to adjust their recovery rate based only on the OAS monthly entitlement amount if OAS is currently recovering based on the CPP and OAS monthly entitlement amounts. Based on the amount of the overpayment, you must ensure the recovery rate guarantees the overpayment is collected within specified timelines (i.e. 5 years or 10 years). Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) Your rationale and decision regarding the recovery rate must be documented on the Undue Hardship, Deferral, Recovery Rates and Set-Offs Decision Rationale Worksheet (ISP-0119) form and placed on the debtor's file.

You do not have to set a recovery rate on a debtor's account in OAS Online when you initially discover an overpayment. The process automation of the Monthly OAS/GIS Overpayment Report will perform this task in most cases. When you add the overpayment amount to the Deductions (DED) screen on a debtor's account in OAS Online, the debtor's account will appear on the Monthly OAS/GIS Overpayment Report at the end of the accounting month (i.e. after monthly cut-off). The automated process will take action on active accounts found on this report when the overpayment is less than $25,000 and when there is no recovery rate set on the account. The automated process will set the recovery rate against the account as long as it does not identify an exception. It will also send a notification letter to the debtor informing them of the amount of recovery and the date when the recovery will start. However, you will be required to send the applicable letter (e.g. Entitlement Change, Overpayment letter, etc.) to the debtor explaining the cause of the overpayment and the amount of the overpayment. The letter may need adjusting, as there are specific paragraphs that need to be included due to process automation. To view these paragraphs and the exceptions, Process Automation—OAS/GIS Monthly Overpayment Report (Knowledge) Process automation exceptions When the automated process identifies an exception, the reason for the exception is recorded in the PWS notes of the work item and the work item status is set to Unassigned . Processing staff will be responsible to review and manually set the recovery rate on process automation exceptions. If you establish an overpayment on a client's account that you know is a process automation exception (e.g. overpayment of $25,000 or more), you can choose to manually set the recovery rate, and this will stop the account from going through the process automation. Setting a recovery rate To set a recovery rate in OAS Online, you must manually add the percentage or dollar value on the Deductions (DED) screen of the debtor's account. When an overpayment is $100 or less on an active account, you can set the recovery rate to 100% so that the full amount of the overpayment will be recovered from the debtor's next monthly benefit payment. If the monthly entitlement is not sufficient, the balance will be recovered from subsequent payments. When an overpayment is more than $100 on an active account, you must: use the Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) to determine the applicable recovery rate to set on the debtor's account; and Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) record the dollar value or percentage on the Deductions (DED) screen of the debtor's account. When determining the recovery rate, you must verify if the debtor is also receiving a CPP program benefit and if a CPP overpayment is already being recovered, including in the International Agreements system. If a CPP overpayment is not being recovered, you must take the CPP program benefit amount into consideration when calculating the recovery rate. If the debtor receives: an OAS pension only (i.e. no GIS), you must calculate the rate at 25% of the total CPP and OAS entitlement amounts; or an OAS pension and a GIS or an ALW benefit or ALWS benefit, you must calculate the rate at 10% of the total CPP and OAS entitlement amounts. If the CPP program is currently recovering their own overpayment, you must: set the applicable rate (i.e. 25% or 10%) in OAS Online only against the debtor's OAS monthly entitlement amount; and notify the CPP program to adjust their recovery rate based only on the CPP monthly entitlement amount, if CPP is currently recovering based on the CPP and OAS monthly entitlement amounts. Based on the amount of the overpayment, you must also determine if the percentage allows the Department to recover the overpayment within a 5- or 10-year period, as applicable. For more information, refer to the Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) Your decision and rationale for setting the recovery rate must be documented on the Undue Hardship, Deferral, Recovery Rates and Set-Offs Decision Rationale Worksheet (ISP-0119) form and retained on the debtor's file for audit purposes. OAS Online will start recovery from the debtor's benefits in the accounting month when the recovery rate is set in the system. For example, if you set the recovery rate on September 26, 2023, which is during the October 2023 accounting month, the recovery will be deducted from the debtor's October 2023 payment. When you set a recovery rate on the debtor's account, you must ensure that the debtor receives 30 days notice before the recovery starts. Do not set a recovery rate on a debtor's account during the last week of an accounting month, as this does not provide the debtor with the required 30 days notice. Wait for the new accounting month to start in the following week (i.e. after cut-off).

When determining the recovery rate and start date for the departmental receivable, refer to Recovery Guidelines (Work Tool) . Recovery will start with the next monthly payment following the creation of the receivable. CPMS will automatically set a recovery rate of 25% in cases where the receivable is over $100.00. The recovery starts the second month following creation of the receivable. When the client is in receiving of an OAS income-tested benefit (i.e. GIS, ALW and ALWS ), the rate of recovery should be reduced to 10%. If there are two or more receivables on an active account, CPMS will automatically set up the recovery rate of 25% on each receivable. This would result in a 50% or more recovery from the client's payment. To ensure that only 25% is recovered, you must: modify the recovery rate of the receivable(s) to ensure no more than 25% is recovered; or select a future start date for the second receivable that is after the projected end date of the first one, if the first receivable will be fully recovered in the near future. When the client is entitled to an arrears or retroactive payment from CPP or OAS, apply the full amount of the arrears or retroactive payment to the debt, if applicable. A minimum period of 30 days, from the time a client is notified of an overpayment, must pass before starting recovery from their monthly benefit. However, you are not required to give 30 days notice to the client when you are applying an arrears or retroactive payment against the debt. In cases where the debtor has claimed undue hardship and a reduced rate is supported, the new rate should be set for recovery within 5 or 10 years; Bring Forward (BF) and review after 12 months. An active account means there is a pension or benefit in pay under any of the programs (i.e. OAS, CPP or CPPD). Effective February 8, 2016, the recovery rates withheld from a monthly pension or benefit payment are as follows: For an overpayment amount of $100 and under : the full amount is deducted from the next or subsequent pension or benefit payments until the overpayment amount is recovered. For an overpayment amount over $100 : The standard recovery rate is equal to a monthly withhold of 25% of all CPP and OAS pensions or benefits until the overpayment amount is recovered (excluding children's benefits unless the overpayment consists of children's benefits). For individuals who are receiving income-tested benefits, the recovery rate will be equal to a monthly withhold of 10% of all CPP and OAS pensions or benefits until the overpayment is recovered. For individuals who are not receiving income-tested benefits and depending on an individual's situation, an initial recovery rate of a monthly withhold of 10% of all CPP and OAS pensions or benefits can be used. The recovery rate must not be less than $10 per month, unless their monthly entitlement is less than $10. When possible, the full overpayment should be recovered within 5 years. However, when there are large overpayments (i.e. $10,000 and over), the full overpayment should be recovered within 10 years. These guidelines are designed to help the Department establish consistent national recovery rates using discretion and good judgment. However, there will be cases where the overpayment cannot be recovered within the stated guidelines. Furthermore, depending on the circumstances, the established recovery rate does not prevent the Department from: determining a lower recovery rate; determining a higher recovery rate; or accepting repayment in full for individuals who request it.

When there is a departmental receivable established on an account and there are no CPP benefits in pay in ITRDS , you must notify the debtor and attempt to recover the overpayment. After 90 days, the CRA will take over the collection of overpayments on all CPP accounts in CPMS where there are no benefits in pay in ITRDS . However, if the debtor is in pay for an OAS pension or benefit, this would not be considered an inactive account. You must request a cross program recovery and for a lock on the overpayment in the Public Sector Collections and Disbursements system. This will prevent the CRA from starting their collection.

For inactive accounts, the CRA is responsible for the collection of all CPP and CPPD overpayments. The CRA will start their collection activities 90 days after a departmental receivable is created in CPMS . When a departmental receivable is established on an account and there are no CPP or CPPD benefits in pay in ITRDS ,the processing staff must notify the debtor and initiate recovery of the overpayment. If the overpayment is not recovered within 90 days, the CRA will take over recovery on all CPP and CPPD accounts in CPMS where there are no benefits in pay in ITRDS . Debts under $5,000 will be automatically sent to the CRA without additional review. As such, it is essential that all receivables in CPMS are reviewed and validated when any work item is assigned to an account in PWS . CRA will use the Public Sector Collections and Disbursements system (PSCD) to view the departmental receivable information. The data in PSCD comes from CPMS .

An informant lead (also known as a third-party complaint) is a notification from an individual that, in their opinion, an investigation should be made into a client's eligibility or entitlement to a CPP pension or benefit. An informant lead can be received by letter, telephone or any other means to CPP. All informant leads must be sent to Integrity Services Branch (ISB) for a potential administrative investigation. It is the Department's obligation to review each lead received to determine if it is valid or has an impact on an applicant or a beneficiary's eligibility or entitlement. You must never indicate receipt of an informant lead on an individual's file or in ITRDS notes, as this could reveal an informant's identity. You must protect the informant, even if they do not indicate they want to remain anonymous. Information that might reveal the identity of an informant must not be divulged or disclosed. For more information, Informant Leads (Policy)

An informant lead (previously known as a third party complaint) is a notification to the Department—communicated by letter or telephone, electronically, in person or by any other means—by an individual (who may remain anonymous) that, in that individual's opinion, an investigation must be made into: CPP contributions made or pensions or benefits applied for or paid to a particular applicant, beneficiary or to a particular group of individuals; or OAS pensions or benefits applied fo r or paid to a particular applicant, beneficiary or to a particular group of individuals. It is essential that all informant leads received from all sources are documented to: investigate instances of alleged abuse; identify overpayments, suspected fraud or misrepresentation; and maintain the integrity of the programs.

You should thoroughly review the client's OAS and CPP files, ITRDS and notes, Cúram and PWS for historical data. To ensure the integrity of the department and our clients and ensure appropriate payments are made, the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) conducts a number of administrative investigations annually. An administrative investigation is an impartial investigative process conducted by ISB on files referred from the Department's employees due to: anomalies and discrepancies identified in the files; or third party complaints and disclosures received by the department. There are a number of triggers that may elicit a case specific review that may lead to an administrative investigation on a client's file. Additionally, ISB initiates annual projects to review client files that ensure: client files are up to date, accurate and complete; appropriate payments are received; and national processes are followed.

An administrative investigation is an impartial investigative process conducted by Integrity Services Branch (ISB) on files Service Canada Benefit Officers (SCBOs) or other departmental representatives referred to them due to anomalies and discrepancies identified in applications, other documentation or files. ISB staff will determine whether an administrative investigation is warranted. There are a number of triggers that, when discovered by departmental officials, may elicit an administrative investigation on the file of an applicant or beneficiary concerning eligibility or entitlement to the CPP or OAS pensions and benefits. Such triggers include: misrepresentation; informant leads; suspected fraud and disclosures. As there is no legislative authority under the Canada Pension Plan or the Old Age Security Act for any surveillance activities, surveillance materials to determine eligibility or continuing eligibility for CPP and OAS pensions are not to be solicited. In this context, "surveillance" is considered any technique consisting of concealed observation of activities to obtain information or to support facts. It includes, but is not limited to: written reports; videotapes; audiotapes or any other recordings (electronic or otherwise).

The security check is completed in 2 parts. Failure to complete these 2 parts constitutes a breach of security. Security Check—Part I Updated If a call centre staff member transfers a caller to you, ask them to provide the caller's name and to confirm if they have authenticated the caller's identity. If yes, you do not need to authenticate the caller again. If the caller has not been authenticated or if you made the call, the client or their authorized representative must correctly answer all questions in Part I of the security check, which includes providing their full name and details about their account number (i.e. their SIN or Client Identifier number). As an added security measure, a client or their authorized representative may request that a password be added to their account. A password can be added on the account only after the client or the authorized representative has been authenticated and is added as an important note in ITRDS . If a password has been added to the ITRDS notes, it must be provided by the client or their authorized representative during Part I of the security check. If you call the client or their authorized representative, you must obtain the last 3 digits of the client's account number. However, you must obtain the full account number when: you receive an Enquiry work item in PWS or a task in Cúram and call the client or their authorized representative back at a phone number that is not on the account; someone calls you directly; or a caller is transferred directly to you without prior interaction with call centre staff. Do not read aloud the information appearing in the systems (e.g. ITRDS , Cúram, PWS ) or on a client's file that you are using for authentication. You must ask the individual on the phone to provide the information or they must volunteer it. Do not acknowledge the existence of a client's CPP or OAS account before the completion of a successful security check. Only provide general information. Security check—Part II Updated If the client or their authorized representative successfully answers the questions in Security Check—Part I , you must obtain additional details about their CPP or OAS account. The client or their authorized representative must successfully answer at least 2 of the questions in Security Check—Part ll . Information from any available system (e.g. ITRDS , Cúram, PWS , Client Correspondence Tool (CCT), Government On Line (GOL)) can be used to authenticate the caller; however, the following restrictions on the release of information apply: For CPP, a PWS barcode or work item ID (prefaced by the letter "W") must not be used to authenticate the caller. For OAS, a task must not be used to authenticate the caller. Medical information cannot be disclosed by telephone. Do not call the client or their authorized representative if the systems are unavailable. If the client or their authorized representative calls you during a time when the systems are unavailable, advise them to call back later, when their identity can be authenticated. To review the list of possible questions, go to the Authenticating a client or their authorized representative section in the What you need to do of the Step by Step tab. Failed security check If an individual fails any part of the security check or confirms that they are an unauthorized third party, you must inform them that client information can only be given to the client or an authorized representative. If the individual requires further assistance, direct them as follows: If the individual called you directly, advise them to go to a Service Canada Centre to authenticate their identity. If you called the individual, advise them that you will contact the client or authorized representative that is on file by mail to obtain or provide the required information. For specific direction, go to the Failed security check section in the What you need to do of the Step by Step tab.

If, for any reason (such as a language or medical barrier), a client asks that you speak with an unauthorized third party (e.g. a friend, relative or translator) who is with them at the time of the call, you can conduct the security check with the assistance of this unauthorized third party. However, the client must be partially authenticated and must consent to the disclosure of their personal information to the other party on the call before any client-specific details are discussed. When the client gives verbal consent to disclose personal information to an unauthorized third party, indicate this consent in the Telephone Call (ISP0112) form and in the ITRDS notes. CPPD staff can record the information on the appropriate template. CPPD Templates and Updated Naming and Saving Conventions This verbal consent is only valid for the duration of the phone call. If the client would like to give consent to communicate with this third party on an ongoing basis, refer them to their My Service Canada Account to provide this consent or send a Consent to Communicate Information to an Authorized Person (ISP1603) form to the client to complete and return. For specific direction, go to the Client asks that you speak with an unauthorized third party section in the What you need to do of the Step by Step tab.

If you are unable to complete the security check with a client and they ask you to speak with an unauthorized third party who is with them at the time of the call, you can complete the security check with the assistance of the unauthorized third party after a partial security check is successfully completed with the client. Proceed as follows: Ask the client for: their full name; their SIN or Client Identifier number; their date of birth (day, month and year); the name of the unauthorized third party. Obtain the client's verbal consent to continue the conversation with the unauthorized third party. Ask the third party to confirm their relationship with the client (e.g. friend, relative or translator). Complete the rest of the security check process with the assistance of the third party. Go to the Authenticating a client or authorized representative section above. Update the client's notes in ITRDS to record details of your actions or decisions made on the account. Include the following details: that the client provided verbal consent to continue the conversation with the third party; the name of the third party; and the third party's relationship to the client. An application can be deemed to have been received on an earlier date when the incapacity provision is applied. The incapacity provision is extended to a child under the age of 18 (-18 child) or a child over the age of 18 (+18 child) who is listed on a CPPD benefits application when the disabled contributor is granted an earlier date of application due to incapacity. For a child aged between 18 and 25, the incapacity provision under the disabled contributor can only be applied if the child submits their own application within the prescribed timeframe. The incapacity provision can also be applied to the +18 child based on their own Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit application and claim of incapacity. For more information, refer to Incapacity Provision (Scenario) and Incapacity Provision (Scenario) Incapacity (Policy)

The incapacity provision can also be applied to a +18 child if they are determined to have been medically incapacitated and unable to apply for the benefit at an earlier time. The +18 child is the applicant in this case. For more information, refer to Incapacity Provision (Scenario) and to Incapacity Provision (Scenario) Incapacity (Policy)

The incapacity provision applies to a child under the age of 18 (-18 child) or over the age of 18 (+18 child) listed on a CPPD benefits application when the disabled contributor is determined incapacitated and granted an earlier application date. The protective date provision applies to most of Canada's International Social Security Agreements (ISSA). The provision stipulates that the date that a benefit application is received in one country is considered the date of application for the corresponding benefit in the other country, provided certain conditions are met. International Operations (IO) processing staff validate protective dates received under the ISSAs by ensuring the various conditions are met. Therefore, a protective date may only be considered as the receipt date of the application if it has been validated and provided by IO.

To apply the protective date provision, the client must have applied for a Canadian benefit that corresponds to the benefit in the other country. When the foreign institution requests the date of receipt or date of claim of an application for Canadian benefits, they will identify the type of foreign benefit on the liaison form. When providing a foreign institution with the date of receipt of an application for Canadian benefits, you must first identify the type of benefit(s) for which the client has applied for in the agreement country. If the liaison form does not include a specific field to provide the date, advise the foreign institution the following in the Other or Other remarks field of the liaison form: "The date of receipt of the corresponding benefit according to Article <Article reference information (i.e.number of article and/or paragraph number> of the <Agreement and/or Administrative Arrangement> is <the protective date>". The protective date provision stipulates that the date on which an application for a benefit is received in one country is considered the date of application for the corresponding benefit in the other country, if certain conditions are met. For more information, Protective Date Provision Under an International Social Security Agreement (Knowledge) Protective date information can be provided to foreign institutions to accompany foreign benefit applications or in response to a liaison request. Foreign institutions will use this information to establish the effective date for a benefit in that country. When a client is in pay for a corresponding pension or benefit under the jurisdiction of QPP and an Understanding is in force, the Bureau des ententes de sécurité sociale is responsible for reporting the protective date for that pension or benefit to the foreign institution. Denial or approval of a Canadian pension or benefit application has no bearing when providing a protective date to a foreign institution. If the conditions of the protective date provision have been met, a protective date can be provided to the foreign institution regardless if the application has been approved, denied or is under review. To report a valid protective date to a foreign institution, you must ensure that the date meets all of the conditions as outlined by that country's International Social Security Agreement (ISSA).

The date on which an application is received can impact the applicant's effective date. This protective date provision is only beneficial to applicants who do not apply within 11 months of their first possible effective date and will therefore not receive the maximum retroactive payments to which they could have received if they had applied on time. Example A client would have been eligible for an OAS pension in M ay 2021 based on their Canadian residence, legal status and age. However, they did not submit an application until April 15, 2023. If a protective date is not applied, the earliest effective date for the pension is May 2022 (i.e. 11 months prior to the date of application). The ISSA country confirms a protective date of August 9, 2021. Using this date as the date of application for the OAS pension, the applicant's pension can be approved effective May 2021. There are no limitations associated with how long the protective date predates the first possible effective date. As long as the protective date is after the date of entry into force of the agreement, it can be applied to the corresponding Canadian benefit application. Example The applicant applied for an OAS pension in May 2023 at age 68, but would have met the eligibility requireme nts (i.e. age, residence and legal status) had they applied in March 2020, the month in which they turned 65. The other country provides a protective date of January 11, 2016. Despite the applicant having applied for the corresponding foreign benefit at age 60, the protective date can still be applied to the OAS pension application. Since a protective date is deemed to be the date of receipt of a Canadian pension or benefit application for administration purposes, the same rules surrounding retroactivity will apply using that date.

A protective date provided by a foreign social security institution under an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) with Canada can assist clients in qualifying for a benefit earlier than the effective date based on the date stamp of their application.

A protective date provision is included in many of Canada’s ISSAs. In general, this provision stipulates that the date on which an application for a pension or benefit is received in one country is deemed to be the date of application for the corresponding benefit in the other country, if certain conditions are met. The protective date provision varies by agreem ent, and each agreement will outline the conditions that must be met for the protective date provision to apply. If an ISSA does not contain a protective date provision, the date of receipt is established with OAS a nd CPP rules only. Under the CPP, the term "dependent child" of a contributor means and includes a child of the contributor who: is younger than 18 years of age; or is 18 to 25 years of age and in full-time or part-time attendance at a school or university. Decision-making responsibility is defined as the responsibility for making significant decisions about a child's well-being, including: Health; Education; Culture, language, religion and spirituality; and Significant extra-curricular activities. Parenting time means the time that a child spends in the care of a person who is a parent of the child, who stands in the place of a parent or who intends to stand in the place of a parent, whether or not the child is physically with that person during that entire time (i.e. times when the child is at school) Maintaining a dependent child of the disabled or deceased contributor (adoption or “in fact” by someone other than the contributor) Updated CPP Regulation 65.1 states that maintaining the child with reference to the child of a disabled contributor means making financial provisions for the child amounting to not less than the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit payable under the CPP. CPP Regulation 65.1 further states that maintaining the child with reference to the child of a deceased contributor means making financial provisions for the child, until the contributor's death, amounting to not less than the Surviving Child's benefit payable under the CPP.

To protect the privacy and personal information of a disabled contributor, the Department will not initiate contact with, or solicit a DCCB application or information from the child or the individual or agency having decision-making responsibility of the child (i.e. an individual other than the disabled contributor) unless the Department receives the disabled contributor's written consent to do so. To ensure that their privacy and personal information is protected, disabled contributors may decide to: inform the child, individual or agency having decision-making responsibility of the child of possible entitlement to the DCCB ; provide their written consent for the Department to contact the child, the individual or agency having decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the child regarding possible entitlement to the DCCB ; or make no contact with the child, the individual or agency having custody and control of the child, and not provide their written consent for the Department to initiate contact with these individuals. If the disabled contributor decides not to make contact and not to provide their written consent for the Department to contact the child and, as a result, no one submits an application for the DCCB , the DCCB cannot be paid. Under the CPP, the Department is obligated to make decisions on all applications received. This includes all DCCB applications, even if the disabled contributor: has not provided written consent to initiate contact with the custodial parent; or instructs the Department not to initiate contact with the child or individual or agency having decision-making responsibility of the child. The disabled contributor may revoke their consent to contact the individual or agency having decision-making responsibility of the child or the child directly, in writing, if contact has not been initiated.

Children's benefits are paid on behalf of the child to the individual or agency for periods during which the individual or agency had decision-making responsibility for the -18 child. If an individual or agency receives Children's benefit payments for periods during which they had no decision-making responsibility for the child or orphan, an overpayment is established and is subject to recovery in accordance with policy. Overpayments—Recovery and Collection (Policy) The recipient or payee of a -18 Child's benefit can be: a disabled contributor or survivor who has decision-making responsibility (at least 20% of the parenting time) for the child; a person or agency who has decision-making responsibility for a deceased or disabled contributor's child; or under exceptional circumstances, a -18 child who is not living with a parent, individual or agency that exercises decision-making responsibility (i.e. a child living alone). Payees must notify the Department when a change of parenting time occurs that rebuts the presumption of decision-making responsibility (the disabled contributor or the survivor are presumed to have decision-making responsibility if they have at least 20% of the parenting time). When these periods are confirmed, payments are made to each payee for the months that they had decision-making responsibility for the child or orphan. When the child reaches 18 years of age and is in full-time or part-time (effective January 1, 2025) attendance at school or university, any retroactive amount for the periods when the child was under age 18 years of age is paid to the individual or agency that had decision-making responsibility for that child. The portion of the Children's benefit owed for any months after the child's 18th birthday is payable directly to the child if the child is in full-time or part-time attendance at school or university.

This policy provides guidelines to identify who the payee should be for CPP Children's benefits for a dependant child under the age of 18 (-18 child) when there is a change in decision-making responsibility. Custody and control has been replaced with decision-making responsibility. When the child is under the age of 18, the payment of Children's benefits is made to the person or agency who has decision-making responsibility for the child or orphan. Decision-making responsibility is defined as the responsibility for making significant decisions about a child's well-being, including: health; education; culture, language, religion and spirituality; and significant extra-curricular activities. Parenting time is a new term introduced in the legislation. Its purpose is to help determine if the disabled contributor or survivor can be presumed, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, to have decision-making responsibility for a child or orphan and receive the benefit on their behalf. Under the new legislation, a disabled contributor or a survivor is presumed to have decision-making responsibility for a child or surviving child, unless they have less than 20% of the parenting time. Parenting time means the time that a child spends in the care of a person who is a parent of the child, who stands in the place of a parent or who intends to stand in the place of a parent, whether or not the child is physically with that person during that entire time (i.e. times when the child is at school).

Disabled contributors are under no obligation to disclose that they have children on their application for CPPD benefits. To protect the disabled contributor's privacy, the Department must not initiate contact with the child, the other parent or guardian or the agency that has custody and control of the child to solicit a Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit application or information unless the Department receives the disabled contributor's written consent to do so. Disclosing a CPP contributor's eligibility for CPPD benefits may put the contributor in a vulnerable position given their medical condition. Some contributors prefer to keep their sensitive information private. This choice is their fundamental right and the Department must respect their decision. Failure of the Department to respect the privacy of a disabled contributor could result in tangible and negative consequences for them. For example, disclosing the disability status of the contributor could provide their former spouse with evidence when seeking to end or limit the contributor's custody of their child(ren). Authorization to communicate with a third party ends when the applicant who has given authorization dies. However, the applicant's consent to contact the guardian or the adult child for the purpose of applying for a child benefit is still valid after the CPPD benefit applicant's death. The reason why the consent is still valid is because it simply provides authorization to mail out an application to the child's guardian or the adult child. It does not provide authorization to communicate personal information from the contributor's file. This was the wish of the CPPD benefit applicant before they died.

Determining the payee for a child under the age of 18 Updated The CPP provides payment of a Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) for a child under the age of 18 to the person or agency that has decision-making responsibility on behalf of that child. Custody and control has been replaced with decision-making responsibility. Decision-making responsibility is defined as the responsibility for making significant decisions about a child's well-being, including: health; education; culture, language, religion and spirituality; and significant extra-curricular activities. Parenting time is defined as the time that a child spends in the care of a person who is a parent of the child, who stands in the place of a parent or who intends to stand in the place of a parent, whether or not the child is physically with that person during that entire time (i.e. times when the child is in school). Unless there is evidence of the contrary, the disabled contributor is presumed to have decision-making responsibility for the child unless they have less than 20% of the parenting time. The DCCB is payable to the disabled contributor when the above is satisfied and they: apply for the DCCB ; and inform the Department that they have decision-making responsibility for the child. Refer to the Disputed dates of custody section of Children's Benefits—Change in Custody and Control (Policy) . Children's Benefits—Change in Custody and Control (Policy) Decision-making responsibility or parenting time includes, but is not limited to: formal and informal parenting arrangements; or sole, shared, joint and similar parenting arrangements. All DCCB eligibility requirements must be met. Child-Contributor Relationship—Children’s Benefit (Policy) By applying for the DCCB and indicating they have a minimum of 20% parenting time for the child, the disabled contributor is making an attestation that they have decision-making responsibility, which is sufficient to determine that they are the payee on the initial application only. The change in payee is effective the month following the change in decision-making responsibility or the current accounting month when the request is actioned (this is for change the payee based on policy updates only). Refer to Children's Benefits—Change in Custody and Control (Policy) for more information. Children's Benefits—Change in Custody and Control (Policy) When the disabled contributor shares decision-making responsibility, the Department will pay the full amount of the DCCB to the disabled contributor as there is no legislative authority to allow the DCCB payment to be split. When the disabled contributor does not live with the child at least 20% of the parenting time, you must determine if the other parent, guardian or child can be contacted (i.e. when they are available to be contacted and how they want to be contacted). Refer to the Protection and disclosure of the disabled contributor's information section of Eligibility Requirements—CPP Disabled Contributor’s Child’s Benefit (Policy)

The date of the CPPD benefits application protects the effective date for all children listed (both a child over the age of 18 (+18 child) and a child under the age of 18), regardless of who is listed as having decision-making responsibility and parenting time on that application. For more information on date protection, Receipt Date and Date Protection (Action) When the CPPD benefit application lists a +18 child and the child does not submit the Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 Years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form within 2 bring forward periods, the date protection afforded by the CPPD application ends. You must record a note in ITRDS to indicate the child's date protection period is closed. If the child submits their ISP-1402 form at a later date, it is subject to a maximum retroactive period of 11 months.

The date on a survivor's application protects the effective date of the children listed (both -18 and +18, no matter who has decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the child) in this application. Refer to Receipt Date and Date Protection (Action) . However, denied applications do not date-protect future applications for children's benefits. Receipt Date and Date Protection (Action) Applications Date of Receipt (Policy) An application is not required to apply for a CPP benefit; an applicant can submit a written request containing all the required information. You must, however, send an official application to the applicant if any information is missing from the written request. The date on an application is protected if the applicant identified children when they submitted their written request or application. When the survivor's pension application lists a +18 child and the child does not submit their Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 Years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form within 2 bring forward periods, the date protection afforded by the survivor's pension application ends. You must record a note in ITRDS to indicate the child's date protection period is closed. If the child submits their ISP-1402 form at a later date, it is subject to a maximum retroactive period of 11 months.

The receipt date of an SVR pension application protects the effective date of a Surviving Child's benefit for all children listed on the application. However, there is a time limit to the date protection afforded to a child over the age of 18 (+18 child). When the SVR pension is approved, you must request a Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 Years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form from the child. If the +18 child does not submit their ISP-1402 form within 2 bring forward periods, the date protection afforded by the SVR pension application ends. You must add a note in ITRDS to indicate the child's date protection period is closed. If the child submits their ISP-1402 form later, their benefit is subject to 11 months retroactivity. For more information on date protection, Receipt Date and Date Protection (Action)

The receipt date of a CPPD benefits application protects the effective date for all children listed under the age of 18 and over the age of 18 (+18 child), regardless of who is listed as having decision-making responsibility and parenting time on that application. For more information on date protection, Receipt Date and Date Protection (Action) However, when the CPPD benefits application identifies a +18 child and the child does not submit their Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 Years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form within 2 bring forward periods, the date protection provided by the CPPD benefits application ends. For children who are between 18 and 25 years of age and attending school or university on a full-time or part-time basis (effective January 1, 2025), the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) can begin the later of: the month the contributor's DSB or PRDB begins; the eleventh month before the month in which the application for a DCCB is made; or the month in which classes begin (a school vacation may be considered part of a full-time or part-time attendance period). A written request to apply for a DCCB which contains all of the required information is acceptable. The 11-month maximum retroactivity period applies to all applications for children's benefits. There is no exception to this rule. If no information about the children is provided on the CPPD benefits application and the Department later learns that the disabled contributor had children, the effective date of payment of a DCCB for any of the children would be subject to the 11 months of retroactivity from the date of receipt of the DCCB application.

For Children under age 18 , the surviving child’s benefit begins the later of : the month after the contributor’s death; the month after the child is born; the 11th month before the month the application is received; or For Children who are 18 to 25 years of age and attending school on a full-time or part-time basis, the surviving child’s benefit begins the later of : the month after the contributor’s death; the 11th month before the month the children’s benefit application is received; or the month in which classes begin (a school vacation may be considered part of the full-time or part-time attendance class period). The date of application is protected for all children who are identified on a CPP Survivor’s pension application, in addition children over the age of 18 must submit their own application within the prescribed timeframes. A written request applying for a children’s benefit which contains all the required information is also acceptable. If no information is provided about the children on the CPP Survivor’s pension application, and the department later learns that there were children of the deceased contributor, the effective date of payment of the surviving child’s benefit would be subject to the 11 months retroactivity from the date of receipt of the surviving child’s application.

CPP Child’s benefit provides monthly payments to the dependent children of disabled or deceased CPP contributors. To qualify, the child must be 18 to 25 years old and in full-time attendance at a recognized school or university. Service Canada currently receives CPP Child’s benefit applications only on paper via the Application for a Canada Pension Plan Child’s Benefit (ISP1400) form or by written communication. Effective October 22, 2021, individuals can choose to apply for the CPP child's benefit online using their My Service Canada Account (MSCA). The online CPP Child’s benefit application does not replace the ISP1400 form. It is another channel eligible applicants can use to apply for the benefit. The online CPP Child’s Benefit application has a dynamic component that displays appropriate application questions based on the information input by the applicant.
