The online Declaration of Attendance at School or University (ISP1401) form is available for students within My Service Canada Account (MSCA). Registered students or students with an existing account are able to access the online ISP1401 form under CPP applications . Students without an MSCA are required to register for one in order to renew their existing children’s benefit, i.e. Disabled Contributor’s Child’s Benefit and/or Surviving Child’s benefit. The eligibility criteria to renew benefits online are as follows: The student must be between the ages of 18 and 25 + 11 months; The student’s account must not be under the c ontrol of a trustee or Power of Attorney; The student must have a Canadian address; The student must be the dependent child of a disabled and/or deceased contributor; The interrelationship must already exist between the contributor and the applicant (interrelated by Social Insurance Number (SIN)); The student must currently be in pay for one of the children’s benefit s and the children’s benefit status must not be: Suspended; Denied; On hold; or Terminated for more than 12 months. The student must currently be enrolled full time at a recognized educational institution; The student must not be an International Agreement account client; The student must have started their first day of class; and The student must be able to upload a signed ISP1401 or a proof of enrolment. Students eligible for 2 children’s benefits can renew their benefits online when their account in ITRDS is linked to both parents through their SIN and not a client identifier. By completing one online declaration in MSCA, students continue to receive the benefits they are entitled to with no requirement for a second declaration. Example of online ISP1401 form Mandatory questions when submitting the online ISP1401 form Mandatory questions when submitting the online ISP1401 form. Leveraging existing MSCA functionalities, students have the opportunity to update their address, direct deposit information and telephone number with the View and Update Personal Information functionality and have this information updated automatically in ITRDS. The online ISP1401 form cannot be saved and retrieved at a later time.

Introduction Effective October 24, 2020, Service Canada introduced 2 CPP service delivery changes: An online Declaration of Attendance at School or University (ISP1401) form that offers an alternate channel for students with a Canadian address to renew their existing +18 ch ildren’s benefit, i.e. Disabled Contributor’s Child’s Benefit and/or Surviving Child’s benefit through their My Service Canada Account (MSCA); and A business process improvement that gives students the option to provide a proof of enrolment from their student portal, a signed Section C on the ISP1401 paper form when renewing online or via traditional paper forms. The online ISP1401 form differs from the paper form in that it will determine the students’ eligibility to use the online service from the onset. First, students using the online option to renew their existing benefits will be prompted to answer mandatory questions to confirm their full-time attendance at a recognized educational institution following their first day of class, as the legislation refers to attendance and not registration in a course. These responses will serve to populate the data fields in ITRDS. In addition, these students are required to upload a proof of enrolment obtained from their online school or university portal containing information about their enrolment (e.g. program of study, enrolment start date, educational institution’s information) or an ISP1401 form signed by their school or university. Students who meet the eligibility criteria to use the online ISP1401 form will have their benefit automatically renewed without agent intervention once they have submitted their declaration . A contributory period is the period of time when an individual is eligible to contribute to the CPP and/or the QPP. For more information, CPP Earnings and Contributions (Policy) For more information, Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge)

The contributory period is the period of time in which the individual makes contributions based on their earnings to the CPP or the QPP. A dual contributor is one who has contributed to both the CPP and the QPP. Under the CPP, individuals pay contributions during their contributory period on annual earnings between a set minimum and a set maximum level: The minimum level, known as the Year’s Basic Exemption, is set at $3,500. The maximum level is set every year by the CPP and known as the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings.

For recipients of the CPP Retirement (RTR) pension who apply for CPP Disability (DSB) benefits and are deemed to have become disabled before the month the RTR pension became payable, the application for DSB benefits is deemed to be a request for the cancellation of the RTR pension. This is referred to as an in-favour cancellation. Effective January 1, 2019, CPP RTR pensioners no longer have to submit a written request to cancel their RTR pension in favour of receiving the CPP DSB benefit. Instead, their application for DSB benefits is deemed to be the request for the cancellation of their RTR pension. Once cancelled, the RTR pension is considered never to have been paid. A Post-Retirement Disability Benefit (PRDB) recipient can cancel their RTR pension in-favour of a CPP DSB benefit if specific conditions are met. When their RTR pension is cancelled, the amounts of RTR pension, Post-Retirement Benefit (PRB), if applicable, and PRDB they received must be repaid. The amount of all RTR pension entitlements paid is recovered from the DSB benefit arrears payment. The balance, if any, is recovered from subsequent monthly DSB benefit payments. An applicant cannot receive both an RTR pension and a DSB for the same period. PRDB is available to a retired pensioner who meets the eligibility requirements and whose: disability Date of Onset (DOO) is determined to be on or after the effective date of their RTR pension; or disability DOO is determined to be before the effective date of their RTR pension and applied 15 months or more after the effective date of their RTR pension. As of January 1, 2019, the Department began phasing in the CPP enhancement, a new component of the CPP. The enhancement is not a separate benefit, but rather a top-up to the original, now referred to as the base component of the CPP. This means working Canadians will receive higher benefits in exchange for making higher contributions. Before January 2019, the RTR pension replaced one quarter (25%) of the average monthly pensionable earnings. This average is based on an individual's work earnings up to the year's maximum pensionable earnings set by CPP. The CPP enhancement increases this to one third (33.33%) of the average pensionable earnings. Individuals will not see the full impact of enhancement before 2065, but their pension will increase based on how much and for how long they contribute to the enhanced CPP. Individuals will get the full increase if they make the maximum contributions to the enhanced CPP for 40 years. The enhanced and base components of the CPP are intended to work seamlessly together. That means there is no separate application process to receive the enhanced component of CPP benefits. The eligibility criteria for CPP benefits are not affected by the enhancement as only the base component is used to determine eligibility and the minimum qualifying period for CPP benefits. The current formula used to calculate the combined benefits under the base CPP continues to apply. However, there is no maximum placed on the enhanced component of a combined SVR and RTR pension or of a combined SVR pension and DSB . For more information, CPP Enhancement (Knowledge)

As of January 1, 2019, the Department phased in enhanced components of the CPP. The first additional and second additional components are not separate benefits, but top-ups to the original, now referred to as the base component of the CPP. This means working Canadians receive higher benefits in exchange for making higher contributions. If the RTR pension amount is calculated using the base, first additional and second additional earnings, then the amount redistributed through PNSH will also include the base, first additional and second additional components. CPP enhancement will not affect the eligibility criteria and calculation of the cohabitation period for the base component of the PNSH amount. As the cohabitation and joint contributory period for the first additional component began on January 1, 2019, and the second additional component began on January 1, 2024, the pension share factor may be different between the base, the first additional and the second additional components. Each component of the pension share will be calculated separately; a couple may have a double base pension share and a single first additional pension share, and a single second additional pension share if only one spouse or common-law partner made enhanced contributions. Similarly, a base pension share may include both CPP and QPP portions, while the first additional and second components may be 100% CPP or 100% QPP, depending on the individual's contributions. For more information, CPP Enhancement (Knowledge)

As of January 1, 2019, the Department began phasing in the CPP enhancement. The increase that individuals receive on their SVR pension will depend on how much and for how long their deceased spouse or common-law partner made enhanced contributions. The current formula used to calculate CPP combined benefits continues to apply, and the maximum payable for a combined benefit cannot exceed the maximum RTR pension or DSB rate. If there is a first additional or second additional SVR pension, RTR pension or DSB component, the additional components will be added to the amount of the base component of the combined benefit. A combined first additional amount cannot be more than the maximum payable amount of a first additional RTR pension or first additional DSB . Similarly, a combined second additional amount cannot be more than the maximum payable amount of a second additional RTR pension or second additional DSB . The following pensions and benefits will have an additional portion and are included in the CPP enhancement: Survivor pension; Retirement pension; Disability benefit; Post-Retirement benefit and Combined benefits. Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) form the basis of benefit calculations. The 2 new contributory periods add 2 new sets of UPE. Under the enhancement, there are a total of 3 sets of UPE: one for each of the Base CPP, the first additional period and the second additional CPP. The UPE details are as follows: Base UPE = UPE up to the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), based on contributions made at 9.9%. First additional UPE = UPE up to the YMPE, based on contributions made at an extra 2% contribution rate. Second additional UPE = UPE from the YMPE to the Year’s Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings, based on contributions made at an extra 8% contribution rate. The base CPP determines eligibility for a pension or benefit. When an individual meets the minimum qualifying period (MQP) in the Base CPP period, they are eligible for the pension or benefit, including any additional portions.

The enhancement of the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) serves as a top-up to the benefits provided by the base CPP. The result is that working Canadians will receive higher amount benefits in exchange for making higher CPP contributions. For people who contributed to the CPP through paid work or self-employment in 2019, and continued to do so thereafter, the enhancement increases the amounts of the following CPP pensions and benefits: Retirement pension; Disability benefit; Survivor’s pension; Post-Retirement Benefit; and Combined benefits. Enhanced benefits will increase over time as people make enhanced contributions, eventually increasing benefit by up to 50%. The features of the enhancement are as follows: The CPP enhancement began in 2019, with the contribution rate of 2% being phased-in gradually from 2019-2023; The upper earnings limit will be 114% of the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) upon full implementation of the enhancement in 2025. This new amount is called the Year’s Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings ; and The enhancement, when combined with the base CPP , offers a replacement rate of 33.33% on earnings up to 114% of the YMPE. The original CPP remains unchanged since its introduction in 1966 and is called the "Base CPP". The CPP enhancement creates a top-up to the "Base CPP" called "Additional CPP". The additional CPP contains its own: contributory periods; contribution rates; replacement rates; and benefit calculations. As a part of the CPP enhancement, the additional CPP will introduce child rearing and disability drop-Ins. For both the child rearing drop-in and the disability drop-in, qualifying earnings are dropped into the periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the CPP enhancement portion of a pension or benefit.

The project was also responsible for implementing system functionalities to accommodate the legislative changes resulting from the 2016-2018 CPP Triennial Review, such as: a flat-rate Death ( DTH ) benefit; the removal of the age-based reduction to the SVR pension; the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) provision; and the Disability Drop-In (DDI) provision. The CRDI and DDI only apply to the first and second additional components of CPP benefits. On November 23, 2019, system functionalities required to split earnings and contributions in ITRDS (between the base CPP and first additional component) were implemented. Certain products such as the Statement of Contributions (SOC), My Service Canada Account (MSCA) and the Canadian Retirement Income Calculator were updated to accommodate the CPP enhancement and Triennial Review legislative changes. On May 21, 2022, system functionalities were introduced in ITRDS and CPMS to pay the first additional component of the CPP. The system release in May 2022 also included the introduction of system functionalities for two of the Triennial Review legislative changes: a flat-rate DTH benefit; and the removal of the age-based reduction to the SVR pension. On May 27, 2023, system functionalities were introduced in ITRDS to attribute or “drop in” credits (Child Rearing Drop-In and the Disability Drop-In provisions) into the calculation of the first additional component of CPP benefits. On February 10, 2024, system functionalities were introduced to allow ESDC to receive second additional contribution data from the CRA . Data transmission between Retraite Québec and ESDC was also updated to accommodate the second additional component.

The CPP enhancement legislative changes were phased-in over seven years, from 2019 to 2025. The enhanced components (i.e., first and second additional) are not a separate benefit, but rather a top-up to the base CPP. The first and second additional components do not affect the eligibility requirements for benefits. Clients must be entitled and eligible to the base CPP benefit and have made enhanced contributions to be eligible for an enhanced component of that benefit: The CRA began collecting first additional contributions in January 2019, and second additional contributions in January 2024. The Canada Pension Plan legislation requires a review every 3 years. The following 6 CPP Triennial changes are being implemented on January 1, 2025: Top-up to the CPP Death ( DTH ) benefit. This change adds a top-up to the CPP DTH benefit for eligible contributors who die on or after January 1, 2025, do not have an SVR pension payable and have never received a CPP or QPP disability or retirement pension. New child's benefit for part-time attendance at a school or university. Effective January 1, 2025, children of disabled or deceased contributors aged 18 to 25 who attend a recognized institution on a part-time basis will be eligible to receive 50% of the CPP benefit currently paid to full-time students. Extension of eligibility for the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) when the disabled contributor reaches the age of 65. This change extends the child's eligibility for the DCCB when their disabled parent reaches the age of 65 on or after January 1, 2025, provided all other eligibility criteria are met. Disentitlement to a CPP SVR pension following a CPP Credit Split. Contributors who are separated from their legal spouse with an approved credit split on or after January 1, 2025, are no longer eligible to receive a CPP SVR pension for that same separated spouse. Extension of the CPP incapacity provisions to DCCB applications. Effective June 20, 2024, if a disabled contributor is found to have been incapacitated and their CPPD benefits application is deemed to have been received at an earlier date, the same deemed date of application would also apply to any children listed on that application. Determination of the payee for CPP children's benefits (i.e. DCCB and Surviving Child's benefit). Effective June 20, 2024, the DCCB and Surviving Child's benefit is paid on behalf of a minor child to the disabled contributor or surviving spouse if they have decision-making responsibility for the child.

Effective 2012, an individual must make mandatory contributions to the CPP when they: have reached age 60 to 64; are receiving an RTR pension; and are still working. An individual who has reached age 65 to 70 must also contribute unless they opt out. Post-Retirement Benefit (Knowledge)

Since January 1, 2012, an individual who works and receives an RTR pension must contribute to the CPP if they: have earnings above the Year's Basic Exemption amount; and are 60 to 64 years of age; or are 65 to 70 years of age, unless the individual has made an election to stop paying CPP contributions and has not revoked that election. Post-Retirement Benefit ( PRB ) contributions: are separate from other CPP contributions; are not used to establish eligibility or increase the amounts of other benefits; cannot be used for credit splitting or pension sharing; and are based on the Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings in the previous year.

The PRB is only payable to a CPP or QPP RTR pension recipient who works and makes valid contributions on earnings above the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE). It is payable even if the recipient is already receiving the maximum CPP RTR pension. Since it is a taxable benefit, it may affect eligibility for other benefits. Payment of the first PRB was made effective January 1, 2013. Individuals will make compulsory contributions to the plan if they are: between the ages of 60 and 65 (including the month of their 65th birthday); receiving a CPP RTR pension; and still working. Individuals may opt out or stop contributing if they are: at least 65 years of age but under 70; receiving a CPP RTR pension; and still working. For more information, Eligibility Requirements—Post-Retirement Benefit (Policy) Enhancement to the CPP As of January 1, 2019, the department began phasing in the CPP enhancement, a new component of the CPP. The enhancement is not a separate benefit, but rather a top-up to the original, now referred to as the base component of the CPP. This means working Canadians will receive higher benefits in exchange for making higher contributions. The base component of the PRB and the additional components of the PRB are calculated using the same formula. The total amount of the PRB is the sum of the base and additional components . To understand how the PRB is calculated, Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge) For more information, CPP Enhancement (Knowledge) Manual adjudication Although the PRB is an automatically adjudicated benefit and staff are not required to manually make calculations, there may be exceptional cases that require manual intervention in order to complete the adjudication process. In these cases, there will be enquiries that require subject matter expertise for responses. Some examples of the situations requiring PRB subject matter expertise are: QPP RTR pension-only clients entitled to a PRB ; QPP and CPP (dual) contributors entitled to a PRB ; PRB adjudication exception report processing; and complex enquiries regarding entitlement amounts and/or the calculation of the PRB .

For individuals who were over 70 years of age on January 1, 2020 , the receipt date of the proactively enrolled RTR application is considered to be January 1, 2020. The effective date of the individual's proactively enrolled RTR pension is the later of: the month following the month of the individual's 70th birthday; or February 2019. For individuals who turned 70 on January 1, 2020 or later , the receipt date of the proactively enrolled RTR application is considered to be the 1st day of the month in which the individual turns 70 years of age. The effective date of the proactively enrolled RTR pension is the month following the month of the individual's 70th birthday. There are 2 types of CPP benefits available to children, based on eligibility: the Surviving Child's Benefit for the children of a deceased contributor; and the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit for the children of a disabled contributor. A child is eligible for a maximum of 2 children's benefits. For more information, refer to Validate a Child-Contributor Relationship (Action) and Validate a Child-Contributor Relationship (Action) Child-Contributor Relationship—Children's Benefit (Policy) Natural child of a deceased contributor A natural child is considered the child of a deceased contributor if born before or after the contributor's death. If the child is born after the death of the contributor, the birth must occur within 301 days of the date of death of the contributor. The child's birth certificate must identify the contributor as a parent. Natural child of a disabled contributor A natural child is considered the child of a disabled contributor, born before or after the date when the contributor's disability benefit was approved. Child who becomes a ward of an agency, such as Children's Aid or Social Services, after birth A child cannot be considered for a child's benefit based on the death or disability of a foster parent. The foster parent is paid by the agency to care for the child. The benefit cannot be paid to the foster parent or parents because they do not have decision-making responsibility of the child—it is the agency that has decision-making responsibility of the child. An agency can be considered for a child's benefit on the death or disability of a legal parent. The child's benefit can be paid to the agency or authority that has decision-making responsibility on behalf of such a child if all other requirements are met.

The following documents may be used to support a parent's claim that the deceased contributor was a legal parent of the child in cases where a child is born after the death of the contributor: a written statement verifying that the birth occurred within 301 days of the date of the contributor's death; and a long form birth certificate. The applicant who is unable to obtain a long form birth certificate must provide a written statement stating that the deceased contributor is the child's parent completed either by: the family physician; or a member of the deceased contributor's family.

Deceased contributor's natural child A natural child may be considered the child of a deceased contributor whether born before or after the contributor's death. If the child is born after the death of the contributor, the birth must occur within 301 days of the date of death of the deceased contributor. The child's birth certificate identifies the contributor as a parent. Disabled contributor's natural child A natural child may be considered the child of a disabled contributor whether born before or after the date the contributor's CPP DSB application is approved.

Students who cannot remain at school or university full-time or part-time because of an illness can still be eligible for benefits. To determine if they are eligible, the student must submit the Canada Pension Plan Illness Certificate (ISP-1403) form. If a student was unable to resume full-time or part-time attendance at the start of an academic year, entitlement to benefits can still exist. To be entitled, the student must submit an ISP-1403 form and resume attendance immediately after the period of illness. If the student is absent for the entire year, they will only be entitled to benefits if they resume full-time or part-time attendance in the following academic year and submit a second ISP-1403 form to support the entire period of the absence (including the vacation period). If a student has not started an education program (instead of being unable to resume attending one), there is no entitlement to benefits, regardless of health. Absences that occur within an academic year If the student was absent due to an illness occurring within an academic year, they must submit a new Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form confirming that they have resumed full-time or part-time studies. If the student does not return to school after the illness, they are only entitled to the benefits during the period of illness. Absences that last until the end of an academic year The student is entitled to benefits if their ISP-1403 form is valid until the end of the academic year, including the normal school vacation period. Absences that extend into the next academic year The student is entitled to benefits if their ISP-1403 form is valid for the entire current academic year, including the normal school vacation period. The student is also entitled to benefits from the start of the next academic year until the end of the period of illness if they resume full-time attendance sometime during that academic year. To confirm they have returned to full-time or part-time attendance, the student must submit a new ISP-1402 form. When a contributor's CPPD benefit stops while the dependent child is absent from school or university due to illness As of January 1, 2025, when a disabled contributor's CPPD benefit ceases because they reach age 65, the eligibility to the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit ( DCCB ) may be extended for the disabled contributor's child. For more information, Children's Benefits After CPPD Beneficiary Reaches Age 65 (Scenario) In all other situations, when a contributor is no longer eligible for the CPPD benefit, the DCCB also stops. If a disabled contributor's child was absent from school due to illness but was receiving the benefit because they submitted the ISP-1403 form, payment stops the same month that the CPPD benefit ends. If a contributor's CPPD benefit stops and their child is absent from school or university due to illness, the child is eligible for benefits up until the cessation date of the CPPD benefit. To be eligible they must: resume full-time or part-time attendance during that year or the next school year; and submit an ISP-1403 form. A child turns 25 while absent from school or university due to illness If a child who is turning 25 years old in the academic year but is unable to start school or is absent due to an illness, they are eligible for a child's benefit from the start of that school year until the month of their 25th birthday. To maintain eligibility, they must: submit an ISP-1402 form to prove that they resumed full-time attendance during that year or the next school year; and submit an ISP-1403 form.

CPP legislation recognizes that although a child may not be attending school, they may be deemed to be in approved attendance in the following situations: School vacations; or An absence due to illness. Children who are absent due to illness can in certain circumstances be considered in approved attendance at school. For benefit payments to continue to be paid to the dependent child, they must submit the required Canada Pension Plan Illness Certificate (ISP-1403) form and it must be consistent with the type of attendance (full-time or part-time) at the time the illness begins. If a disabled contributor's child was absent from school due to illness but continued to receive benefit payments as they provided the ISP-1403 form, their benefit payments will cease the month the contributor's benefit payments cease. If a disabled contributor's child was absent from school or university due to illness and the DSB ceases, that child will be eligible for benefits up to the date the DSB ceases. This is only applicable if the child resumes full-time or part-time attendance during that year or the following school year. They must also submit an ISP-1403 form confirming that the absence was due to illness. Upon notification from a student that their school is not able to provide classes (teacher strike, temporary closure, etc.) and they have returned to school with an extended end date, proof is required to extend the end date. Proof can come in the form of: a letter from the school with all relevant information; a completed CPP Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form that confirms approved attendance; or official proof of enrolment signed by an authorized school official that contains all required information.

An automated Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402-A) form is sent to a child over the age of 18 (+18 child) one month before the end of the current school period. An automated Cancellation of the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) - Surviving Child's Benefit/Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit (ISP-1365) letter, including reconsideration rights, is sent to the +18 child if a current school period is not entered in the ITRDS School Declaration field within 60 days of the first letter. If a school period is entered in ITRDS more than one month after it has ended, you must send a manual ISP-1365 letter and an ISP-1402-A form to the child.

Standard vacation period A standard vacation period may begin as early as April 1 and end as late as September 30. Students who have been in full-time or part-time attendance at school or university immediately prior to a vacation period falling within these dates are entitled to receive the CPP child's benefit for the entire vacation period. Although international schools or universities schedule vacation periods other than April to September, the vacation period is acceptable for CPP purposes. Non-standard vacation period A student whose vacation period does not fall within the April to September time frame may be deemed to be in full-time or part-time attendance during their chosen 4-month vacation period. For this to occur, they must attend school or university on a full-time or part-time basis for 8 consecutive months in the 12 months ending with the vacation period. Most universities and colleges offer students the opportunity to take courses during all three semesters (fall, winter and summer). This allows students to go to school and complete their program earlier or to choose their own vacation period. In addition, some universities can offer Co-op programs that are set up to allow for a schedule that alternates between a semester of school and a semester of work experience. During these schedules, students are considered to be in full-time or part-time attendance. This enables students to acquire work experience in their field of study as part of the requirements of the program. Some technical or trade schools have courses that begin at any time during the year. Eligibility to a child's benefit for a +18 child begins during a school vacation period The following are events that make a +18 child eligible to a child's benefit: The contributor dies; The contributor becomes disabled; or The child reaches age 18. When any of these events occur during a school vacation period, the child must complete and submit a Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form and provide proof of attendance from the school or university for the previous academic year. The current school vacation period is connected to the academic year that just ended. Therefore, the +18 child must have been in attendance in the past academic year to be paid the child's benefit for the school vacation period following the event. For subsequent school years, school vacation period entitlement depends on meeting full-time or part-time attendance requirements and the completion of another ISP-1402 form. Vacation periods when the year or semester has not been completed If a child did not complete a school year or semester for reasons other than illness, the child is not entitled to receive benefits for the vacation period or any month after the month the child last attended school. CPP Children's Benefits—Attendance at School or University (Policy)

Normal vacation periods Example Miranda is the 20-year-old child of a CPP contributor who receives disability benefits. Miranda, who had been out of school for some time, attended university during the January to April term as a full-time student. Because she was in full-time attendance, she was paid children's benefits for the January to April (winter) term. After she completed the winter term, Miranda was absent from school for the normal academic vacation period associated with her university program (May-Aug). Because she had attended a university program full-time up to the end of the semester or school year that immediately precedes the school's vacation period, Miranda was entitled to continued children's benefits payments during the summer vacation. When a child successfully completes an academic year before the beginning of the normal period of school vacation, the child is entitled to receive CPP children's benefits up to the end of the scholastic vacation period. Non-standard vacation periods Michael, the 22-year-old child of a deceased CPP contributor, attended university during the January to April term and continued as a full-time student during the May to August term. He was considered to be in full-time attendance and entitled to children's benefits during the period he was attending school. Michael chose to take his vacation period from September to December. His school vacation period was considered to be from September to December, because he had attended school during 8 of the last 12 months. As a result, Michael was entitled to children's benefits from September to December. The next semester began on January 10. Michael did not return to university for the winter semester and lost his entitlement to children's benefits on February 1. He is no longer in full-time school attendance as of January 10, the date his school vacation period ended. As a result, Michael is not entitled to children's benefits as of the month following the month in which he left school. When the event leading to children's benefits eligibility occurs during a school vacation period, i.e. when: the contributor dies; the contributor becomes disabled; or the child reaches age 18, The child must obtain a Declaration of Attendance at School or University (ISP1401) for the previous academic year to be paid any benefits during the vacation period. This is necessary because the current school vacation is related to the academic year that just ended. If the child attended school during the school year just ended, that child is eligible for children's benefits payments for the school vacation period which follows the event. For subsequent school years, school vacation period entitlement depends on meeting full-time attendance requirements and the completion of another ISP1401 form. Vacations related to internships or articling Heather, the 23-year-old child of a disabled contributor, was attending school on a full-time basis and obtained her law degree in June. She attended university full time up to the end of the spring semester that immediately preceded the school vacation period. As a result, she was entitled to children's benefits during the summer vacation period that followed. Classes at her university resumed on September 10. CPP considers her a full-time student until that date and to be entitled to children's benefits for the month of September. In October, Heather started articling with a medium-sized law firm. Although she is required to article with a law firm in order to practice law in Canada, her entitlement to CPP children's benefits ends after the payment for the month of September. She is not entitled to it because she now has her degree and is no longer attending school on a full-time basis.

Use the information provided by the child and the educational institution on the Canada Pension Plan Child's Benefit Application and Declaration for a Student Over 18 years of Age in Attendance at School or University (ISP-1402) form to determine if the child is in full-time or part-time attendance. A child is considered to be in full-time attendance if they are deemed full-time by an acceptable educational institution, regardless of the number of courses in which they are enrolled. A child is considered to be in part-time attendance if they are not considered full-time by the educational institution. In addition, they must be enrolled in courses that make up at least 20% of a full course load as recognized by the educational institution. For more information, CPP Children's Benefits—Attendance at School or University (Policy)

Effective January 1, 2025, a determination of what constitutes part-time school attendance is essential in deciding eligibility for benefits. Dependent children of deceased or disabled contributors can be eligible for a benefit when they are attending part-time school and meet all eligibility requirements. The educational institution determines the part-time status. The amount they could receive is 50% of the rate for full-time students. A dependent child is normally considered to be in part-time attendance at school for CPP purposes if they: are recognized to be a part-time student by an acceptable educational institution; and enrolled in courses that make up at least 20% of a full course load as recognized by their educational institution.

For spouses or common-law partners to qualify for a single PNSH or a double PNSH, they must: submit an application in writing; be at least 60 years of age; be living together or cohabiting in a common-law relationship for a continuous period of at least one year immediately before the PNSH approval date; have made valid contributions from at least one applicant to CPP or QPP and have applied for or is currently receiving an RTR pension or a QPP RTR pension; not be voluntarily separated at the time of application; and not have a spousal agreement that is binding on the Minister indicating their intention of not sharing their RTR pension under CPP. For more information, Pension Sharing (Policy)

Spouses or common-law partners may choose to share their CPP RTR pensions if the following eligibility requirements are met: A written application must be made in the prescribed manner using the Application for Canada Pension Plan Pension Sharing of Retirement Pension(s) (ISP-1002) form. Both spouses or common-law partners must be at least 60 years of age at the effective date. At the time the couple applies for Pension Sharing (PNSH): spouses must be legally married and living together; or persons cohabiting in a common-law relationship who must have so cohabited for a continuous period of at least one year immediately before the date the PNSH is approved. Couples living apart for reasons beyond their control are considered to be living together at the time of application for PNSH purposes. Neither spouses nor common-law partners can be voluntarily separated at the time of application. At least one of the applicants must have valid CPP or QPP contributions and either be receiving or have applied for a CPP or a QPP RTR pension.
Double pension sharing Single pension sharing

There are 2 types of CPP Pension Sharing (PNSH): Single PNSH When only one spouse or common-law partner receives a CPP RTR pension and the other spouse or common-law partner is at least 60 years old and a non-contributor to CPP, the pension share is: single . The term "non-contributor" means that an individual has: never made a valid contribution to either CPP or QPP; and not been credited with earnings from a division of unadjusted pensionable earnings (credit split). Double PNSH When both spouses or common-law partners are receiving CPP RTR pensions or when one is receiving an CPP RTR pension and the other is receiving an CPP RTR pension from the QPP RTR , the pension share is: double .

Usually, both spouses or common-law partners apply using one application form or letter. If each spouse or common-law partner submits an application, treat them as one. Compare and verify the information on each application. A spouse or common-law partner can apply by submitting one of the following: an Application for Canada Pension Plan Pension Sharing of Retirement Pension(s) (ISP-1002) form; an online Application for CPP Pension Sharing of Retirement Pension via My Service Canada Account; or a signed letter indicating their wish to apply for PNSH.

Both or either one of the spouses or common-law partners can apply for Pension Sharing (PNSH) on the same application form. If two applications are received, the information is verified and treated as one application. When only one spouse signs, the other spouse must be informed in writing of the application. In all cases, whether or not a PNSH application is approved, both spouses or common-law partners must be notified in writing of the decision and advised of their right to request a reconsideration.

Currently, Service Canada receives all PNSH applications by paper or written communication only. Both or either one of the spouses or common-law partners can apply for PNSH on the same application form. If two applications are received, the information is verified and treated as one application. If only one spouse or common-law partner signs the application, the other spouse or common-law partner must be informed in writing of the application. Third party contacts may apply on behalf of the applicant if the third party administrator provided the supporting documentation with the paper application.

A spouse or common-law partner can request in writing or by submitting a Pension Sharing (PNSH) application to have their PNSH reinstated. If only one spouse or common-law partner requests a reinstatement, the other spouse or common-law partner must be notified. Before reinstating the PNSH, review the file to ensure there is continued eligibility. Request any information necessary from the applicants to verify that eligibility continues or resumes (i.e. the spouses or common-law partners may have been separated during the period the PNSH was cancelled). Reinstate a single PNSH Reinstating a single PNSH can result in a different ratio if, at the time of approval of the first PNSH, the non-contributor spouse or common-law partner had not yet reached age 70. The joint contributory period and period of cohabitation will be extended to the month in which they reach 70 or the month in which the request for reinstatement is approved, whichever is earliest. Reinstate a double PNSH When reinstating a double PNSH, the ratio is the same ratio that was calculated at the time the first PNSH was approved. If the reinstatement is approved, the effective date is the month following the month of approval, i.e. the accounting month in which the PNSH is accepted by the system.

Reinstating a single PNSH Reinstating a single Pension Sharing (PNSH) could result in a different sharing ratio if, at the time of approval of the first PNSH application, the non-contributor spouse had not yet reached age 70. In such cases, the joint contributory period and the period of cohabitation are extended to the month in which the contributor reached age 70 or the month the request for reinstatement of PNSH is approved, whichever is earliest . Reinstating a double PNSH When a double PNSH is reinstated, the ratio of the number of months in the period of cohabitation to the number of months in the joint contributory period remains the same ratio that had been calculated at the time of approval of the first PNSH.

The CRDI only applies to the enhanced earnings calculation of a CPP benefit or pension. The drop-in adds UPE to the periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the CPP enhanced components of a benefit or provision. The CRDI is applied for any contributor who, at the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the child, is eligible to receive the CCB and acts as the primary caregiver. An eligible contributor will receive UPE dropped into the calculation of the enhanced portion of their CPP benefit beginning the month after the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility for the child and ending the month of the child's 7th birthday. After January 1, 2019, the CPP enhancement will drop in an amount equal to the primary caregiver's average first additional earnings during the 5 years before the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the child for each year the child is under the age of 7. After January 1, 2024, the CPP enhancement will drop in an amount equal to the primary caregiver's average second additional earnings (i.e. earnings between the year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (MPE) amount and the year's additional MPE amount) during the 5 years before the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the child for each year the child is under the age of 7. The drop-in provisions are only applied to the first additional and second additional contributory periods if: the drop-in amount is higher than the contributor's actual earnings during that period; and the child is under the age of 7. When a contributor loses decision-making responsibility and parenting time for a child but regains it later, separate CRDI calculations are required for each period the contributor had decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the child. Therefore, some contributors may have multiple first additional CRDI and second additional CRDI periods per child. When first additional or second additional CRDI periods are attributed for the year of the child's birth, the child's adoption, or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the child, the attributed amount covers the whole year regardless of when the date of birth, adoption or assumption of decision-making responsibility falls within the year. However, when a contributor's first additional and second additional contributory periods end within 7 years after the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date on which the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the child (e.g. the contributor starts receiving their CPP RTR pension, reaches age 70 or dies), the calculated amount of the CRDI must be prorated over 12 months. The CRDI will not help individuals meet the eligibility requirements or Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) for CPP benefits, as the CRDI only applies to the enhanced earnings calculation. It is only the base earnings and contributions that are considered in determining eligibility and MQP. UPE's dropped in as a result of the CRDI are eligible for a Credit Split provision (division of pensionable earnings). When a client is in pay for a DSB and has UPE attributed from the CRDI for any year during which they are in pay, it will trigger a recalculation of the additional components of their DSB every year following the attribution of the CRDI UPE. Recalculations will occur in January, coinciding with the indexation of the DSB . For more information on how the CRDI is calculated and its impact on the calculation of benefits, refer to Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation and Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge) For more information about the CRDI and CPP enhancement, CPP Enhancement (Knowledge)

The CRDO only applies to the base calculation of a CPP pension or benefit. The CRDO removes contributory months with low or zero earnings from the base calculation, starting with the month after the child's birth, the child's adoption or the date the contributor gained decision-making responsibility for the child, and ending with the month of the child's 7th birthday. This reduces the total number of months used in the calculation and results in a higher average of monthly pensionable earnings. The CRDO applies only to the time period when the individual was the primary caregiver for children under the age of 7. The CRDO can help individuals meet the eligibility requirements for CPPD benefits. In the event of an individual's death, the CRDO can also help their estate and survivors qualify for benefits.

When an individual requests the CRP, the request is applied to both the Child Rearing Drop-Out (CRDO) and Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) provisions. The CRP prevents the financial penalization of individuals who stopped working or reduced their paid employment or self-employment to raise children under the age of 7. Periods of time with low or no contributions result in lower payment amounts for CPP benefits. The purpose of the CRP is to help eligible individuals qualify or receive a higher entitlement amount for CPP benefits. The CRP is only applied if it is to an individual's advantage. If it reduces eligibility or entitlement, it is not applied. The CRP applies only to the time period when the individual had little to no earnings and was eligible for the Family Allowance or Canada Child Benefit (CCB). The primary caregiver is the person who was most responsible for the day-to-day needs of a child or children. An individual who worked at home while taking care of a child or children also meets this requirement. The CRP can only be applied to one individual's account for a given time period and particular child, even if there were multiple primary caregivers for the same child. For more information, Child Rearing Provision (Policy) Individuals are urged to request the CRP when they first apply for a CPP benefit or pension. However, the individual or their authorized representative can request the CRP even after the initial benefit amount has been calculated. The CRDO allows for the removal of months or years of low or no earnings from an individual's contributory period when calculating a CPP benefit. This can help an individual meet the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) for CPP pensions or benefits. The CRDO can also improve the MQP for CPPD benefits. The CRDI adds Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) to periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the CPP enhanced component of a benefit.

As of January 2019, the Child Rearing Provision includes the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI). The CRDI adds Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) to periods of low or zero earnings in the first or second additional contributory period for the time when the child was under 7 years of age. As CRDI amounts are UPE, they are subject to credit splitting upon divorce or separation. The CRDI UPE amount is determined using earnings from the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child, or the date the contributor gained decision making responsibility and parenting time of the child. If a credit split occurs before the CRDI calculation and any earnings from the 5 years before the child's birth, adoption or date they came under the decision making responsibility and parenting time of the contributor were split, the divided earnings are used in the CRDI calculation. If a credit split occurs after CRDI amounts are attributed, and the credit split changes any of the earnings amounts in the 5 years prior to the birth or adoption of the child, the CRDI amounts that were originally attributed within the period of cohabitation are not recalculated, however, they are divided along with the other UPE. If a credit split occurs after CRDI amounts are attributed, the credit split changes any of the earnings amounts in the 5 years before the child's birth, adoption or date they came under the decision making responsibility and parenting time of the contributor, and the CRDI period extends past the period of cohabitation, then CRDI amounts for the post-cohabitation period are recalculated taking into account the newly divided earnings. For an example of a CRDI subject to the division of UPEs, Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation

Effective January 2019, the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) and Disability Drop-In (DDI) provisions were introduced to protect the value of CPP benefits during periods of low or no earnings (e.g. due to child rearing or disability). The drop-in provisions only apply to a contributor's first additional earnings (as of January 2019) and second additional earnings (as of January 2024). These drop-in provisions are used to calculate the enhanced components of a CPP pension or benefit. For more information on CPP enhancement, go to the CPP enhancement section below. If the contributor's earnings are higher than the drop-in value, the drop-in provision will not be applied. In the calculation for the first and second additional contributory periods under the CPP enhancement, the number of contributory months is fixed at 480 months (40 years). The Department will use the best 480 months in the calculation of the enhanced components. Given that 480 months is always the number of months used, earnings are dropped in to increase the total amount of earnings, resulting in a higher average over the set number of months. For CPP base calculations, the disability exclusion and the drop-out provisions remove months from the total number of contributory months to increase the average monthly pensionable earnings. In May 2023, system functionalities were introduced to "drop in" credits into the calculation of the first additional component of CPP benefits for periods of the CRDI and the DDI. In August 2025, system functionalities were introduced to "drop in" credits into the calculation of the second additional component of CPP benefits for periods of the CRDI and the DDI. Child Rearing Provision—CRDI (applicable to first additional and second additional components of the contributory period only) For contributors with low or no earnings due to raising children under the age of 7 for a period that includes 2019 or later, drop-in earnings may be included in the calculation of the first additional and second additional components of CPP benefits. When applied, the CRDI drops earnings into periods of low or no earnings from the month after the child's birth, adoption or the date the contributor assumed decision-making responsibility of the child until the month of the child's 7th birthday. The amount dropped in is equal to the contributor's average earnings for the 5-year period immediately before the child's birth, adoption or the date the contributor assumed decision-making responsibility of the child. The earnings are only dropped in when the amount is higher than the contributor's actual first additional or second additional earnings during that period. The dropped-in credits act as Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) in the first additional or second additional contributory period when calculating the first or second additional component of a benefit. The CRDI does not help individuals meet the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) eligibility requirement for benefits as the CRDI only applies to the enhanced components. As CRDI credits are essentially first additional or second additional UPE, they are subject to credit splitting if a credit split occurs after CRDI credits are attributed. Where a credit split occurs after CRDI credits are attributed and the credit split changes the earnings amounts in any of the 5 years before the child's birth, adoption or the date the contributor assumed decision-making responsibility for the child, any CRDI credits that were originally attributed within the period of cohabitation are not recalculated. The original CRDI credits are divided along with any other affected UPE. If a credit split occurs after CRDI credits are attributed and the credit split changes any of the earnings amounts in the 5 years before the child's birth, adoption or the date the contributor assumed decision-making responsibility for the child, and the CRDI period extends past the period of cohabitation, the CRDI credits for the post-cohabitation period are recalculated taking into account the newly divided earnings. If a credit split occurs prior to the CRDI calculation and any earnings from the 5 years before the child's birth, adoption or the date the contributor assumed decision-making responsibility for the child were split, the credit split earnings are used in the CRDI calculation. For an example of a CRDI subject to the division of UPE, Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation (Work Tool) If the contributor does not have valid earnings in the period used to calculate the average earnings for the drop-in, they do not receive the drop-in. If there are less than 5 years in the first additional or second additional contributory periods, the average is determined by the actual number of available months in the contributory period, down to a lower limit of 36 months (3 years). If there are less than 3 years in the first additional contributory period, the client is awarded 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e 1/12 of the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for each month outside of the contributory period, up to a maximum of 36 months for the CRDI. This is only applicable to the first additional contributory period, as second additional contributions are made on earnings between the YMPE and the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE) amount. For CPP base calculations, the drop-out provisions remove months from the total number of contributory months to increase the Average Monthly Pensionable Earnings. For the enhanced components, the total number of months is always 480 months. Therefore, earnings are dropped in to increase the total amount of earnings, resulting in a higher average over the set number of months. For more information and calculation details on the CRDI, Child Rearing Provision (Policy) For additional examples of how to determine CRDI values, Examples—Child Rearing Drop-In Calculation (Work Tool) DDI (applicable to the first additional and second additional components of the contributory period only) For contributors with low or no earnings due to severe and prolonged disability, drop-in earnings may be added to the calculation of the first additional and second additional components of their RTR pension for the period they were deemed disabled if it is to the contributor's advantage. If a deceased contributor was receiving a DSB , the DDI can be applied to the enhanced components when calculating the SVR pension payable to the surviving spouse or common-law partner. The DDI does not help individuals meet the MQP eligibility requirements for benefits. DDI values are determined at the Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (APE) stage of calculating the enhanced component of a contributor's RTR pension, or the enhanced component of the SVR pension payable to a deceased contributor's surviving spouse or common-law partner. Because they are determined at the APE stage of the enhanced calculation, DDI values are not UPE and are not subject to credit splitting. The amount dropped into the contributor's first additional CPP contributory period equals 70% of their average first additional earnings compared to the YMPE made in the 6 years before the contributor became disabled. The amount dropped into the contributor's second additional contributory period is 70% of the average second additional pensionable earnings, made between the YMPE and the YAMPE. If a contributor does not have valid earnings in the period used to calculate the average earnings amount for the drop-in, they will not receive the drop-in. If there are less than 6 years in the first or second additional periods, the drop-in rate is calculated using the actual number of available months in the contributory period; if the number of months is 0, there will be no drop-in amount. If the DSB beneficiary returns to work for a period of less than 6 years before qualifying for and receiving a second DSB , the higher DDI rate between the previous period of disability and the second period of disability is calculated. This will be applied to the second disability period in the beneficiary's contributory period. For more information on the DDI provision and for examples of its calculation, refer to Disability Drop-In (Knowledge) . For information on the formula and calculation details of the DDI, refer to Disability Drop-in Provision (Policy) and to Disability Drop-In (Knowledge) Disability Drop-in Provision (Policy) Examples—Disability Drop-In (Work Tool)

When fewer than 36 months exist in the first additional contributory period, the formula applicable to the first additional contributory period attributes 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e. 1/12th of the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings ( YMPE ) for each missing month up to 36 months. However, the minimum number of contributory months required is 36 months, and in this case, the contributor has a first additional contributory period of only 18 months (from January 2019 up to and including June 2020). Since there are fewer than 36 months in the contributor's first additional contributory period, 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e. 1/12th of the YMPE will be attributed for each missing month up to 36 months.
