When there are fewer than 5 years (60 months) in the first additional contributory period, because the individual either had a child before the age of 23 or had a child before 2023, only the actual number of contributory months will be used to calculate the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) attributed to the first additional contributory period. The minimum number of contributory months required in the first additional contributory period is 36 months. Similarly, when there are fewer than 5 years (60 months) in the second additional contributory period because the individual either had a child before the age of 23 or had a child before 2028, only the actual number of contributory months will be used to calculate the CRDI for the second additional contributory period. The minimum number of contributory months required in the second additional contributory period is 36 months. Example: A contributor had a child in February 2022 and was eligible to receive the Canada Child Benefit ( CCB ) in March 2022. Ratios are calculated by dividing the first additional Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) by the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for each of the 5 years (60 months) prior to the recipient's start date for a CCB . Each ratio is then multiplied by the number of months in the first additional contributory period for that year. As there are not 60 months in the contributor's first additional contributory period, the value of the contributor's CRDI for 2022 is calculated based on the actual number of contributory months. In this case, the contributor has a first additional contributory period of 38 months (from January 2019 up to and including February 2022). [[(M1 × A) + (M2 × B) + (M3 × C) + (M4 × D) + (M5 × E) + (M6 × F) + Q] / R = [[(0) + (0) + (12 × ($52,124 / $57,400)) + (12 × ($54,225 / $58,700)) + (12 × ($56,235 / $61,600)) + (2 × ($4,753 / $10,817) + Q))] / 38] × YMPE = [[(12 × 0.90808) + (12 × 0.92376) + (12 x 0.91291) + (2 × 0.43940) + 0] / 38] × YMPE Next, the average is calculated and multiplied by the YMPE for the year the drop-in is attributed. The YMPE for 2022 is $64,900. = [(10.89696 + 11.08512 + 10.95492 + 0.8788) + 0 / 38] × 64,900 = (33.8158 / 38) × 64,900 = 0.88989 ( CRDI Factor) × 64,900 = a CRDI of $57,754 for 2022. Since this amount is greater than the contributor's actual 2022 earnings of $4,753, the drop-in amount will be attributed for 2022. It will cover the whole year despite the fact that the contributor had their child in February 2022. There are no second additional UPE in this example because this period is prior to the second additional contributory period.

Formula for the first additional contributory period Where: M1 to M6 represent the number of months in the first additional contributory period for each of the 5 years (60 months) before the contributor becomes a Family Allowance recipient. There is a special calculation for M1 and M6 . If, for example, a child is born or adopted in May, the value of M6 will be 5 months (January to May) and the value of M1 will be 7 months for a total of 12 months. A to E represent the ratio calculated by dividing the first additional Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings ( UPE ) by the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings ( YMPE ) for each of the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child. ( A to E = UPE ∕ YMPE ) F is the ratio that applies to the year in which the drop-in period begins (i.e. the year in which the child is born or adopted). In case of overlapping child-rearing periods—if there was a previous child— F provides that a previous drop-in amount be used in the calculation. If not applicable, the first additional UPE for the months before the birth or adoption of the child are to be divided by a prorated YMPE amount. If the child is born or adopted in January, the value of F is zero. Q attributes 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e. 1/12th of the YMPE for each missing contributory month, up to 36 months. R is the denominator used to calculate the average ratio of earnings to YMPE . The value of R will be between 36 and 60 and represents the number of contributory months in the 5 years (60 months) before the birth or adoption of the child. T represents the YMPE for the year to which the drop-in is attributed. The product of multiplying the average ratio by T is the value of the child-rearing drop-in (CRDI) for the year to which it is attributed. Formula for the second additional contributory period This formula is similar to that applied to the first additional contributory period. The only differences are: A to E represent the ratio calculated by dividing the additional UPE by the difference between the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings ( YAMPE ) and YMPE , for each of the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child. YAMPE is the new pensionable earning ceiling introduced by the CPP enhancement. Its value is 114% of YMPE . ( A to E = UPE ∕ YAMPE − YMPE ). F is the ratio that applies to the year in which the drop-in period begins (i.e. the year in which the child is born or adopted). In case of overlapping child-rearing periods (i.e. if there was a previous child) F allows a previous drop-in amount to be used in the calculation. If not applicable, the second additional UPE for the months before the birth or adoption of the child are to be divided by the difference between the prorated YAMPE and YMPE amounts. If the child is born or adopted in January, the value of F is zero. There is no Q in the second additional contributory period formula. 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e. 1/12th of the YMPE cannot be attributed to the second additional contributions, since contributions to that period are made on earnings between the YMPE and YAMPE . For more information, Child Rearing Provision (Policy) When a contributor’s first additional and second additional contributory period ends within 7 years after the birth, adoption, or date on which the contributor gained decision-making responsibility and parenting time of the child (e.g. the contributor starts to receive their CPP RTR pension, reaches age 70 or dies) the calculated amount of the CRDI must be prorated over 12 months, using the following formulas: First additional CRDI: First additional CRDI value = first additional CRDI factor × Prorated YMPE Second additional: Second additional CRDI value = Second additional CRDI factor × (Prorated YAMPE – Prorated YMPE)

The Child Rearing Drop-In supports primary caregivers who stop working or reduce their work hours to care for children under the age of 7. The drop-in is only applied if it benefits the client. Each year after 2019, the CPP enhancement will "drop in" an amount equal to the primary caregiver's average earnings during the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child if the following are met: the drop-in amount is higher than their actual earnings during that period; and the child is under the age of 7. The Child Rearing Drop-In is also applied for any contributor who, at the birth or adoption of a child, receives the Canada Child Benefit and acts as the primary caregiver. An eligible contributor will receive earnings dropped into the calculation of the enhanced portion of their CPP benefit for the time when the child was under 7 years old. The earnings dropped in as a result of the Child Rearing Drop-In are eligible for a Credit Split provision (division of pensionable earnings).

The Child Rearing Drop-In will drop in unadjusted pensionable earnings (UPE) in the first and second additional contributory periods. For the first additional contributory period, the UPE will be equal to the average percentage of earnings the contributor has made in relation to the year's maximum pensionable earnings (YMPE) for the 5 years before birth or adoption of the child. For the second additional contributory period, the UPE are based on earnings between the YMPE and the year’s additional maximum pensionable earnings, which equals to 114% of the YMPE. Only higher earners who make more than the YMPE will contribute to the second additional contributory period.

The Child Rearing Drop-Out only applies to the base calculation of the CPP. The drop-out removes contributory months with low or zero earnings from the base calculation. This reduces the total number of months used in the calculation and results in a higher average of monthly pensionable earnings. The Child Rearing Drop-In only applies to the enhanced earnings calculation. The drop-in adds earnings into the periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the CPP enhancement portion of a benefit. The eligibility requirements for the Child Rearing Provision remain the same.

The Child Rearing Drop-In is based on the first and second additional pensionable earnings. It is possible for a client to receive a drop-in with a $0 value. This can occur when a client is a valid contributor but has no earnings in the period used to calculate the average earnings for the drop-in. If there are less than 5 years in the first or second contributory periods, the average is determined by the actual number of available months in the contributory period, down to a lower limit of 36 months (3 years). If there are less than 3 years in the first contributory period, the client is awarded 40% of the YMPE for each month outside of the contributory period, up to a maximum of 36 months for the Child Rearing Drop-In.

In the calculation for the first and second additional contributory periods under the CPP enhancement, the number of contributory months is fixed at 480 months (40 years). The Department will use the best 480 months in the calculation of the enhancement. With the CPP base calculations, the drop-outs remove months from the total number of contributory months to increase the average monthly pensionable earnings. With the enhancements, given that 480 months is always the number of months, earnings are dropped in to increase the total amount of earnings, resulting in a higher average over the set number of months.

The Disability Drop-In (DDI) rate (credits) for the first additional contributory period is determined by taking 70% of the contributor's average first additional pensionable earnings made in relation to the year's maximum pensionable earnings (YMPE) in the 6 years (72 months) before the Date of Onset (DOO), including the month of the DOO. For the second additional contributory period, the drop-in is similarly determined by taking 70% of the contributor's average second additional pensionable earnings, made between the YMPE and the year's additional maximum pensionable earnings in the 6 years (72 months) before the DOO, including the month of the DOO. A client can receive a first additional or second additional drop-in rate with a $0 value. This can occur when a client is a valid contributor but has no earnings in the period with which to calculate the average earnings amount for the first additional or second additional drop-in. If there are less than 6 years in the first or second additional contributory period, the drop-in rate is calculated using the actual number of available months in the contributory period. If the number of months is zero (0), there is no DDI amount provided. If a contributor's disability ceases due to a return to work, and the contributor becomes disabled again and has additional pensionable earnings for less than 6 years, the amount of drop-in for the second disability is the greater of: the drop-in rate for the previous period of disability; or the drop-in rate for the second period of disability (calculated using the previous 6-year period, including unadjusted additional pensionable earnings plus the drop-in from the previous period of disability). If the Child Rearing Drop-In or credit split Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (APE) amounts within the 6 years before the contributor became disabled are higher than the first additional or second additional DDI value, the greater value will be used. These credits are dropped in during the APE calculation for an RTR or SVR pension. This means the additional APE resulting from the DDI are added to the total first additional APE and total second additional APE during the calculation of the pension. For more information, Examples—Disability Drop-In

The Disability Exclusion only applies to the base calculation. The exclusion removes contributory months when the client was disabled, starting with the month following the month of DOO, from the calculation of the CPP base rate. This reduces the total number of months used in the calculation and results in a higher average monthly pensionable earnings. The eligibility requirements for the Disability Exclusion remain the same. The Disability Drop-In (DDI) only applies to the enhanced calculations and only if it is to the advantage of the contributor. The drop-in adds earnings into the periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the first additional and second additional components of an RTR or SVR pension. The DDI will not help individuals meet the eligibility and minimum qualifying period requirements for CPP benefits. If a contributor becomes disabled and receives a DSB in 2019, but never makes CPP enhanced contributions, the drop-in earnings for those months or years of disability will be $0 and will not affect the CPP benefit or pension calculations.

On January 1, 2019, changes to the CPP legislation came into effect as a result of the 2016-2018 Triennial Review. The DDI provision was introduced as a support for contributors with disabilities. The DDI provision is not used in the calculation of a DSB amount; rather, the DDI helps to protect the value of the enhanced components of CPP benefits during periods of low or no earnings for individuals who were in receipt of DSB . Earnings are credited to the contributor's first additional and second additional CPP contributory periods for the months when they were disabled as defined by the CPP. The drop-in amounts are used only for the purpose of calculating future RTR or SVR pension amounts, and are only calculated if the RTR or SVR pension is calculated. To apply the DDI provision to the enhanced components of the RTR or SVR pension calculations, the following criteria must be met: the contributor's disability Date of Onset (DOO) must be on or after January 1, 2019; to apply the DDI provision to the first additional component of the applicable benefit, the contributor must have first additional pensionable earnings in 2019 or thereafter; and to apply the DDI provision to the second additional component of the applicable benefit, the contributor must have second additional pensionable earnings in 2024 or thereafter. The DDI provision can only be attributed if it is to the advantage of the disabled contributor. The provision might not necessarily be to their advantage, as while the contributor cannot work and contribute during the disability period, they may have already received the following other credits: as a result of a Credit splitting provision; or from the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI). The DDI is only applied if it is greater than the credit split or CRDI earnings amount. An eligible contributor will receive earnings dropped into the calculation of the enhanced components of their CPP RTR pension and any SVR pension paid to their eligible surviving spouse or common-law partner. Earnings are dropped in for the month-based period of time the contributor is disabled, beginning the month after the contributor's DOO and ending the month their DSB ceases. The DDI values are not subject to a credit split (division of pensionable earnings between former spouses or common-law partners). The values may change if there is a division that affects the 6 years before the DOO, including the month of the DOO. If a division of unadjusted pensionable earnings occurs after the drop-in values have been calculated and there is a change to the pensionable values used to calculate the drop-in values, then both the drop-in earnings and benefit amount must be recalculated. For more information, Disability Drop-In Provision (Policy) The dollar amount of earnings dropped into the client's first additional and second additional CPP contributory period equals 70% of the client's average first additional pensionable earnings and 70% of the client's average second additional pensionable earnings for the 6 years (72 months) before the DOO, including the month of the DOO. A disability beneficiary may cease to be disabled and return to work. If they have contributions and additional pensionable earnings for less than 6 years and then becomes disabled again, the value of the drop-in for the second period of disability will be the greater of: the drop-in value for the previous period of disability; or the drop-in value for the second period of disability, calculated using the previous 6-year period, which will include unadjusted additional pensionable earnings from pensionable employment plus the drop-in amounts from the previous period of disability. This is applicable even in cases when a contributor returns to work and then suffers a relapse within 2 years ( DSB Auto Reinstate).

Effective January 2019, the drop-in provisions will help to further protect the value of the enhanced component of CPP benefits during periods of low or no earnings for primary caregivers and individuals with disabilities. Pension credits are "dropped in" for these periods based on an average of their earnings prior to the child's birth, adoption, date they came under the custody and control of the client or the date the client became disabled. Similar to the child rearing drop-out provision and the disability exclusion, the drop-in provisions can help increase the amount of CPP benefits. However they will not be considered when determining eligibility or the minimum qualifying period for CPP benefits. The child rearing drop-out provision and the disability exclusion apply to the base component of CPP benefits and the drop-in provisions apply to the enhanced component. Eligibility criteria for the child rearing drop-in and drop-out provisions are the same. For more information, refer to Child Rearing Provision (Scenario) and Child Rearing Provision (Scenario) Disability Drop-In (Knowledge)

Contributory periods cannot be excluded from the CPP enhancement portions. Therefore, Child Rearing Drop-in ( CRDI ) amounts are used to drop earnings into the contributor's first and second additional contributory periods for the purpose of CPP benefit calculation. Pension credits equal to the amount of the primary caregiver’s average earnings during the 5 years before the birth or adoption of the child are dropped into their first additional contributory period. There will be a maximum of 7 years of drop-ins per child. When there are overlapping drop-in periods due to the birth of more than one child in a given time frame, the highest of the 2 or more drop-in average earnings amounts is used. Beginning January 1, 2024, the provision will attribute to the primary caregiver’s second additional contributory period an amount equal to the average of their second additional UPE in the 5 years (60 months) before the birth or adoption of the child. Child-Rearing Drop-ins result in additional UPE The drop-in amounts function like additional UPE . They are used to calculate the additional CPP portion of the RTR pension and the additional CPP earnings-related portions of the DSB (including the PRDB and SVR pension). Their value must be adjusted upward at the time a pension or benefit is calculated. Use the same adjustment methodology as that used for the upward adjustment of the value of UPE . Child-Rearing Drop-ins and CPP Credit Splitting The drop-in amounts will be subject to division upon divorce or separation. The drop-in amount, once attributed to the contributory period, is not recalculated during the period of cohabitation due to the division. Changes to the earnings in the years before the birth or adoption of the child due to the division do not trigger a recalculation of the amount of the drop-in within the period of cohabitation. (The original amount attributed is divided along with the other UPE.) If the CRDI period extends past the period of cohabitation (i.e. the period subject to division), then the CRDI amount for that post-cohabitation period is recalculated, taking into account the newly-divided earnings. Therefore, if a division of additional UPE occurs after the CRDI has been attributed and affects the pension credits that were used to calculate the drop-ins, the amount of the CRDI must be recalculated. If there is a benefit in pay, the benefit amount must also be recalculated as the CRDI impacts other provisions. Bookend years The amount of the CRDI must be prorated for both the first and second additional contributory periods for the year in which the contributor: reaches 18 years of age; reaches 70 years of age; dies; or begins their RTR pension. The calculated amount of the CRDI for such years is prorated over 12 months. Less than 5 years in the contributory period If the individual either had a child before they turned 23 years of age or had a child before the year 2023, there are less than 5 years (60 months) in the first additional contributory period. In such cases, only the actual number of contributory months is used to calculate the average since CPP contributions can only begin at age 18. The minimum number of contributory months required is 36. In cases where there are less than 36 months in the first additional contributory period, the formula used for the first additional contributory period attributes 40% of the monthly maximum pensionable earnings, i.e 1/12 of the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for each missing month, up to 36 months. Child rearing period ends and then restarts There are cases in which one period of child rearing may end when custody and control of a child is lost. When this occurs, the individual no longer receives the CCB . If, however, custody and control of the child is regained, the individual again receives the CCB . In such cases, the drop-in value for the second period of child rearing is calculated using the previous 5 year period, which, will include (if the individual worked during this time), additional UPE from pensionable employment in addition to the drop-in amounts from the previous child rearing period. ( A to E = UPE ∕ YMPE ) F is the ratio that applies to the year in which the drop-in period begins (i.e. the year in which the child is born or adopted). The value of R will be between 36 and 60 and represents the number of contributory months in the 5 years (60 months) before the birth or adoption of the child. The product of multiplying the average ratio by T is the value of the child-rearing drop-in for the year to which it is attributed. In case of overlapping child-rearing periods, (i.e. if there was a previous child) F allows a previous drop-in amount to be used in the calculation. If not applicable, the first additional UPE for the months before the birth or adoption of the child are to be divided by the difference between the prorated YAMPE and YMPE amounts. The CPP Child Rearing Drop-out ( CRDO ) provision helps contributors maintain their level of pensionable earnings by excluding eligible child rearing years from their contributory period when calculating their CPP benefits. The purpose of the CRDO is to ensure that a CPP contributor will not be penalized for periods of low or zero earnings while they cared for a child under 7 years of age. The provision may help a contributor to qualify for benefits or to increase the amount payable.

The CPP Child Rearing Provision ( CRP ) has 2 ways to help contributors maintain their level of pensionable earnings during the time when the child was under 7 years old: excluding eligible child rearing years from their CPP calculation. This is called the Child Rearing Drop-out ( CRDO ); and dropping earnings into the CPP calculation of the enhanced portion of the contributory period. This is called the Child Rearing Drop-In ( CRDI ).

The Child Rearing Provision (CRP) may help an applicant qualify for CPPD benefits or receive a higher DSB amount. The CRP can also be used to improve a Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO). The CRP applies only to the time period when the individual had little or no earnings and was the primary caregiver for children under the age of 7. The CRP includes the Child Rearing Drop-Out (CRDO), which allows for the removal of months or years of low or no earnings to be removed from an individual's contributory period when calculating a CPP pension or benefit. As of January 1, 2019, the CRP includes the Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) which adds Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) to periods of low or zero earnings when calculating the CPP enhancement component of a benefit for the time when the child was under the age of 7. The CRDI will not help individuals meet the eligibility requirements or Minimum Qualifying Period, as the CRDI only applies to the enhanced earnings calculation. When a client is in pay for a DSB and has UPE attributed from the CRDI for any year(s) during which they are in pay, it triggers a recalculation of the additional components of their DSB every year following the attribution of the CRDI UPE. Recalculations occur in January to coincide with the indexation of the DSB entitlement. For more information, Child Rearing Provision (Scenario) If using the CRP can help an applicant to qualify for CPPD benefits or improve their LPDOO, CPPD Earnings and Contributions Criteria (Scenario)

The Child Rearing Provision (CRP) helps an applicant maintain their level of pensionable earnings by excluding periods of low or no earnings during the years spent raising children under the age of 7. The CRP can help an individual meet or improve the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) or increase the monthly rate of their CPPD benefit. For more information, Child Rearing Provision (Scenario)

Disability Drop-in values and Adjusted Pensionable Earnings when calculating a benefit Disability Drop-in (DDI) values are dropped in during the Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (APE) calculation for an RTR or an SVR pension. The first additional or second additional DDI value will only be dropped into the benefit calculation if it is greater than the actual first additional or second additional APE amount and is to the client's benefit. If the DSB recipient has received additional pension credits as a result of a credit split or has had Child Rearing Drop-In (CRDI) amounts attributed for the period of disability, the actual APE may be higher than the DDI amount. The DDI amount cannot be attributed to any month that is outside the period the client is deemed disabled. The DDI and the actual APE values must be broken down into monthly amounts and compared because there could be some months where the DDI amount is greater and others where the actual APE is greater. The greater of the monthly DDI amount or the actual APE is applied to each month excluded due to disability for the year the amount is attributed and used in the benefit calculation. Using Taylor from Example 1, let us assume Taylor's DSB converted into an RTR pension when they reached age 65 in January of 2024. The Average Yearly Maximum Pensionable Earnings (AYMPE) used to calculate the RTR-FBC for an RTR is: The AYMPE of the year the DSB started, if a DSB was paid after age 60; or The AYMPE of the year the RTR starts, if there was not a DSB paid after age 60. The phase-in factor must be applied to the first additional DDI values for 2021-2023. To determine the Yearly DDI Value with a Phase-in, the formula is: 1st DDI factor (rounded to 5 decimal places) × phase in factor (rounded to 4 decimal places) × AYMPE used in the calculation of the Retirement or Survivor = Yearly DDI factor (rounded to 0 decimal places) In Taylor's case, they were paid a DSB after age 60 and it began in 2021, so the 2021 AYMPE of $57,780 will be used. 2021 - 0.64966 × 0.5000 × $57,780 = $18,769 2022 - 0.64966 × 0.7500 × $57,780 = $28,153 2023 - 0.64966 × 1.0000 × $57,780 = $37,537 To determine the monthly DDI, divide the DDI value by 12. 2021 - $18,769 ∕ 12 = $1,564.08 2022 - $28,153 ∕ 12 = $2,346.08 2023 - $37,537 ∕ 12 = $3,128.08 The phase-in factor must also be applied to first additional APE values for 2021-2023. To determine the yearly APE Value with a phase-in factor, the formula is: (CPP UPE + QPP UPE, rounded to 0 decimal places) × Adjustment Factor (rounded to 5 decimal places) × Phase-in factor (rounded to 4 decimal places) As we saw in Example 1, Taylor's UPE in 2021 was $40,410. In Taylor's case, they were paid a DSB after age 60 and it began in 2021, so the 2021 AYMPE of $57,780 will be divided by the 2021 YMPE amount of $61,600 to find the adjustment factor of 0.93799. The phase-in factor for 2021 is 0.5000. 40,410 × 0.93799 × 0.5000 = $18,952 To determine the monthly amount of the first additional APE, divide the APE amount by the number of contributory months with earnings and contributions. 2021 - $18,952 ∕ 12 = $1,579.33 2022 - $0 ∕ 12 = $0 2023 - $0 ∕ 12 = $0 Compare the monthly DDI amounts and the monthly APE amount and apply the greater amount. 2021 - The APE amount of $1,579.33 is higher than the DDI amount of $1,564.08 therefore the client gets 12 months of APE. 2022 - The DDI amount of $2,346.08 is higher than the APE amount of $0 therefore the client gets 12 months of DDI. 2023 - The DDI amount of $3,128.08 is higher than the APE amount of $0 therefore the client gets 12 months of DDI.

Sarah had two periods of disability. The Date of Onset (DOO) of their first disability is September 2021. That first disability ended in March 2023. The value of their first additional Disability Drop-in (DDI) for this first disability was calculated at 0.62718, or 62.718% of the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE). There is no second additional factor as contributions to the second additional do not start until January 2024. The DOO of their second disability is May 2026. Calculation of the first additional contributory period DDI Ratios are calculated by dividing the first additional unadjusted pensionable earnings by the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the 6 years (72 months) prior to the onset of disability. Each ratio is then multiplied by the number of months in the first additional contributory period for that year. The 6-year average is used because those are the earnings considered when determining eligibility for a CPP DSB benefit. Providing a 70% credit is consistent with most private disability insurance plans in Canada. Drop-ins are calculated when the department converts unadjusted additional pensionable earnings into adjusted additional pensionable earnings. Therefore, they are dropped into the benefit calculation and not the individual’s earnings history. The month they are deemed disabled is included in the range for calculating the DDI values for the first and second additional contributory periods; however, the DDI starts the month after they are deemed disabled. As of January 1, 2019, (first additional), and January 1, 2024, (second additional), the contributory period of CPPD beneficiaries will also be credited with drop-in amounts. The Disability Drop-in ( DDI ) provision is applicable only where the disability date of onset is after December 31, 2018. The DDI amounts are attributed only if they are advantageous for the disabled contributor. They might not necessarily be to their advantage, as while the contributor cannot work and contribute during the disability period, they may have received credits: as a result of a credit-split following divorce or separation; or from the child rearing drop-in . The drop-in amounts are used only for the purpose of calculating future benefit amounts, apart from the DSB benefit (i.e. the retirement pension and SVR pension). DDIs are applied only at the time of a benefit calculation. In 2018, Québec enhanced the QPP in the same way as the CPP enhancement. Therefore, for dual contributors, the first additional and second additional pensionable earnings under the QPP will be taken into account in calculating the DDIs. If, in the 6 years before the disability, there are child rearing drop-in amounts, these amounts will be used in the calculation of the amount of the DDI . The period covered by the DDI is the month-based period of time that an individual is disabled (rather than the period of time in receipt of a DSB benefit, which starts the fourth month after an individual is deemed disabled). Therefore, in those years where a disability starts or ends, the amount of the drop-in is prorated to take into account the fraction of the year that an individual is disabled.

The Child Rearing Drop-Out (CRDO) excludes periods that the deceased client had low or no earnings while they were the primary caregiver for children under the age of 7. The CRDO can help applicants qualify for a DTH benefit, SVR pension or Surviving Child's benefit. If the CRDO may help the applicant meet the MQP, send the Supply: Sending applications and information (ISS-6191) letter to the applicant before making your decision. For more information, refer to Child Rearing Provision (Policy) and Child Rearing Provision (Policy) Child Rearing Provision (Scenario)

The Child Rearing Drop-In ( CRDI ) only applies to the enhanced component of the CPP , while the Child Rearing Drop-Out ( CRDO ) will continue to apply to the base CPP . The CRDI protects individuals from reduced wages due to providing care for a child under age 7 and will increase the amount of DSB benefit, RTR and SVR pensions paid by the CPP enhancement. In each year while a child is under age 7, a credit equal to the average of the primary caregiver’s earnings in the 5 years prior to the birth or adoption of a child will be “dropped-in” if that amount is higher than their actual earnings. The CRDI does not help individuals meet the Minimum Qualifying Period eligibility requirement for benefits. Clients are not required to submit a separate application for CRDI . The department will leverage the information provided in the Request for a Child Rearing Provision (ISP1640) form. When the client applies for the Child Rearing Provision they are applying for both the CRDO and CRDI .

The Disability Drop-In ( DDI ) only applies to the enhanced component of the CPP , while the Disability Exclusion will continue to apply to the base CPP . The DDI is provided to individuals with disabilities. It is equal to 70% of their average earnings in the six years prior to the onset of the disability. The DDI protects the value of their RTR pension and any subsequent survivor’s pension they may leave to their families. Earnings will be “dropped in" or credited for the years when individuals received the CPP DSB , increasing the amount of their RTR pensions (as well as their SVR pension). The DDI does not help individuals meet eligibility and Minimum Qualifying Period for benefits. Clients are not required to submit a separate application for DDI . The Department will leverage the information it has to calculate or apply the DDI . Additional system changes related to the calculation of the second additional component of the CPP will be implemented at a later date.

The Child Rearing Drop-In ( CRDI ) and Disability Drop-In ( DDI ) provisions were introduced on January 1, 2019, to help protect the value of CPP benefits during periods of low or no earnings. The drop-in provisions only apply to the enhanced component (first additional and second additional) of the CPP . The CRDI protects the enhanced component of CPP benefits of individuals who reduce their earnings to be the primary caregiver of young children. It has the same eligibility criteria as the Child Rearing Drop-Out ( CRDO ) provision in the base CPP but is calculated differently. The DDI protects the enhanced component of CPP benefits for individuals with severe and prolonged disabilities and is calculated differently from the disability exclusion, which will continue in the base CPP . On May 27, 2023, system functionalities were introduced to calculate drop-in credits for the first additional component of the CPP . For clients who begin receiving a CPP benefit in June 2023 or later and who are eligible for CRDI and/or DDI , drop-in credits will be calculated as part of the adjudication process. Accounts in pay with a Child Rearing Provision that include a period between January 2019 and May 2023 will require re-adjudication to calculate the CRDI component of the provision. Accounts in pay for a CPP RTR pension and/or SVR pension that had a previous period of disability with a date of onset on or after January 2019, will require re-adjudication to calculate the DDI . The re-adjudication process is currently scheduled to begin in June 2023 and will calculate the CRDI and DDI credits and pay any retroactive amount to the client. For more information, refer to CPP Enhancement and Triennial Review Reforms—Child-Rearing Drop-In and Disability Drop-In Provisions (Implementation Bulletin) . CPP Enhancement and Triennial Review Reforms—Child-Rearing Drop-In and Disability Drop-In Provisions (Implementation Bulletin)

The CRDI protects individuals with low or no earnings, who are the primary caregiver of a child under age 7, and increases the amount of the benefit paid by the CPP enhancement. A contributor who is eligible for the CRDI will receive earnings dropped into the calculation of the enhanced component of their CPP benefit for the time when the child was under age 7, for a period that includes 2019 or later. Each year that a child is under age 7, credits equal the average of the primary caregiver's earnings in the 5 years prior to the birth or adoption of a child. These credits will be dropped in if that amount is higher than their actual earnings. These credits become 1st Additional Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings ( UPE ) on the individual's Record of Earnings. The first UPE dropped in as a result of the CRDI are eligible for a Credit Split provision. The CRDI only applies to the enhanced component of the CPP , while the Child-Rearing Drop-Out ( CRDO ) will continue to apply to the base CPP . Clients are not required to submit a separate request for the CRDI ; information submitted on the Request for a Child Rearing Provision (ISP1640) form will be used to determine eligibility to both the CRDO and CRDI .

The DDI applies to individuals who were previously in receipt of a CPP DSB with a date of onset on or after January 2019. This new drop in will attribute to their first additional contributory period an amount equal to 70% of the average of their first additional pensionable earnings in the 6 years (72 months) preceding the date of onset. It is only applied when calculating the individual's CPP RTR or SVR pensions. The DDI provision protects the value of their RTR pension and any subsequent SVR pension owed to the survivor. The DDI only applies to the enhanced component of the CPP , while the Disability Exclusion will continue to apply to the base CPP .

The Canada Child Tax Benefit (1998-2016)—Income-tested. The CCB (2016-present)—Income-tested. An individual or their spouse or common-law partner who was in the Canadian Armed Forces and posted outside of Canada between 1966 and 1973 is considered to have been a Family Allowance recipient, although the Family Allowance was not paid to them during that time. The following eligibility conditions must exist before a contributor can be considered under the Child Rearing Provision ( CRP ): The contributor or the contributor's survivor must have made an application for a pension or benefit under the CPP . The CRP declaration is also built into the application form for the CPP Retirement ( RTR ) pension as well as the application for CPP Disability ( DSB ) benefits. The contributor must be deemed to have been either a Family Allowance recipient or the individual eligible for the Canada Child Benefit ( CCB ) for the children for which the CRP is requested. This condition is met when the contributor: received Family Allowance payments; or remained at home and was the primary caregiver for the child(ren) under 7 years of age and is the spouse or common-law partner of the person who received Family Allowance payments and the Family Allowance recipient waives their rights to the CRP ; and/or is the individual eligible for the CCB ; or is the person who would have been eligible for the CCB had they applied for the benefit and no other person was considered to be an eligible individual in respect of the same child for the same period of time. The contributor must have been the Family Allowance recipient and/or a CCB -eligible individual for at least one child under 7 years of age, however, the month of the child's: birth cannot be included since the Family Allowance and the CCB are not payable for that month; and 7th birthday is included.

The level of misrepresentation is important for the overall penalty determination process because it helps to determine the maximum penalty amount that can be applied. First misrepresentation A first misrepresentation occurs when there are no records of a previous penalty or conviction under the same program, CPP or OAS, within the last ten years. The maximum penalty amount for the first level of misrepresentation is: 10% of the gross overpayment amount (resulting from the misrepresentation); or 10% of the maximum monthly benefit or pension payable at the time of the misrepresentation if there was no overpayment. Subsequent misrepresentation A subsequent misrepresentation occurs when: the individual makes another misrepresentation under the same program (e.g. CPP or OAS); and the penalty imposition date for that misrepresentation is within ten years from the date of imposition of a prior OAS or CPP penalty or conviction. The maximum penalty amount for a subsequent misrepresentation is: 20% of the gross overpayment amount (resulting from the misrepresentation); or 20% of the maximum monthly benefit or pension payable at the time of the misrepresentation if there was no overpayment. Multiple misrepresentations discovered at the same time When there is a false statement or declaration made under both the CPP and OAS program, each program can impose its own penalty. If there are multiple misrepresentations detected under the same program during the same investigation, only one penalty will be imposed.

First misrepresentation A first misrepresentation occurs when the Department determines that an individual has knowingly made a misrepresentation for the first time. Even if the statement or declaration contains several falsehoods, it is still considered as one misrepresentation because it all relates to the same event. The initial value of the penalty percentage for a first misrepresentation is 10% of the overpayment amount. If there is no overpayment, then the initial value of the penalty is 10% of the maximum monthly benefit or pension payable at the time of the misrepresentation. Subsequent misrepresentation When the Minister becomes aware of a new misrepresentation by the same individual under the OAS or CPP, and the penalty imposition date for that misrepresentation is within 10 years from the date of imposition of a prior OAS or CPP penalty or conviction, this new misrepresentation would be considered as a subsequent misrepresentation. Any misrepresentation identified after an individual has been notified in writing, and beyond the reconsideration and appeal period, is treated as a subsequent misrepresentation. A subsequent misrepresentation is to be penalized at a higher rate than a first misrepresentation. The initial value of the penalty percentage for a subsequent misrepresentation is 20% of the overpayment amount. If there is no overpayment, then the initial value of the penalty is 20% of the maximum monthly benefit or pension payable at the time of the misrepresentation.

When the Integrity Services Branch determines that a misrepresentation was knowingly made and makes a recommendation to apply a penalty, determine the penalty amount to be imposed. To determine the penalty amount, consider the following: The maximum legislated penalty allowed for each misrepresentation is $10,000. In a first misrepresentation, the penalty is based on an amount not more than 10% of the accumulated overpayment or, if there is no overpayment, on an amount not more than 10% of the maximum monthly benefit rate for that program. In a subsequent misrepresentation, the penalty amount is based on an amount not more than 20% of the accumulated overpayment or, if there is no overpayment, on an amount not more than 20% of the maximum monthly benefit rate for that program. To determine whether a misrepresentation should be penalized as a first or subsequent misrepresentation , the Minister must be aware of the subsequent misrepresentation and it must be within 10 years from the date a previous penalty was imposed. The penalty amount may be reduced depending on an individual’s mitigating circumstances, outlined in the Report of Investigation. Mitigating circumstances determined to be valid may allow the penalty amount to be reduced by any percentage up to 100%. The minimum penalty amount is $0.00. A $0.00 amount still counts as a penalty. This is an important consideration when establishing a subsequent misrepresentation.

Once it is determined that an individual has knowingly misrepresented, mitigating circumstances must be considered. Mitigating circumstances are situations, facts or actions that can offer some explanation of the individual's actions and lead to a possible reduction of the penalty amount. Although these circumstances offer some explanation, they do not excuse the misrepresentation. The Integrity Services Branch (ISB) will investigate the information surrounding these mitigating circumstances and will clearly document them in their Report of Investigation (ROI). The ISB will not take mitigating circumstances into consideration when making a recommendation to impose a penalty. However, you must consider the mitigating circumstances when determining the penalty amount. For more information, refer to Suspected Fraud and/or Misrepresentation (Policy) and Suspected Fraud and/or Misrepresentation (Policy) Assessing Mitigating Circumstances (Action)

“Mitigating circumstances” are situations, facts or actions that do not condone the misrepresentation(s) but can provide some explanation to the individual's actions, which could lead to a reduction of up to 100% of the penalty amount. It may also include situations when the individual takes responsibility for their actions or assists in the investigation. Mitigating circumstances are only considered after the criterion of “knowingly” has been established and a penalty has been recommended. Many personal situations, as well as other factors, can be considered as mitigating circumstances. There are two types of mitigating circumstances: Situations present at the time of the misrepresentation To be considered as mitigating circumstances, situations provided or found must: be present at the time of the misrepresentation; be credible; and help explain the individual's actions. The existence of mitigating circumstances must never be assumed. There must be clear indication that such circumstances exist. The following examples attempt to provide an overview of situations or factors that might constitute mitigating circumstances and may justify a lower penalty. The following is not an exhaustive list: Physical or mental illness serious illness of a close relative or immediate family member; medical circumstances or condition of the beneficiary or individual; or compulsive disorders (such as addictions, gambling, drug, or alcohol dependency, etc.). Emotional death of spouse, partner, relative or immediate family member; financial, physical or mental abuse by a spouse, partner, family member, or other; or separation from a spouse or partner (loss of marital income). Other the beneficiary or individual demonstrates an urgent need due to personal or family circumstance(s); personal theft; other debt obligations; or states of emergency such as wildfires, flooding, earthquakes, etc. Other factors or situations present at the time of the investigation or penalty Other factors or situations that are only present at the time of the investigation or penalty may be considered as mitigating circumstances to reduce a penalty to be imposed. The following is not an exhaustive list: individual expresses genuine regret; individual admits to the misrepresentation without resistance or further misrepresentation; and individual cooperates with, or even assists in the investigation, providing documentation, etc. In addition, the following situations may develop after the misrepresentation but are still present by the time the penalty is applied and may further be considered as mitigating circumstances: individual now lacks the ability to understand, or to judge right from wrong (for example, individual is deemed medically incapable or is incapacitated). Deterrent value Administrative penalties have an important deterrent value in discouraging individuals from committing further misrepresentations and protecting the integrity of the programs. When it is determined that an individual has knowingly made a misrepresentation, the delegated departmental representative must review the Report of Investigation and the individual's file for any mitigating circumstances, to determine if the penalty amount should be adjusted accordingly. The responsible BDS official must rely upon written record and documentation in order to identify any “mitigating circumstances”. However, as a rule, individuals do not need to provide proof. All decisions are made on a case-by-case basis, and a record of all decisions made shall be maintained. The records of decision shall help BDS determine which level of mitigating circumstances may be appropriate. Assessing mitigating circumstances A proper assessment of both types of mitigating circumstances constitutes the cornerstone of the Minister's discretionary authority to establish the amount of a penalty. The Minister always has the discretion to determine if mitigating circumstances exist and to consider those circumstances when setting the penalty amount. Subject to the judgement of the delegated authority, agent or department representative, case-related mitigating circumstances shall have the following impact when determining if there are mitigating circumstances and how significant they are in reducing the penalty amount: where the mitigating circumstances are very significant , the penalty amount will be reduced on the scale 80, 90 or 100% ; where the mitigating circumstances are significant , the penalty amount will be reduced on the scale 50, 60 or 70% ; where the mitigating circumstances are moderately significant , the penalty amount will be reduced on the scale 10, 20, 30 or 40% ; or where there are no mitigating circumstances 0% reduction and full penalty. The existence of increments, however, does not imply a "mechanical" approach to the consideration of case-related circumstances. There is no correlation such as "one case-related circumstance equals one increment. Any single case-related circumstance may be more significant, or less so, and be weighted accordingly. Many situations or factors may be considered as mitigating circumstances. Judgement will be required in determining if case-related circumstances exist to a degree warranting consideration. Consideration should be given to the individual's particular situation and severity, from moderately significant to very significant. The number of circumstances should also be considered in the reduction and may help explain the individual's actions at the time of the misrepresentation.

There must be clear indication that mitigating circumstances existed.The information surrounding these circumstances must be identified and documented by the Integrity Services Branch in their Report of Investigation. An administrative penalty is an amount that is charged to a beneficiary or third party who knowingly misrepresented information in relation to CPP or OAS benefits or pensions. The intention of an administrative penalty is: to be a deterrent to discourage individuals from committing further misrepresentations; and to protect the integrity of the programs. The imposition of administrative penalties was implemented on July 21, 2011. Misrepresentations that occurred before that date are not subject to an administrative penalty. The ISB determines that an individual knowingly misrepresented. They are responsible for making a recommendation to Benefits Delivery Services (BDS) to impose an administrative penalty. Once complete, the ISB Report of Investigation (ROI) will be returned to BDS where it will be added to the individual's file for action. The report will include Prior Offences/Misrepresentation, Facts, Contributing Circumstances and Recommendation sections. Contact the ISB immediately if you have any questions or clarifications needed regarding the investigation or the recommendation of an administrative penalty before taking any action on the account. Under no circumstances are you to contact the individual during the assessment phase of a penalty. For more information, refer to Suspected Fraud and/or Misrepresentation (Policy) and Suspected Fraud and/or Misrepresentation (Policy) Administrative penalties (Policy)

When a couple reconciles and the separation was for a period less than the required time period to be considered separated, the marital status will not change, meaning that the couple will continue to be considered married or common-law. When a married couple reconciles after the required time has elapsed to be considered separated, they are considered married again effective the month following the month of reconciliation. When a common-law couple reconciles after the required time has elapsed to be considered separated, they are required to live together for one year before they are considered common-law again. The following describes how CPP and OAS benefits are affected when a couple reconciles: Program Benefits CPP A new Pension Sharing application is required to resume the provision after a separation of more than 12 months. A Credit Split application can be withdrawn if the criteria to withdraw are met. Refer to Withdraw an Application (Scenario) . Withdraw an Application (Scenario) A separated spouse with a credit split approved on or after January 1, 2025 is not eligible for an SVR pension after the death of their same separated spouse. However, if the couple reconciled for at least one year immediately before the death of their spouse, they may be eligible for the SVR pension if all other requirements are met. Program Benefits OAS The GIS is calculated based on combined income the month following the month: the one-year requirement of living together is met if the couple resumes a common-law relationship; or the couple resumes living together if they are married. A new ALW benefit application is required after a separation of more than 3 months as the lifetime renewal designation (i.e. GIS for Life) is lost.

A couple is considered to be "reconciled" when they have resumed cohabitation. Separated married couples OAS benefits When a separated married couple reconciles, they are considered to be “married”, effective the month after the month of reconciliation. Separated common-law partners OAS benefits When a separated common-law couple reconciles after a breakdown period of less than 3 months, the marital status does not change from the "married rate". A separation of more than 3 months is seen as evidence that the relationship has ended. If more than 3 months have passed after the month in which the separation occurred and the couple resumes cohabitation, they are required to live together for one year before they may be considered as common-law partners under the OAS Act.

If there is a dispute between the parties about the periods when each individual or agency had decision-making responsibility for the -18 child, the party requesting such a change must provide the following documents to the Department in support of their request: a court order detailing the allocation of decision-making responsibility and parenting time for the -18 child to an individual or agency; or a written statement from the individual or agency requesting the change which includes details about the dates the change in decision-making responsibility occurred; and a description of the circumstances that led to the change in parenting time, causing the change in decision-making responsibility. In such situations, to verify the date of the change in decision-making responsibility between the parties in the dispute, one or more of the following documents should be obtained: the record of the person who received the Canada Child Benefit for the periods under review; a written statement from third parties (e.g. family physician, school teacher) who are familiar with the situation; or separation agreements or court orders. The following documents can be used as additional supporting evidence: school registration forms; provincial health care registration; and private insurance records. Review the information or the evidence to determine who the child lives with (i.e. schedule). The disabled contributor or survivor must have 20% of parenting time or more to be the eligible payee. Once the actual periods of decision-making responsibility are verified through examination of the required evidence, separate -18 Children's benefit payments can be made to each party for the appropriate periods.
To change the payee of a -18 Children's benefit, the person or agency who requests the change must submit documentation to the Department to substantiate their claim of parenting time.

In most situations, a request for a change in payee for a -18 child is not disputed by any other parties. The start date for the payee after the Department receives a request to change the decision-making responsibility and parenting time is the month following the notification of the change. The effective date of the change in decision-making responsibility for payment purposes is the month after the month that a notification of the change in decision-making responsibility is received. However, notification of a change in decision-making responsibility may be received months or even years after a change has occurred. In these situations, the party requesting the change in decision-making responsibility must provide documents that support their claim. In some cases the evidence provided by the requesting party demonstrates that they did not understand the meaning of decision-making responsibility. For example, the requester may state that they provided financial support for the -18 child but confirm that they had no parenting time for the -18 child during the disputed period.

Absences from Canada may be considered as periods of Canadian residence, and could change your eligibility and entitlement if you were accompanying a spouse/common-law partner or were an accompanying dependant yourself, and if the absences from Canada stated on your application fall under one of the following circumstances: stationed abroad as a member of the Canadian Forces; missionary activities performed abroad; working abroad for the United Nations; attending school or university abroad; performing services abroad for an international charitable organization; working in lumbering, harvesting, fishing or other seasonal employment; a transport worker on trains, aircraft, ships or buses running between Canada and points outside Canada or other similar employment; temporary absences exceeding one year that do not interrupt Canadian residence (i.e. extended vacation, caring for a sick relative, etc.). If any of your absences fall under the circumstances above, notify Service Canada in writing within 90 days of the date of this letter.

Applicants may indicate that they lived outside of Canada, unaware that the period abroad could be deemed as Canadian residence. Although a complete residence statement may not require further review, it is important to consider whether absences of more than one year could be deemed as Canadian residence. Review the application and the residence statement for indications that the stated absences can be deemed as Canadian residence and do not interrupt residence. The following are some of the factors that could indicate that an absence can be deemed as Canadian residence: the applicant made CPP contributions during periods of absence; the applicant or their current or ex-spouse or common-law partner is or was a member of the Canadian Forces; or the applicant is or was a missionary or member of an international charitable organization (e.g. the applicant states their name is Reverend John Smith and has multiple absences from Canada). For more information, Defining Residence (Policy) Documentary evidence for specified circumstances Specific documents must be provided as documentary evidence depending on the type of absence. Applicants must provide official documentation to support that they were employed or engaged outside of Canada by one of the specified occupations or organizations. For example, a Record of Employment or Military Personnel Records Resumé can be used to support the applicant's employment or engagement outside of Canada. If the applicant declares that they returned to Canada within 6 months of completing their employment or activity, or if they reached the age of 65 while still engaged abroad, no further documents are required. Family members and specified circumstances A family member refers to the applicant's: spouse or common-law partner; mother; father; mother-in-law; father-in-law; brother; sister; and any natural, adoptive or foster children. Similar documentary requirements apply to family members living abroad with the applicant who is absent under specified circumstances. Family members who lived abroad with the applicant must provide documentary evidence to support that they accompanied the applicant who was employed or engaged outside of Canada under a specified circumstance. The supporting documentary evidence must be on an official letterhead and signed by an official. The date of return to Canada indicated on the family member’s residence statement must be within 6 months after the return or death of their family member upon whom they are or were dependent. Unless there is a discrepancy or inconsistency on file, documents to prove the date of return are not required. Changes in marital status while absent from Canada under a specified circumstance An applicant who is absent under one of the specified circumstances and exceptions who enters into a marriage or a common-law union, needs to provide documentary evidence to support their marriage or common-law union. For more information, Defining Residence (Policy)

Generally, an individual's residence is determined by the location and activity they themselves undertook while outside of Canada. However, the OAS regulations also recognize that there can be situations where individuals find themselves absent from Canada while accompanying their spouse or common-law partner. Spouses and common-law partners residing with an individual absent from Canada under a specified circumstance or attending school or university In situations where individuals are absent from Canada while accompanying their spouse or common-law partner, their absence from Canada can be considered residence in Canada provided the individual on whom they are dependent is absent from Canada under one of the specified circumstances or for the purpose of attending school or university. In simpler terms, if an individual is considered a resident of Canada by virtue of a specified circumstance, their spouse or common-law partner will also be considered a resident of Canada during this period. The spouse or common-law partner's absence while accompanying the individual on whom they are dependent will only be considered as Canadian residence if: the spouse or common-law partner returns to Canada either before or within 6 months after the return of the individual on whom they are dependent; the spouse or common-law partner returns within 6 months of the death of the individual on whom they were dependent; or the spouse or common-law partner reaches an age at which they would be eligible for the OAS pension while absent from Canada. If the spouse or common-law partner worked and contributed to the social security scheme of the other country for the same period, these periods may not be considered deemed periods of residence in Canada. Entering into a marriage or common-law relationship while absent from Canada under a specified circumstance If a resident of Canada who was absent under a specified circumstance marries or enters into a common-law relationship during the absence,the spouse or common-law partner must count the period after the date of the marriage or date the common-law partnership as residence in Canada. The spouse or common-law partner's absence while accompanying the individual on whom they are dependent will only be considered as Canadian residence if: the spouse or common-law partner returns to Canada either before or within 6 months after the return of the individual on whom they are dependent; the spouse or common-law partner returns within 6 months of the death of the individual on whom they were dependent; or the spouse or common-law partner reaches an age at which they would be eligible for the OAS pension while absent from Canada. If the spouse or common-law partner worked and contributed to the social security scheme of the other country for the same period, these periods may not be considered deemed periods of residence in Canada. Dependants residing with an individual absent from Canada under a specified circumstance Similar requirements apply to dependants, including an individual's mother, father, mother-in-law, father-in-law, brother, sister and the natural, adoptive or foster child(ren) living abroad with the individual who is absent from Canada under a specified circumstance. These individuals may be considered residents in Canada during this period provided they: return within 6 months of the return of the individual on whom they were dependent; return within 6 months of the death of the individual on whom they were dependent; or reach an age where they would be eligible for an OAS pension under the OAS Act while absent from Canada.

Although an individual may be physically present in Canada, this does not always mean that these periods can be considered as Canadian residence for OAS purposes. Situations may arise where you need to obtain clarification to determine if a period in Canada should be considered as residence or presence. There are also situations where an applicant may reside in Canada but is not considered a resident of Canada. You must determine whether the period should be considered residence or presence if an applicant claims residence in Canada, and: made contributions to the social security scheme of a fo reign country; or was living in Canada but not considered a resident of Canada for specific reasons as outlined in the OAS Regulations. Refer to KA-03434 Validate Periods not Considered Residence in Canada (Action) Evaluations of Canadian residence versus presence occur when: the applicant entered Canada via a temporary legal status (e.g. visitors, international students, work permit) and was absent from Canada before obtaining a permanent legal status in Canada (e.g. landed immigrant, permanent resident, Canadian citizen); the applicant was in Canada via a temporary legal status and never obtained a permanent legal status in Canada; or the applicant maintained strong ties with and spent a significant amount of time in another country. In these situations, an applicant's intention to reside in Canada permanently cannot be assumed. Contact the applicant to clarify their intent to reside in Canada permanently to determine if the period in Canada should be considered as residence or presence. For more information, Defining Residence (Policy)

The OAS pension, ALW benefit and ALWS benefit are based, in part, on the applicant's years of Canadian residence (actual or deemed). The applicant must meet the minimum residence requirements to be eligible for the pension or benefit. When an applicant applies for an OAS pension, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit, their declared residence can be accepted without the need for further review or additional documents if: a signed, complete residence statement is provided; there are no inconsistencies between the residence statement and documentation on file; the applicant has a permanent Canadian legal status (e.g. Landed Immigrant, Permanent Resident or Canadian Citizenship); and the applicant did not declare any absences from Canada after the later of; their 18th birthday; or their initial arrival into Canada. An International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) may allow an applicant to meet the minimum residence requirements to be eligible for a pension or benefit under the OAS program. Residence for OAS purposes is determined by ensuring that the time an individual is physically in Canada is actually residence and not merely presence. Similarly, an individual who may not be physically (i.e. present) in Canada, may be considered as having residence in Canada (deemed). The documentary evidence to support dates of entry into, departures from and re-entries to Canada to establish periods of residence in Canada may not always be required as described below. However, where applicable, the requirement for documentary evidence when determining residence rather than presence, and when deeming periods of absences from Canada under specified circumstances, still applies. The policy Defining Residence describes the circumstances when these residence determinations are required. Section 20 of the OAS Regulations does not specifically require documentary evidence to support the residence history on an OAS application or residence statement. An application or residence statement that has been signed and that provides a statement of all periods of residence and absences from Canada relevant to eligibility and entitlement fulfills the residence requirement. Defining Residence Since June 5, 2017, provided the eligibility requirements of age and legal status are met, residence for all initial OAS pension applications processed under domestic legislation can be established through a review of the residence history on the application against all available documents currently on file. If there are no inconsistencies between the residence history provided on the application and any documents on file, there is no requirement for proof of all dates of entry into, departures from and re-entries into Canada. On November 20, 2017, the policy was extended to include all initial OAS pension applications processed under an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA). As of July 2019, this policy was extended to situations when confirmation of residence in Canada is required by a foreign institution with which Canada has an ISSA in force. This operational policy applies to both full and partial pensions, including those that may qualify under transitional rules or ISSAs and all OAS applications. This also includes applications for the Allowance or the Allowance for the Survivor benefit and conversion applications. This operational policy must be applied when there are no inconsistencies between the residence history or residence statement and the available documents currently on file, even if proof is missing for some or all of the dates of entry into, departures from and re-entries into Canada. Any requests for reconsideration will require applicants to provide documentary evidence of residence, even if the initial decision on the application was made under this interim process. However, if the beneficiary has requested a reconsideration of an approved benefit under the above policy on the basis that the entitlement is incorrect and a specific period is being disputed, it would be acceptable to request documentation for that period only. Documentary evidence to support residence is waived for individuals who are selected for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension. These individuals must meet all the eligibility requirements for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension through a combination of data elements when an individual is in the following situations: was not selected for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension; submits a paper application to apply for a full OAS pension under the 40 year rule; and meets the data elements to substantiate eligibility for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension. In these cases, an individual may have their eligibility determined for an OAS pension by using the same combination of data elements. In October 2013, the Department was given the authority through a Service Level Agreement to go directly to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada to verify the initial date of entry for residence purposes as long as the Department obtains the written consent from the applicant or their authorized representative.

To be considered eligible for an OAS pension and, if applicable, the related supplementary benefits such as the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), Allowance ( ALW ) and the Allowance for the Survivor ( ALWS ), the applicant must have sufficient residence in Canada to meet the legislated eligibility requirements. There are several ways in which an individual's residence can satisfy the residence eligibility requirements for OAS benefits. The residence requirements vary depending on whether an individual qualifies for a partial or a full OAS pension or related income tested benefit.

Residence in Canada is one of the three primary eligibility factors for OAS benefits. In order to pay benefits under the Old Age Security Act (OAS Act), the Department must ensure that the residence, age and legal status requirements have been met. Residence Specified circumstances and exceptions to residence rules There are several provisions where individuals may be deemed a resident of Canada despite being physically absent. These exceptions to the general residence rules are frequently referred to as specified circumstances . The deeming of residence is also considered for individuals who are subject to the legislation of another country's pension scheme with which Canada has an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) in force. At the same time, provisions exist that prevent the Department from considering certain periods of physical presence to be considered as residence in Canada. The following subsections describe the various circumstances under which an individual may be considered to reside in Canada despite being physically absent. Residence requirements To be found eligible for an OAS pension and where applicable, the related supplementary benefits: GIS, ALW , and ALWS ; the Department must be satisfied that the applicant has sufficient residence in Canada to meet the legislated eligibility requirements. There are several ways an individual will satisfy the residence eligibility requirements for an OAS pension. Similarly, there are various residence requirements depending on whether an individual qualifies for a partial or full OAS pension, or a related income-tested benefit (i.e. GIS, ALW , ALWS ). Residence must not be confused with presence. To be considered a resident of Canada for the purpose of OAS benefits, an individual must ordinarily live and make their home in Canada. An individual is considered present in Canada when they are physically present in any part of Canada. An individual who is present in Canada is physically within Canada,but is not necessarily a resident of Canada. Similarly, an individual can be considered a resident of Canada although they are not present in Canada. Some scenarios involving residence versus presence include: An individual resides in Canada but is not considered to be a resident of Canada (e.g. foreign diplomats); An individual is present in Canada but does not reside in Canada (e.g. United States residents who own a summer cottage in Canada); An individual resides in another country but is considered a resident of Canada (e.g. members of the Canadian Armed Forces, Canadian diplomats). The Department must determine whether an individual is a resident of Canada or simply present in Canada. When making this determination, the primary assumption is that an individual can only be resident of one country at any given time. While an individual may own property in many countries and spend some time in each of them, only one country will be considered their place of residence. This country will be the one with which the individual has the most significant attachment. An individual's attachment to a country is measured by evaluating the residential ties between the individual and the country.
