These procedures provide you with the steps to process a Statement of Estimated Income after Retirement or Reduction in Pension Income Year 20XX (ISP-3041) form, commonly referred to as an Option.

The following table provides you with guidelines for accepting and processing a Statement of Estimated Income after Retirement or Reduction in Pension Income Year 20XX (ISP3041) form that is received before the event.

The Statement of Estimated Income after Retirement or Reduction in Pension Income Year 20XX (ISP-3041) form must be received by the Department within the timeframes established by legislation. These time limits are based on the timing of the optionable event. The time limits for the current year and previous year options are as follows: timeframes Current year option: The Department must receive the ISP-3041 form no later than the end of the second payment period following the payment period in which the event occurs. Previous year option: The Department must receive the ISP-3041 form no later than the end of the payment period following the payment period in which the effective date of the previous year option occurs. If an ISP-3041 form is received too late to grant a current year option, a previous year option may still be granted in the following payment period if that form is received within the prescribed time limit for the previous year option. Examples—Time Limits for Submission of a Statement of Estimated Income If it is determined that the ISP-3041 form was not received within the prescribed timeframes, the statement of estimated income form and event details must still be data captured in Cúram. Once the event details are data captured, Cúram will: continue to calculate entitlement using the base calendar year income; and display No in the Time Limit Met field of the Estimated income data evidence. For more information, refer to Options (Policy) and Options (Policy) Time Limit Tables for Submission of a Statement of Estimated Income

The statement of estimated Income must be submitted within the legislated timeframes. The timeframes are calculated based on the date of the event. All requests must be date stamped to ensure the time limits are correctly applied. The following rules apply to time limits: If the event occurs in the current payment period, the statement of estimated income must be submitted no later than the end of the second payment period following the current payment period. If the event occurs in the previous payment period or in the 6-month period immediately before that payment period, the statement of estimated income must be submitted no later than the end of the payment period following the current payment period. If a statement of estimated income is received too late to grant a current year option, the individual may still exercise a previous year option, in the following payment period, as long as the Statement of Estimated Income after Retirement or Reduction in Pension Income Year 20XX (ISP-3041) form is received by the deadline.

Entitlement to income-tested benefits (i.e. GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits) is based on the income that was received for the previous calendar year (i.e. base calendar year income). When a client or their spouse or common-law partner retires from employment or self-employment, or suffers a loss of pension income, their current income may no longer be as high as it was in the previous calendar year. To lessen the financial impact of this income reduction, clients can choose to have their benefit entitlement calculated with an estimate of their income for the current calendar year (after the retirement or loss) instead of with their income for the base calendar year, if it is to their advantage. This choice is called an option. A retirement, cessation of a business, and a loss or reduction of pension income are all known as events. Since these events relate to the types of income that can be granted an option, they are called optionable events. For more information, Options (Policy)

An option may be granted to an individual who has retired from employment or self-employment, has ceased to carry on a business, or has a loss of income due to termination or reduction of pension income. These are called "optionable events". When an option is granted, entitlement to an income-tested benefit is determined based on estimated income for the current calendar year rather than on actual income for the base calendar year. The base calendar year is the last calendar year ending before the current payment period. Estimated income is what an individual foresees receiving after the event. One event may result in two options referred to as the "Current Year Option" and the "Previous Year Option". The event date determines the type of option. If the event occurs in the current payment period or the previous 6 months, it is a current year option. If the event is in the calendar year immediately preceding the payment period, it is a previous year option. An option is intended to act as a buffer from the financial impact of retirement, or from the termination or reduction of a pension income. It must only be granted if it is to the pensioner's or beneficiary's advantage. Each payment period is looked at separately to determine if an option is beneficial. If the current year option is not beneficial but the previous year option is, then the previous year option may be granted and vice versa. They are not dependent on one another.

If the optionable event occurs during the current payment period or within the previous 6 months, the option is called a "current year option". If the optionable event occurs during the calendar year immediately preceding the payment period, it is called a "previous year option". The exception to this rule is when an option is effective in January. Current year option All employment, self-employment and pension income must be estimated for the option. The estimated income is added to the actual income from the base calendar year to calculate the total income. The total income is used to establish the benefit entitlement for the remaining months of the payment period after the event. Termination of employment or self-employment To calculate the estimated income in a current year option situation, any employment or self-employment income received from the source of retirement before or after the event took place is excluded from the calculation of estimated income. Any employment and self-employment income received from other sources in the calendar year of the event are included. All earnings exemptions and deductions must be applied and included in the estimated income. All pension income received the month after the event to the end of that calendar year is prorated to a yearly amount and included in the calculation of estimated income. Termination or reduction of pension income To calculate the estimated income for a current year option where pension income terminates , the pension income received from that source is excluded from the calculation of estimated income. To calculate the estimated income for a current year option where a pension income reduces , any pension income received from that source will be prorated to a yearly amount beginning the month of the event using the reduced rate. All other pension income received the month of event to the end of that calendar year is prorated to a yearly amount and included in the calculation. If an option is granted due to the termination or reduction of pension income in the current payment period, all employment or self-employment income for the calendar year in which the loss or reduction of pension income took place will be included in the estimate. All earnings exemptions and deductions must be applied and calculated for statements of estimated income in the same manner as indicated in the Employment and self-employment income section. Previous year option To calculate the estimated income for a previous year option where employment or self-employment income or pension income terminates , any income from the source of the event is excluded from the calculation. To calculate the estimated income for a previous year option where a pension income reduces , any pension income received from the source will be included in the calculation using the reduced rate. All other pension income that is not part of the event is also included in the calculation and estimated for the calendar year. All employment income or self-employment income and pension income which are not part of the event should be estimated for the calendar year. All earnings exemptions and deductions must be applied and calculated for statements of estimated income. January effective dates Generally, when an option is processed for an event, 2 options or statements of estimated income are offered. A current year option that coincides with the calendar year in which the event occurs, followed by a previous year option for the payment period that follows the calendar year in which the event occurs. The exception to this is when an option is effective in January. When an option is effective in January, only one option is offered because the terminated income, or the higher income in the case of the reduction of pension income, no longer impacts the individual's base calendar year income. If the individual retired from employment or self-employment in the month of December, the event is considered to have occurred in December, but the option is effective January. As the event occurred in the calendar year immediately before the effective date, a previous year option calculation is performed for January to June and again for July to the following June, resulting in only 2 previous year option calculations. If the individual's pension income is reduced or terminated in January, the event is considered to have occurred in January and the option is effective January. Since the event occurred in the same calendar year as the effective date, a current year option calculation is performed for January to June and again for July to the following June, resulting in only 2 current year option calculations.

When an applicant meets all the eligibility requirements, an application can be approved. An application is approved the later of: the day an individual turns 65; the day after an individual meets the minimum residence requirements; the day after an individual meets the legal status requirement; 12 months before the date of receipt of the application; or the month immediately before the date specified in writing (where the applicant is already 65 when the application is received). For more information, Approval Date—OAS Pension and Benefits (Policy) The approval date is not the same as the effective date. For examples of approval date versus effective date, Examples—Approval and Effective Dates (OAS)

When an applicant meets all the eligibility requirements, an application can be approved. When a client is entitled to an OAS pension, there may be situations where the pension is subject to a tax withhold or the client can request one. Non-resident tax Clients that do not live in Canada may be subject to non-resident tax. Tax treaties between Canada and other countries allow varying percentages of Canadian tax to be deducted. The country in which a client resides determines whether or not non-resident tax is applicable and, if so, the percentage of tax to be withheld. For more information, Non-Resident Tax (Scenario) OAS recovery tax The OAS recovery tax applies to higher-income OAS pensioners who file an income tax return and whose individual net income (for a given base taxation year) is above the threshold set by the Department of Finance. OAS pensioners who receive an OAS income-tested benefit (GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits) are not subject to the OAS recovery tax. For more information, refer to KA-04549 OAS Recovery Tax (Scenario)(article not available). Voluntary tax withhold The OAS pension is a taxable benefit. However, it is not automatically subject to a federal or provincial (e.g. Quebec) tax withhold. Pensioners can request a withhold amount on their OAS application by written request, or online through their Client Portal. For more information, Voluntary Tax Withhold (Scenario)

The OAS Recovery Tax applies to higher-income OAS pensioners who file an income tax return and whose individual net income (for a given base taxation year) is above the threshold set by the Department of Finance. Criteria for applying the OAS Recovery Tax OAS pensioners who file an income tax return and whose individual net income including the OAS pension exceeds the established indexed threshold, have a calculated portion of their monthly OAS pension payment deducted as Recovery Tax at source. Those pensioners with a net individual income higher than the ceiling threshold have their OAS pension payment 100% recovered at source. The total Recovery Tax amount may not exceed the total monthly OAS pension entitlement. Recovery tax calculation Each July, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) calculates the total amount of the OAS Recovery Tax payable for the entire payment period from July of the current year to June of the year following. The amount of Recovery Tax calculated is based on the pensioner's assessed income for the calendar year (often referred to as the "base calendar year") preceding the start of the deduction period. The Recovery Tax amount is equal to 15% of the amount by which the pensioner's net income (reported on line 234 of the income tax return), including the OAS pension, exceeds the established threshold amount. The 15% amount is then divided by 12 to determine the amount of OAS Recovery Tax to deduct monthly. To determine the "base calendar year" in relation to the months January to December, proceed as follows: for OAS pensions paid from January to June, the "base calendar year" is the calendar year before the preceding year. For example, for pensions paid from January to June 2019, the Recovery Tax calculation is based on the pensioner's income reported for 2017. for OAS pensions paid from July to December, the "base calendar year" is the immediately preceding calendar year. For example, for pensions paid from July to December 2019, the OAS Recovery Tax calculation is based on the beneficiaries income reported for 2018. The notice of assessment issued by the CRA notifies OAS pensioners of the OAS Recovery Tax amount to be deducted at source from their monthly pension payments. Affected pensioners receive a letter indicating the: effective date; amount; and, where applicable; and voluntary tax amount deducted at source.

For non-residents of Canada, the OAS Recovery Tax is an additional monthly tax on higher-income OAS pensioners whose individual net world income for a given base taxation year exceeds the threshold amount set by the Department of Finance. The OAS Recovery Tax generally applies to residents of any non-exempt country that have a 25% non-resident tax withhold rate. OAS beneficiaries who reside in a non-exempt country are subject to the OAS Recovery Tax as well as the non-resident tax withhold. Criteria for applying the OAS Recovery Tax Non-resident OAS pensioners may be subject to the OAS Recovery Tax if they meet both residence and income criteria. Residence OAS pensioners are considered non-resident OAS pensioners for the purposes of the OAS Recovery Tax when: they do not reside in Canada; their residential address is identified by the Department as being in a country with a non-resident tax withhold rate of 25%; and they file with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) as a non-resident. Residents of countries which have concluded tax treaties with Canada that reduce the rate of the non-resident tax withhold below 25% are exempt from the OAS Recovery Tax. In some cases, pensioners identified as non-residents are considered by the CRA as factual or deemed Canadian residents and file taxes as such. These pensioners may still be subject to the OAS Recovery Tax if their income is above the established threshold amount. Income Non-resident OAS pensioners: must file an annual OAS Return of Income form. The CRA, however, will not insist that pensioners residing in a tax-recovery-exempt country file an OAS Return of Income form; who reside in a non-exempt country must submit an annual OAS Return of Income form to the CRA declaring their net world income. Pensioners whose income exceeds the established threshold amount are subject to the OAS Recovery Tax. If the CRA grants a beneficiary a reduction or waiver in the non-resident tax withhold rate (NR5) for a given calendar year, the system automatically stops the Recovery Tax deduction for that specific calendar year also. Recovery tax calculation The CRA calculates the OAS Recovery Tax amount using the individual's declared net world income, including the OAS pension. The OAS Recovery Tax amount is calculated yearly for the payment period beginning in July and ending in June of the following year, by referring to a preceding year defined by the CRA as the "base taxation year". The "base taxation year" is the calendar year that precedes the start of the OAS Recovery Tax withholding period. In relation to a calendar year (i.e. January to December), for OAS pensions paid during the first 6 months of a year, the "base taxation year" is the year before the preceding year; for benefits paid during the last 6 months of a year, the "base taxation year" is the immediately preceding year. The OAS Recovery Tax amount equals 15% of the amount by which the beneficiary's net world income reported on the OAS Return of Income form exceeds the established threshold amount for the "base taxation year". The 15% amount is then divided by 12 to determine the amount of OAS Recovery Tax to deduct monthly. However, because the pension is also subject to a 25% non-resident tax withhold, the rate of the OAS Recovery Tax is reduced from 15% to 11.25% of the amount by which the beneficiary's reported net world income exceeds the established threshold amount. The actual OAS Recovery Tax amount as calculated by the OAS system is 75% of the posted amount posted by the CRA. For pensioners whose net world income, including the OAS pension exceeds the ceiling threshold amount, their OAS pension is 100% recovered. However, the combined total of the non-resident tax withhold and the OAS Recovery Tax amounts cannot exceed the total OAS pension amount. The CRA advises beneficiaries who file an OAS Return of Income form about their calculated OAS Recovery Tax amount by means of a notice of assessment. The CRA issues an advisory letter to all affected beneficiaries, including those whose OAS pension is recovered at 100%. The letter indicates the following: the effective month of the OAS Recovery Tax withhold; the non-resident tax withhold amount; and the OAS Recovery Tax amount: OAS Recovery tax—100% withhold.

If the spouse or common-law partner of the incarcerated individual is in pay for the GIS or the ALW benefit, their account may require an adjustment by the Incarceration team to calculate their entitlement based on their individual income if it is to their advantage. Calculating the spouse or common-law partner’s entitlement based on their individual income Once eligibility and entitlement have been established, the spouse or common-law partner of the incarcerated individual may be entitled to have their entitlement to the GIS or the ALW benefit calculated based on their own income if it is to their advantage. If it is not advantageous, the benefit will be based on the combined income of the couple as usual. For more information on marital status and rate tables, Marital Status and Rate Tables for Income-Tested Benefits Payment based on individual income will begin the later of: the month following the month the spouse or common-law partner is incarcerated; or at the effective date of the benefit (normal retroactivity applies) if the spouse or common-law partner is incarcerated on this date. Entitlement at this rate continues to be paid until the month before the incarcerated individual is released. The spouse or common-law partner must be notified in writing when their payment rate has been adjusted due to this provision. If the spouse or common-law partner is paid based on their own income, they must notify the Department in writing of: a change in marital status; and the date of release of their incarcerated spouse or common-law partner. The release date they provide must match the release date of their spouse or common-law partner from the Correctional Service of Canada transfer of information.

Eligibility to the ALW benefit during the incarceration of a spouse or common-law partner When an application for the ALW benefit is submitted by the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual, the application may be approved provided that the applicant meets all the ALW eligibility criteria. The incarcerated spouse or common-law partner must also apply and be eligible for an OAS pension and the GIS in order for the spouse or common-law partner to receive an ALW benefit. Payment of the ALW benefit to eligible spouses or common-law partners of incarcerated OAS pensioners Payment of the ALW benefit to eligible spouses or common-law partners of incarcerated OAS pensioners will continue even though the incarcerated individual's OAS pension and GIS are suspended. During the period of incarceration, the ALW beneficiary will maintain their entitlement to the ALW benefit and their benefit may be calculated on the basis of their individual income. The ALW benefit can be paid based on Rate Table 4, using either combined income or individual income, whichever is more advantageous. The new payment rate may be paid at the effective date (i.e. the normal rules regarding retroactivity apply) as long as the ALW benefit applicant's spouse or common-law partner meets the definition of incarcerated on the effective date. Otherwise, the new payment rate would be effective the month following the month of the individual's incarceration. The new payment rate may be paid until the month before the incarcerated individual's release. Should the individual be released to a transitional living facility (i.e. halfway house), the combined income test does not apply until the couple resumes living together. Although the incarcerated individual must notify the Department of the date of their release, the legislation prescribes that spouses and common-law partners of incarcerated individuals who are in receipt of a more advantageous rate by this measure will have to notify the Department of their spouse or common-law partner's release date, if known, or of any change in their marital status in a timely manner in order to avoid overpayments. The date of release provided by either the incarcerated individual or their spouse or common-law partner must correspond to the release date on the transfer of information from Correctional Services Canada or the province or territory.

GIS payments will be suspended simultaneously with the OAS pension since this benefit can only be paid to individuals who are receiving the OAS pension. At the time of the individual's release, the GIS may be resumed at the same time as the OAS pension, as long as the pensioner meets all of the OAS eligibility requirements to receive the GIS and provided that the Department has their income information. The individual must notify the Department in writing of the date of their release. Entitlement to the GIS during the incarceration of a spouse or common-law partner When an application for the GIS is submitted by the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual, the application may be approved provided that the applicant meets all the GIS eligibility and entitlement criteria. In addition, payment of the GIS to eligible spouses or common-law partners of incarcerated ALW beneficiaries continues even though the incarcerated individual's ALW benefit is suspended. During the individual's period of incarceration, their spouse or common-law partner's GIS entitlement should be paid based on which ever rate is to their advantage. If a pensioner is married or in a common-law relationship with an incarcerated pensioner, the GIS can be paid based on Rate Table 2 using combined income or Rate Table 1 using individual income. If a pensioner is married or in a common-law relationship with an incarcerated ALW recipient, the GIS can be paid based on Rate Table 4 using combined income, Rate Table 3 using combined income or Rate Table 1 using individual income. Exception: If the incarcerated spouse or common-law partner is a non -pensioner, the pensioner spouse or common-law partner will continue to be paid GIS based on Rate Table 3 using combined income. The income information for both individuals is still needed. The single rate may be paid at the effective date (i.e. the normal rules regarding retroactivity apply) as long as the GIS applicant's spouse or common-law partner meets the definition of incarcerated on the effective date. Otherwise, the single rate would be effective starting the month following the month of the individual's incarceration. The single rate may be paid until the month before the incarcerated individual's release. If the individual is released to a transition living facility (i.e. halfway house), the combined income test does not apply until the couple resumes living together. Although the incarcerated individual must notify the Department of the date of their release, the legislation prescribes that spouses and common-law partners of incarcerated individuals that are advantaged by this measure have to notify the Department of their spouse or common-law partner's release date, if known, or of any change in their marital status in a timely manner in order to avoid overpayments. The date of release provided by either the incarcerated individual or their spouse or common-law partner must correspond to the release date on the transfer of information from the Correctional Services Canada or the province or territory.

When a notification of incarceration is received for a client and they or their spouse or common-law partner is in pay for or has applied for the GIS or ALW benefit, you must determine whether it is more advantageous for the spouse or common-law partner’s entitlement to be calculated: at a couple’s rate using their combined income; or at a single rate using their own individual income. If it is more advantageous, the benefit can be calculated based on their individual income for the duration of the incarceration, excluding the month of incarceration and the month of release. For more information on marital status and rate tables, Marital Status and Rate Tables for Income-Tested Benefits For examples of determining the most advantageous rate, Examples—Incarceration—Limiting Payment of OAS Benefits GIS entitlement for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated GIS client (MS2 (rate table 2)) When the couple is being paid for or has applied and been approved for the GIS at the MS2 (rate table 2) rate, you must review the entitlement for the spouse or common-law partner of the incarcerated client and determine which rate is to their advantage. Compare the GIS entitlement at the following rates to determine which is most advantageous: MS2 (rate table 2) using the couple’s combined income; or MS4 (rate table 1) using their own individual income. If it is not advantageous to calculate the GIS entitlement based on their individual income, the GIS will remain based on the couple’s combined income at the MS2 (rate table 2) rate as usual. GIS entitlement for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated ALW client (MS5 (rate table 4)) When the couple is being paid for or has applied and been approved for the GIS and ALW benefit at the MS5 (rate table 4) rate, you must review the GIS entitlement for the spouse or common-law partner of the incarcerated ALW client and determine which rate is to their advantage. Compare the GIS entitlement at the following rates to determine which is most advantageous: MS5 (rate table 4) using the couple’s combined income; MS3 (rate table 3) using the couple’s combined income; or MS4 (rate table 1) using their own individual income. If it is not advantageous to calculate the GIS entitlement based on their individual income, the GIS will remain based on the couple’s combined income at the MS5 (rate table 4) rate as usual. ALW entitlement for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated GIS client (MS5 (rate table 4)) When the couple is being paid for or has applied and been approved for the GIS and ALW benefit at the MS5 (rate table 4) rate, you must review the ALW entitlement for the spouse or common-law partner of the incarcerated GIS client and determine which rate is to their advantage. Compare the ALW entitlement at the following rates to determine which is most advantageous: MS5 (rate table 4) using the couple’s combined income; or MS5 (rate table 4) using their own individual income. If it is not advantageous to calculate the ALW entitlement based on their individual income, the ALW will remain based on the couple’s combined income at the MS5 (rate table 4) rate as usual. GIS entitlement for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated non-pensioner spouse (MS3 (rate table 3)) Since the non-pensioner spouse or common-law partner is not in receipt of any benefits, no action is necessary as the couple is not disadvantaged by one member’s entitlement being limited. The GIS will continue to be calculated based on the couple’s combined income at the MS3 (rate table 3) rate. System limitations OAS Online cannot pay a benefit in the following situations and, therefore, a monthly manual priority payment is required: An ALW benefit cannot be issued by the system when the OAS pensioner’s account is suspended; and The GIS cannot by issued by the system at the MS5 rate when the ALW benefit is suspended. When a couple’s accounts are linked to each other in the International Agreements systems, the system is designed to determine entitlement and issue the appropriate benefits to a couple. When one account is suspended, the system cannot automatically pay a benefit for the other account in the following situations and, therefore, the monthly payment must be issued online manually: at rate table 3 using the couple’s combined income; at rate table 1 using their own individual income; or at rate table 4 using combined income or their own individual income.

An applicant's residency status can impact their eligibility or entitlement if they submit a GIS application when they reside outside of Canada. Refer to the following situations and outcomes: Situation 1 Outcome The applicant left Canada more than 6 months before the GIS effective date. The application will be denied because there is no eligibility or entitlement to the GIS outside of Canada beyond the 6 months after the month of departure. If the applicant returns to reside in Canada permanently, they must submit a new GIS application. Situation 2 Outcome The applicant left Canada within 6 months of the GIS effective date. The application will be approved if all the eligibility criteria are met. The applicant can receive payments for the remainder of the 6-month period after the GIS effective date. For more information, Eligibility Requirements—GIS New Business (Policy)

Departure date from Canada is more than 6 months before the effective date When the applicant's departure date from Canada is more than 6 months before the effective date of the GIS, the application must be denied.

When a valid application for the GIS is submitted, it protects the date of the application (and possible retroactivity) based on the date the application was received. If the statement of income or the income information received from the CRA is not for the correct base calendar year, the requirement for the statement of income is met. However, entitlement to the GIS cannot be determined until the required income for the applicable payment period is obtained from the CRA or the applicant. To determine which base calendar year income is required, you must consider the earliest possible effective date of the GIS. Refer to the examples below: Example: Situation 1 Direction A client has been in pay for an OAS pension since June 2021. They submit an Application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement (ISP-3025) form on July 2, 2023. The GIS application is processed on July 24, 2023. The GIS application can be approved with an effective date of August 2022 (11 months before the application was received). To pay the full retroactive entitlement of August 2022 to July 2023, the following statements of income are required: 2021 (July 2022 to June 2023 payment period); and 2022 (July 2023 to June 2024 payment period). The CRA income feed has been received for 2022; however, the 2021 income is not available from the CRA . The requirement for the statement of income is met and payments for the client's GIS can begin effective July 2023. The period of August 2022 to June 2023 is date protected and can be considered once the 2021 income has been obtained from the client or the CRA . Example: Situation 2 Direction An Application for the Old Age Security Pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement (ISP-3550) form is received on October 2, 2023. The applicant's 65th birthday is at a future date of August 5, 2024. The application is processed on November 13, 2023, and the OAS pension is approved with an effective date of September 2024. In this case, the client is being considered for the GIS at the same time as the OAS pension (i.e. in November 2023). Once an individual indicates that they wish to receive the GIS, a request is made to the CRA for the applicant's income information. Since the application is being processed in the July 2023 to June 2024 payment period, the income for 2022 is received from the CRA feed. The requirement for the statement of income has been met; however, entitlement cannot be determined until the income that coincides with the payment period of the effective date (2023) is received. Since the 2023 income is not available at the time of processing, the application will have to be held until the 2023 income is available and entitlement can be determined. The payment period of the effective date is date protected. However, any subsequent payment year is reviewed individually and is subject to the conditions of the lifetime renewal designation.

When a valid application for the ALW benefit is submitted, it protects the date of the application (and possible retroactivity) based on the date the application was received. If the statement of income or the income information received from the CRA , is not for the correct base calendar year, the requirement for the statement of income is met. However, entitlement to the ALW benefit cannot be determined until the required income for the applicable payment period is obtained from the CRA or the applicant. To determine which base calendar year income is required, you must consider the earliest possible effective date of the ALW benefit. The CRA income feed has been received for 2022; however, the 2021 income is not available from the CRA . The requirement for the statement of income is met and payments for the client's ALW benefit can begin effective July 2023. The period of August 2022 to June 2023 is date protected and can be considered once the 2021 income has been obtained from the client or the CRA . The applicant's 60th birthday is at a future date of August 5, 2024. The application is processed on November 13, 2023, and the ALW benefit is approved effective September 2024. Once an individual applies for the ALW benefit, a request is made to the CRA for the applicant's income information. Since the application is being processed in the July 2023 to June 2024 payment period, the income for 2022 is received from the CRA feed. The requirement for the statement of income has been met; however, entitlement cannot be determined until the income that coincides with the payment period of the effective date (2023) is received. An application for the ALW benefit must be made on a form prescribed by the Department, and the Department must receive the applicant's statement of income information. The statement of income may be received: as part of the pensioner's GIS application; as part of the ALW applicant's statement of income form; on a separate written statement; or through the CRA income feed (e.g. one-way or two-way transmission). If the income information provided by the applicant or the CRA does not coincide with the relevant payment period (e.g. 2019 income is received for the 2021-2022 payment period), the application can still be approved as the receipt of income information fulfills the legislative requirement to provide a statement of income. However, the entitlement to the ALW benefit cannot be determined until the income information for the applicable payment period is received (e.g. when the 2020 income is received for the 2021-2022 payment period).

An application for the ALWS benefit must be made on a form prescribed by the Department, unless this requirement has been waived, and the Department must receive the applicant's statement of income. The statement of income may be received: as part of the ALWS benefit applicant's statement of income form; on a separate written statement; or through the CRA income feed (i.e. one-way or two-way transmission when an ALWS benefit application has been submitted). If the income information provided by the applicant or the CRA does not coincide with the relevant payment period, e.g. 2019 income is received for the 2021-2022 payment period, the application can still be approved as the receipt of income information fulfills the legislative requirement to provide a statement of income. However, the entitlement to the ALWS benefit cannot be determined until the income information for the applicable payment period is received, e.g. when the 2020 income is received for the 2021-2022 payment period.

When a valid application for the ALWS benefit is submitted, it protects the date of the application (and possible retroactivity) based on the date the application was received. If the statement of income or the income information received from the CRA , is not for the correct base calendar year, the requirement for the statement of income is met. However, entitlement to the ALWS benefit cannot be determined until the required income for the applicable payment period is obtained from the CRA or the applicant. To determine which base calendar year income is required, you must consider the earliest possible effective date of the ALWS benefit. Refer to the examples below: Example: Situation 1 Direction An applicant submits an Application for the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor – Under the Old Age Security Program (ISP-3008) form on July 2, 2023. The ALWS benefit application is processed on July 24, 2023. The ALWS benefit application can be approved with an effective date of August 2022 (11 months before the application was received). To pay the full retroactive entitlement of August 2022 to July 2023, the following statements of income are required: 2021 (July 2022 to June 2023 payment period); and 2022 (July 2023 to June 2024 payment period). The CRA income feed has been received for 2022; however, the 2021 income is not available from the CRA . The requirement for the statement of income is met and payments for the client's ALWS benefit can begin effective July 2023. The period of August 2022 to June 2023 is date protected and can be considered once the 2021 income has been obtained from the client or the CRA . Example: Situation 2 Direction An Application for the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor – Under the Old Age Security Program (ISP-3008) form is received on October 2, 2023. The applicant's 60th birthday is at a future date of August 5, 2024. The application is processed on November 13, 2023, and the ALWS benefit is approved effective September 2024. Once an individual applies for the ALWS benefit, a request is made to the CRA for the applicant's income information. Since the application is being processed in the July 2023 to June 2024 payment period, the income for 2022 is received from the CRA feed. The requirement for the statement of income has been met; however, entitlement cannot be determined until the income that coincides with the payment period of the effective date (2023) is received. Since the 2023 income is not available at the time of processing, the application will have to be held until the 2023 income is available and entitlement can be determined. The payment period of the effective date is date protected. However, any subsequent payment year is reviewed individually and is subject to the conditions of the lifetime renewal designation.

When a partial OAS pension application is approved, the entitlement of the pension does not increase with additional years of residence in Canada. However, if the applicant has resided in Canada for less than 10 years at the effective date and they are eligible for the OAS pension under an International Social Security Agreement, the applicant may be entitled to a prorated GIS, provided all eligibility and entitlement criteria have been met. Entitlement to prorated income-tested benefits is calculated at 1/10th of the benefit rate for each year of residence in Canada and increases with each additional year of residence in Canada after approval of the benefit, up to a maximum of 10 years. This is known as the special qualifying factor or pro-ration of income-tested benefits. For more information, Special Qualifying Factor (Work Tool)

When an ALW benefit application is approved with 10 years of Canadian residence, the entitlement of the benefit does not increase with additional years of residence in Canada. However, if the applicant has resided in Canada for less than 10 years at the effective date and they are eligible under an International Social Security Agreement, the applicant may be entitled to a prorated ALW benefit, provided all eligibility and entitlement criteria have been met. Entitlement to prorated income-tested benefits is calculated at 1/10th of the benefit rate for each year of residence in Canada and increases with each additional year of residence in Canada after approval of the benefit, up to a maximum of 10 years. This is known as the special qualifying factor or proration of income-tested benefits. For more information, Special Qualifying Factor (Work Tool)

Non-sponsored individuals who qualify for benefits under an International Social Security Agreement are entitled to receive prorated GIS benefits. The rate increases each year by 1/10th to reflect the additional year of residence they accumulate after age 18. For instance, an individual who is approved for a benefit with one year of residence in Canada is only entitled to 1/10th of the benefit. After 9 years of continued Canadian residence, they are entitled to 9/10th and after 10 years, they are entitled to the full GIS benefit. This is referred to as a “special qualifying factor”.

Non-sponsored individuals who qualify for benefits under an International Social Security Agreement are entitled to receive prorated ALW benefits. The rate increases each year by 1/10th to reflect the additional year of residence they accumulate after age 18. For instance, an individual who is approved for a benefit with one year of residence in Canada is only entitled to 1/10th of the benefit. After nine years of continued Canadian residence, they are entitled to 9/10th and after 10 years, they are entitled to the full ALW benefit. This is referred to as a “special qualifying factor”.

Non-sponsored individuals who qualify for benefits under an International Social Security Agreement are entitled to receive prorated ALWS benefits. The rate increases each year by 1/10th to reflect the additional year of residence they accumulate after age 18. For instance, an individual who is approved for a benefit with one year of residence in Canada is only entitled to 1/10th of the benefit. After nine years of continued Canadian residence, they are entitled to 9/10th and after 10 years, they are entitled to the full ALWS benefit. This is referred to as a “special qualifying factor”.

When an ALWS benefit application is approved with 10 years of Canadian residence, the entitlement of the benefit does not increase with additional years of residence in Canada. However, if the applicant has resided in Canada for less than 10 years at the effective date and they are eligible under an International Social Security Agreement, the applicant may be entitled to a prorated ALWS benefit provided all eligibility and entitlement criteria have been met. Entitlement to prorated income-tested benefits is calculated at 1/10th of the benefit rate for each year of residence in Canada and increases with each additional year of residence in Canada after approval of the benefit, up to a maximum of 10 years. This is known as the special qualifying factor or proration of income-tested benefits. For more information, Special Qualifying Factor (Work Tool)

The Special Qualifying Factor (SQF) determines how much income-tested benefits a client can receive when they have not reached 10 full years of Canadian residence after age 18. Since April 1996, clients may receive 1/10th of the full benefit for each full year of residence in Canada, up to a maximum of 10 years (i.e. the full benefit means an SQF of 1.0). How the SQF works The SQF increases by 0.1 each year as the client reaches their next anniversary date of residence. For example, a client that entered Canada on March 15 would reach a year of residence the next year on March 14. Therefore, March would be the anniversary month and the SQF would increase effective April. Cúram uses the Residence Period evidence to calculate the SQF. In the absence of a complete Residence Period evidence, an SQF override equal to the client's total years of Canadian residence up to a maximum of 10 years can be entered. Residence Period evidence considerations for migrated accounts Updated The GIS New Business application only asks for the applicant's residence history in the last 2 years. If that period is the only Residence Period evidence in Cúram, the system assumes that is the total residence for the SQF calculation. This underrepresents a client’s full residence history, leading to incorrect GIS entitlement. The client’s complete residence history should be added to Cúram to ensure an accurate client record and avoid the need for overrides when possible. The residence history can be obtained through the client file (e.g. residence calculation sheet, validated residence histories) and the system (e.g. ITRDS notes, address history). How to fix the SQF Updated Access the client file to determine if client’s residence from age 18 to the OAS effective date is present. If yes, add the client’s complete residence period history in Cúram. Refer to Residence Period—Add, View and Edit in Cúram (Action) . Residence Period—Add, View and Edit in Cúram (Action) If no, go to Step 2 . Step 2 Add an entitlement override for the SQF. Refer to Eligibility and Entitlement Override Evidence—Add, Edit, View, and Delete in Cúram (Action) . For OAS approved without an ISSA, enter an SQF of 10. For OAS approved under an ISSA, enter an SQF of 1 to 10 based on the number of full years of Canadian residence at the start date of the override. For more information, GIS Take-Up Applications (Knowledge) Marital status rate tables A rate table provides a listing of income ranges and corresponding monthly entitlements to income-tested benefits according to a predetermined maximum allowable income level for a specific marital status. There are 5 rate tables. They are used to determine the monthly benefit entitlement for the GIS, the ALW and the ALWS benefits based on the applicant's income level and marital status. Under most circumstances when the non-pensioner spouse or common-law partner becomes eligible for an OAS pension and the GIS, the couple will receive more GIS between them than they did when only one of them was a pensioner. However, there are situations where the combination of income levels and years of entitlement results in a lower combined amount. Bill C-31 was enacted on April 1, 1996, and allows the Department to pay a married or common-law couple using separate rate tables to ensure their total benefits are not less than they were receiving before the non-pensioner spouse became a pensioner. In this situation, Cúram will calculate the future and any retroactive entitlement according to the appropriate rate table. Income is required to determine initial and ongoing entitlement to the ALW benefit. Entitlement is generally based on the income of the couple from the calendar year preceding the payment period. This is referred to as the base calendar year income. Income is assessed using the information found on the: Application for the Guaranteed Income Supplement with Statement of Income (ISP-3025B) form; Statement of Income for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor for payment period of July (20XX) to June (20XX) with Information Sheet (ISP-3026) form; CRA income feeds; or Liaison forms provided by International Social Security Agreement partners. For more information, Calculating Income (Policy) If you receive income from both the applicant and the CRA , the income provided by the applicant must be confirmed against the income provided by the CRA . You must reconcile any variances to ensure the initial income used to determine entitlement is accurate. In specific circumstances, a client's ALW benefit entitlement may be calculated based on an estimate of their current year's income instead of their previous year income. For more information, refer to: Estimated Income (Options) (Scenario) ; and Estimated Income (Options) (Scenario) Validate Income for Income-Tested Benefits (Action) . Income-tested benefits are renewed in July each year based on: the income received for the previous calendar year (i.e. base calendar year income); and marital status. After eligibility is established based on an initial application for income-tested benefits, entitlement to benefits can be renewed every year without the client having to reapply, if they provide the required income information. The renewal of the client's entitlement to benefits can be automatic if their income information is received directly from the CRA .

Clients' income-tested benefit can be automatically renewed if: their income is received through the CRA income feed; and they have a lifetime renewal designation. Clients may also renew their benefits by providing a statement of income (i.e. a Statement of Income for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Allowance the Allowance for the Survivor for payment period of July (20XX) to June (20XX) (ISP-3026) form or written statement of income). Renewal of income-tested benefits (Policy) If income information has not been received from the CRA income feed or from the client directly by the July accounting month, the client's entitlement to income-tested benefits will not be renewed in Cúram in time for the new payment period. Starting in the July accounting month, these clients may be able to provide their income information by phone. The renewal of benefits by phone is a temporary measure to help pensioners maintain entitlement to their income-tested benefits until the CRA income feed or a statement of income is received. If income information is accepted by phone, the client is advised that they must provide a statement of income or file their income tax return within 30 days. This requirement also applies where the income of a spouse or common-law partner is provided over the phone. Clients (or their spouse or common-law partner) who have reported their income by phone will continue to receive their income-tested benefits until the account is reviewed by the processing centre to confirm the income. If confirmation of the income information has not been received within 60 days (to allow for mailing time or CRA tax assessment beyond the 30 days), the income information received over the phone must be manually deleted from Cúram. Cúram will then recalculate the client's entitlement and create an overpayment for any payments received within the applicable payment period. The client must be notified in writing that their entitlement has stopped and of the overpayment details. The deleted income can be viewed in the manually entered income history on the Integrated Case.

Benefits will be renewed every year effective in July as long as the beneficiary has a lifetime renewal designation (formerly GIS for Life) and their income information is consistently provided through: the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) one-way transmission of income feed; or a paper statement of income from the beneficiary. However, their effective date is based on the date the income is received if the beneficiary has a lifetime renewal designation and is: inconsistent about providing their income information; or late filing their Income Tax and Benefit Return.

The requirement for a renewal application is waived when: one-way transmission is received from Canada Revenue Agency (CRA); or a statement of income is received directly from the beneficiary. For beneficiaries who do not file their income tax and benefit returns or are late filers, Service Canada may not receive income information from the CRA in a timely manner. Renewal of benefits and any retroactivity for previous months of entitlement are protected based on the date the income is received via the CRA one-way income transmission or the date of receipt of a paper income statement. When income information is received, the beneficiary has satisfied the requirement to waive the renewal application and thus retroactivity rules apply based on the date the income information is received up to a maximum of 11 months.

The renewal of income-tested benefits is an annual process that occurs in July, which is the start of a new benefit payment period. If a client is eligible for an income-tested benefit and their income information from the previous calendar year has been received, Cúram will automatically process the renewal of the benefit. In addition to the renewal of benefits, several supporting activities are performed around the same time in Cúram. These activities include: reviewing existing overrides; sending appropriate correspondence (e.g. renewal notices, decision letters); reviewing income variances that may indicate inconsistencies between reported and actual income; and reconciling estimated income that was used for the prior benefit period with the actual income now received. Some clients may need to fill out a Statement of Income for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Allowance or Allowance for the Survivor for payment period of July (20XX) to June (20XX) with Information Sheet (ISP-3026) form to keep receiving their benefits. This usually happens when their income information is missing, because they have not filed a tax return, or they don't meet the eligibility rules for automatic renewal based on the information available (e.g. there is a bankruptcy reported by the CRA ). The ISP-3026 form is mailed in March to the address the client has on file at the end of the March accounting month. If the ISP-3026 form is not returned by late June, Cúram automatically sends a second form. If the ISP-3026 form is still not returned in time, benefit payments may be delayed starting in July. Before income-tested benefits are paid for the new payment period, Cúram goes through a process called "reversion", which takes place in June. This process includes: moving all new income information into the current income fields; deleting any data that is no longer needed from the previous payment period; calculating eligibility for the GIS, the ALW benefit, and the ALWS benefit based on the updated income; and capturing information for issuing entitlement correspondence. As part of the supporting activities during the renewal process, Cúram will automatically generate tasks based on pre-defined trigger conditions. These tasks are applied to the client profile which are assigned to processing agents to review and resolve. Below is a list of tasks that Cúram generates along with their associated trigger conditions: Once a client meets all the necessary requirements (e.g. having pending tasks resolved or overrides cleared) Cúram will automatically proceed with renewing the benefits. The system continuously checks for these conditions and benefit renewal is triggered once the conditions are satisfied. If a client does not meet the eligibility requirements for renewal, Cúram will create a task for an agent to review and resolve. Once the task is completed and the eligibility requirements are met, Cúram will automatically renew the benefit. Tasks that are not part of the eligibility rules do not stop the renewal of income-tested benefits. The ITB For Life status is automatically updated to Yes as a result of the eligibility determination process. Correspondence plays an important role in the renewal process. The effective date of the approval of the credit split is the last day of the month in which the request or application is received. Pensionable Earnings will be attributed the month following the month in which the credit split is approved. When an existing benefit in pay is to be adjusted or a new benefit is put into pay as a result of earnings from a credit split, the effective date will be the month following the month the credit split is approved. A benefit that was not payable in the absence of the credit split cannot be paid for any months before the month in which the earnings are attributed. For example, if a request or application is received in March, the earnings resulting from the approval of the credit split will be attributed to the record of earnings effective April. For information on the effective date of the attribution of pensionable earnings, Credit Splitting (Policy)

Under the CPP, the same effective date of attribution should apply equally to former spouses, and former common-law partners. The effective date of the taking place or approval of the credit split is the last day of the month in which the request or application is received. The effective date of the attribution of pensionable earnings is the first day of the month following the month that the division takes place. For example, if a request or application is received in March, the earnings resulting from the approval of the credit split will be accredited to the record of earnings effective April. Any benefits requiring a credit split cannot be paid in the month the division takes place or any month prior. Any benefits currently in pay will be adjusted to be effective the month the division takes place.

The attribution date is the month following the month in which the credit split is approved. When a new benefit is put in pay as a result of earnings from a credit split, the effective date will be the month following the month the credit split is approved. A benefit that was not payable in the absence of the credit split cannot be paid for any months before the month in which the earnings are attributed. Prior to January 1, 1998, valid earnings must be above the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) and effective January 1, 1998, valid earnings must be above the Disability Basic Exemption (DBE). The exception to this rule applies when a credit split causes the earnings to drop below the DBE. Effective 1998, if a contributor's earnings for any year are greater than the DBE before the credit split, and after the credit split are less than the DBE but more than the YBE for that year, the earnings are used as a valid year when determining if the Minimum Qualifying Period has been met. For more information, refer to Credit Split Application (Scenario) and to Credit Split Application (Scenario) CPP Credit Splitting (Policy) When considering the Late Applicant Provision and the Credit Split provision, as long as the applicant was separated from their spouse or common-law partner for at least one year or divorced before the Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO), the divided earnings could be used to meet the earnings and contributions requirements. If the Department uses the CPP Credit Splitting provision to improve the LPDOO, ensure the earnings investigation worksheet includes the LPDOO with and without the applied credit split. Refer to IO Earnings Investigation Worksheet – MQP External link . IO Earnings Investigation Worksheet – MQP For more information, Credit Split and the Late Applicant Provision for CPPD benefits (Policy)

Earnings attributed after a Credit Split may help an individual meet the MQP for a DTH benefit, SVR pension or Surviving Child's benefit. A Credit Split is approved effective the last day of the month the request or application was received. This is the effective date of the division of pensionable earnings. The attribution of pensionable earnings is effective the first day of the month following the month the division takes place. Therefore, when considering the earnings attributed after a Credit Split, the MQP cannot be met in the same month the division takes place. Earnings attributed as a result of a Credit Split can be used to meet the MQP the month following the month the Credit Split is approved. For the DTH benefit, the applicant must submit a new DTH benefit application with a receipt date after the date of attribution, unless they have requested a reconsideration of the initial DTH benefit application.

Credit splitting is a provision that allows Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) or pension credits, earned by both spouses during the marriage or common-law union, to be divided equally between the 2 persons. The division can only take place after a divorce, legal annulment or separation from a legal marriage or common-law union. The effective date of the credit split approval is the last day of the month in which the request or application is received. Any benefits requiring a credit split cannot be paid in the month the credit split was approved or any month before. Benefits may begin on the date of attribution (i.e. the month following the month in which the credit split is approved). For example, if a request or application is received in March, the earnings resulting from the credit split approval will be accredited to the record of earnings effective April. For CPPD, if the applicant had a qualifying period without credit splitting and the date of attribution is within the 11 months before the date of application, it is more beneficial to the applicant if they are found disabled by the Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) from their own credits than it would be if they were found disabled by the LPDOO with the credit split. When medically adjudicating a CPPD benefit application and a credit split is applied, it is important that you consider both LPDOOs, if applicable, in determining when severe and prolonged criteria was met. This ensures that the applicant receives all the benefits to which they are entitled. Examples when the date of attribution is less than 11 months before the date of application An applicant applies for CPPD benefits in August 2026 with an Earliest Possible Date of Onset (EPDOO) in May 2025. The applicant previously applied for a credit split in September 2025 and has a date of attribution of October 2025. With the credit split, the LPDOO is December 2027. Without the credit split, the LPDOO is December 2023. If this applicant met the severe and prolonged criteria by December 2023, they will be entitled to a benefit for the full retroactive period. If they became disabled after December 2023 but before December 2027, the effective date for payment of their benefit would be the same date as the later of: the date of attribution; 4 months after the Date of Onset (DOO); or for subsequent applications, the month after the DOO if the DOO is within 5 years after the cessation date of a previous CPPD benefit. Example when the date of attribution is 11 months or more before the date of application An applicant applies for CPPD benefits in July 2025 with an EPDOO in April 2024. The applicant previously applied for a credit split in August 2023 and has a date of attribution of September 2023. With a credit split, the LPDOO is December 2022. As this date is before the maximum retroactivity the LPDOO without credit split should not be considered as the date of attribution is before any possible effective date. If the applicant is found disabled, the effective date would be August 2024, the full retroactive period. Credit splitting is a provision that allows CPP pension credits (unadjusted pensionable earnings) to be divided equally between 2 individuals following the dissolution of their relationship. CPP credits that were earned during a period of cohabitation in a marriage or common-law union can be divided between former spouses or former common-law partners, except for Post Retirement earnings. Post Retirement earnings are considered outside of an individual's contributory period and cannot be included in the division of earnings following a request for a credit split. As of January 1, 2019, the CPP enhancement was implemented and former spouses or former common-law partners who apply for a credit split will divide both their base and first additional CPP credits; as of January 1, 2024 second additional CPP credits will be divided as well. In order to divide first additional and second additional CPP credits, at least one of the former spouses or common-law partners must have made enhanced contributions during their cohabitation period. Credit splitting can only take place after: divorce; legal annulment separation from a legal marriage; or separation from a common-law union. A credit split is mandatory for divorces or legal annulments that occurred on or after January 1, 1987. Effective January 1, 2025, when a credit split application is received and approved for separated legal spouses, there is no eligibility to a CPP SVR pension when one of the separated legal spouses dies. If a separated legal spouse is receiving an SVR pension and the Department receives a credit split application on or after January 1, 2025 for the same deceased separated legal spouse, the SVR pension ceases as of the effective date of the credit split approval. The effective date of the credit split approval is the last day of the month in which the credit split application or request was received. Pension credits are attributed the first day of the month after the effective date of the credit split approval. For more information on credit splitting and CPP enhancement, refer to CPP Enhancement (Knowledge) and Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge) . For additional important information regarding credit splitting, CPP Enhancement (Knowledge) Calculation of CPP Benefits (Knowledge) Credit Splitting (Policy)

Credit splitting allows Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings or pension credits to be equally divided between 2 former marital or common-law partners. Additional pension credits attributed to a contributor's record of earnings following the approval of a credit split can improve an applicant's qualifying period or establish one when they do not qualify with their own pensionable earnings. Refer to Credit Split Application (Scenario) and the policy on Credit Split Application (Scenario) Medical Adjudication with Credit Splitting (Policy) Earnings as a result of credit splitting do not represent work capacity.

The Credit Split provision allows CPP unadjusted pensionable earnings earned by both common-law partners or spouses during the common-law union or marriage to be divided equally between both individuals. The attributed pensionable earnings following the approval of a request for a Credit Split provision may help an individual meet or improve the Minimum Qualifying Period for a CPPD benefit. The CPP Credit Split is a provision allowing the equal division of CPP contributions accumulated by both the applicant and their former spouse or common-law partner while they were living together. If the SVR pension application has been processed and you receive an application from another applicant, you must determine who is eligible to the SVR pension. The new applicant must provide evidence that they are the surviving spouse of the deceased contributor as defined by CPP. For more information, Survivor's Pension—Contesting Applications (Policy) If you initially obtained substantial information and evidence, the decision to change the SVR pension from one individual to another should rarely occur. To make this change, the evidence submitted to support the second application must challenge the information that was submitted by the first applicant. In cases where another individual submits a contesting application for an SVR pension already in pay, you must: review the original decision and all supporting documentation; review the new application and documentary evidence; and analyze and compare the applications to determine who is eligible. If you determine that there are anomalies or discrepancies in either applicant's information, refer the file to the Integrity Services Branch. Referral Process for Administrative Investigations—CPP (Scenario) Only one person can be the survivor for the purpose of the CPP SVR pension. If the information and evidence collected establish the eligibility of the second applicant as the survivor, you must terminate the first SVR pension. You must send the Benefit Status - Cancel or Terminate (ISS-4559) letter to the first applicant to notify them of the decision to terminate the SVR pension, provide details of any receivables generated from the termination and give reconsideration rights. Departmental Receivables (Overpayments) (Scenario) As only one person can be the survivor for the purpose of the SVR pension, payments made to any other person—regardless of whether they were thought to be the survivor at the time of approval—are payments to which the person was not entitled. The overpayment is a debt to the Crown and as such must be recovered. The overpayment cannot be automatically remitted. Review the evidence and information on the file. An overpayment can only be considered for remission, in full or in part, in cases where the Minister is satisfied that a person meets one of the 4 conditions, as set out in the remission provisions. Remit an Overpayment (Scenario) This direction is for all new cases effective November 17, 2020. Closed cases will not be overturned or reviewed. To process these applications, go to the Exceptions and special cases section in What you need to do .

A survivor is only entitled to receive one SVR pension. However, they are entitled to receive whichever SVR pension provides the highest payment between their previous and current deceased contributor spouses or common-law partners. You must process the new SVR pension application, and ITRDS will always determine which SVR pension to pay. ITRDS will terminate the lesser SVR pension with the reason Pay Greater SVR . You must advise the applicant of the results in writing, with either the Award - Survivor's Pension Award (ISS-4525) letter or the Denial - Survivor's pension (ISS-4520) letter to advise the applicant that they are already receiving a larger SVR pension from their former spouse or former common-law partner. If the survivor requests to receive the lesser of the 2 SVR pensions, refer to The applicant wants to receive the lesser of the 2 SVR pensions in the Exceptions and Special Cases section below.

Under the CPP, an applicant is only entitled to receive one Survivor’s (SVR) pension at a time. Where an applicant is the survivor of 2 or more deceased contributors, only the greatest of the calculated SVR pensions will be paid. Note the following examples: If the SVR pension that is already in pay is the greater amount, the subsequent SVR pension application is denied. The applicant must be informed in writing of the decision. If the subsequent SVR pension application has the greater entitlement, the first SVR pension must be cancelled effective the month following the date of death of the subsequent deceased contributor. The cancellation results in an overpayment of the first SVR pension. The overpayment is then withheld from the arrears payment of the subsequent SVR pension and the balance is paid. The applicant must be informed in writing of the decision. If the greater SVR pension is subsequently reduced by a Credit Split, then the survivor becomes entitled to receive the previous SVR pension if it is the greater of the 2 SVR pensions. If the common-law partner of a deceased contributor either does not apply for the SVR pension, or applies and their application is denied based on the greater of 2 SVR pensions, the legal spouse is not eligible for the SVR pension.

Under CPP, only one person can be considered to be the survivor of the deceased contributor. As a result, only one individual can be entitled to receive the Survivor’s (SVR) pension. If there is more than one applicant for the CPP SVR pension, the applicant who meets the definition of "survivor" is the eligible beneficiary. There are times when the first beneficiary's SVR pension must be terminated in favour of the contesting applicant. To make such a change, the evidence submitted to support the second individual’s application must disprove the information and evidence submitted by the first person. In cases where it appears either applicant may have provided false or misleading information, the case is to be considered for referral to the Integrity Services Branch as per existing policies and procedures. If the second applicant is found to be eligible and the second application is approved: the SVR pension currently in pay must be cancelled; an overpayment must be set up; the original applicant must be advised: of the decision; and of their reconsideration rights; and the effective date of the SVR pension on the second application is the month after death or eleven months before the date of receipt of the application, whichever is later.

In situations where individuals are widowed twice (or more), the greater of the calculated Survivor's (SVR) pension entitlements will be paid. If a pensioner’s SVR pension is subsequently reduced following a credit split, as the SVR entitlement amount is based on: the deceased contributor’s earnings and contributions; age at the time of death; and the deceased ex-spouse submitted a credit split application within the legal time frame from the date of death, then the pensioner becomes eligible for the other pension, which is now the greater of the 2.

The PRDB is a flat rate benefit paid to qualified RTR pension recipients. The combined benefit calculation is the RTR pension plus PRDB amounts. When combining RTR pension, PRDB and SVR pension, the Department will only pay the higher flat rate portion of the SVR pension or PRDB . The Specialized Processing Centres process all PRDB payments. When the client is eligible for a combined RTR pension, PRDB and SVR pension, the Specialized Processing Centres will subtract the SVR pension flat rate from the PRDB , pay the remainder by manual priority payment (a workaround due to system limitations), send the applicable letter and BF the account to amend the tax slip. Go to the Exceptions and special cases section in What you need to do .

The Post-Retirement Disability Benefit ( PRDB ) is a flat-rate benefit that is equal to the Disability ( DSB ) benefit yearly flat rate. The contributor may receive a combined PRDB and RTR pension amount that is above the maximum RTR pension or DSB benefit amount. When a pensioner is eligible for both a combined Retirement and Survivor's pension and a PRDB , the greater of the survivor's flat rate or the PRDB flat rate is used in the formula. For more information, refer to CPP Benefit Calculation Guide Internal link . CPP Benefit Calculation Guide

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government of Canada introduced emergency benefits to support Canadians by providing temporary income support for workers (employed and self-employed) who were directly impacted by the pandemic. These emergency benefits are: Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB); Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB); Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); and Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). Federal emergency benefits received in 2020 are considered income for the 2021-2022 payment period. Clients who received EI-ERB and saw a reduction of their income-tested benefits during the 2021-2022 payment period might have qualified for an option when the emergency benefit ended. Effective July 2022, these benefits are no longer considered income when calculating entitlement to income-tested benefits. For more information about these benefits and how this income was reported to the Department by the CRA , refer to: Calculating Income (Policy) ; and Calculating Income (Policy) COVID-19: Interim Measures—Emergency Benefits (Action) .
