Effective July 2022, the following emergency benefits received in 2021 or later are exempted from the calculation of income-tested benefits, i.e. the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), the Allowance (ALW) and the Allowance for the Survivor (ALWS) benefits. Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB); Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB); Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); and Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). Emergency benefits received in 2020 For the July 2021 to June 2022 payment period, based on an individual’s 2020 income, the EI-ERB, CERB, CRB, CRSB, CRCB and CWLB are considered income when determining entitlement to income-tested benefits. In some cases, the receipt of these emergency benefits in 2020 resulted in a reduction or cessation of income-tested benefits in July 2021. To alleviate the financial hardship of GIS, ALW and ALWS recipients who received emergency benefits in 2020, individuals may qualify for the One-time grant for GIS Recipients who received Pandemic Benefits Options Under the OAS Regulations, pension income for the purpose of an "option" includes amounts received as “employment insurance benefits”. Therefore, prior to July 2022, EI ERB is considered “pension income” in the same manner as EI benefits. However, CERB, CRB, CRCB, CRSB and CWLB are not considered pension income. The cessation of EI ERB can trigger an "option". However, the cessation of the CERB, CRB, CRCB, CRSB and CWLB cannot trigger an "option” as these benefits are not considered pension income under the OAS Regulations. An "option" for the cessation of EI-ERB may be granted even if an individual qualifies for the "One-time grant for GIS Recipients who received Pandemic Benefits", if it is to their advantage. When estimating income for a separate event (i.e. retirement or reduction in retirement pension), EI ERB is included in the estimated income. Any EI ERB received would continue to be part of the estimated income for the July 2021 to June 2022 payment period. Effective July 2022, any EI ERB would be removed from the estimated income. The CERB, CRB, CRBC, CRSB and CWLB continue to be part of the base calendar year income of an estimate until June 2022. Effective July 2022, the base calendar year will no longer include income from these sources. Claims of dire need For accounts where individuals claimed they were in a dire need situation and were granted options when their emergency benefits ended, the option is still valid as this was the direction in place at the time. In addition, these options will continue until the income from the emergency benefit no longer forms part of the base calendar year income. In other words, if a beneficiary was granted a current year option due to their emergency benefit ending, they may continue to be granted a previous year option for this event. Claims of suspected CERB/EI ERB fraud or identity theft For accounts where income-tested benefits stopped or were reduced in July 2021 due to CERB/EI ERB income, but individuals claim they did not receive this income and are victims of fraud or identity theft, the income cannot be removed without confirmation that the Canada Revenue Agency will be amending the taxpayer’s 2020 income.

Income-tested benefits July 2021 to June 2022 payment year The following emergency benefits will be considered income for the 2021-2022 payment period: Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB); Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB); Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); and Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). Process applications and accounts for the July 2021 to June 2022 payment year as usual, including this income. A Questions and Answers document was also developed to assist staff when interacting with clients or responding to questions related to income-tested benefits and CERB/EI ERB. Questions and Answers document When received by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) income feed, the emergency benefits received in 2020, will be displayed and treated as follows: July 2022 to June 2023 payment year and forward Effective July 2022, the following emergency benefits will not be considered income for income-tested benefits: Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB); Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB); Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); and Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). As a result, the CRA will exclude CERB, CRB, CRSB, CRCB and CWLB from the regular income feed, beginning with the 2021 income year. However, income from EI ERB received in 2021 or later, will not be excluded from the income feed. National Headquarters was created account verification work items in PWS using the barcode NHQ-2021-C12-EIERBINCOME , for two groups of accounts: Group 1 includes urgent work items for accounts where: EI has confirmed that EI-ERB was received in 2021; the client or their spouse or common-law partner are in pay for Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), Allowance (ALW) or Allowance for the Suvivor (ALWS); and an income amount is reported on Line 119/11900 in the CRA income feed for 2021. Group 2 includes non-urgent work items for accounts where: EI has confirmed that EI-ERB was received in 2021; the client or their spouse or common-law partner is a GIS for Life client and is not in pay for GIS, ALW or ALWS; and an income amount is reported on Line 119/11900 in the CRA income feed for 2021. The PWS work item includes a note that provides the amount of EI-ERB and EI benefits received in 2021. The amount of income identified as EI ERB, must be manually removed from the client’s income. In order to provide similar support for workers who would generally be eligible for the Employment Insurance (EI) program, the Minister made an interim order on March 31, 2020, providing for the Employment Insurance Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB) to be administered through Service Canada. Where continued support is needed, the Government of Canada introduced additional temporary recovery benefits to support those who are still unable to work for reasons related to COVID-19. These new benefits are: the Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB); the Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB); the Canada Recovery Caregiving Benefit (CRCB); and the Canada Worker Lockdown Benefit (CWLB). Not all individuals who were in receipt of the CERB/EI ERB will be eligible for continuing support under the new Government of Canada initiatives. The CERB/EI ERB, CRB, CRSB, CRCB and CWLB are taxable benefits that are considered income under the Income Tax Act and are considered income when determining entitlement to income-tested benefits up to June 2022. The analysis of this factor helps determine the potential impact of the applicant's education on their employability, including the ability to retrain. Formal education completed in the distant past may not be relevant in terms of current employability. More weight should be given to education, training and knowledge used in the applicant's more recent work. Consideration must also be given to the medical conditions, treatment and any cognitive or functional limitations and their impact on the applicant's ability to retrain. Consider the following elements: the applicant's level of education; any physical and cognitive functional limitations related to the medical condition that may affect the ability to retrain; any other work-related skills that have been acquired; if their skills would support the capacity for any work now; and if upgrading their skills would result in the ability to pursue regular gainful work. Education includes formal and informal education as well as training. Higher levels of education or training demonstrate the likelihood an individual will be capable of additional training in the future. Formal education completed many years ago may no longer be relevant in terms of the applicant’s or beneficiary’s capacity to pursue any substantially gainful occupation (SGO). Therefore: less emphasis should be given to formal education which occurred in the remote past; and consider education, training, or knowledge acquired or used in their most recent work in the context of their capacity to perform other types of SGO. In order to make a determination of eligibility or continuing eligibility for CPP disability (DSB) benefits, including the Post-retirement Disability Benefit (PRDB), a holistic assessment of work capacity must occur and consider: the medical condition(s); functional limitations affecting work capacity; and personal characteristics . personal characteristics

Personal characteristics, factors unique to a particular applicant that directly affect their ability to pursue any substantially gainful occupation, are considered when making a disability eligibility decision. Personal characteristics including age, education, work experience and language proficiency, on their own, are not sufficient to entitle an applicant or beneficiary to a disability pension. These personal characteristics are considered in combination with the medical condition and evaluated for impact on the applicant in the same way a medical condition is evaluated.

Personal characteristics must be considered when determining whether the combination of medical condition(s) and personal characteristics make it more likely than not that the contributor is disabled according to the CPP. Consideration must be given in a real world context, regarding what effect the combination of the applicant’s or beneficiary’s medical condition(s) and personal characteristics have on their functional capacity and ability to pursue any substantially gainful occupation (SGO). Consideration must be given to the combined effect of the applicant or beneficiary’s medical condition(s) and their: age; education; work experience; and language proficiency. Examples of socio-economic factors not to consider: Regional unemployment rates; Local access to specific jobs; Types of major industry in the region; Types of occupations offered by regional industries; and Occupational skills needed for those industries. The included parameters serve only as a baseline to help in decision making, not to quantify how to consider personal characteristics. Personal characteristics should be considered in the same manner that a medical condition is evaluated. A simple diagnosis may not always be sufficient to evaluate an applicant’s or beneficiary’s level of disability.

An applicant's work history and life experience is relevant as it provides information regarding transferable skills that could enhance their ability to pursue regular gainful work. Variation in work experience indicates a capability of adjusting to other work. In addition, persons with transferable skills generally have an advantage over low skilled workers in the labour market. Consider the following elements: the reason the applicant stopped working: e.g. medical condition, illness, care of a family member, shortage of work or contract end, maternity or paternity, dismissed or quit, lay off, company closure, etc.; whether the applicant has always worked for the same employer or had multiple employers; duration working with the employer or employers(s); the nature of the previous occupation; what the physical and cognitive demands were of the last job held; the applicant's past pattern regarding the type of work (regular or seasonal, contract, casual, etc.); whether the medical condition limited the applicant to part-time work; if the applicant was working in an accommodated workplace that provided specialized equipment, access for persons with disability, etc.; if there are gaps in the record of earnings or work history; whether there has been a decline in earnings that can be related to the medical condition; whether or not the evidence supports that the applicant can do their current job or a job they have done in the past; whether the evidence supports the capacity for regular gainful work suited to their education and work experience; and any attempts to return to work and the outcome. For the Work Experience Guide, Consideration of Personal Characteristics (Policy)

A determination must be made as to whether the applicant ’s or beneficiary’s past work and life experience may have provided them with any transferable skills that could enhance their capacity for substantially gainful work, including: on-the-job training; occupation-specific courses ; or volunteer work, etc. Impact of medical condition on ability to work It should be confirmed as to whether there are physical or cognitive limitations related to the applicant’s or beneficiary’s medical condition(s) that would affect their ability to use skills they had previously obtained. Impact of work experience on employability While in the past, many individuals worked for the same employer during their entire career, it is common today for an individual to work in a variety of jobs during their working years. This variation in work experience indicates they are likely capable of adjusting to other work. Similarly, individuals with transferable skills commonly have an advantage over low-skilled workers in the labour market. Skill level corresponds to the type or amount of training and education required to work in an occupation. It also reflects the experience required and the complexity of the responsibilities involved in the work. In most cases, progression to a highly skilled occupation is not possible without the completion of additional formal education, whereas progression from a low skilled occupation to one with higher skills is often achievable through on-the-job training and experience. Essential skills are the skills that provide the foundation for learning all other skills and enable individuals to better prepare for, get and keep a job, and adapt and succeed at work. Essential skills are used in the workplace in different ways and at different levels of complexity. The level of complexity can range from basic to advanced, and varies based on the work being performed. Where the applicant or beneficiary has a work history characterized by physically active work, consideration must be given as to whether it is likely they can perform sedentary work. Usually, these jobs require the ability to do light work with your hands, to do repetitive tasks which require fine motor skills, and literacy. Foreign benefits Individuals may be eligible for benefits from another country if they have lived or worked in that country. They may also be eligible if they are the surviving spouse or common-law partner of someone who lived or worked in another country. A foreign benefit is any benefit paid by the social security administration of a country other than Canada. Benefits from other countries are comparable to Canada's social security benefits and include: retirement old age disability death survivor Many countries have minimum requirements regarding contributions or residence for an individual to qualify for benefits. If the minimum requirements are not met, an International Social Security Agreement (ISSA) may help an individual qualify for a foreign benefit. If an individual resides in Canada and wants to apply for a benefit from another country where they lived or worked, they must complete a foreign benefits application form. Most countries with an agreement with Canada have their own unique foreign benefits application form. These forms are available in English, French and in the language of the particular country, if applicable. The applicant completes the form and sends it to International Operations (IO) where it is reviewed for completeness. IO then forwards the form to the other country, along with all supporting documentation and information. When to send a foreign benefit application to an applicant A foreign benefits application form must be sent to an individual that has requested an application, an applicant or the surviving spouse or common-law partner of an individual who has indicated on their Canadian benefits application that they have lived or worked in a country with which Canada has an ISSA. The applicant can indicate periods of residence and employment in foreign countries on Canadian applications for: ALW benefit ALWS benefit CPP Death benefit CPPD benefits CPP RTR pension CPP SVR pension OAS pension New versions of paper and online applications can provide applicants with information and a website link to investigate their eligibility or possible entitlement to benefits from another country. You no longer need to send a foreign benefit application to the client when they apply using the following forms: Application kit for Canada Pension Plan Disability benefits (ISP-1151) form; and Terminal Illness Application Kit for Disability Benefits under the Canada Pension Plan (ISP-2530A) form. If the client submits any other versions of the form, you must determine the correct foreign benefits application form and send it to them. If the client has indicated that they lived or worked in the United States and has not already requested or applied for United States benefits, you must notify the IO-Atlantic (ATL) region. The IO-ATL region will communicate with the client and send a foreign benefit application to the United States, if applicable. Interim Application form You must only send the applicant a Foreign Benefits under an Agreement on Social Security, Interim Application for (ISP-5005) form when the foreign benefit application form for their country is not available online.

A foreign benefit refers to any pension or benefit that is paid by a social security administration of a country other than Canada. Benefits from other countries are comparable to Canada's social security benefits and include retirement, old age, disability and survivor benefits. International Operations staff provide information to be sent with foreign benefit applications to assist the foreign institution in determining whether the individual is eligible to that country's benefits based on the terms of the social security agreement. An individual's Canadian creditable periods (i.e. Canadian residence and/or CPP creditable periods) may assist the individual to meet the eligibility criteria of the other country's pension scheme when an International Social Security Agreement exists between Canada and that country. In all cases, the foreign institution determines an applicant's eligibility. The action that you will take with a foreign benefit application is dependent on the foreign institution's requirements. You may be required to: verify that all of the required documents and information have been received prior to forwarding the application; or send the application without verifying the completeness of documentation or the application, in which case the foreign institution will communicate directly with the applicant to obtain the required information or documents .

You must consider an application under the incapacity provision i f: the applicant has regained capacity after indicating on their application that they were incapacitated; and the applicant has submitted their application within the required timeframe: one month of regaining capacity, if the period of incapacity was less than 30 days; the number of days equal to the number of days the person was incapacitated, if the period was less than one year; or one year, if the period of incapacity was greater than one year. The MA must deem the application to be received the later of: the start of the period of incapacity; or the month before the benefit could have started. Example Mr. Brown became incapacitated as a result of a severe head injury in November 2015, 4 months after his 65th birthday in July 2015. After extensive treatment, he has recovered to the point of having regained capacity by December 2017. He submits an application for an OAS pension in March 2018, with a note explaining his prior incapacity. An ISP1800 form is sent to Mr. Brown for completion. When it is returned to Service Canada, the complete file is sent to an MA for review. The MA determines that Mr. Brown was indeed incapacitated from November 2015 to December 2017 and returns the file for processing. Because Service Canada received the application within the prescribed timeframe for consideration under the incapacity provision, the deemed date of receipt is November 2015. You must use November 2015, and not March 2018, to calculate the entitlement. In addition, if all legislative requirements are met, the effective date can be as early as August 2015, the month following Mr. Brown's 65th birthday.

An application meets the eligibility criteria for the incapacity provision when the period of incapacity was continuous. In a case where the applicant regains capacity, the incapacity provision may be applied if the benefits application was submitted within the following time limits: within one month if the period of incapacity was less than 30 days; within the number of days the person was incapacitated, if the period of incapacity was less than 365 days (e.g. if the period of incapacity was 45 days, the applicant must submit their application within 45 days of regaining capacity); or within one year if the period of incapacity was more than 365 days. For more information, refer to Incapacity (Policy) and to Incapacity (Policy) Examples—Incapacity Provision (Work Tool)

The Correctional Service of Canada will provide the release date information to the Department on the monthly Correctional Service of Canada report. Before the Incarceration team can reinstate the benefit to the incarcerated client, the client must advise the Department in writing of their release. Adjustments must be made immediately to their spouse or common-law partner’s income-tested benefit, if applicable, even if the incarcerated client has not provided written notification. If the client submits written notification of their release to the regional processing office, advise the Incarceration team in Timmins using the OAS Incarceration Enquiry (ISP-5014) form. The Incarceration team will confirm that the date matches the Correctional Service of Canada’s record on the report. If there is a discrepancy, the Incarceration team will verify the date with the Correctional Service of Canada. The Correctional Service of Canada's release date is the authoritative source. If the client insists the wrong release date is being used, they may contact the Correctional Service of Canada to clarify the information. The applicant can notify the Department in advance if they know their release date. Payments can be reinstated by the Incarceration team the month the individual is released if they are still eligible and entitled. The applicant is entitled to receive up to 11 months of retroactivity for any months in which they were not incarcerated (including the 1st month of incarceration and the month of their release). OAS benefits are in pay prior to incarceration If the incarcerated individual is receiving OAS benefits when the notice of incarceration is received, the initial suspension of benefits is effective the month following the transfer of information from the Correctional Service of Canada or from the province or territory. Once the information regarding the incarceration is reviewed, the OAS account will need to be suspended effective the month following the month of incarceration. If the suspension is retroactive, an overpayment may be incurred. For more information on the impact of the incarceration on the spouse or common-law partner’s OAS benefits, refer to the OAS benefits for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual section below. OAS benefit applications processed during incarceration If an incarcerated individual or their spouse or common-law partner submits an application for an OAS pension or benefit, the application is processed in the regional or International Operations (IO) processing office as usual, along with any related work items (e.g. a Statement of Estimated Income after Retirement or Reduction in Pension Income Year 20XX (ISP-3041) form) to determine eligibility and entitlement. Application is approved If the application is approved, payments are not released by the regional or IO processing office. The regional or IO processing office will advise the Incarceration team of the outcome using the OAS Incarceration Enquiry (ISP-5014) form and the Incarceration team will perform the necessary actions to issue payments, release the account and notify the client and their spouse or common-law partner, if applicable. The Incarceration team cannot perform the required actions in the International Agreements systems. Therefore, the Incarceration team will advise the applicable IO processing office of any system actions required. These actions must be performed as a priority. If they are eligible and entitled, the incarcerated client's benefit payments will begin the month they are released. The incarcerated client is entitled to receive up to 11 months of retroactive payments for any months in which they were not incarcerated (including the 1st month of incarceration and the month of their release). If the application is approved for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual, the Incarceration team will review the account to determine which entitlement rate is more advantageous to them. Individuals incarcerated in a federal penitentiary or in a provincial correctional facility are not eligible to accrue an actuarial adjustment for the months they are incarcerated (i.e. the month after the month of incarceration up to the month before release). Entitlement—Voluntary Deferral and Pension Choices (Policy) Individuals will be able to accumulate residence while incarcerated up until their OAS pension or benefit application has been approved. After the approval of an application, individuals will be able to accumulate residence while incarcerated for the purpose of portability, but they may not accumulate residence for a higher payment rate. For more information on the impact of the incarceration on the spouse or common-law partner’s OAS benefits, refer to the OAS benefits for the spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual section below. Application is denied If the application is denied, the regional or IO processing office will perform all required actions on the account as usual, including: systems actions; sending denial letters; and updating ITRDS notes. If the Incarceration team in Timmins requested that the application be processed, notify them of the type of application processed and the pension or benefit that was denied using the ISP-5014 form.

OAS clients will not receive OAS pension or income-tested benefit payments during a period of incarceration in Canada: of 2 years or more to be served in a federal penitentiary; or exceeding 90 days to be served in a provincial correctional facility in a province where an Information Sharing Agreement (ISA) has been negotiated. Incarceration—OAS Pension and Benefits (Policy) In January 2011, the Correctional Service of Canada started transferring information to the Department on a monthly basis, identifying incarcerated and released individuals aged 60 and over. International Operations in National Headquarters was responsible for managing the exchange of information between the Department and the Correctional Service of Canada. As of March 19, 2020, this responsibility was transferred to a specialized team in the Timmins regional processing office, the Incarceration team. Administration of OAS benefits for incarcerated individuals UPDATED While the individual is incarcerated, regional processing offices are responsible for determining eligibility and entitlement to benefits. The Incarceration team in the Timmins processing office is responsible for: administering the benefits; managing the account; and communicating with the incarcerated individual and their spouse or common-law partner, if applicable.

Although different situations can necessitate the suspension of a benefit, OAS pensions or benefits are usually suspended for the following reasons: the Canada Revenue Agency notifies the Department that the OAS pension recipient is living in a foreign country and has not submitted the OAS Return of Income form; reviewing residence for OAS pension, GIS, ALW and ALWS benefits if entitlement is questioned; the pensioner or beneficiary is not entitled due to incarceration. Suspension of all OAS benefit payments are effective the month following the month of incarceration; if the pensioner leaves Canada for a period exceeding 6 months, not including the month of departure, and the pensioner has fewer than an aggregate of 20 years of residence in Canada after the age of 18. Payment of the OAS pension may resume the month in which the pensioner returns to Canada or the month residence in Canada is resumed.

No OAS benefit may be paid for any period of incarceration (exclusive of the first month of that period) to an individual who is incarcerated. The suspension of all OAS benefit payments is effective the month following the month of incarceration. Only incarcerated pensioners and beneficiaries will have their OAS benefits suspended. Low income spouses or common-law partners of incarcerated individuals will not lose their entitlement to the GIS or ALW benefit. Initial suspensions of OAS benefit payments following Royal Assent or Information Sharing Agreements concluded with provinces or territories The initial suspensions of OAS benefit payments were effective the month following the first transfer of information from Correctional Services Canada or from the province or territory that identifies the OAS pensioner or beneficiary as incarcerated. Subsequent suspensions of OAS benefit payments for existing pensioners and beneficiaries Based on the transfer of information from Correctional Services Canada or from the province or territory, OAS benefit payments will be suspended effective the month following the month of incarceration. OAS benefit applications submitted during incarceration When an application for an OAS benefit is submitted by an individual while they are incarcerated, the application may be approved at that time provided that the applicant meets all the OAS benefit eligibility criteria. However, payment of the benefit will only begin the month the individual is released, provided that they continue to meet all the eligibility requirements. The individual must notify the Department in writing of the date of their release. An individual whose OAS benefit application is approved while incarcerated is entitled to receive retroactive payment for any months (within 11 months) in which they were not incarcerated, including the first month of incarceration. OAS benefit applications submitted after release from incarceration If an application for an OAS benefit is received within 11 months of the individual's release from prison, no retroactive payment may be made for any month in which the individual was incarcerated (except for the first month of incarceration and the month of release). The application will be assessed to determine if the period of incarceration falls within the provision to limit payment of the OAS benefit based on sentence period and jurisdiction.

OAS applicants, pensioners and beneficiaries sentenced to imprisonment do not receive OAS benefit payments during of a period of incarceration. The provisions limit payment of OAS benefits to pensioners and beneficiaries by suspending their OAS benefits while they are incarcerated. They also limit payment to those who apply for OAS benefits while incarcerated. Should an individual apply after release from incarceration, the legislation also provides that there is no entitlement to retroactivity for any periods of incarceration except for the first month of incarceration and the month of release. Incarceration under the provisions of the OAS Act means that due to a sentence of imprisonment, an individual is confined in a penitentiary or a correctional facility for a period: of 2 years or more to be served in a federal penitentiary; or exceeding 90 days to be served in a provincial correctional facility in a province where an Information Sharing Agreement has been negotiated. There are 2 implementation stages for these provisions: In the first stage , OAS benefit payments are suspended during the period of incarceration to an individual who is sentenced to imprisonment in a federal penitentiary for a term of 2 years or more. In the second stage , Information Sharing Agreements will be pursued with the provinces and territories and implemented as they are concluded. Once an Information Sharing Agreement is in place with a province or a territory, the suspension of payments will be extended to individuals during the period of incarceration serving a term exceeding 90 days in a prison in that jurisdiction. This provision does not apply to individuals incarcerated outside of Canada. The Department has a one-way agreement with Correctional Services Canada that permits the disclosure of Correctional Services Canada information to the Department for the purpose of administering the OAS program exclusively. Currently there are no Information Sharing Agreements (ISAs) with provinces or territories allowing for the exchange of personal information between the Department and the province or territory for the purpose of limiting OAS benefit payments. Until ISAs are reached with provinces or territories, OAS payments cannot be withheld from these individuals. OAS benefits Murder or manslaughter of a spouse or common-law partner A spouse or common-law partner who has been convicted of 1st or 2nd degree murder or manslaughter will not be eligible to the Allowance for the Survivor ( ALWS ) benefit as a result of the death of the murdered individual. Benefits are either denied or cancelled back to the effective date. In these cases, there is no eligibility to the ALWS benefit due to the murdered spouse or common-law partner policy as opposed to limiting payments of OAS benefits due to incarceration. Pension income splitting To ensure that the lower income spouse or common-law partner of an incarcerated individual is not disadvantaged by a pension income split when calculating the GIS or the ALW benefit based on their own income, the non-incarcerated spouse or common-law partner may ask to exclude the amount of pension income split they received from their spouse or common-law partner. Notifications on the limitations of OAS pension and benefits payments OAS pensioners or beneficiaries must be informed in writing immediately of the suspension of their pension and benefits once it has happened. However, the limitations on payment of OAS benefits generated by the provision do not require that the pensioner or beneficiary be notified 30 days before the suspension of their OAS benefits. The non-entitlement to OAS benefits has been already determined by the information received from Correctional Services Canada or the province or territory. Letters will need to be sent to the spouses and common-law partners of incarcerated individuals who have had their GIS or ALW benefit adjusted due to the provision. Overpayments As of January 2011, any OAS payment received or obtained by the pensioner or beneficiary to which they are not entitled due to incarceration will be set up as an overpayment and will be recovered according to the overpayment policy and procedures. Reconsiderations and appeals Individuals whose OAS benefits are suspended or reinstated under this provision have recourse via the regular appeal process. If an individual is dissatisfied with a decision made, they may request a reconsideration of the decision by writing to the Minister within 90 days of being notified of the original decision. Individuals that remain unsatisfied with the reconsideration decision may request an appeal to the Social Security Tribunal-General Division. Family Orders and garnishment If an account suspended under this provision is also subject to a garnishment order under the Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act or a set-off agreement with the CRA , the withhold or garnishment activity on the account will also be suspended. The Department will notify the appropriate department (i.e. Department of Justice, the CRA ) of the suspension of OAS payments and the suspension of the garnishment or withhold. Reinstating OAS benefits when incarceration period ends New The OAS benefit payment will resume the month the individual is released, provided that they continue to meet all the eligibility requirements. The individual must notify the Department in writing of the date of their release. The individual can send the notification before or after the date of release. The date provided must correspond with the release date on the transfer of information from Correctional Service Canada or the province or territory before payments are resumed. There is no requirement for a new application as the beneficiary was eligible for the benefit throughout the period of incarceration but was not entitled to receive it. For income-tested benefits, a statement of income is required in order to calculate entitlement. The statement of income can be submitted by the beneficiary on a prescribed form or as a separate written statement. The requirement of a paper statement of income can be waived if the income information is received from the CRA .

Therefore, the Incarceration team will communicate with the IO processing office to advise of the system actions required. While the individual is incarcerated, regional and International Operations (IO) processing offices are responsible for determining eligibility and entitlement to benefits. However, the Incarceration team in Timmins is responsible for: administering the benefits; managing the account; and communicating with the incarcerated individual and their spouse or common-law partner, if applicable.

The Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act serve to make government more open and transparent and allow Canadians to fully participate in the democratic process. Under these Acts, individuals have the legal right to: obtain information, in any form, that is contained in government records; and the protection of their privacy and personal information held by the government.

The Access to Information Act gives Canadian citizens, permanent residents and any person or corporation present in Canada a right to access records of government institutions that are subject to the Act. The Privacy Act gives Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and individuals present in Canada the right to access their personal information held by government institutions that are subject to the Act. The Act also protects that information against unauthorized collection, use, retention and disclosure. Individuals present in Canada can access their government-held personal information by making an Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) request through the ATIP website. For more information on the collection, use, disclosure and retention of personal information, refer to Privacy and Personal Information . Refer to Employment and Social Development Canada’s Corporate Secretariat Branch ’s website for more information on the Department’s ATIP Division and its units, as well as these ATIP-related details: ATIP Privacy and Personal Information Corporate Secretariat Branch Steps required to access records held by federal government departments; and Forms to fill out. Refer to the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat for information on ATIP policies and directives. For a list of the names, addresses, and telephone numbers of the ATIP privacy coordinators in all ATIP offices across the federal government by institution, refer to the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat

The OAS pension and benefits amounts increase every 3 months by a factor based on the Consumer Price Index. Since 1975, CPP benefits are adjusted every year in January by a factor based on the Pension Index. For CPP purposes, the Pension Index for a year cannot be less than the previous year. In other words, benefits will never be adjusted downwards, even if the cost of living decreases. Escalation of CPP pension s and benefits payment rates CPP pensions and benefits payment rates may be adjusted or escalated each year in January to reflect increases in the cost of living as measured by the Consumer Price Index. The average of the monthly Consumer Price Index figures for the 12-month period ending October 31 of the previous year is the Pension Index. The pension and benefits payment rates are adjusted by a factor based on the Pension Index. The adjustment factor for each January is not available until mid-November of the preceding year because the Consumer Price Index for October must first be received from Statistics Canada. For CPP purposes, the Pension Index for a year cannot be less than that of the previous year. This means that the dollar amount of a CPP pension or benefit cannot drop to correspond with a similar drop in the Consumer Price Index. Escalation of OAS pension and benefits payment rates OAS pension and benefits payment rate increases are legislated under the Old Age Security Act . The rates are calculated 4 times a year (January, April, July and October) using data from the Consumer Price Index's All-Items Index so that pensions and benefits payments keep up with the cost of living. OAS pension and benefits rates are increased every 3 months by a factor based on the Consumer Price Index. For example, the factor used for increasing OAS benefits in April is equal to the ratio between the average Consumer Price Index for the 3-month period ending the previous January to the average Consumer Price Index for the 3-month period ending the previous October.

The contributory period is the period during which the individual is eligible to contribute a portion of their earnings to CPP. With CPP enhancement, there are up to three components to an individual's contributory period: the Base contributory period (as of January 1, 1966); the First additional contributory period (as of January 1, 2019); and the Second additional contributory period (as of January 1, 2024). The base contributory period starts on the latest of: January 1, 1966; or the month after the contributor's 18th birthday. The first additional contributory period starts on the latest of: January 1, 2019; or the month after the contributor's 18th birthday. The second additional contributory period starts on the latest of: January 1, 2024; or the month after the contributor's 18th birthday. All three contributory periods end with the earliest of the following: the month before the start of the contributor's RTR pension; the month of the contributor's 70th birthday; or the month of their death. For more information, CPP Earnings and Contributions (Policy)

The enhancement adds 2 additional contributory periods to the base CPP contributory period. The first additional contributory period begins January 1, 2019, or the month an individual reaches age 18 (whichever is later ) and ends the earliest of: the month before a contributor reaches age 70; the month in which the contributor dies; or the month before the month in which the retirement pension commences. The second additional contributory period begins January 1, 2024, or the month an individual reaches age 18 (whichever is later ) and ends the earliest of: the month before a contributor reaches age 70; the month in which the contributor dies; or the month before the month in which the retirement pension commences.

With the implementation of CPP enhancement, First Nations employees on reserves will still be able to choose whether to contribute to the CPP. However, if First Nations employees and employers contribute to the CPP, they and their employers will do so at the new contribution rates resulting from the enhancement. These higher contributions will increase the amount of their CPP benefits. If their employer chooses not to participate, First Nations employees may still elect to be covered by the CPP. They are required, however, to pay both the employee and employer contributions to the base, first additional and second additional components. First Nations people who are employed off reserves have always participated in the CPP and will participate in the CPP enhancement. For more information, refer to the CPP Earnings and Contributions (Policy)

Send all requests for medical information to your Regional Privacy Coordinator. Be cautious when releasing medical information. Requests for medical information must be made in writing. You cannot release medical information on the basis of a verbal request—the Regional Privacy Coordinator may want to consult with the Medical Adjudicator (MA) before releasing the information. Do not release medical information unless the participating program authorizes its release. This includes the disclosure of medical information to other program areas of the Department. Based on the MA's advice, the Regional Privacy Coordinator can exempt the report if the disclosure of part of a medical report may have an adverse effect on the physical, mental or emotional health of the client or may not be in the best interests of the client. In some instances, the physician indicates “Not to be released” on the medical report. The medical report is the property of the CPP Program. As such, the decision to release or not rests with the Regional Privacy Coordinator, based on the best interests of the client or third party. Before releasing medical information, ensure that: you clearly identify the need for the requested information; the doctor's report does not specify that the information must not be released because it could cause harm to the client or to someone else; you release only information that is relevant for the administration of the program; you apply due diligence when disclosing medical information. Example Employment Insurance (EI) requests a copy of a letter contained in the DSB benefit file. The client references work activity in the letter. However, the letter also contains information on the client's medical condition.Because substantiating work activity is relevant to the administration of the EI Act, you can release the specific information about the work activity. Do not release the medical information, because it is not relevant to the administration of the EI Act.

Individuals may request medical information from their file under the Privacy Act . Requests for copies of medical information must be in writing and not released on the basis of a verbal request. However, medical adjudicators have the flexibility of discussing medical evidence with the applicant, contributor or their legal representative over the phone. Medical adjudicators may also confirm the receipt of a medical report based on a verbal request. Requests for copies of medical information are forwarded to the regional or National Headquarters Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) coordinator. Medical information cannot be released unless the program authorizes the release. The coordinator will consult with a medical adjudicator before releasing the information. In situations where the disclosure of a medical report may not be in the best interests of the individual, the ATIP coordinator will obtain written confirmation from the physician who wrote the report on whether or not to release the medical information. The physician will advise the coordinator whether or not the release of the information would have an adverse effect on the physical, mental or emotional health of the individual or cause harm to a third party. In cases where the ATIP coordinator consults with a medical adjudicator before releasing information, the medical adjudicator may provide the ATIP coordinator with a recommendation, along with a rationale, as to why the medical information should not be released.

Any request for personal information not mentioning the Privacy Act and not submitted using the Treasury Board TBC/CTC 350-58 form or TBC/CTC 350-57 form are considered informal requests. Forward informal requests to your Regional Privacy Coordinator immediately. There is no time limit for a response. In some situations, the Department cannot provide access to all the personal information it holds about an individual. Exceptions to the access requirement must be limited and specific. The reasons for denying access will be provided to the individual upon request by the Regional Privacy Coordinator. Exceptions can include: information that contains references to other individuals; sensitive medical information; information that cannot be disclosed for legal or security reasons; information that is subject to solicitor-client or litigation privilege. The Department also provides an account of the use that has been made or is being made of this information. It also provides an account of the third parties to whom the information has been disclosed.

Generally, when receiving a written request that does not mention the Privacy Act specifically, it is considered an informal request for information. Once the Department identifies the identity and authority of the individual who will receive the information, they release the information under the legislative provisions of the Department of Employment and Social Development Act , the CPP legislation and the OAS Act. However, if information on an individual's file is exempt from disclosure, the Department cannot respond to an individual's informal request to provide them access to the personal information on their file. The privacy coordinator will provide the reasons for denying access to the individual. Denying access can occur for information that contains the following: references to other individuals; sensitive medical information; information that cannot be disclosed for legal or security reasons; and information that is subject to solicitor-client or litigation privilege. Requests for copies of the following are to be referred toAccess to Information and Privacy: medical reports; statements made by a third party; applications for benefits; letters sent to a third party; documents related to an integrity investigation; entire files, as they usually contain personal information of another individual (e.g. SIN and date of birth); information on another individual's file; and documents that contain the personal information of other individuals.

Personal information includes any recorded detail about an identifiable individual, including: race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age or marital status of the individual; education, the medical, criminal or employment history of the individual; financial transactions in which the individual has been involved; any identifying number, symbol or other particular assigned to the individual, such as a social insurance number (SIN); the address, fingerprints or blood type of the individual; the personal opinions or views of the individual, except where they are about another individual; correspondence sent to a government institution by the individual that is implicitly or explicitly of a private or confidential nature, and replies to such correspondence that would reveal the contents of the original correspondence; the views or opinions of another individual about the individual; the name of the individual where it appears with other personal information relating to the individual or where the disclosure of the name itself would reveal information about the individual. For a description of what Protected A, B and C information is and how to safeguard it when transmitting it by hand, mail, fax and email, refer to the Information Classification Tool

The Privacy Act defines personal information as information about an identifiable individual that is recorded in any form. Personal information includes: race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age or marital status of the individual; education and medical, criminal or employment history; financial transactions in which they were involved; any identifying number, symbol or other particular assigned to the individual, such as a SIN; an address, fingerprints or blood type; their personal opinions or views, except where they are about another individual; correspondence sent to a government institution by the individual that is implicitly or explicitly of a private or confidential nature, and replies to such correspondence that would reveal the contents of the original correspondence; the views or opinions of another individual about the individual; and their name where it appears with other personal information relating to them or where the disclosure of the name itself would reveal information about them.

An annual Bring Forward (BF) must be set on the accounts of couples living apart for reasons beyond their control to determine if it continues to be to the couple's advantage to have their entitlement based on individual income. The timing of the BF depends on whether they are being paid under the provision or not. A June BF is set on the control account of couples that are being paid based on their individual income. This annual review should occur before the beginning of every new payment period (i.e. June each year) to look for: a change in the couple's living arrangements; or a change in income information that makes the provision: no longer to the couple's advantage; or to the couple's advantage, where it was previously determined it was not. If no information has been received to suggest otherwise, it can be presumed that the couple is still living apart for reasons beyond their control. If the couple is no longer living apart for reasons beyond their control, their accounts must be updated effective the month following the month they resumed living together. The CRA and Revenu Québec are responsible for collecting Earnings and Contributions (E & C) data from copies of T4 and Relevé 1 forms by employers or T1 and TP1 general forms submitted by the self-employed. The agency responsible for administering a client's income tax is based on the client's province of residence on December 31st of the tax year. For dual contributors, Revenu Québec collects E & C, but QPP electronically transfers the information from Relevé 1 and TP1 to the Department. The Department receives regularly scheduled Record of Earnings (ROE) updates from the CRA . The CPP ROE is a record of the yearly earnings and contributions of a contributor. A person's CPP ROE is used to: determine eligibility for a CPP benefit; update client information; calculate CPP benefits; calculate any financial adjustment with QPP, in the case of a dual contributor; calculate RTR and post-retirement pensionable earnings by year; and prepare and issue a CPP Statement of Contributions. When a CPP benefit application is processed and approved for payment, the monthly entitlement is calculated based on the information contained in the contributor's CPP ROE at the time the decision is released in ITRDS (interim earnings). When the ROE is updated, ITRDS recalculates the benefit on the finalized earnings.

The SOC provides contributors with a year by year summary statement of their: CPP earnings and contributions (and QPP , if applicable); and estimates of their CPP pension and benefit dollar amounts. Canada Revenue Agency ( CRA ) and Revenu Québec are responsible for collecting CPP and QPP earnings and contributions data from the following documents: copies of T4 and Relevé 1 forms submitted by employers; or T1 and TP1 general forms submitted by the self-employed. CRA and Revenu Québec regularly transfer this data to Employment and Social Development Canada ( ESDC ) where it is posted to each contributor's Record of Earnings (ROE). A contributor's CPP ROE account is used to: determine eligibility for CPP benefits; calculate the CPP benefits entitlement amount; calculate the estimated monthly CPP benefits on the CPP SOC ; display earnings and contributions data on the CPP SOC , including any divided pensionable earnings and any Child Rearing Drop-in credits; calculate the Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings ( UPE ) by year; and prepare and send a manual CPP or CPP / QPP SOC . When a CPP pension or benefit application is processed, the CPP benefit entitlement amount is often based on interim earnings due to the delay between the moment CRA reports the contributor's income and the income appearing on the contributor's ROE. When ESDC receives earnings updates from CRA or QPP , the new data will trigger a recalculation. When the account is readjudicated in ITRDS , the CPP benefit amount is adjusted accordingly.

Under the Income Tax Act , when a client receives a CPP or QPP retroactive payment of which $300.00 or more relates to previous years, they can choose to exclude the previous year(s) retroactive amounts from their current tax year. The CRA can apply the notional tax provision to exclude any previous year’s portion from the current tax year if it reduces the client’s tax liability. When the notional tax provision is applied, the portion of the retroactive payment that relates to previous years can be attributed to the corresponding tax assessments for income tax purposes. Every year in mid-January, the Department transfers 2 files to the CRA. The first file has last year's T4 information for all clients who received a lump sum payment of which $300.00 or more is for a previous year. This file also includes a breakdown of the lump sum payment by year, for up to 10 years. The CRA then uses this information to apply the notional tax provision automatically if this action reduces the client's tax liability. However, if the provision does not benefit the client for taxation purposes, the CRA does not subtract the previous year's arrears payments when calculating the client's total amount for the current taxation year. The second file has a list of rejected accounts where ITRDS could not automatically break down the lump-sum payme nt by year. CRA uploads these 2 files to their system, which will compare the T4 information with the clients’ accounts. For any rejected accounts, the CRA will request breakdowns of the lump-sum payments from the Department by email. For clients who are eligible for an income-tested benefit, if the notional tax provision is applied to their CPP or QPP income, their benefits are based on this adjusted income and not the gross amount. If the CRA has not applied the notional tax provision automatically but the client meets the criteria to have it applied, staff will manually calculate the CPP or QPP with the notional tax provision and adjust the income as required.

The notional tax provision applies when a retroactive CPP or QPP lump sum payment or the total of multiple lump sum payments: was or were paid in the base calendar year; and includes a total amount of $300.00 or more that relates to a previous calendar year. When determining entitlement for income-tested benefits, the notional tax provision is applied for all clients who meet the above criteria, regardless of whether there is a tax benefit. The income removed from the current year is not retroactively applied to previous years and is not considered income for the previous years. For more Information, Calculating Income (Policy) In most cases, the base calendar year portion can be calculated by taking the December gross CPP or QPP rate and multiplying it by 12. Any retroactive CPP or QPP lump sum payments that do not extend to a previous calendar year, or any amount for the previous year that is less than $300.00, must be included in the base calendar year income in which the underpayment was issued. Although this adjustment is automatically applied by OAS Online and the IA system, the following situations may require manual adjustment: The income information is reported on an application or a statement of income and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) income information is not available. The client may not be aware of the notional tax provision and may include the full amount of CPP or QPP benefits received, including the full arrears portion; At reversion time (end of June), if both CRA income and client-reported income exist in the system, the system compares the income provided by the CRA to the client-reported income and retains the higher of the 2 amounts. If the client-reported income contains the full retroactive payment, the system will not retain the CRA income where the notional tax provision was applied; The notional tax provision was not applied by the CRA as it did not benefit the client for income tax purposes; The client did not file a federal Income Tax and Benefit Return; and An information link with the CRA has not been established for the account. To identify situations where the notional tax provision must be applied manually, verify the CPP and QPP amounts reported on all applications and statements of income.

International social security agreements allow a province or territory of Canada to conclude "Understandings" concerning social security with other countries. Quebec is currently the only province to enter into Understandings under social security agreements with other countries. Quebec has its own provincial pension plan, the QPP, which is Quebec’s counterpart to the CPP. The BESS is the liaison agency between Quebec and other countries when an Understanding is in force. The BESS is responsible for processing foreign benefit applications and providing information to social security agencies of other countries for individuals within the QPP's jurisdiction.

The Bureau des ententes de sécurité sociale (BESS) is responsible for the application of social security agreements between Quebec and other countries where there is an understanding in force. Foreign benefit applications that fall under the responsibility of BESS must be transferred to BESS to action with all accompanying documentation. A foreign institution's liaison request for QPP information from a client's file must be transferred to BESS to action with any documentation sent by the foreign institution. For more information, Determine Jurisdiction of a Foreign Benefit Application or Liaison Request (Action)

The established Date of Onset (DOO) is a term used for late applicants only. The established DOO is the date on which the applicant's disability started. It is a medically determined date that is separate from the DOO and the LPDOO. However, there will be instances where the established DOO may be adjusted for administrative purposes, i.e. setting the established DOO results in dropped years of earnings needed to qualify, or when the applicant is found disabled prior to the year of a possible prorate date. The CPPD benefit can be approved using the LAP only if the established DOO is on or before the LPDOO. Determine and Record the Established Date of Onset (Action)
