It is a medically determined date that is separate from the DOO and the LPDOO. The CPPD benefit can be approved using the LAP only if the established DOO is on or before the LPDOO. Determine and Record the Established Date of Onset (Action)

The established Date of Onset (DOO) is a medically determined date that and is separate from the Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO). At times, the medical evidence will not be sufficient to determine the established DOO. In such cases, the balance of probabilities approach must be considered.

If attempts to obtain medical evidence for the appropriate time frame (i.e. on or before the LPDOO and continuously thereafter) are not successful, or there are gaps in information, it does not necessarily mean the applicant was not disabled when the contributory requirements were last met. Refer to CPPD—File Development (Scenario) KA-01878 (article not available). You must consider if it was more likely than not the applicant was disabled by the LPDOO. Consideration of the progressive nature of the medical condition is particularly pertinent when adjudicating under the LAP. Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy)

The balance of probabilities is used to determine if the applicant was more likely than not disabled at the Latest Possible Date of Onset. All medical and non-medical evidence on file, as well as the progressive nature of the applicant’s medical condition (s) and whole medical history must be considered. Consideration of the progressive nature of the medical condition (s) is particularly pertinent when adjudicating under the LAP.

As of January 1, 1998, earnings are valid if they are above the Disability Basic Exemption (DBE) in a given year External link . Earnings below the DBE are not considered to be a valid year of earnings for the purposes of CPPD and do not require investigation. Disability Basic Exemption (DBE) in a given year The DBE is 10% of the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings. The applicant can have one to three years of valid earnings after they last met the contributory requirements. The SCBO will identify any years of valid earnings after the LPDOO from the Contributions screen as the Benefits screen in ITRDS only identifies the LPDOO. Earnings after the LPDOO may represent earnings from several sources. This may include, but is not limited to: regular work activity; private benefits; pensionable earnings not from work; foreign work activity; credit splitting; or paid out vacation credits or severance pay. For more information, Valid Earnings after the Latest Possible Date of Onset (Policy)

As of January 1, 1998, valid earnings are earnings that exceed the Disability Basic Exemption (DBE) in a given year. Earnings below the DBE are not considered to be valid earnings for the purposes of the CPP Disability benefit and do not require investigation. An applicant may have valid earnings after their Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) because they wanted to maintain a connection to the workforce or were attempting to continue working despite their disability and were unsuccessful. To recognize and support the applicant's attempt to remain in the workforce, these years must be investigated to determine if the applicant had capacity for work after their LPDOO. If an applicant has one to 3 years of valid earnings after they last met the contributory requirements, investigation of the valid earnings after the LPDOO will determine their work capacity. The assessment of work capacity for those years is based on: performance; productivity; and profitability. If an applicant has valid earnings after the LPDOO and it is determined that the earnings do not represent the work capacity, it must be established if the applicant had a severe and prolonged disability: on or before their LPDOO; and continuously since their LPDOO to the date of application and into the future. Both employer and medical evidence is required to determine capacity from the LPDOO, including the valid years of earnings. The evidence is to be used to support the continuous nature of the disability determination. There are times when information regarding an applicant’s work activity may not be available (e.g. the business has closed, the files destroyed). When this occurs, consider all evidence (medical and non-medical): what is known about the applicant’s work activity; information about the applicant’s medical condition; and the Medical Adjudicator's knowledge of CPP legislation and policy. The balance of probabilities standard is used to determine if the applicant was more likely than not disabled at their LPDOO.

Fast-track reapplication is an accelerated application process for applicants whose benefits ceased within the last 5 years. This process receives priority attention through all stages of service. To qualify, applicants must meet the severe and prolonged eligibility criteria under the fast-track reapplication process. The fast-track reapplication is available to applicants who meet all the following criteria: They previously received a CPPD benefit. Their CPPD benefit ceased (i.e. not suspended), and they are not: in an active appeal period; or appealing the cease decision, including an appeal to the SST (General Division or Appeal Division) or Federal Court of Appeal. They worked or participated in work-like activities(e.g. volunteer or educational activities) after their CPPD benefit ceased and have since stopped. They stopped work or stopped work-like activities within: one year of the date of the fast-track reapplication; and five years of the cease date. They stopped work or stopped work-like activities due to a recurrence of the same or related disability for which they were originally approved. They are applying for the same benefit that was previously in pay. They are not receiving a CPP RTR pension at the date of the recurrence (for DSB applicants only). They are under the age of 65. They meet the earnings and contributions requirements. The fast-track reapplication process is not available to applicants whose benefits ceased due to regained capacity or non-compliance, without evidence the past beneficiary returned to work. For more information, refer to Fast Track Reapplication (Policy) and Automatic Reinstatement & Fast Track Reapplication Reference Guide Share Point link . Fast Track Reapplication (Policy) Automatic Reinstatement & Fast Track Reapplication Reference Guide

The fast-track reapplication process is offered to beneficiaries who stop working within 5 years of their CPPD benefit being ceased due to a recurrence of the same or related disability. They must reapply within 1 year of recurrence of the same or a related disability. For more information, refer to Process a Fast-Track Reapplication (Scenario) or Process a Fast-Track Reapplication (Scenario) Fast Track Reapplication (Policy)

The fast track reapplication is an incentive offered to past CPPD beneficiaries who attempted to return to work or participated in work-like activities. The fast track reapplication is an accelerated process for previous CPPD beneficiaries who stop working within 5 years of their benefit cease date. It is offered if the beneficiary stopped work due to a recurrence of the same or related disability for which they were originally granted benefits. Fast-track reapplication only applies to the same benefit that was previously in pay. A past beneficiary may request a fast track reapplication kit: in writing or via the My Service Canada Account (MSCA); by phone; or in person. Eligibility criteria To qualify for a CPPD benefit under the fast track reapplication, the past beneficiary must meet the following eligibility criteria: be under the age of 65; for DSB , not be receiving a CPP retirement pension at the date of the recurrence of the same or related medical condition; have received a CPPD benefit in the past; have had their CPPD benefit ceased (i.e. benefit is not currently suspended) and they must not be appealing the cease decision; have stopped work or work-like activity due to a recurrence of the same or related disability for which they were previously granted a CPPD benefit; reapply within 1 year of the recurrence of the same or a related disability within 5 years of the date their DSB or PRDB was ceased; meet the earnings and contributions requirements. Earnings and contributions considerations Refer to the Eligibility Requirements— PRDB (Policy) . Commencement of payments Past beneficiaries who are deemed eligible under the fast track reapplication process and are found to be disabled are to receive payment within 2 months of the date of reapplication. The date of Onset will be the later of: The month after the month in which the past beneficiary stopped work or is found to be disabled, if maximum retroactivity has not been provided; or 12 months before the date of application (maximum retroactivity). If the fast-track reapplication is refused, a subsequent application may be date protected to the receipt of the fast-track reapplication.

To request the reinstatement of a CPPD benefit, a past beneficiary or authorized third party must provide information about the recurrence of the same or related disability. They must also provide the date the past beneficiary: stopped working; or was unable to participate in volunteer or educational activities. When a benefit is ceased, the past beneficiary is provided with personalized AR request forms, if applicable. These AR request forms for a CPPD benefit include the: Automatic Reinstatement of CPP Disability Benefits form; and Automatic Reinstatement of CPP Disability Benefits Physician or Nurse Practitioner Confirmation form. The following documents can also be considered as a request for an AR, if received within the appropriate timeframes: A Fast-Track Re-Application for Canada Pension Plan Disability Benefits form; A Terminal Illness Application Kit for Disability Benefits under the Canada Pension Plan (ISP-2530A) form; An Application kit for Canada Pension Plan Disability benefits (ISP-1151) form; or A signed written statement requesting the reinstatement of their CPPD benefits. If any of these documents are received and accepted as a request for an AR, the PWS work type is changed to Disability Auto Reinstate . These documents are accepted as confirmation of entitlement and generally no additional information is required. However, in some circumstances, file development may be required to support the AR of the benefit. A past beneficiary can upload a copy of their AR request forms to My Service Canada Account by selecting Other/correspondence . This information is uploaded into PWS as a Correspondence work type and the work type must be manually changed to Disability Auto Reinstate . Requests for an AR receive priority attention through all stages of service. It is the intent of the legislation to ensure that payments resume within 30 days of receipt of the AR request.

Past beneficiary dies after completing an automatic reinstatement request If the Department receives the required documentation from the past beneficiary or their legal representative prior to their death and within one year of the date the same or related disability reoccurred, their DSB or PRDB can be reinstated. Post-Mortem Applications (Policy) In pay for the CPP RTR pension A past beneficiary cannot cancel their Early Retirement (ERTR) pension in favour of a DSB if the recurrence of their medical condition occurred after the start of their ERTR pension. They must have become unable to work due to a recurrence of their medical condition prior to the effective date of their ERTR pension. If the recurrence of the past beneficiary's medical condition occurs after the effective date of their ERTR pension, they may be eligible for the PRDB if specific conditions are met. Documentation An AR request must be made in writing. The past beneficiary is required to supply information about the recurrence of the same or related disability and the date they: stopped working; were unable to participate in educational activity; or were unable to participate in volunteer activity. When the benefit ceased, the beneficiary was provided with: a personalized Reinstatement of CPPD Benefits form; and a Physician or Nurse Practitioner Confirmation form. These completed forms will be accepted as a confirmation of AR eligibility. Generally, no additional information is requested unless further clarification is required. Earnings and Contributions If the past beneficiary does not meet the eligibility criteria for AR, they will be required to meet the Earnings and Contributions (E & C) requirements if they choose to apply using the fast-track reapplication or the initial application for a CPPD benefit. Although past beneficiaries do not require E & C to be eligible for AR, any valid contributions made while they were working will be included in the entitlement calculation for the: DSB ; RTR pension; DTH benefit; and SVR pension. Past beneficiary returning to work or residing in Québec Past beneficiaries whose CPPD benefit ceased due to a return to work are eligible for the AR even if they contribute to the Québec Pension Plan (QPP) or reside in Québec. Their QPP contributions will be used to recalculate their reinstated DSB . The eligibility is established when the DSB is ceased. Effective date If it is determined that the past beneficiary meets the criteria for AR, their CPPD benefit will start the month following the month they stopped work activity or work-like activity or 12 months prior to the date of the request (maximum retroactivity). If the past beneficiary was laid off, dismissed, terminated, or quit and subsequently has a recurrence of the same or related disability, their CPPD benefit will be reinstated effective the month following the date when their disability recurred and not the date stopped work or work-like activity. Payment amount The amount of the reinstated CPPD benefit will generally not be less than what the past beneficiary would have received However, if their personal or family situation (e.g. credit splitting, change in custody of children) changed since the cessation of benefits, the CPPD benefit monthly entitlement amount could be affected. In the case of PRDB , the amount of the RTR pension could be affected. Other CPP benefits The Disabled Contributor's Child Benefit will be paid if the eligibility requirements are met at the time the CPPD benefit is reinstated.

AR is not a readjudication of CPPD benefits. It is a return-to-work incentive available to past beneficiaries who were previously in receipt of CPPD benefits and who now meet specific eligibility criteria. There is no limit to the number of times a past beneficiary can request an AR.

AR is not a re-adjudication of eligibility for CPPD benefits. When the DSB or PRDB is approved, the beneficiary is determined to have met the severe and prolonged criteria for that medical condition. If a past beneficiary stops work activity or work-like activity (i.e. volunteer or educational activities) due to a recurrence of the same or related medical condition, the criteria do not need to be met again and a review of eligibility is not undertaken. Past beneficiaries who request the reinstatement of benefits do not have to meet earnings and contributions requirements and are not required to undergo a medical review of eligibility. If the past beneficiary does not meet the AR requirements as outlined below, they are still able to reapply for a CPPD benefit as a fast-track reapplication or a new application.

Past beneficiaries may request AR if they have stopped work or work-like activities (i.e. volunteer or educational activities) due to a recurrence of the same or related medical condition for which they were originally approved. The CPPD benefit that was previously in pay must be the same benefit that is reinstated. For example, a PRDB cannot be reinstated if a DSB was the benefit previously in pay. To be eligible for AR, the past beneficiary must meet all of the following criteria: They are under the age of 65. They had a recurrence of the same or related medical condition prior to the start date of an Early Retirement (ERTR) pension (for DSB beneficiaries only). Their DSB or PRDB ceased due to a: return to work; participation in an educational activity; or participation in a volunteer activity. They had a recurrence of the same or related disability within 2 years of the date their DSB or PRDB ceased. They submitted a request for a reinstatement within one year of the recurrence of the disability that caused them to stop work or work-like activities (e.g. volunteer or educational activities). Their cease decision is not under appeal, including an appeal to the SST (General Division or Appeal Division) or Federal Court of Appeal. If a past beneficiary requests an appeal of a cease decision and also requests an AR before the appeal decision is finalized, the AR request will be held in abeyance until the outcome of the appeal is determined. A past DSB beneficiary who started to receive their ERTR pension may be eligible for an AR if they: are deemed disabled before the start date of their ERTR pension; and have been receiving their ERTR pension for less than 15 months. If the above criteria is not met, they may be entitled to a PRDB. However, a new application specifically for the PRDB is required. Automatic reinstatement (AR) is an incentive which provides financial security to beneficiaries of CPPD benefits who are unsuccessful at their: return to work; participation in educational activities; or participation in volunteer activity. AR allows past beneficiaries of CPPD benefits who meet the AR eligibility criteria to have their CPPD benefit reinstated if they are unable to continue working or participating in educational or volunteer activities due to the same or related disability. This incentive is available for 2 years following the month benefits were ceased. AR is particularly helpful to past beneficiaries with episodic or recurring conditions. Each additional recurrence of the medical condition has an impact on treatment, recovery and likelihood of deterioration. Recurrences may result in: shorter intervals between relapses; additional functional limitations or a further reduction in functional abilities; more aggressive treatment and medical interventions; and longer absences from the workplace. A beneficiary may experience multiple episodes of exacerbation and remission over their lifetime while receiving a CPPD benefit. Eligibility requirements Appeal rights AR decisions are subject to reconsideration and appeal to the SST . Protection of initial and fast-track reapplication If it is determined the past beneficiary does not meet the criteria for AR, the date the signed reinstatement form was received may be used as the application date for a subsequent CPPD benefit application or fast-track reapplication. For more information, Severe Criterion—Work Activity and Earnings (Policy)

Legislation defines a school or university as a "school, college, university or other educational institution that provides training or instruction of an educational, professional, vocational or technical nature." Acceptable institutions include, but are not limited to: Universities Composite High Schools Comprehensive Schools High Schools Colleges (regular) Community Colleges Military Colleges Business Colleges Bible Colleges Colleges of Applied Arts and Technology Collegiate Institutes Convents Novitiates Institutes of Technology Music Academies (School) Polytechnic Schools Schools of Applied Arts and Technology Schools of Nursing Technical Schools Vocational Schools The institution can be located in Canada or abroad. Use the following factors to determine if an institution is acceptable for CPP purposes. It is recognized as an educational institution by a province or territory, or its course of study is affiliated with an institution that is so recognized. It offers the student a diploma or certificate upon completion of the course of study. It provides training that will directly prepare the student for further study at a recognized educational institution. It can demonstrate that the student must attend or otherwise participate in courses (e.g. submit papers, make presentations, write tests, pass examinations and other activities that indicate full-time study).

The requirement for documentation to support legal status will be waived when processing all initial OAS pension, ALW or ALWS benefit applications, if the applicant meets one of the following criteria: The applicant is selected for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension; The applicant is not selected for automatic enrolment but submits a paper application and has their eligibility for an OAS pension determined by a combination of automatic enrolment data elements. Refer to Eligibility Requirements—Automatic Enrolment (Policy) ; or Eligibility Requirements—Automatic Enrolment (Policy) The applicant meets certain criteria to have this requirement waived. Refer to Documentary Evidence—Legal Status (Policy) . Documentary Evidence—Legal Status (Policy) Once the client's legal status has been confirmed for the ALW or ALWS benefit, it does not need to be confirmed again when converting the benefit to the OAS pension, unless there is an indication that the legal status has changed. Although documentation to support legal status may not be required, documentary evidence can be requested at any time before or after approval of the OAS pension and ALW or ALWS benefits. When validating the declared legal status, examine the documents you receive from the applicant to ensure they are valid (e.g. the document is acceptable, the document is not expired on the day legal status is required). If there are discrepancies between the provided documents and the information on the application or in the file, you must request clarification from the applicant before making a decision. For more information, Documentary Evidence—Legal Status (Policy) Acceptable documentation There are multiple legal status categories and a vast number of documents exist to support proof of legal status. For more information on the various types of acceptable documents to support legal status, Documentary Evidence—Legal Status (Policy) Foreign-born applicants The Landed Immigrant document or the Permanent Resident card can be used to confirm legal status in Canada, even if the individual has subsequently obtained their Canadian citizenship. If the applicant indicated on their application that they are a Canadian citizen, but only provided their Landed Immigrant document (e.g. IMM 1000) or Permanent Resident card, they do not need to provide proof of Canadian Citizenship if they: originally entered Canada as a permanent resident or landed immigrant and have provided acceptable proof of this status; have no absences from Canada where legal status may have been lost; are currently residing in Canada; and have no discrepancies or conflicting information on their account.

The requirement for documentation to support legal status will be waived when processing all initial OAS pension, ALW or ALWS benefit applications, provided the applicant: completes the appropriate sections of the application pertaining to their legal status (this will meet the requirement of confirming their legal status in writing); has a Canadian address; indicates one of the following legal statuses on the application: Canadian citizen; Permanent resident (landed immigrant); or Status Indian; is not currently under a sponsorship agreement. This operational policy will be applied only when there are no changes or inconsistencies between the information on the application or any documentation submitted with the application(s) currently on file. If there are changes or inconsistencies, a review will be completed and evidence of legal status is required. OAS automatic enrolment For individuals who are selected for automatic enrolment of the OAS pension, documentary evidence to support legal status is waived as these individuals meet the eligibility requirements through a combination of data elements. Although documentation to support legal status may not be required, documentary evidence can be requested at any time before or after approval of the OAS pension.

The applicant must indicate their legal status on their OAS pension application and their ALW and ALWS benefit application. The applicant's legal status declaration must be in writing, unless the requirement has been waived through automatic enrolment of the OAS pension. You must validate the applicant's declared legal status to determine their eligibility for an OAS pension or an ALW or ALWS benefit.

All applicants must provide proof of legal status, with the exception of individuals for whom the requirement for documentation has been waived. Legal status evidence must be requested, where applicable, and examined when determining an applicant's eligibility for OAS benefits.

You must review the file to determine if there is any evidence that the applicant lost their legal status (e.g. long absences reported in the residence statement, stamps in passport). An applicant who has lost their legal status must prove that it has been reinstated before the application's approval. Before February 15, 1977, Canadian citizens could not have a dual citizenship. If a Canadian citizen was absent for a period greater than 5 years or became a citizen of another country before or by this date, they may have lost their Canadian citizenship. If there is any indication on the file that the applicant may have lost their legal status during an absence before February 15, 1977, they must either: complete a statutory declaration confirming that they were not granted citizenship in another country during their absence over 5 years; or provide a Canadian citizenship certificate as proof that their Canadian citizenship has been restored. Applicants who are Canadian citizens and became citizens of another country on or after February 15, 1977, do not lose their Canadian citizenship. They hold dual citizenship. For more information, refer to Legal Status—Examples and Legal Status—Examples Defining Legal Status (Policy) Applicants resuming residence in Canada Applicants who resume residence in Canada and apply for an OAS pension, ALW benefit or ALWS benefit must meet the legal status requirement on the day before the application is approved. An applicant who lost their citizenship due to departing Canada and becoming a citizen of a foreign country before February 15, 1977, may have had their Canadian citizenship automatically reinstated under the amendments to the Citizenship Act that came into force on April 17, 2009. In this case, citizenship is reinstated back to the day the applicant was born or the day they lost their citizenship, depending on the situation. These applicants do not have to apply for citizenship but may need to request a Canadian Citizenship certificate. For more information, Defining Legal Status (Policy)

Foreign-born applicants fall into one of several categories when determining their legal status. The following individuals must provide proof of legal status: Applicants who were born in the United Kingdom Applicants who were born in the United Kingdom and arrived in Canada before January 1, 1947 may be considered to be legal residents in Canada if they can: produce a Class A birth certificate; and establish that there have been no absences from Canada that would interrupt residence for the purposes of OAS since their date of arrival. Naturalized British subjects Before January 1, 1947, immigrants to Canada could become naturalized as British subjects and receive a naturalization certificate. When the Canadian Citizenship Act became law on January 1, 1947, naturalized British subjects with at least 5 years of residence in Canada automatically became Canadian citizens. Naturalized Canadians who have had no absences from Canada may be considered to have retained their status in the same way as Canadian-born applicants. If the applicant had any absences of 5 years or more before February 15, 1977, they must complete a statutory declaration declaring that they have not become citizens of another country before February 15, 1977. All members of a family were frequently included as British subjects in Canada in certificates of naturalization issued before 1947. Where the applicant is named as a dependant in such a certificate, you may accept it as proof of status, provided there is no indication of a change since that time. Immigrants with permanent resident/legal resident status For applicants, who immigrated to Canada in 1925 and later, the process of confirming their status is simplified because of the central alphabetical index that was established by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) authorities at that time. Immigrants who became Canadian citizens In addition to proving their citizenship, Canadian citizens who have been absent for a period of 5 years or more before February 15, 1977, may be asked to complete a Statutory Declaration stating that they have not become citizens of another country before February 15, 1977. For those individuals who may have automatically had their Canadian citizenship reinstated as of April 17, 2009 by IRCC, a Statutory Declaration is not required.

For CPP applications, where the applicant has a life-long developmental disability and they have made earnings and contributions, the incapacity provision would be assessed, but only applied if it is to the advantage of the applicant. The Incapacity provision should not be applied in cases of a CPPD benefits application where the life-long disability is the incapacitating condition and the application of the incapacity provision would remove earnings and contributions made, thereby disqualifying the applicant from being entitled to a benefit.

Life-long developmental disability In cases where an applicant has a life-long developmental disability and they have made contributions to the CPP, the incapacity provision should be assessed but would only be applied if it is to the advantage of the applicant. In the case where the life-long disability is the incapacitating condition and the application of the incapacity provision would negate the earnings and contributions made, thereby disqualifying the individual from being entitled to a benefit, the incapacity provision should not be applied. For OAS benefits, earnings and contributions are not a factor when determining eligibility, therefore if the applicant has a life-long developmental disability, the incapacity provision can be assessed and could be applied. Determining a medical date of onset for disability For CPP Disability benefits (CPPD benefits) (both DSB and the PRDB ), an applicant cannot be deemed to have become disabled earlier than 15 months before the date of their CPPD benefits application. If the applicant is found to be incapacitated, the 15-month retroactivity begins from the new deemed date of application. For applicants in pay for benefits in the previous 5 years, the maximum retroactivity of 12 months applies to the earlier deemed date of application. Determination using the Late Applicant Provision It is possible to consider the incapacity and the late applicant provisions when reviewing an application for disability benefits. The provisions operate together without any conflict between them. The incapacity provision is applied first, and then, if necessary, the late applicant provision is considered. If as a result of a determination of incapacity, the disability application is deemed to have been received at an earlier date: it must be determined if the person has sufficient contributions to meet the Minimum Qualifying Period at an earlier date; and whether the person met the CPP definition of disability before or at their Latest Possible Date of Onset and continuously thereafter.

Should the medical evidence not meet the reasonably satisfied standard of proof for incapacity, development for medical reports or ISP-1800 form is suggested. Definition of terminal illness For CPP purposes, a Terminal Illness (TI) is defined as a medical condition that cannot be cured or adequately treated and is reasonably expected to result in death within 6 months. When a doctor, nurse practitioner or a registered nurse in a geographically isolated area completes a medical attestation or medical report, they use this definition to attest that an applicant has a TI. TI attestation The Terminal Illness Medical Attestation for a Disability Benefits Application under the Canada Pension Plan (ISP-2530B) form or section 4 a) of the Medical Report for Canada Pension Plan Disability Benefits (ISP-2519) form is sufficient evidence to determine that an applicant has a severe and prolonged disability. The attestation should be taken at face value and development should only be undertaken in unique circumstances, such as late applications or if the applicant is working at the date of application. In cases where the medical condition is suggestive of a TI, but an attestation is not completed, screening for a grave medical condition should take place.

The Late Applicant Provision (LAP) is for individuals applying for a DSB or a PRDB who do not have sufficient earnings and contributions in the 6 years prior to the date of their application. The LAP protects contributors who would have met the earnings, contributions and medical criteria had they applied at an earlier time. There is no restriction to the number of times an individual can apply for benefits or the number of times the LAP can be used. Conditions of the provision For the DSB , the LAP can be considered if: other applicable provisions, such as: the Child Rearing Provision (CRP); the proration of earnings; credit splitting; additional earnings; International Agreements (IA); and previous DSB periods have been considered and the applicant still does not meet the current DSB contributory requirements. the applicant meets the contributory requirements at an earlier date. For the PRDB , when the Date of Onset (DOO) or established DOO falls between January 2019 and April 2023, the LAP can be considered if: the applicant does not meet the contributory requirements at the date of application; the applicable provisions (e.g. credit splitting and IA) have been considered; the applicant still does not meet the contributory requirements; and the considered date of application cannot be earlier than the individual’s Early Retirement (ERTR) pension effective date. Considered Date of Application The application for the LAP with respect to a PRDB Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) calculation requires that the application must be received earlier than it was. The considered date of application creates a new 6-year window during which the earnings and contributions must be present. The considered date of application cannot be before 2019, the year PRDB came into force, or the year the individual started receiving their ERTR pension. Determination of the DSB Latest Possible Date of Onset The Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO) will be established based on an applicant’s earnings, contributions and all applicable legislative provisions. The legislative contributory requirements in effect at the DOO or established DOO must be met to determine the LPDOO. LPDOO and PRDB For the purpose of a PRDB , it is not necessary for the individual’s DOO to have started within the MQP. It is only necessary that the individual meets the contributory requirements, has a DOO or established DOO on or after January 2019 and before their 65th birthday.

The Late Applicant Provision (LAP) is for individuals applying for a DSB or a PRDB who do not have sufficient earnings and contributions in the 6 years prior to the date of their application. The LAP protects contributors who would have met the earnings, contributions and medical criteria had they applied at an earlier time. There is no restriction to the number of times an individual can apply for benefits or the number of times the LAP can be used. Conditions of the provision The LAP can be considered if other applicable provisions and considerations have been reviewed and the applicant still does not meet the current DSB or PRDB contributory requirements. These include: the Child Rearing Provision; the proration of earnings; Credit splitting; additional earnings; International Agreements; and previous DSB or PRDB periods. In addition, the individual must: meet the contributory requirements at an earlier date; and have been disabled at an earlier date and continuously since then. Determination of the LPDOO The LPDOO will be established based on an applicant's earnings, contributions and all applicable legislative provisions. The legislative contributory requirements in effect at the Date of Onset or the established Date of Onset must be met to determine the LPDOO.

To be eligible for a CPPD benefit under the Late Applicant Provision, the applicant must meet the following criteria: Be considered disabled within the meaning of the CPP when they last met the contributory requirements. Have continuously met the severe and prolonged criteria since the Latest Possible Date of Onset. Be disabled at the date of application. Be likely to remain disabled in the foreseeable future and be considered incapable of regularly pursuing any substantial gainful occupation. For more information, refer to: Non-Medical Processing and the Late Applicant Provision (Policy) . The Late Applicant Provision (LAP) can extend eligibility to CPP disability (DSB) benefits to protect those contributors who would have met the earnings and medical eligibility had they applied for a CPP DSB benefit at an earlier time. The LAP can be applied if the applicant meets the following contributory requirements: they were conside red disabled within the meaning of the CPP when they last met the contributory requirements, th e Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO); they continue to meet the severe and prolonged criteria since their LPDOO; they were disab led at the date of adjudication; and they are likel y to be disabled into the future and considered incapable of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation (equal to 12 times the maximum monthly disability amount). The LAP allows for the determination as to whether or not an applicant qualifies for CPP DSB benefits at a time when they had coverage under the CPP . Once it is established that the applicant has met the contributory requirements at some point in time, it must be determined if the applicant meets the definition of “disabled” within the meaning of the CPP. T o make a medical determination, it must be established if the applicant met the definition of a “severe and prolonged” disability when they last qualified for a benefit and continuously thereafter. In order to make a defendable and sustainable denial decision, the evidence must demonstrate: the applicant was not disabled at their LPDOO; and the information supports the applicant’s work capacity after their LPDOO.

The PRDB and DSB are 2 distinct benefits. The PRDB came into effect January 1, 2019. It provides disability coverage for CPP Early Retirement pensioners who meet the legislative criteria of severe and prolonged and have not reached age 65. A legislative change to the PRDB came into effect in May 2023. The Date of Onset (DOO) or established DOO will determine which legislation applies.

Effective Date: January 2019 to April 2023 To be eligible for PRDB , the contributor must: apply with a valid application (in writing or online); be in receipt of a CPP Early Retirement (ERTR) pension; be under age 65; meet the contributory requirements by having valid earnings and contributions in at least 4 of the last 6 years, or 3 of the last 6 years in the case of a contributor with 25 years or more of contributions, immediately prior to the date (year) of the CPPD application; and, have a severe and prolonged disability as defined in the CPP. Eligibility for PRDB ends: when the beneficiary ceases to be disabled; when the beneficiary reaches 65 years of age; or the month in which the beneficiary dies. For more information, Non-Medical Processing and the Late Applicant Provision (Policy)

The DSB and the PRDB are monthly benefits for CPP contributors who are determined to have a severe and prolonged medical condition. Before a determination on medical eligibility can be made, contributors or their representatives must submit an application in the prescribed manner. To qualify for a DSB or a PRDB , the applicant must: be under the age of 65; and meet the CPP contributory requirements. The PRDB provides protection to RTR pensioners who have either: been in pay for an Early Retirement (ERTR) longer than 15 months and have become disabled; or received an ERTR and subsequently became disabled.

The Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act allows for garnishment of federal monies. A spouse or common-law partner may petition a court for a judgment order. These petitioning documents are submitted to the Minister of Justice. The Department of Justice then requests the search of all eligible funds which can then be intercepted, including the following payments: OAS pension; Allowance benefit; Allowance for the Survivor benefit; Guaranteed Income Supplement benefit; and/or CPP pensions and benefits, excluding: benefits payable in respect to children; benefits payable on behalf of a beneficiary to a province, territory or municipality; and the Death benefit. The Department notifies the Department of Justice of the dollar amounts and dates of current and future applicable pensions and benefits. The Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Unit The Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Unit at the Department of Justice: evaluates the funds available against the financial terms of the garnishee summons; and instructs the source program (i.e. OAS, CPP or International Operations) to transfer all or some of the money to the Department of Justice . The transferred funds are deposited into a trust account and a cheque is issued to the court or enforcement service which issued the garnishee summons. The Department of Justice is responsible for transferring the funds to the creditor. Tracing requests are processed through an electronic exchange of data between the Department and the Department of Justice. The Department does not release information directly to a creditor. The creditor must contact the court or enforcement service that issued the garnishee summons for information. The Department also does not deal directly with clients regarding garnishments. The Department of Justice is responsible for notifying clients in writing with respect to garnishments. The client is not advised from which department the monies will be intercepted, and therefore, any client inquiries must be referred to the Department of Justice website where the client will find contact information relevant to their province or territory. An application for CPP Retirement Pension Sharing must be processed even if the garnishment action has started because the Department cannot terminate the processing of an application if there is entitlement. The amount that can be garnished may change as a result of the application for Pension Sharing. Department of Justice

Part II of the Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act provides for the garnishment of designated federal monies to satisfy support orders or provisions. The following creditor types who are owed money under the terms of a defaulted support order can initiate a request for garnishment: the spouse or former spouse (creditor); the common-law partner or former common-law partner (creditor); the creditor's lawyer; or provincial or territorial enforcement services or social service agencies. To apply for assistance, a creditor can petition a court for a garnishee summons against the judgment debtor. In some jurisdictions, it is possible to obtain a garnishee summons without proceeding to court. The garnishee summons and an application for garnishment and support documents are then submitted to the Federal Minister of Justice. Upon receipt of a valid application, the Department of Justice informs the debtor that garnishable monies can be intercepted. As applicants do not specify the funds they believe will be paid to the debtor, the Department of Justice automatically requests searches of all eligible funds. The following federal monies can be intercepted at the source department: income tax refunds; employment insurance benefits; interest on unmatured Canada Savings Bonds held by the Bank of Canada; training income supplement; OAS benefits; benefits payable under the CPP, excluding: benefits payable in respect of children; and benefits paid on behalf of a beneficiary to a province or municipality and death benefits; agricultural stabilization payments; Western Grain stabilization payments; and Canadian Dairy Commission payments. Following notification, source departments report to the Department of Justice as to whether garnishable monies are payable (or may be payable in the future) to the debtor. If funds are available, the source department indicates to the Department of Justice both the amounts and the dates when those funds are payable. The Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Unit evaluates the funds available based on the information received from source departments, against the financial terms of the garnishee summons and instructs the source department to transfer all or some of the money to the Department of Justice. The funds are deposited in a trust account and a cheque is issued to the court or enforcement service that issued the summons. The garnishment order is binding for a period of 5 years or until the summons is satisfied in full. Exception An exception occurs where funds are garnished periodically. If a garnishee summons is of continuing effect and remains unsatisfied in full at the end of the 5-year period, it continues to bind any sources of money until the summons is satisfied. If, however, after the 5-year period is expired, no funds are garnished for a period of 180 consecutive days, the summons ceases to bind the government. Public trustee Note that applications received from the public trustee must be actioned even when a garnishment action has started.

When a single medical condition does not support a severe disability, a holistic assessment considers all medical conditions in combination to determine the functional limitations affecting work capacity, even if the medical conditions are not related. When an individual has two or more medical conditions, this holistic assessment must include the consideration of all relevant physical and mental health conditions identified in the file, as well as the cumulative effect on the capacity to work. Each medical condition is not to be considered individually or in isolation when determining whether the individual's medical conditions prevent them from working. For more information, Consideration of Multiple Medical Conditions (Policy) In assessing the cumulative effect of all the medical conditions, consider the impact of the following: progressive nature of chronic conditions; impact on activities of daily living and increased complexity of self-care; response to medication; impacts of various interventions and treatments; barriers to treatment (e.g. wait list times) and impact of delayed treatment; increased likelihood of having multiple medical appointments; and stress and uncertainty from the impact of all of the above.

When an applicant applies for a CPP Disability (DSB) benefit, they can b e found to meet the severe criterion on the basis of a single medical condition. However, if a single medical condition is insufficient to make a determination of severe, the combined impact of all of the applicant or beneficiary’s medical conditions on their functional capacity is assessed to see if the severe criterion is met. Whenever the applicant or beneficiary has 2 or more medical conditions that, when considered individually, are not sufficient to meet the severe criterion, an assessment must be made regarding the combined effect of all of the relevant medical conditions on their work capacity. Each medical condition is not to be considered individually or in isolation when determining if the applicant or beneficiary meets the definition of severe and prolonged under the CPP. All medical conditions that are likely to affect an applicant or beneficiary’s employability (i.e. not just the main or dominant medical condition) must be considered. This includes taking into consideration all relevant physical and mental conditions identified on their file. When there is insufficient information on file to substantiate a condition, including a self-reported condition, the decision-maker should determine whether additional information is available. Other considerations When considering the combined effect of all reported medical conditions, consideration must also be given to the progressive nature of chronic conditions and the impact they have on an applicant or beneficiary’s overall functional capacity. The following factors need to be considered as all may contribute to higher stress levels: the impact on activities of daily living; the responses to medication (e.g. trials, dosage, and side effects); the impacts of various interventions and treatments; the increased complexity of self-care (e.g. eating, bathing); and the increased likelihood of having multiple medical appointments.

Combined impact of multiple medical conditions All medical conditions that are likely to affect work capacity, not just the main or dominant medical condition, are to be considered. Refer to the Consideration of Multiple Medical Conditions policy. Consideration of Multiple Medical Conditions Late applicant provision The evolving nature of the medical condition(s) is even more pertinent when assessing eligibility under the late applicant provision The signs and symptoms of a disability can occur: before diagnosis; or before the Latest Possible Date of Onset. Consideration should be given to when the functional limitations began to affect the individual’s ability to work. Review of longitudinal medical records may demonstrate when the functional limitations prevented the individual from regularly pursuing any substantially gainful occupation. Personal characteristics The combined impact of the medical condition(s), functional limitations, and personal characteristics of the individual must be considered when determining eligibility and ongoing eligibility. Refer to the Consideration of Personal Characteristics policy. Consideration of Personal Characteristics

When the individual is not working, you will assess their medical condition(s) and determine how their functional limitations impact their ability to pursue work. If the applicant or beneficiary does not demonstrate work capacity, consider the Prolonged Criterion (Policy) Functional limitations occur when a disability interferes with a person's physical, cognitive or psychological ability to perform the routine activities of daily living and their ability to pursue work. All medical conditions that are likely to affect an individual's ability to pursue work must be considered. A medical condition can affect the following functional abilities: physical abilities: stamina, strength, resistance and flexibility; behavioural abilities: interacting with others and the environment; emotional abilities: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness and relationship management; and cognitive abilities: learn, remember, concentrate, plan and execute a goal. The focus for CPPD is on the limitations of functional abilities arising from the medical condition or the cumulative effect of multiple medical conditions.

During the assessment of eligibility and continued eligibility, it is to be determined if the associated functional limitations related to the medical condition(s) impact the applicant’s or beneficiary’s ability to regularly pursue any substantially gainful occupation. A functional limitation hinders an individual’s ability to perform tasks or participate in activities. For CPP DSB and PRDB purposes, the focus is on those functional limitations affecting an individual’s work capacity. How these limitations affect the ability to function in both daily and work life requires a holistic assessment to determine eligibility and continued eligibility. Limitations may occur in one or more domains: physical abilities; behaviours and emotional abilities; communication and thinking abilities; and other daily abilities. Consideration should be given to possible linkages across domains in order to understand how difficulty in one domain may be affecting another. Both the individual’s self-reported functional limitations and the perspectives of their healthcare provider(s) should be considered.

In rare circumstances, it may be determined an applicant or beneficiary is employed in a truly sheltered employment setting. The primary purpose of this type of therapeutic work is for social connection and cognitive stimulation, rather than to provide an income. Examples of these types of settings include: employment of institutionalized individuals in mental health facilities; and community run programs for individuals with specific disabilities, often for those with developmental delays. A defining characteristic of this work is the highly supportive nature of this type of work. Thus a modified approach to assessment of work activity and income earned should occur.

Accommodation allows applicants or beneficiaries with disabilities to participate fully in the workplace. An example of accommodation can include a flexible schedule or fewer work hours than others are afforded. Use the same approach for these applicants or beneficiaries when assessing work activity as any applicant or beneficiary with paid work. For an example of workplace accommodations , go to example 1 in the Case Examples section below. Accommodated work is different from sheltered or inclusive work, which is for therapeutic reasons to keep a social connection, rather than provide an income. Sheltered or inclusive work is an exception occurring in rare circumstances.

Sheltered or inclusive work is an exception occurring in rare circumstances. This is a highly supportive work environment with no or significantly low pay. While hours and predictability may be met, this alone does not demonstrate work capacity. When assessing seasonal work, it is important to identify the time, length of the seasonal work, and determine if the work activity is aligned with that type of work. For example, if a season lasts only a few months and the beneficiary is able to complete the work required for the position, the beneficiary returning for a second consecutive season shows predictability aligned with this type of work. Seasonal work is work activity that occurs at around the same time each year for the duration of a season, or longer if required for the completion of a specific job. Generally, seasonal work has predetermined beginning and end dates due to seasonal factors. Assessment of work capacity for individuals engaged in seasonal work is the same as for those engaged in other work activities. For more information, refer to the Assessment of earnings from work activity section above. Additional considerations for seasonal work include: work history; earnings history; identified patterns of work activity; and a determination as to the beneficiary having stopped working due to: a shortage of work; their medical condition; or a combination of both. If the applicant or beneficiary demonstrates the ability to work predictably in a seasonal capacity, they are demonstrating work capacity and benefits will likely be denied or ceased. If annual SGO amount is not reached in the season: The return to work is case managed; and The pending cease date is set on a case-by-case basis and may be extended into a second season. If the work trial is extended into a second season and the second season ends before the end of the continued work trial, a holistic review is completed, and a decision is made. Observation Month (Policy) A beneficiary who self-reports a return to seasonal work is entitled to all work incentives including: allowable earnings; an observation month (a 1-month period after the month the beneficiary reaches allowable earnings). A beneficiary is no longer required to earn the monthly SGO amount during the observation month. The observation month is completed once the beneficiary is able to work regularly and predictably; a 3-month paid work trial beginning after the observation month (monthly SGO is no longer required to be met during each month of the 3-month paid work trial period); automatic reinstatement, and fast-track reapplication. For more information, refer to Automatic Reinstatement—CPPD Benefits (Policy) and Automatic Reinstatement—CPPD Benefits (Policy) Fast Track Reapplication (Policy) Earnings from work activity above the annual Substantially Gainful Occupation (SGO) benchmark likely indicate work capacity. Some individuals employed on a seasonal basis work short seasons and can reach above the annual SGO benchmark in a short period of time. In this situation, the beneficiary does not have to work for the duration of the work trial to demonstrate work capacity. The following lists demonstrate how to apply the 3-month work trial period for a beneficiary engaged in seasonal work. If the annual earnings are: below or above the SGO benchmark; and the beneficiary continues the seasonal work beyond the completion of the 3-month paid work trial then: cease the benefit at the end of the 3-month paid work trial. If the annual earnings are: below the SGO benchmark; and the beneficiary stops work because the season ends, which is before the completion of the 3-month paid work trial; then: pause the 3-month paid work trial until the following season; and cease the benefit at the end of the remainder of the work trial in the consecutive season; the 3-month paid work trial cannot be extended to a third season. If the annual earnings are: above the SGO benchmark; and the beneficiary stops work because the season ends, which is before the completion of the 3-month paid work trial then: cease the benefit at the end of what would have been the third month of the work trial.

The observation month is a work incentive offered only to beneficiaries who self-report their return to work and reach the allowable earnings benchmark while remaining compliant during the reassessment process. The observation month is a one-month period after the month the beneficiary reaches the allowable earnings amount. If the allowable earnings have already been reached for the calendar year, the month the beneficiary returns to work is considered an observation month. For more information on the allowable earnings, Allowable Earnings (Policy) Beneficiaries are not required to earn the monthly substantially gainful occupation amount. When the beneficiary is able to work regularly and predictably during the observation month, the 3-month work trial begins the following month, regardless of earnings.

The 3-month paid work trial is not a one-time entitlement. Each time a beneficiary attempts a reported Return to Work (RTW), they are given a 3-month paid work trial. This work trial becomes effective: the month after the observation month (i.e. allowable earnings reached, observation month, 3-month paid work trial); or the 1st month after the beneficiary's RTW, if the allowable earnings have already been reached for the calendar year (i.e. observation month, 3-month paid work trial). The month the beneficiary returns to work is considered the observation month. For more information on allowable earnings or the observation month, refer to Allowable Earnings (Policy) and Allowable Earnings (Policy) Observation Month (Policy)

A 3-month paid work trial is available to all CPPD beneficiaries who are engaged in paid work and are compliant with the reassessment process. For beneficiaries who report their Return to Work (RTW) to the Department, the 3-month paid work trial begins when the beneficiary: reaches the allowable earnings amount; and demonstrates work capacity during the observation month. Monthly Substantially Gainful Occupation (SGO) earnings do not need to be met in each month of the work trial for it to be considered successful. The Department also removed the requirement to meet monthly SGO earnings before the 3-month work trial begins. For more information, Observation Month (Policy) For beneficiaries who do not report their RTW to the Department but remain compliant during the reassessment process, the 3-month paid work trial begins: the month following the month they returned to work if the RTW date is known; or January 1st of the first year of SGO earnings if the RTW date is unknown. Beneficiaries who report their RTW are entitled to all work incentives including: allowable earnings; an observation month; a 3-month paid work trial starting the month after the observation month; an automatic reinstatement; and a fast-track reapplication.

A decision on initial or continuing eligibility for CPPD benefits is made in “respect of whom the determination is made”. Evidence to the contrary is evidence on file (e.g. medical, employment) that shows that the individual does not have the work capacity for any SGO despite their earnings or work activity. Cases with evidence to the contrary are rare. If information is identified that suggests an individual does not have work capacity despite engaging in paid work, the decision rationale must clearly articulate what information (e.g. medical evidence, predictability) led to the determination of initial or continuing eligibility.

You will then use the information and recommendation provided by ISB as the basis for making your decision. If an individual is dissatisfied with a decision made in accordance with ministerial discretion, that individual cannot request a reconsideration or an appeal to the Social Security Tribunal. The individual must apply to the federal court for judicial review of the Minister’s decision.

The Minister's refusal to accept a disclosure cannot be reconsidered to the Minister or appealed to the Social Security Tribunal—General Division. However, an applicant or beneficiary can make an application to the Federal Court for a judicial review of the Ministers' decision.

Reassessment Reassessment review is the only area where the burden of proof lies primarily on the Minister. The Department, on behalf of the Minister, must show the beneficiary has ceased to be disabled according to the CPP legislation. When CPPD benefits are ceased, the onus is with the Minister to show the beneficiary is no longer disabled. At the reassessment level, there is also an onus on the Department to periodically review cases of individuals who are receiving a CPPD benefit to ensure continuing eligibility. The beneficiary or their authorized representative is responsible for providing or reporting: a return to work once they have gross earnings at or above the allowable earnings threshold; if they are participating in education or volunteer activities after four months at 15 hours or more per week; if there has been an improvement in their medical condition; and/or all documents and information required to support the beneficiary's continuing eligibility, including information related to: earnings; hours worked or participated in volunteer or educational activities; absences; nature of the activity or tasks; any accommodations; and any changes to the above that occurred since the last decision. all documents and information required to support the beneficiary's continuing eligibility. The Department is responsible for reviewing and investigating any: reported return to work or educational or volunteer activities; triggers related to unreported earnings or work activity; pre-scheduled return to work triggers; reported regained capacity; and/or third party complaints.

The Department may conduct a reassessment of beneficiaries receiving a CPPD benefit to determine if they continue to be disabled in accordance with CPP legislation and policy. For the purposes of this process, CPPD benefits refer to both the DSB and the PRDB . There are several reasons to initiate a review of a beneficiary's file. To confirm if a beneficiary remains eligible for the benefit, the Department may assess continuing eligibility based on: new or recent earnings information; or a pre-scheduled return to work notification; or notification from the beneficiary or other parties of a change in circumstances, including: self-reported Return to Work (RTW); unreported RTW; improvement in the beneficiary's medical condition; and participation in volunteer or educational activities. If a beneficiary self-reports work, volunteer or educational activities, it is considered an assessment. Triggers associated with unreported work activity are considered a reassessment. When conducting a review, you must examine all evidence on the file since the last time the beneficiary received a decision. There may be times when it is necessary to request additional information from sources other than the beneficiary. You have the discretion to make a decision based on information on file and any information obtained during the reassessment. A decision only needs to ensure that the contributor is more likely disabled than not. For more information, refer to Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) . In most cases, the beneficiary should be able to: Satisfied on a Balance of Probabilities (Policy) provide all necessary information concerning their overall work capacity; and serve as the primary source of information to determine continuing eligibility during an assessment or reassessment. For more information, refer to Final Decision section below.

To continue receiving CPPD benefits, beneficiaries must continue to meet the eligibility requirements. To ensure that beneficiaries remain eligible, the Department may reassess them to determine continuing eligibility. The regulations give the Minister the authority to request information regarding: the beneficiary's occupation and earnings for any period; and changes in the beneficiary's medical condition. This policy guidance addresses a beneficiary's non-compliance to requests for this information. It does not address non-compliance with health care treatment. Non-Compliance with Health Care Treatment (Policy) A beneficiary is considered non-compliant when: the Minister receives no response from the beneficiary after 2 written requests have been sent (the original request and the reminder to the original request) asking for specific information by a prescribed date; or the beneficiary responds to the Minister's written request but fails to provide the specific information sought, as solicited by the Department, which is necessary to make a decision regarding their continuing eligibility for CPPD benefits. A beneficiary is not considered non-compliant when: the beneficiary has good cause; the nature of the beneficiary's medical condition is such that it could be reasonably anticipated they will be unable to respond to the request for information (i.e. incapacity); or the beneficiary is missing. Suspending CPPD benefits based on non-compliance When a beneficiary does not respond to the Minister's requests for information, the payment of CPPD benefits is generally suspended. Suspending payment of the benefit when a beneficiary becomes non-compliant: may prompt the beneficiary to respond to the Minister's request for information; and limits the potential of any overpayment of benefits that the beneficiary could incur. While benefits are suspended, the beneficiary does not have the right to request a reconsideration or to appeal. Reaching a decision concerning the beneficiary's continuing eligibility and informing them of the decision enables the beneficiary to exercise these rights. Ceasing CPPD benefits when non-compliance occurs If a beneficiary fails to provide the information requested by the Minister within the suspension period, their DSB benefits can be ceased. These files may be transferred to the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) for further investigation before determining a cease date. If confirmed that earnings are from work activity, the cease date is based on the evidence rather than non-compliance. Files with evidence of fraud, misrepresentation or missing beneficiaries must be sent to ISB for investigation. Establishing a CPPD benefits cease date In situations where a beneficiary has not provided the required information requested by the Department to determine their continuing eligibility, CPPD benefits are ceased based on the available earnings information. The following are not to be used when determining a CPPD benefits cease date: Earnings confirmed through an employer to be from sources other than work activity such as: earnings related to sickness benefits; or payment to the beneficiary for unused vacation leave. Earnings that have been fully investigated either: at the time of the initial eligibility determination; or during a previous reassessment.

Erroneous advice Erroneous advice (EA) is false or misleading oral or written communication containing incorrect or misleading information provided by a departmental employee in the course of administering the CPP or the OAS Act. As a result, the EA affects a beneficiary or applicant’s actions or conduct in relation to the CPP and OAS programs to their detriment. EA includes the omission of crucial information. If a departmental employee does not give an applicant information that could affect them making an informed decision in regard to an application, the omission is considered to be just as erroneous as providing incorrect information. Information provided by anyone outside of the delegated administration of the CPP and the OAS Act (the Canada Revenue Agency or a private sector human resources expert) cannot be remedied under the Erroneous Advice/Administrative Error (EA/AE) provisions under any circumstances. Information communicated to the applicant or beneficiary may or may not be indicated on the file or in ITRDS notes. The legislative requirement is that the Minister be satisfied. For the purposes of the EA/AE provisions, the term "satisfied" means "convinced". There is no statutory onus on the Minister to prove that EA/AE occurred. However, all available documents and additional information provided by the applicant or beneficiary must be reviewed. Administrative Error An administrative error (AE) is an action by an official of the Department acting in an official capacity in the administration of the CPP and the OAS Act. This action causes: a benefit; a provision; a portion of a benefit; or a provision to be denied. This includes access to a credit split and pension sharing. The sole purpose of the EA/AE provisions is to enable the Department to take remedial action when an error is made by departmental officials. "Administrative" (from "administration") relates to the management or conduct of business. Administrative actions in the context of the CPP and the OAS Act are necessary to carrying out legislation, policies, procedures and practices. For the purposes of the CPP and the OAS Act, an AE is an incorrect action or a failure to act of a departmental employee while administering the policies, procedures and practices related to the CPP and the OAS Act. Time limit There is no time limit on a request for, or on the approval or non-approval of an allegation of EA/AE, nor is there a time limit to implement the provision. This applies to both minister-initiated reviews of a potential EA/AE or a request from an applicant or beneficiary-initiated allegation. However, the legislation, policies, procedures and practices in place at the time the alleged EA/AE is said to have occurred, must be used to determine if EA/AE occurred. Clerical error For program administration purposes, clerical errors are not considered under the EA/AE provisions. There is no discretion or decision made on clerical errors as is the case with EA/AE. A clerical error (e.g. missing a step in a calculation or process, keying in the wrong date of birth) is an evident error that simply needs to be corrected. While clerical errors are not administrative errors for program administration purposes, federal courts make no such distinctions. From a court and an applicant or beneficiary’s perspective, when an error is found to have occurred, it must be corrected. There may be cases where an error occurred while administering an applicant or beneficiary’s file, but did not cause any loss of benefits to the applicant or beneficiary or prevent access to a credit split or pension sharing. As there was not a loss of benefits or access to a provision, it is not a case of EA/AE as detailed under the legislation. Depending on the situation, the error must be corrected or the individual must be informed although nothing in the file changes. EA/AE and overpayments (remission) The EA/AE provisions (subsection 66(4) of the CPP and section 32 of the OAS Act) do not apply to cases where an overpayment has occurred due to EA/AE. Overpayments resulting from EA/AE are considered under the remission provisions of the CPP and OAS Act. The remission provision for EA/AE provides the Minister with discretion, when satisfied, in cases where an overpayment is caused by EA/AE, to remit all or any portion of that overpayment.

The purpose of the EA/AE criterion under the remissions provisions is to enable the Department to remit an overpayment (in full or in part) when that overpayment was from erroneous advice or the result of an error by a Departmental employee. Erroneous advice Erroneous advice occurs when incorrect or misleading information is communicated or provided to an individual by a Departmental employee (i.e. orally or in writing) during the administration of the CPP or the OAS Act. This erroneous advice affects an individual's actions or conduct to their detriment in relation to the CPP or OAS program. Erroneous advice includes the omission of crucial information related to eligibility and entitlement to benefits. Specifically, if a Departmental employee does not provide an individual with all the required information available at that time and it affects the making of an informed decision regarding their benefit, it is considered just as erroneous as providing information that is incorrect. Administrative error An administrative error is an incorrect action, an error made or the failure to act by a Departmental employee during the administration of the CPP or the OAS Act that causes or increases an overpayment on an individual's account. Failure to act due to workload is not an administrative error. However, the failure of an employee to act on or to overlook information pertinent to eligibility and entitlement while administering the legislative provisions of the CPP or the OAS Act is an administrative error. When an overpayment is a result of EA/AE by a Departmental employee, it may be considered for remission in whole or in part. However, an overpayment caused by an employee's failure to act (e.g. not acting upon information on file) or to take corrective action when an error is found could result in the overpayment being considered for remission. In these situations, accounts should be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. When overpayments are increased because of an employee's actions or inactions, there is flexibility to consider remitting all or portions of the overpayment in part or in full, depending on the circumstances of the case. There are also situations where the Department made an error that resulted in an overpayment and the individual is not aware that an error was made on their account. Specifically, the Department has determined that the overpayment is a result of EA/AE and that it is solely responsible for the overpayment. In these situations, the error is a clear fact and the individual was not aware of the error or that they were being overpaid. Situations where the Department made an error and is solely responsible for an overpayment include: systems errors where many beneficiaries were overpaid; encoding errors where the wrong benefit amounts are paid; or administrative errors where an individual is not aware that an error was made on their account. It would be unreasonable in these situations to request full recovery of the overpayment from the individual if the Department made the error and the individual could not have known they were being overpaid. This would create inequities and is inconsistent with the principles upon which the overpayment policy is based. Full remission—EA/AE An overpayment can be remitted in full if the Department's or a departmental employee's error is the sole cause of the overpayment and the individual could not have been aware of the error and that they were being overpaid. Partial remission—EA/AE An overpayment can be partially remitted when: the overpayment is originally caused by the Department or a departmental employee and the individual could have been aware of the error; or the overpayment is originally caused by an error or the actions or inactions of the individual and: an employee of the Department could have been aware of information on the account or in the file (including the error made by the individual) and could have taken corrective action but did not; or an employee of the Department made subsequent errors or omissions that increased the overpayment. In partial remission situations, it is appropriate for the Department to accept a percentage of the responsibility for the overpayment and remit that portion of it. For national consistency, this is generally set at 50%, but can be set to any percentage deemed appropriate, depending on the facts of the case. Discretion can be used to remit different percentages of an overpayment, as long as a rationale is provided for the recommended percentages based on the facts of each case. Depending on the case, certain portions or periods of the overpayment can be considered for a full or partial remission, while certain portions or periods may be fully recovered. When part of the overpayment is remitted, the balance remains as a recoverable overpayment and recovery action will continue.

Failure to advise individuals of a legislative amendment is not an administrative error by the Department as per the legislation in these cases. Credit split—Kempling remedy Documentation for cases that are a result of applying the Kempling provisions is not required. Although an EA/AE submission is prepared in these cases, the authority to remedy these situations does not fall under the EA/AE provision but under the provision where a credit split is denied.

Pursuant to the CPP, the maximum retroactivity of a SVR pension is 11 months preceding the month in which the application is received by the Minister. Previous decisions will not be revisited. This update is for any pending and future decisions.
