The Department administers the Old Age Security Act (OAS) and the Canada Pension Plan (CPP). The administration of the payments relating to these programs includes a requirement to prevent overpayments and underpayments of program funds. If initial and continuing eligibility and entitlement conditions are met due to false and misleading information or due to the withholding of information, action is mandatory. In the daily course of a departmental employee's duties, anomalies or discrepancies may be identified in applications or documentation. After going through a standard review process, if reasonable explanations for an anomaly or a discrepancy are not revealed or explained; all relevant documentation and other evidence received must be referred to the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) for an administrative investigation. Until the nature and extent of the misrepresentation against the CPP and OAS programs is determined, and the entire administrative investigation process is completed, benefits cannot be cancelled. However, benefits can be temporarily suspended.

The Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act authorize the suspension of pension and benefit payments when a beneficiary's continuing eligibility or entitlement is in question and requires an investigation. If an individual is the subject of an investigation either by the Department or by the RCMP on behalf of the Department, consultation with the Integrity Services Branch (ISB) is required before any action to suspend the benefits is taken. The suspension of a benefit is an administrative measure used to temporarily stop the payment of a benefit to: confirm ongoing eligibility or entitlement; or take administrative actions. Suspensions are usually followed by an action to either resume the payments or to cancel the benefit. Beneficiaries expect that the benefit will be paid continuously after they have applied and been found to be eligible. Interruption in payments can have serious ramifications for beneficiaries. Therefore, all living CPP and OAS beneficiaries with a known address must receive a written notice a minimum of 30 days before the suspension of the benefits. A benefit remains suspended until the Minister is satisfied that the beneficiary continues to meet the eligibility criteria, in which case the benefit is reinstated. If an ISB investigation reveals a beneficiary is not eligible to the benefit in question, the payment of the benefit may be cancelled. A suspension must not remain in place for any longer than it takes to confirm continuing eligibility or to process transactions to correct the type, amount or method of benefit payment.

Until the exact nature and extent of the suspected fraud or misrepresentation against the CPP and OAS programs is determined, and the entire administrative investigation process is completed, benefits must not be cancelled. However, they can be suspended: when advised by ISB; when eligibility has ceased due to death; or when the individual does not reside in Canada. Each case must be evaluated to ensure that any action taken will not interfere with, or obstruct, any investigation by the RCMP.

Applicants, beneficiaries and other individuals or groups have attempted and will continue to attempt defrauding our programs. It is everyone’s responsibility to report any information which may identify fraudulent situations. Files referred to Integrity Services Branch (ISB) for an administrative investigation may result in the imposition of an administrative monetary penalty when it has been discovered that the applicant or beneficiary knowingly made a misrepresentation (i.e. they knowingly provided false or misleading information or knowingly withheld or omitted relevant information). Until the exact nature and extent of the suspected fraud or misrepresentation against the CPP and OAS programs is determined, do not cancel benefits before the entire administrative investigation process is completed. However, benefits can be suspended when advised by ISB in cases where eligibility or entitlement has ceased due to death, or due to residence outside of Canada. Each case must be evaluated to ensure that any action taken will not interfere or obstruct any investigation by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

Under the CPP and the OAS Act, the Minister has the discretionary authority to reduce the penalty amount or rescind penalties where appropriate. When a penalty is reduced in part or in full, the penalty itself remains valid and can be used in the future to potentially establish a subsequent misrepresentation. The rescission of the imposition of a penalty reflects the determination that the penalty should never have been imposed in the first place. In relation to upon whom the penalty was imposed, it will be as if the penalty (and any penalty amount assigned) never existed in the first place. The circumstances surrounding the situation will no longer be considered to be a misrepresentation and cannot be used in the future to establish a subsequent misrepresentation. Because of this, the rescission of the imposition of a penalty or the reduction in the penalty amount must only be considered under the CPP and the OAS Act in the following circumstances: the presentation of new facts; the satisfaction that: the penalty was imposed without knowledge of a material fact or based on a mistake regarding that fact; the penalty cannot be collected within the reasonably foreseeable future; or payment of the penalty would cause undue hardship to the debtor. A penalty is meant to be collected in full or until such time as there is a reason to reduce or rescind the penalty or any outstanding balance. All reasonable efforts to recover the receivable must be attempted.

The Minister can rescind or reduce a penalty amount, after the penalty has been imposed, in the following situations: on the presentation of new facts; on being satisfied that the penalty was imposed without knowledge of some material fact, or on the basis of a mistake; on being satisfied that the penalty cannot be collected within the reasonably foreseeable future; or on being satisfied that payment of the penalty will cause undue hardship to the debtor. A penalty amount can be reduced to zero, but the penalty is still considered to have been imposed.

Tax treaties between Canada and other countries allow varying percentages of Canadian tax to be deducted, and in some cases, eliminates Canadian taxation. The individual's country of residence determines: whether or not non-resident tax is applicable, and, if so, the percentage of tax to be withheld from payments . When a new or revised tax treaty changes the non-resident tax rate, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) notifies the Innovation, Information and Technology Branch. The Department then changes the tax rate in the CPP and OAS systems and sends the Advisory Letter - Non Resident Tax to individuals affected by the change in the tax rate. These system-generated letters are issued each time a non-resident tax withhold is established, or if the percentage rate of a tax withhold changes. Corporate Finance forwards non-resident tax withheld on OAS and CPP accounts to CRA on a monthly basis using an interdepartmental settlement notice.

In most cases, the tax withhold rate for a non-resident receiving Canadian social security benefits is 25% of the benefit unless it is reduced or exempted by a tax treaty between Canada and the individual's country of residence. Tax treaties between Canada and other countries result in taxation rates varying between 0% and 25%. Individuals can apply for a reduced rate of non-resident tax withhold as per Section 217 of the Canadian Income Tax Act . The OAS and CPP systems apply the correct non-resident tax rate according to the residential address and country code. Events that can change the non-resident tax rate are: the submission and processing of an application by a non-resident of Canada for a reduction in the amount of non-resident tax required to be withheld for a given tax year (NR5); a new or revised tax treaty between Canada and other countries; a change of address to a different country; and when the Canada Revenue Agency advises the Department that the individual is a deemed resident of Canada. The amount of tax to be withheld is determined by applying the non-resident tax rate percentage to the gross amount of the pension or benefit payment. CPP pensions and benefits are indexed annually and the system automatically applies the tax rate to the new indexed benefit amount every January. OAS benefits are indexed quarterly ; therefore, the non-resident tax rate is adjusted every January, April, July, and October. System-generated letters [Advisory Letter - Non Resident Tax (ISP3525)] are issued to beneficiaries at month-end to advise of changes in the non-resident tax withhold rate.

The Income Tax Act allows the taxation of Canadian social security benefits paid to non-residents. The NRT is 25% unless there is a tax treaty between Canada and the country of residence, or the client has applied for and received a reduction in their NRT rate. The country in which a client resides determines whether or not the NRT is applicable and, if so, the percentage of tax to be withheld. NRT rates can vary for OAS and CPP payments. A country can have up to 3 rates: CPP (other than the Death (DTH) benefit) DTH OAS NRT rates are only percentages, not dollar amounts. Withhold rates are reviewed every January and revised accordingly. ITRDS displays the adjusted NRT rates or ends the tax withhold entirely if a client does the following: changes their address and leaves Canada; moves from one country to another; or returns to Canada.

Applicants who were Canadian citizens and became citizens or nationals of another country prior to February 15, 1977, automatically lost their Canadian citizenship if: they resided outside Canada; were 21 years of age or over; and acquired another nationality or citizenship by a voluntary and formal act other than marriage. If they return to Canada, they are required to apply through the normal immigration channels to be legally re-admitted. Certain categories of individuals can qualify under the amendments to the Citizenship Act that came into force April 17, 2009 to automatically reinstate their Canadian citizenship. Applicants who are Canadian citizens and became citizens or nationals of another country on or after February 15, 1977 have not lost their Canadian citizenship, they hold dual citizenship. Citizenship is complex because of the great variety of citizenship laws throughout the world. Some countries allow dual citizenship, while others take away the citizenship of an individual who acquires another citizenship.

Where an individual ceased to reside in Canada, then resumed residence in Canada and subsequently applies for an OAS pension, ALW or ALWS , the legal status requirement must be met on the day before the approval of the OAS application. Amendments to the Citizenship Act came into force April 17, 2009 (Bill C-37). Individuals who may be affected by these amendments to the Citizenship Act are those who were Canadian citizens (including Canadian-born individuals) who lost their citizenship when they departed from Canada, then became citizens of a foreign country before February 15, 1977. These individuals lost their Canadian citizenship automatically as Canada did not allow dual citizenship at that time. Until April 17, 2009, such individuals had to apply to IRCC to re-establish their legal status if and when they returned to Canada. These amendments to the Citizenship Act allow IRCC to automatically reinstate the Canadian citizenship of certain categories of individuals without requiring them to officially apply to have their citizenship reinstated. The categories for these amendments are as follows: The law restores citizenship to individuals who: became citizens when the first Citizenship Act took effect on January 1, 1947, including individuals born in Canada before 1947 and war brides. It also applies to other British subjects who had lived in Canada for at least 5 years before 1947, became citizens on January 1, 1947, then lost citizenship; and were born in Canada or became Canadian citizens on or after January 1, 1947, then lost their citizenship. The law also gives citizenship to some individuals who have never been citizens. This includes individuals who: were born outside Canada on or after January 1, 1947; are in the first generation born abroad; and were born to a Canadian citizen. OAS, ALW or ALWS applicants in any of the above situations are required to provide proof that citizenship has been restored by means of a citizenship certificate issued by IRCC. The citizenship goes back to the day the individual was born or lost citizenship depending on the situation.

Effective January 1, 2019, a full Survivor’s (SVR) pension is paid out to every survivor regardless of their age, the contributor’s date of death or the existence of dependent children or disability. That is, as of January 1, 2019, the SVR pension is always paid at the full rate with no reduction.

Legislative changes to the DTH benefit and SVR pension were introduced as part of the CPP 2016-2018 Triennial Review. DTH benefit The DTH benefit has been changed to a flat-rate amount of $2,500.00 for all eligible contributors. SVR pension Age-based reductions for survivor’s under the age of 45 were removed. These legislative changes have been manually processed since they were implemented in January 2019. As part of the CPP enhancement, May 21, 2022 system release, ITRDS and other systems have been modified to pay a flat-rate DTH benefit of $2,500.00, and remove the age-based reduction to the SVR pension. As a result, the manual intervention and workarounds introduced in January 2019 are no longer required.

To determine the RTR pension(s) amounts to be shared by the spouses or common-law partners, you must determine: the joint contributory period; and the period of cohabitation. Joint contributory period The joint contributory period for both single and double Pension Sharing (PNSH) starts with the later of: January 1, 1966; or the month in which the elder spouse or common-law partner reached 18 years of age. For single PNSH, the joint contributory period ends with the later of: the month in which the contributor's contributory period ends; or the earlier of the month in which: the non-contributor reaches 70 years of age; and PNSH is approved. For double PNSH, the joint contributory period ends: the month before the later of the 2 CPP RTR pensions began. The spouses' and common-law partners' joint contributory period excludes any contributory months during which either person: was in receipt of a CPP DSB ; or could apply for the Child Rearing Provision (CRP) to their contributory period. Period of cohabitation The period of cohabitation represents the years that CPP contributions will be shared between the spouses or common-law partners. The period of cohabitation starts with the latest of: January 1, 1966; the month of marriage; or the month in which a common-law relationship starts. Periods when spouses lived together in a common-law relationship before getting married can also be included in the period of cohabitation. The period of cohabitation ends the month the joint contributory period ends.

Spouses or common-law partners may share a portion of each other's RTR pension based on the joint contributory period and their period of cohabitation. As of January 1, 2019, contributors who have made contributions to the enhanced CPP will be able to share their first additional RTR ; as of January 1, 2024, they will be able to share their second additional RTR . To calculate a pension sharing (PNSH), you must find the PNSH ratio for the spouses or common-law partners. Determine the base Joint Contributory Period To calculate the base PNSH, you must first calculate the number of months in the base joint contributory period. The base joint contributory period begins with the latest of either: January 1, 1966; or the month in which the eldest spouse/partner reached 18 years of age. The base joint contributory period for a single PNSH ends with the latest of: the month in which the contributor's contributory period ends; or the earlier of the month in which the non-contributor reaches age 70 and the month that the PNSH is approved. If only one spouse or common-law partner is a contributor, the base joint contributory period does not include those contributory months excluded due to disability or any month where the Child Rearing Drop-Out (CRDO) is applied. If both spouses or common-law partners are contributors, the base joint contributory period for a double PNSH ends with the month before the later of the 2 RTR pensions began and any months excluded from the base joint contributory period due to disability or the CRDO can only be excluded if they apply to both base contributory periods. Determine the base period of cohabitation Calculate how many months are in the base cohabitation period. Deduct any periods when they were voluntarily separated for a period of more than one year. If the spouses provide periods of cohabitation before marriage, include these months in your calculation. Cohabitation begins with the later of: January 1, 1966; or the earlier date between the month of marriage or the month the common-law relationship begins. Cohabitation ends with the earlier of: the month the base joint contributory period ends; the month following the month of separation; or the month following the month of a death of one of the beneficiaries. As of January 1, 2019, determine the first additional joint contributory period when there is a first additional RTR pension to share The first additional joint contributory period begins with the latest of either: January 1, 2019; or the month in which the eldest spouse/partner reached 18 years of age. The first additional joint contributory period for a single PNSH ends with the latest of: the month in which the contributor's contributory period ends; or the earlier of the month in which the non-contributor reaches age 70 and the month that the PNSH is approved. The first additional joint contributory period for a double PNSH ends with the month before the later of the 2 RTR pensions began. Determine the first additional period of cohabitation Calculate how many months are in the first additional cohabitation period. Deduct any periods where they were voluntarily separated for a period of more than one year. If spouses provide periods of cohabitation before marriage, include these months in your calculation. Cohabitation begins with the later of: January 1, 2019; or the earlier date between the month of marriage or the month the common-law relationship begins. Cohabitation ends with the earlier of: the month the first additional joint contributory period ends; the month following the month of separation; or the month following the month of a death of one of the beneficiaries. As of January 1, 2024, determine the second additional joint contributory period when there is a second additional RTR pension to share The second additional joint contributory period begins with the latest of either: January 1, 2024; or the month in which the eldest spouse/partner reached 18 years of age. The second additional joint contributory period for a single PNSH ends with the latest of: the month in which the contributor's contributory period ends; or the earlier of the month in which the non-contributor reaches age 70 and the month that the PNSH is approved. The second additional joint contributory period for a double PNSH ends with the month before the later of the 2 RTR pensions began. Determine the second additional period of cohabitation Calculate how many months are in the second additional cohabitation period. Deduct any periods where they were voluntarily separated for a period of more than one year. If spouses provide periods of cohabitation before marriage, include these months in your calculation. Cohabitation begins with the later of: January 1, 2024; or the earlier date between the month of marriage or the month the common-law relationship begins. Cohabitation ends with the earlier of: the month the first additional joint contributory period ends; the month following the month of separation; or the month following the month of a death of one of the beneficiaries. The contributor's RTR monthly pension amount will be reduced by the amount shared to their spouse or common-law partner. To calculate a double PNSH, you must use the calculation above on each spouse or common-law partner to determine the RTR pension amount that each will share. Disability benefits Proration of UPE may apply for a year in which DSB or PRDB ( PRDB with a DOO of May 2023 or later), either starts or ceases to be paid (in a month other than December), and the UPE are below the Disability Basic Exemption (DBE). Proration of earnings or UPE for DSB or PRDB purposes may apply to a year in which the disabling event occurs (in a month other than December), where the earnings/UPE are below the DBE and the date of onset is: before 1998 and the earnings are equal to or below the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE); or January 1998 and later and the UPE are below the DBE. When establishing the earnings eligibility requirements needed for a subsequent DSB or PRDB , proration may also apply to the remainder of the year in which a previous disability ceased (in a month other than December). A contributor must have made contributions for at least the Minimum Qualifying Period to be eligible to receive a benefit. A contributor will be considered to have made such contributions in a year only if they have made contributions on earnings that are not less than the YBE or DBE. Repayment of refunded contributions for current applications using proration New For a prorate year to be valid for the applicant, the contributor must repay some or all contributions that were refunded to them by CRA . The amount of the prorated UPE for the year will be used for benefit calculation purposes. Repayment of refunded contributions for Late Applicant Provision using proration New Late applicants who meet the Minimum Qualifying Period with a prorate date are no longer required to repay refunded contributions for the year of the established Date of Onset. The prorated year is not used for benefit calculation purposes in the case of a late applicant. General CPP An individual's Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) must be at least their basic exemption for the year to be deemed to have made a valid contribution. Normally, an individual's basic exemption for the year is the same as the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE), however, the legislation provides an exception to that provision. An individual whose UPE are equal to or less than the YBE can be deemed to have made a valid contribution for a year, for a proportion of the YBE months in that year, if during that year any of the following occur: the person reaches age 18 or 70 or has died; a retirement pension under the CPP or QPP becomes payable; the contributory period ends by reason of disability under the CPP or QPP, or a DSB or PRDB under the CPP or QPP ceases to be payable (other than in the month of December). In all cases, if a contributor has earnings but did not pay CPP contributions on them, the earnings are equivalent to zero for CPP purposes. CPP contributions, not earnings, are what allow a contributor to be entitled to receive CPP benefits. For example, if an individual earns over $100,000 a year for a few years, but never makes CPP contributions, the earnings may not be considered valid for CPP purposes.

Proration of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) may apply to a year in which "triggering" events occur (in a month other than December), where the UPE are equal to or below the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE), or Disability Basic Exemption (DBE) for CPPD benefits. Triggering events include: reaching age 18; commencing a CPP or QPP Retirement pension; reaching age 70; and death. Years in which such events occur are prorated by the Canada Revenue Agency ( CRA ); however, if the Department needs to use a year in which a triggering event occurs to qualify an individual for a benefit, a manual calculation can be done if the CRA hasn't already prorated that particular year. The UPE can only be prorated if sufficient CPP contributions have been deducted from the individual's earnings. If the contributions are insufficient to cover the earnings, the UPE will be less than the actual earnings. The number of months that can be prorated will be reduced. An individual cannot make CPP contributions before the age of 18.

Earnings with CPP contributions that are below the Year's Basic Exemption (YBE) (before 1988) or below the Disability Basic Exemption (effective January 1998) can be prorated if the applicant is deemed disabled in the prorate year by the end of the prorated month. If earnings are available on the Record of Earnings, ITRDS calculates and displays a prorated latest possible date of onset. If earnings are available on the Record of Earnings, ITRDS calculates and displays a prorated Latest Possible Date of Onset (LPDOO). The Canada Revenue Agency assesses the CPP contributions of self-employed individuals at the end of the year when they file their income tax return. If 100% of their earnings are below the YBE and are self-employed, no contributions are made to the CPP, and there are no valid CPP contribution to prorate. Following the cessation of a CPPD benefit, the contributory period restarts the month following cessation of the benefit. If the year during which the benefit ceased is required to meet the earnings requirements, that year may be prorated. Proration can be used to establish or extend an LPDOO for PRDB for applicants with a Date of Onset (DOO) or an established DOO in May 2023 or later. For more information, refer to Proration of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (Policy) and to Proration of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (Policy) Process a PRDB (Scenario)

Proration of Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings may be completed by the CRA in the year in which the death occurs, provided the earnings are equal to or below the Year's Basic Exemption. This may have an impact on the deceased contributor's ability to meet the MQP for a DTH benefit, SVR pension or Surviving Child's benefit. If the Department needs to use a year in which a triggering event occurs to qualify an individual for a benefit, staff can complete a manual calculation if the CRA has not yet prorated that year. You must complete the prorate worksheet and include the month the MQP is met and the next month the MQP is not met. Since January 1, 1987, credit splitting is mandatory for spouses upon divorce or for legal spouses and common-law partners upon separation. In the case of spouses following a divorce or a legal annulment of marriage, credit splitting may only be considered if the following eligibility requirements have been met: Cancellation Credit splitting can be cancelled when it is detrimental to both spouses. It must be evident, immediately before credit splitting or within 60 days after, that credit splitting would adversely affect both spouses. This is only applicable when both spouses are beneficiaries at the time of credit splitting or both spouses become beneficiaries within 60 days of credit splitting. Having 2 benefits in pay is the only way it can be determined with any accuracy that credit splitting is detrimental to both spouses. No projected calculations are to be done to determine if credit splitting may be detrimental to both spouses at some time in the future. Withdrawal Withdrawal of the credit split request is not permitted for divorced individuals. Credit splitting is mandatory upon the Minister being informed of a decree absolute of divorce, a judgment granting divorce under the Divorce Act or a judgment of nullity in a marriage.

Credit splitting provision The credit splitting provision in the CPP allows for the equal division of pension credits earned by: former spouses upon divorce; or separated legal spouses; and common-law partners. Credit splitting was introduced in the CPP on January 1, 1978. Under the 1978 provisions, all CPP credits earned by both spouses during the period of a marriage when the spouses cohabited were divided equally between the 2 spouses in the event of: a divorce; an annulment of a legal marriage upon application by either spouse within 36 months of the final divorce decree; or a judgment of nullity. Former spouses had to have cohabited for at least 36 continuous months during the marriage. Credit splitting did not extend to separated legal spouses and common-law partners. From the date of implementation of the credit splitting legislation in 1978, requests for a credit split were processed regardless of any separation agreement or court order entered into by the parties. The Minister was identified as a third party and, therefore, was not bound by the provisions of the agreement. In 1983, in Minister of N.H.W. v. Lawrence C. Preece et al. (the 1983 Preece decision), the CPP Pension Appeals Board ruled that if spouses had waived their rights to property claims other than those contained in a separation agreement or court order they were precluded from receiving a division of CPP pension credits. Because many separation agreements and court orders included a general property waiver against all future claims, the Preece decision often prevented Credit splitting. In March 15, 1991, the CPP was amended to add the Kempling remedy. This amendment allowed applicants denied by the 1983 Preece decision to qualify for credit splitting. By applying this remedy, credit splitting applications are not denied due to separation agreements or court orders made before June 4, 1986 having general property release clauses. The credit splitting provision applies to the first and second additional UPE in the same way as it is applied to the base CPP. As with the base CPP, the additional earnings for each individual will be added and then divided equally, and the divided earnings will be attributed to each person. Additional pensionable earnings under QPP will be used to calculate the division. The first and second additional CPP contributory periods do not end with the month in which a beneficiary is determined to have become disabled. The disability exclusion does not apply. Therefore, unlike the Base CPP, it is possible to divide first and second additional pensionable earnings in periods where a beneficiary is in receipt of a DSB .

The credit splitting provision applies to the first and second additional unadjusted pensionable earnings in the same way as it is applied to the base CPP. As with the base CPP, the additional earnings for each individual will be added and then divided equally, and the divided earnings will be attributed to each person. Additional pensionable earnings under the QPP will be used to calculate the division. The first and second additional CPP contributory periods do not end with the month in which a beneficiary is determined to have become disabled. The disability exclusion does not apply. Therefore, unlike the Base CPP, it is possible to divide first and second additional pensionable earnings in periods where a beneficiary is in receipt of a CPP disability (DSB) pension.
The Post-Retirement Benefit is paid during the lifetime of the beneficiary. Payments end with the final payment made the month of the beneficiary’s death.

The last month that a RTR pensioner and PRB beneficiary are eligible for payment is the month of their death. If the beneficiary was alive on January 1 of the year in which the PRB is payable, any outstanding payments are made to the beneficiary's estate or, where there is no estate, to an individual or agency designated by the Minister.
The RTR pension and Post-Retirement Benefit ( PRB ) continue to be paid during the lifetime of the beneficiary, ceasing with the payment for the month in which the beneficiary dies.

OAS pension For an OAS pension, the Department must receive the application within one year of the Date of death (DOD) of the deceased individual. CPP CPP has similar provisions to OAS in that, for some benefits, the Department may receive the application within one year of the DOD of the deceased individual. However, for other benefits, the application must have been received by the Department on or before the individual's DOD. Specific rules for each benefit follow. RTR pension Where a contributor's DOD occurs in the month the individual turned age 70, or earlier, their RTR pension application must have been received by the Department on or before their DOD. Applications received after their month of death must be denied. For example, there is no provision to process an application on behalf of a deceased person where: the contributor dies: before age 70; or in the month of their 70th birthday; and the application is received after the month of their death. However, the application can be processed if: the contributor's date of death occurs anytime after the month the individual turned age 70; valid earnings and contributions have been made to the CPP; and the Department receives the RTR pension application within one year of the contributor's date of death. Credit splitting provision An application or request for a post-mortem credit splitting may be made by: the estate or succession of either spouse or common-law partner; a personal representative; the deceased individual's child; or someone on behalf of that child, if the child is under the age of 18. Applications or requests for credit splitting received after the death of an individual are treated differently than those for benefits and pensions under the CPP and OAS programs. The timelines for the submission of a post-mortem credit splitting request or application are based on whether the members forming the couple are: former spouses upon divorce or legal annulment; separated spouses; or former common-law partners requesting a Credit Split. The date of death is taken into consideration when applying the timelines for accepting a request. For more information on credit splitting application timelines, Canada Pension Plan – Credit Splitting (Policy)

Under OAS and CPP legislation, there are limitations based on when an application for pensions or benefits can be submitted on behalf of a deceased individual. If an application is not received within the prescribed time-frame for that pension or benefit (normally one year from the individual's death), the application would normally be denied. For more information, Post-Mortem Applications (Policy) However, if the deceased had applied for the corresponding foreign benefit prior to their death, a protective date could be applied. If there is a valid protective date that predates the date of death or the date of receipt of the post-mortem application, that date is considered to be the date of application when determining eligibility and entitlement. Example A post-mortem RTR pension application is received on March 15, 2023, on behalf of an individual that died on November 9, 2021. The foreign institution provides a protective date of April 23, 2020. For administrative purposes, including those related to system input, the date of application is now April 23, 2020.

If a pensioner has less than 20 years of residence in Canada after the age of 18 and is absent from Canada for more than 6 months, their OAS pension payments are suspended. Payment of their OAS pension is reinstated the month in which the pensioner returns or resumes residence in Canada. Payment of the OAS pension can also be reinstated after a suspension when the pensioner has: provided all of the information necessary to establish eligibility and entitlement; and complied with the provisions of OAS legislation. A pensioner who requests the cessation of their OAS pension after July 13, 1995 can request, in writing, the reinstatement of their pension at a later date. In such cases, the pension is reinstated either: the month after the month in which the written request for reinstatement is received; or the month chosen by the pensioner, whichever is later . A pensioner cannot accumulate additional periods of residence for any period before the date of reinstatement. However, they can still accumulate periods of time towards pension portability.

In most cases, the amount of an OAS pension that is portable will be the same as the pensioner's original entitlement. This includes any escalation to the pension amount based on changes in the Consumer Price Index since the pension originally became payable. Once a partial pension has been approved, the amount may not be increased based on subsequent residence in Canada or deemed residence while outside of Canada. While the net amount could change, as it could now be subject to additional non-resident and recovery tax deductions, the gross entitlement will remain the same. Some scenarios include: A pensioner receiving a full OAS pension based on 40 years of Canadian residence is entitled to continued payment of the pension despite leaving Canada. A pensioner receiving a partial OAS pension based on 24 years of Canadian residence is entitled to continued payment of the pension when they leave Canada. A pensioner has been receiving a partial OAS pension for 3 years. As the partial pension was based on 18 years of Canadian residence, the pensioner is entitled to continued payment of the pension despite leaving Canada. A pensioner receiving a partial OAS pension based on 4 years of Canadian residence in combination with 18 years of residence or contributions in a country with which Canada has an ISSA has satisfied the portability requirements and is entitled to continued payment of the pension when they leave Canada. A pensioner receiving a partial OAS pension based on 16 years of Canadian residence and who does not have sufficient foreign creditable periods under an ISSA is not entitled to continued payment of the pension upon leaving Canada. A pensioner receiving a partial OAS pension based on 18 years of Canadian residence is living outside of Canada working as a Missionary (i.e. is considered a deemed resident) is entitled to 6 months after the month of departure from Canada. Once the pensioner returns to Canada, the pension is reinstated. The absence can be counted as an uninterrupted residence towards the 20 years required for portability purposes. An applicant applies for an OAS pension. Upon reaching age 65, the applicant is absent from Canada but considered a deemed resident. All residence before age 65 is used to determine eligibility. If the applicant has a minimum of 10 years of residence after age 18 but less than 20, the benefit can be paid for 6 months after the month of departure. The pension is reinstated the month of return or the month residence is resumed in Canada.

Combined benefits are subject to maximum payment amounts as follows: The most that can be paid to a person eligible for both CPP DSB benefit and the SVR pension is the maximum CPP DSB benefit (which is more than the maximum SVR pension); The most that can be paid to a person eligible for the RTR pension and the SVR pension is the maximum RTR pension (which is more than the maximum SVR pension); or The total amount of a combined RTR/SVR pension is adjusted based on the survivor's age (under 65 and 65 and over). When an individual is eligible for a combined RTR pension/SVR pension/PRDB, the greater of the2 flat rates (SVR or PRDB) is used in the calculation formula. A beneficiary cannot receive a full SVR pension and also receive a full RTR pension or DSB benefit.

If an applicant meets the eligibility requirements for more than one benefit, they are eligible for and are required by CPP legislation to receive a combined benefit. CPP legislation states that a beneficiary must receive a combined benefit when they are eligible to receive a SVR pension and either: a CPP DSB benefit or a RTR pension; The PRDB is available and paid to disabled CPP RTR pension recipients who meet the PRDB eligibility requirements. A combined benefit can include either: a RTR and a SVR pension; a CPP DSB benefit and a SVR pension; or a RTR pension, a PRDB and a SVR pension. QPP Combined benefits may include a benefit paid under the QPP.

The CPP allows beneficiaries to receive the following combined benefits: Retirement (RTR) and Survivor (SVR); RTR and SVR, or RTR and Post-Retirement Disability Benefit (PRDB), whichever provides the greater flat rate; or SVR and CPP Disability (DSB) benefit. A combined benefit consists of 2 CPP benefits. One of the benefits could be paid under a provincial program (i.e. QPP).

The RTR pension provides a monthly benefit payment to eligible applicants. Eligible applicants can choose to receive: a full RTR pension at age 65; a reduced RTR pension if they begin receiving it as early as age 60; or an increased RTR pension if they defer receiving it until age 70. The Canada Pension Plan legislation contains drop-out and exclusion provisions to minimize any adverse effects that life events (unemployment, illness, attending school, caring for a child or other family member, etc.) may have on CPP benefit calculations. The exclusion provisions remove months of low or zero earnings from the applicant's contributory period and may increase the Retirement For Benefit Calculation ( RTR -FBC). The Over Age 65 drop-out provision allows months of higher pensionable earnings, after reaching age 65, to replace months of low or zero pensionable earnings before reaching age 65, as long as this substitution does not reduce their contributory period below 120 months, minus any number of months of disability. Flexible retirement was introduced in January 1987 through Bill C-116, to allow contributors to take: a reduced RTR pension as early as age 60; and an increased benefit as late as age 70. At the same time, the Over Age 65 drop-out provision was modified to become a full drop-out, allowing individuals who defer their retirement pension after 65 to drop additional months of low earnings from their contributory period on a one-for-one basis. Exclusion provisions are applied to the contributory period, as applicable, in the following order: Disability Exclusion Child Rearing Provision (Policy) Child Rearing Provision (Policy) Over Age 65 Drop-Out Provision General Drop-Out Provision (Policy) General Drop-Out Provision (Policy) Therefore, when an individual's contributory period ends after age 65, deduct the number of months accumulated in their contributory period after age 65 from the total number of months remaining in their entire contributory period.

The CPP Retirement (RTR) pension provides a monthly pension to eligible applicants. Applicants can receive a CPP RTR pension: at age 65, paid in full; as early as age 60, with a reduction; and as late as age 70, with an increase. The amount of an RTR pension is decreased by 0.6% for each month the contributor starts receiving the pension before reaching age 65. Alternatively, the pension amount is increased by 0.7% for each month the contributor starts receiving the pension after reaching age 65. Monthly Increase of RTR Pension All RTR pension calculations are based upon the Retirement For Benefit Calculation (RTR-FBC). The RTR-FBC is 25% of the contributor's Average Monthly Pensionable Earnings (AMPE). The AMPE is determined by escalating each year of the contributor’s Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings (UPE) (the average of the last 5 years of Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE)) to current year value. This escalation of earnings is called the Adjusted Pensionable Earnings (APE). The APE is divided by the remaining number of contributory months and is multiplied by 25%, resulting in the applicant's RTR-FBC. The CPP provides drop-out and exclusion provisions to allow for periods of unemployment, illness, attending school, caring for a child or other family member, for instance, to be excluded from the applicant's contributory period. These provisions exclude months of low or zero earnings from the applicant's contributory period and may increase the RTR-FBC. Drop-out and exclusion provisions are applied in the following order: Disability Exclusion Child Rearing Provision Over Age 65 Provisions General Drop-Out Provision The General Drop-Out Provision was introduced to allow for a defined percentage of months to be dropped from an applicant's contributory period when calculating their RTR pension's RTR-FBC. Over time, the percentage of periods that can be excluded has been amended. Effective January 2014, 17% of years with low or zero earnings may be excluded from a contributory period. A maximum of 96 months (8 years) may be excluded. Once all applicable drop-out provisions and exclusions are applied, the RTR-FBC is used in the calculation of the original CPP benefit and any subsequent CPP benefit when that subsequent CPP benefit starts the month after the original CPP benefit's cease date. Some benefit calculations will require a new RTR-FBC to be calculated and possibly a new General Drop-Out Provision rate to be used when there is at least one month between the original CPP benefit's cease date and the subsequent CPP benefit's start date. It is important to note that the drop-out provisions or exclusions will not be applied if the result is a disadvantage to the applicant.

To be eligible for a CPP Retirement (RTR) pension, an individual must meet the following requirements. Application An application for an RTR pension must be made to the Minister in writing or electronically using the My CPP Retirement application. The electronic process does not require a wet signature, but instead allows applicants to meet the "in-writing" requirement with an electronic signature. In the majority of cases, all the necessary information to process an RTR pension application is not always included in the written request. As a practice, a completed application form should be obtained, if possible . For more information on proactive enrolments, such as in cases where the legislative requirement for an RTR pension application has been waived for clients who have reached age 70 and meet the eligibility requirements, RTR70—Proactive Enrolment Age The contributor must have reached age 60. Contributions The contributor must have unadjusted pensionable earnings in at least one year of their contributory period.

The standard age to begin receiving the CPP RTR pension is 65. However, the CPP allows contributors to start as early as age 60 with a permanent reduction in the pension amount, or to defer until up to age 70 with a permanent increase. Because there are no actuarial increases to the pension past the age of 70, there is no financial advantage in waiting to start the pension. Due to a retroactive payment limitation of 12 months, an individual who waits too long to apply would be unable to collect all of the benefits they would have received if they had applied at age 70. Under the CPP, an application must be made before an RTR pension is paid to a beneficiary. As a result, a small but significant number of eligible seniors miss out on receiving their RTR pension because they apply late or not at all. In an effort to ensure that payments are made to eligible clients aged 70 years or older, effective January 1, 2020, the Department is waiving the requirement for an RTR pension application.

A CPP Retirement (RTR) pension is payable to CPP contributors who have reached the eligible age. Legislation allows an individual to begin receiving their RTR pension as early as age 60 with a permanent reduction in the pension amount or to defer up to age 70 with a permanent escalation. Current legislation requires that an application or a request in writing be made in order for a beneficiary to receive their RTR pension. A significant number of eligible seniors have not applied for their RTR pension by age 70 and, therefore, may not be receiving benefits to which they may be entitled. Effective January 1, 2020, Bill C-97 will allow the Minister to waive the requirement for an application for an RTR pension under specific criteria and proactively enroll eligible individuals for their RTR pension at age 70. In situations where there is insufficient information for the Minister to assess these criteria, the requirement to submit an application for the RTR pension still applies. The CPP regulations allowing a CPP beneficiary to cancel their benefit has been amended to extend the current 6-month window for requesting the cancellation and repayment of a CPP benefit to 12 months.

Eligibility requirements To establish eligibility for a Death ( DTH ) benefit, all of the following requirements must be met: Effective January 1, 2025, the following eligibility requirements must be met for the DTH benefit top-up of $2,500: The contributor's death occured after January 1, 2025; The deceased contributor must not have received a DSB , PRDB , or an RTR pension and; No SVR pension is payable as a result of the contributor's death, with the exception of a Surviving Child's benefit. Minimum contributory requirements The minimum contributory requirements are met if the deceased contributor had unadjusted pensionable earnings in the lesser of: at least one third of the total number of years in their contributory period, subject to a minimum of 3 calendar years; or 10 years. To help contributors meet the minimum contributory requirements for a DTH benefit to be paid, the following can also be considered, where applicable: Credit Split Provision; Child Rearing Provision; Disability Exclusion; Social Security Agreements. A proration of the last year in the contributory period can also be performed when it is needed to meet the minimum contributory requirements.

To meet the Minimum Qualifying Period (MQP) for a CPP pension or benefit, the contributor must have valid base contributions for a certain number of years in their base contributory period. A valid base contribution appears as a base Unadjusted Pensionable Earnings amount in the contributor's Record of Earnings. The number of years required to meet the minimum contributory requirement is dependent on the CPP pension or benefit. To be eligible for a CPP RTR pension, a contributor must have at least one valid base contribution. Eligibility Requirements–Retirement Pension To meet the MQP for a CPPD benefit, the disabled contributor must have made valid base contributions: in 4 of the last 6 years; for at least 25 years with at least 3 valid contributions made within the last 6 years; or for each year after the month of cessation of the individual's previous DSB or PRDB . For more information on the minimum contributory requirements for a disabled contributor, refer to the Non-Medical Eligibility—CPPD Benefits (Policy) and Non-Medical Eligibility—CPPD Benefits (Policy) Eligibility Requirements— PRDB (Policy) To meet the MQP for the Death benefit, the SVR pension or the Surviving Child's benefit, the deceased contributor cannot have less than 3 calendar years of contributions. The deceased contributor must have made valid base contributions in the lesser of: at least one third of the total number of years in their base contributory period with a minimum of three calendar years; or ten years. For more information on the minimum contributory requirements for a deceased contributor, Eligibility Requirements—Death Benefit (Policy)

The RTR pension replaces the DSB effective the month after the beneficiary reaches age 65. The individual's DSB will automatically be converted to an RTR pension. A child's eligibility to the Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit may continue even after the beneficiary reaches age 65, Eligibility Requirements—CPP Disabled Contributor's Child's Benefit (Policy) An application is not required, however the beneficiary must be notified of the conversion in writing.

When a Disability (DSB) beneficiary reaches age 65, the benefit is automatically converted to an Retirement (RTR) pension. An RTR pension is calculated for the year the disability started. Full price indexing to the effective date of the RTR pension is provided. There is also a further adjustment if the beneficiary’s disability commenced in 1987 or earlier to account for the manner in which the Year’s Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) was calculated before that time. Former DSB beneficiary becomes eligible for an RTR pension If a DSB benefit was paid for an y period age 60 or beyond the special conversion calculation i s applicable. If DSB benefits are ceased before age 60, conversion from DSB benefit to RTR pension is not applicable. The calculation of the RTR pension is based on the YMPE average for the year the RTR pension starts.

An adoption "in fact" can involve an agreement in which the legal parents or a guardian agree to place a child under the decision-making responsibility and parenting time of an adopting parent (the contributor) who cares for the child as they would for their own child. On the other hand, situations can occur where no actual agreement exists. Examples of no actual agreement being in place are situations: where a child has been abandoned and a contributor assumes long-term parental responsibility for the abandoned child; or where the contributor is living with the child's legal parent and cares for the child as though the child was their own. Adoption "in fact" is based on a factual situation normally involving a long-term or permanent child-contributor relationship. The contributor cares for, and behaves towards the child, as if the child was their legal child. The child-contributor relationship must be supported by obtaining evidence described later in this document. Adoption "in fact" ends when the child-contributor relationship ends. A child adopted "in fact" by the deceased contributor When the contributor is deceased, the child may be considered to have been adopted "in fact" by the deceased contributor provided: the "in fact" adoption occurred before the child's 21st birthday; and the relationship between the child and the contributor existed at the time of the contributor's death. A child adopted "in fact" by the disabled contributor When the contributor is disabled, the child may be considered adopted "in fact" provided the "in fact" adoption: occurred before the child's 21st birthday; and was in effect before the date the disability is deemed to have commenced for any date before January 1, 1992; or may be effective before or after the date the disability is deemed to have commenced on January 1,1992,or any date after January 1,1992.

Under the CPP, adoption "in fact" describes a long-term relationship between a contributor and a child provided the adoption "in fact" occurred before the child's 21st birthday. Adoption "in fact" must be based on a factual situation where, usually , a natural or legal parent or legal guardian of the child agrees to submit the child into the care and responsibility of the "in fact" parent. The natural or legal parent or legal guardian may be the partner of the "in fact" parent.

You can select Ineligible Applicant or Insufficient Documentation/Proof as reasons to force deny a Death ( DTH ) benefit. If an application for a DTH benefit is received and the applicant is not the individual eligible to apply for it, you must first create a Contact to allow the Data Capture - DTH screen to become available. On the Data Capture - DTH screen, select Ineligible Applicant from the Force Deny Reason block and click Force Deny to submit. The Benefits screen opens and displays a DTH benefit Status of: Denied . If there is no proof of birth on the deceased's account and the applicant did not supply the documentation in the allowable time frame, force deny the DTH benefit with the reason Insufficient Documentation/Proof . If the deceased client does not have a social insurance number and there are no valid contributions, force deny the application with the reason Insufficient documentation and update the client's notes with the denial reason: Does not meet MQP . Then send the applicable denial letter to the applicant.

When you are processing a new or an incomplete data capture in ITRDS , you can click Force Deny to forward an application or a provision to the Adjudication System without performing any validations, except for the date of birth. Applications or provisions that have been force denied cannot be modified or readjudicated. Insufficient documentation Click Force Deny when you must deny an application or provision because the applicant did not provide the documentation in the allowable time frame to adjudicate a benefit. If mandatory documents are missing (other than birth evidence), force deny the application or provision with the reason Insufficient documentation . Send the appropriate denial letter to the client based on the eligibility criteria that they did not meet and update the client's notes in ITRDS accordingly. When considering whether a severe disability will be of indefinite duration, it is important to consider factors such as: the likelihood that existing or expected treatment(s) or intervention(s) will be successful; treatment failures; and the side effects associated with treatment(s). The prolonged criterion is met when, based on the factors listed above and any other factors, the duration of the severe disability is uncertain and cannot be predicted.

If a disability is found to be severe and is long continued and of an indefinite duration, that is, there is no reasonable end in sight for the disability based on existing or expected treatment(s) or intervention(s) or any other relevant factors, the disability is considered prolonged. It is possible that evidence demonstrates a disability is long continued but does not demonstrate that it is of indefinite duration. Such applications should be denied. The following examples illustrate this concept. Examples An applicant or beneficiary with a severe medical condition who is expected to recover following treatment or therapy, or who has a favourable prognosis for recovery despite the length of time does not meet prolonged criterion; When a disability is of indefinite duration, it is also long continued and therefore prolonged. However, a disability that is long continued is not necessarily of indefinite duration.

Determining whether an applicant is disabled or a beneficiary continues to be disabled, according to the CPP, is an administrative decision. Administrative decisions are to be made based on the civil standard of proof: a balance of probabilities. To grant or continue paying a CPP Disability (DSB) benefit, the civil standard of proof must be met. That is, on a balance of probabilities, the applicant or beneficiary in respect of whom the determination is made, is determined to: be disabled; or continue to be disabled. The civil standard of proof is not a standard of certainty but rather a nuanced approach intended to give the decision-maker, when reviewing all of the evidence, the ability to come to a conclusion as to which is more likely to be true, the applicant or beneficiary is: disabled or not disabled.

The satisfied on a balance of probabilities standard is to be applied in determining an applicant or beneficiary's eligibility or continuing eligibility for a Disability (DSB) benefit under the CPP. All of the objective and subjective evidence provided to the decision-maker to determine whether an applicant or beneficiary meets the CPP definition of disability, must be weighed. That is, a decision-maker must be satisfied that the applicant or beneficiary has, or continues to have, a severe and prolonged disability. Absolute proof of disability is not required. For the purposes of determining eligibility or continuing eligibility for a DSB benefit, the standard of proof used is the civil standard on a balance of probabilities rather than the criminal standard of beyond a reasonable doubt. To say that something is proven on a balance of probabilities means that it is more likely than not to have occurred—it is probable. Therefore, an applicant or beneficiary must be found more likely than not to be, or still be, disabled according to the definition of disability under the CPP. Additionally, a balance of probabilities standard of proof requires the disability be considered in the context of the whole person. That is, not only the medical condition(s) are considered, but also how the capacity to work and personal characteristics affect the particular applicant or beneficiary.

The number of hours an applicant or beneficiary participates in paid employment each week is part of a holistic assessment in determining if this activity is reflective of work capacity. General Guidelines for Work Activity
Individuals participating in paid employment between 15 and 30 hours per week may be demonstrating work capacity. A holistic assessment to determine work capacity should occur.
Individuals participating in paid employment for less than 15 hours per week are usually not demonstrating work capacity. A holistic assessment to determine work capacity is required.
Individuals participating in paid employment over 30 hours per week are likely demonstrating work capacity, unless the evidence on file supports otherwise.
The number of hours an applicant or beneficiary participates in paid employment each week is part of the assessment in determining if this activity is reflective of work capacity.

The predictability of attendance may be reflected in an individual’s ability to work scheduled shifts, in a predictable manner, over a sustained period. Consideration must be given to individuals with unpredictable or irregularly occurring medical conditions and resulting functional limitations (for example, those with mental health diagnoses or cyclical conditions which have periods of exacerbations and remissions). The limitations associated with these condition may prevent them from being able to sustain predictable employment. These applicants or beneficiaries may therefore not be regularly capable of work. For applicants and beneficiaries with varied weekly hours of work or work attendance, a longitudinal assessment of work activity may be necessary to determine their work capacity. Development may be required.

Since the inception of the CPP disability program in 1966, there has been a significant shift in how disability and persons with disabilities are seen in relation to their ability to participate in the workforce. Disability is now seen as the result of environmental, social, and attitudinal barriers preventing an individual from fully participating in society. Persons with disabilities have the right to full and equal participation and inclusion in society. Considering this, a consistent and equitable approach to assessment of work activity and SGO criteria are applied to all individuals engaged in any type of work. Accommodation Employers have an obligation to accommodate employees as long as the accommodation(s) do not result in undue hardship to the employer. Sheltered Work Exception In rare circumstances, it may be determined an applicant or beneficiary is employed in a truly sheltered employment setting. The primary purpose of this type of therapeutic work is for social connection and cognitive stimulation, rather than to provide an income. Examples of these types of settings include: employment of institutionalized individuals in mental health facilities; and community run programs for individuals with specific disabilities, often for those with developmental delays. A defining characteristic of this work is the highly supportive nature of this type of work. Thus a modified approach to assessment of work activity and income earned should occur.

A self-employed individual invoices others for services rendered or goods sold; oversees their own work activities; sets their own work hours; chooses business clients and partners; can accept or refuse work; provides and maintains their own work tools and equipment; and has a relationship with the payer for a specific job. An employer pays the employee's wages; oversees work activities; determines the schedule or priority of work; assigns work clients; decides what work the employee does; supplies work tools and equipment; and maintains a relationship with the employee that is usually continuous. The following lists the differences between a self-employed individual and one who is an employee. A self-employed individual has capital investment in their business; determines the overall direction of the business; pays taxes as a self-employed person or is paid by a business which they own; and can hire, manage and pay staff. An employee typically has no capital investment in the business; cannot determine the direction of the business; is paid by the business that they do not own; and does not hire or pay others to do the work. When determining eligibility to a CPPD benefit, foreign creditable periods under a valid ISSA can be used to meet the MQP. When totalizing CPP contributions or dual CPP and QPP contributions with foreign creditable periods under an ISSA, the contributions are added to the foreign creditable periods. The ISSA must allow the totalization of the CPPD benefit or DCCB . An ISSA may specify that the date of the event causing the disability must be after the date the ISSA came into force. The foreign institution is the primary source for the totalization of the individual's foreign creditable periods under the ISSA. If a client provides evidence of their foreign creditable periods, you can accept the evidence under certain circumstances. In all cases, International Operations must receive an acceptable breakdown of foreign creditable periods to determine eligibility under an ISSA.

When a self-employed beneficiary fails to provide the information requested by the Minister regarding their self-employed earnings and/or business activities, an assessment of their work activity in the business is more difficult and may not be possible. In cases where a non-compliant, self-employed beneficiary has a gross income above the SGO amount, it is reasonable to conclude that the business is profitable. Since the beneficiary has not provided the information requested by the Minister, work capacity cannot be confirmed. However, it is reasonable to conclude since their self-employed work activity is profitable, that the beneficiary has the capacity to regularly pursue some type of work. Failure on the beneficiary's part to provide information or details to explain their self-employed earnings, results in their CPPD benefit being ceased. In these cases, the cease date is based on the available earnings information. When the period of self-employment of a non-compliant beneficiary cannot be determined, January of the first year of SGO earnings is deemed to be the month in which the beneficiary returned to work and their CPPD benefits are ceased at the end of that month (January).

In some cases, information available to the Minister (e.g. work activity with SGO earnings since the beneficiary began receiving CPPD benefits) suggests the beneficiary may have become ineligible for CPPD benefits at some point before the date their non-compliance occurred. Beneficiaries who are non-compliant and have earnings equal to or greater than the SGO amount must have these earnings investigated to determine: the period of employment; the source of those earnings; and if those earnings are reflective of the beneficiary being able to work at any SGO. If the earnings are confirmed and a period of employment is verified, CPPD benefits are ceased at the end of the month the beneficiary returned to work. Files may be transferred to ISB to confirm the source of earnings, if required. If the earnings cannot be confirmed or verified, January of the first year of SGO earnings is deemed to be the month in which the beneficiary returned to work. In such a case, the beneficiary's CPPD benefits are ceased at the end of January.

Bill C-97 allows the Minister to waive the requirement for an RTR pension application and enrol a client for an RTR pension if the Minister is satisfied that the person: has contributed to the CPP; has reached 70 years of age; and either: is in receipt of at least one of the following: another CPP benefit; an OAS benefit; a QPP benefit; or has filed an income tax return for the tax year that precedes the year in which the Minister intends to waive the requirement. For more information, Proactive Enrolment—CPP Retirement Pension at Age 70 or More (Policy)

Proactive enrolment allows the Minister to waive the requirement for an application for an RTR pension if the Minister is satisfied that: the person has contributed to the CPP; the person is 70 years old or older; and the person either: receive: another CPP benefit; an OAS benefit; a QPP benefit; or has filed an income tax return for the tax year that precedes the year in which the Minister intends to waive the requirement. The amended legislation provides that an application for an RTR pension is deemed to have been made and received on the day the requirement for an application is waived. When the requirement for an application is waived, an approved RTR pension is payable for each month after the month the requirement is waived.

There are 2 categories of proactive enrolment that allow the Minister to waive the requirement for a CPP RTR pension application. Individuals who meet the following criteria: Contributors aged 70 or older who are in receipt of at least one of an OAS benefit and/or a Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) or a CPP Survivor’s pension; Contributors aged 70 or older who are not in receipt of an OAS benefit, a GIS or a CPP Survivor’s pension, but who have recently filed taxes with Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). On an ongoing basis, individuals will be enrolled using the following criteria: Contributors who turn age 70, who are in receipt of at least one of an OAS benefit and/or GIS or a CPP Survivor’s pension; Contributors who turn age 70, who are not in receipt of an OAS benefit, a GIS or a CPP Survivor’s pension, but who have recently filed taxes with CRA.

Following legislative changes contained in Bill C-97, effective January 1, 2020, the Department will proactively enrol eligible clients aged 70 or over who have not yet applied for an RTR pension to which they are entitled, in the absence of an application and under specific criteria. The CPP regulations allow a CPP beneficiary to request the cancellation of their benefit within 12 months of receiving their first proactive enrolment payment.

Budget 2021 increased the OAS pension by 10 percent for seniors 75 and over as of July 2022.

The Federal Government announced an increase to the OAS pension for seniors aged 75 and over as part of Budget 2021. The increase will be implemented in 2 stages: A taxable one-time payment of $500.00 in August 2021 to seniors who are 75 and over as of June 30, 2022. For more information, refer to One-time Payment for Older Seniors ; and One-time Payment for Older Seniors A permanent 10% increase to the monthly OAS pension for seniors aged 75 and over beginning in July 2022.

OAS pensioners aged 75 or over by June 30, 2022 will be entitled to the increase beginning in July 2022. Pensioners turning 75 as of July 1, 2022 or later will receive the increase automatically the month following their 75th birthday. Pensioners will be automatically issued a 10% Increase to OAS for Older Seniors (ISP3175B) letter earlier in the month the increase takes effect. Manual letters are not required. The 10% increase in the maximum OAS pension rate will not affect the calculation of the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) for full pensioners. For partial pensioners or those with higher actuarially adjusted pensions, the GIS top-up portion is impacted by the increase as it is directly linked to the OAS partial pension amount. H owever, the regular GIS portion is not impacted. The guaranteed minimum income formula will be maintained.
A 10% increase will be applied to the monthly OAS pension for seniors aged 75 and over as of July 2022.

The purpose of this report is to identify entitlement to an income-tested benefit for the year in which a client declared bankruptcy. Income is displayed in the OAS Online system on the CRA Income screen with a match code 7–Bankruptcy . Unlike the regular one-way process, this income is not displayed in the future fields of the Monetary screen. Both pre-bankruptcy and post-bankruptcy income information must be obtained in order to verify the client’s total yearly income. The combined pre-bankruptcy and post-bankruptcy income will be used to calculate the client’s entitlement to the income-tested benefits. However, due to OAS Online system limitations, either the pre-bankruptcy or the post-bankruptcy income information received from CRA can be displayed in OAS Online, not both.
